# PREFATORY NOTE

This volume contains the seventh course of lectures offered by New York University through the foundation known as the Charles F. Deems Lectureship of Philosophy. On April 15, 1895, the University contracted with the American Institute of Christian Philosophy—a corporation chartered on December 1, 1891—to maintain this lectureship for at least twenty years. This was to be accomplished by securing a distinguished Lecturer in Science and Philosophy every two years. This lecturer would deliver at least six lectures on one of the most important questions of Science and Philosophy, with a special focus on its relation to the revealed truths of the Holy Scriptures and the fundamental principles of Theistic Philosophy.

The Lecturer was to be chosen by the University’s Committee on the Charles F. Deems Lectureship. This committee consisted of the Chancellor of the University, two members of the Faculty of Arts and Science, and two members of the University Council, appointed as the Council directed. The subject for each year’s lectures was agreed upon between this Committee and the Lecturer.

The University provided a room for the lectures free of charge and, at its own expense, publicly announced the time and place of each lecture. The University was responsible for publishing each series of lectures in book form and offering them for sale through one or more reputable book firms, provided this could be done using only the surplus income remaining after the costs of maintaining the lectures were met.

<vocab>New York University, Charles F. Deems Lectureship of Philosophy, American Institute of Christian Philosophy, Science and Philosophy, Theistic Philosophy</vocab>

# PREFATORY NOTE

The various volumes of lectures from the Deems Foundation have been published as follows:

1. "*Theism in the Light of Present Science and Philosophy*," by James Iverach, M.A., D.D.: The Macmillan Company, New York and London.
2. "*Theism*," by Borden P. Bowne, D.D., Professor of Philosophy in Boston University: American Book Company, New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago.
3. "*Religions of Eastern Asia*," by Horace Grant Underwood, D.D.: The Macmillan Company, New York.
4. "*The Teaching of Paul in Terms of the Present Day*," by Sir William Mitchell Ramsay, D.C.L.: Hodder & Stoughton, London, New York, and Toronto.
5. "*Ethics and Modern Thought — A Theory of Their Relations*," by Rudolf Eucken, Professor of Philosophy, University of Jena: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, New York and London.
6. The failing health of the late Principal Fairbairn of Oxford, England, after the delivery of his lectures, prevented them from being prepared for the press.
7. The present volume, published by The Macmillan Company, is the seventh and final volume of the first series of lectures; it is written by the youngest of the seven lecturers on this Foundation.

Dr. August Karl Reischauer was born in Jonesboro, Illinois, on September 4, 1879. He was, therefore, in his thirty-fourth year when he lectured for the Deems Foundation, being the first of the lecturers who was under forty years of age. He studied at Hanover College, Indiana, and at the McCormick Theological Seminary in Chicago. After his ordination in 1905, he went immediately to Japan to teach Ethics and Philosophy at the mission college in the southern part of the city of Tokyo. The school is named Meiji Gakuin in honor of the Meiji era of Japanese history, which was ushered in during the year 1868 by the abolition of the Shogunate government and the restoration of supreme power to the Mikado, who had been kept in subjection to the military Shogunate for centuries. # PREFATORY NOTE

Japan a catechism on Buddhism of the Shin Sect, *Buddhist Gold Nuggets*, and a treatise on personal immortality. Dr. Reischauer’s lectures on the Deems Foundation have not appeared earlier because he did not return to Japan for several months after their delivery and required considerable time to prepare them for the press. No libraries outside of Japan contain more than a mere fraction of the Buddhist authorities from whose writings the material for these lectures was obtained.

The lecturer, in his first lecture, presented the origins of Buddhism. In the second, he traced the development of Primitive Buddhism into Mahayana Buddhism, as this form of Buddhism holds the lead in Japan. He presented the historical development of Japanese Buddhism in his third lecture. His fourth lecture discussed the Buddhist Canon. In his fifth, he sketched the Japanese sects and their chief tenets, and in the sixth, Buddhist ethics. The closing lecture presented, in comparison with Buddhism, the strength of Christianity in Japan.

The twenty-year contract between the American Institute of Christian Philosophy and New York University having expired by its own limit, these two parties are now considering the question of renewing it. It falls to me, as both a member of the University Committee and President of the Institute of Philosophy, to supply this prefatory statement.

->HENRY MITCHELL MACCRACKEN.<-

UNIVERSITY HEIGHTS,
NEW YORK CITY.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

In sending this book out to the public, I am keenly aware that the magnitude of the subject it deals with is such that it may seem absurd to try to cover it in such a short space. Any single chapter might easily be expanded into a large volume without even then going into very great detail. And yet I feel that a general, brief survey of the subject, such as this book attempts to give, is on the whole the wisest plan when one considers the current degree of interest in Oriental religions and philosophies on the part of Western readers. There is still so very little in English books on Japanese Buddhism, even of a general nature, that no author can hope to be heard who does not confine himself largely to the outstanding facts and characteristics of his theme. Furthermore, it should be said that even the interested student who enters this field must always be on his guard lest, in the multiplicity of details—and in Japanese Buddhism there is a wealth of these—he lose sight of the main trend of the subject.

As stated in the preface by Dr. H. M. MacCracken, this volume comprises the Deems Lectures for the year 1913, but it should be said that the lectures as originally given have been almost entirely rewritten and considerably expanded. The form of the lectures has, however, determined the general trend of thought in the book.

Naturally, I feel indebted to many writers and to other friends with whom I have spoken on this great subject during my eleven years of residence in Tōkyō. Regarding books written in European languages, this has been partly acknowledged, but I wish to make special mention here of the late Professor Arthur Lloyd, whose pioneer work was of great value to me at the beginning of my studies

## CHAPTER VI. BUDDHIST ETHICS . . . . . 268

### A. General Aspects . . . . . . 268

The separation of religion and ethics — The philosophy of the Good — The Arhat and Bodhisattva ideals — Enlightenment of the mind rather than enrichment of the entire personality — Mahāyāna ethics are more altruistic — The contradiction between Buddhist psychology and the goal of Buddhist ethics.

# STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM

## INTRODUCTION

Not many years ago, a remarkable picture was on display in a Tokyo art gallery. The picture was not exactly a masterpiece, but its subject matter was extremely suggestive. In the center stood a child, and grouped around it were four men, each beckoning it to follow. The child's face showed an expression of bewilderment, of apparent perplexity as to what it should do. The child was intended to represent Japan, and the four men represented a Shintō priest, Confucius, Gautama Buddha, and Jesus. The average visitor to the gallery gave this picture little more than a passing glance, but to the student of modern Japan, it was of deep interest.

If there is anything characteristic of the life of the rising generation in Japan, especially of its intellectual life and the spiritual realm, it is bewilderment and confusion; for Japan is the meeting place of four great religions—namely, Shintō, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Christianity—not to mention other currents of thought and life which have been pouring into this land from all parts of the world during the last fifty or sixty years. It is not strange that the youth of Japan especially should be like the child in the picture—confused and perplexed as to whom or what they should follow. On one hand are the voices and beckonings of the past—the currents of thought and the habits and customs of their fathers. These they would follow instinctively. But on the other hand, they hear the persistent

These seem to promise more than the old, but if followed without reservation, they threaten to create too great a gap between the Japanese people of today and past generations.

There is, of course, no insurmountable difficulty in readjusting old habits and customs to fit in with the new in the physical realm, though even here it is not as simple as it might seem to an outsider. For instance, standing at a modern railway station and listening to the clatter of wooden clogs as the crowds hurry up and down the stairs strongly suggests that one is hearing something of the “clash of civilizations.” Or seeing airplanes and dirigibles speeding over rice fields in which poor peasants use tools as primitive as those used by Abraham makes one feel that modern Japan still has great gaps to bridge, even in the physical realm. And even where they are being bridged, the country's limited resources tend to make economic adjustments a very painful process. But, after all, it is in the realm of the spirit, in higher and deeper sentiments and feelings, that the real difficulty of adjustment lies for the current generation. What adds to the difficulty is the fact that among the so-called leaders in the nation's intellectual life, there are very few who truly understand the nature of the forces at work. On one hand are the old-fashioned leaders who would keep the younger generation bound to the things of the past. On the other hand are the advocates of the new, who apparently think they have done all that is required of them when they have handed out the contents of the latest book to their followers. Those who are successfully bridging the gap between the old and the new are few indeed, and it is no wonder that there is so much confusion in the intellectual life of modern Japan.

This is hardly accurate, for as a matter of fact, the three old religions of Japan are not separate and distinct from one another. Shintō—as we shall show in Chapter III—though it is the native religion of old Japan, was virtually incorporated into Buddhism about a thousand years ago. While it was officially separated from Buddhism in the modern period, it is impossible to draw any clear line between the two. Furthermore, Confucianism never really existed as an independent religion in Japan; instead, it was fostered largely by Buddhist leaders as a part of their own system. It is true that the Neo-Confucianism of the Tokugawa period had a measure of independence and even opposed Buddhism to some extent, but even this was first introduced and spread by Buddhists and was itself as much Buddhism as it was Confucianism. In fact, the three old religions of Japan have interpenetrated each other so completely that for centuries the average Japanese person has regarded himself as more or less an adherent of all three. It is Buddhism, however, which has supplied the matrix that holds the various elements together, and so it may be said to represent all three in one. It has so completely adapted itself to Japanese life and incorporated everything it found in its way that one can be a good Buddhist without being disloyal to anything for which the other two ever stood.

When it comes, however, to the fourth religion—the religion of Jesus Christ—the matter is very different. No Japanese Christian in good and regular standing would regard himself as anything but a Christian, though he would insist that, as such, he can retain all that is good in the other three and all that is essential to being a true and loyal citizen of the empire. On the other hand, few good Shintoists, Confucianists, or Buddhists would pretend to be also good Christians, for it was the custom for almost three centuries to look upon Christianity as an enemy of Japanese traditions; thus, the line between it and the old religions is drawn quite sharply. One naturally wonders which of these spiritual guides the child of Japan will follow. There was a time a few years ago—and it is not altogether past now—when it almost looked as if the expression on the child’s face was changing from one of confusion and bewilderment to one of indifference. Japan had followed the old guide for many centuries, sometimes very eagerly and at times only from afar. But during the last fifty years or so, as the rising tide of intelligence has made it impossible for many to rest content with the beliefs and practices of the past, there developed a surprising indifference to the old religious ideals, and in fact an indifference to religion as such. But no one familiar with human nature or human history can regard this as anything but a passing phase, for man is “incurably religious” and even a person like Auguste Comte must have at least a “Religion of Humanity,” though he may regard the historical religions as phases of life which the race should outgrow as it advances. There are many signs that this indifference to religion, so characteristic of young Japan a few years ago, was only a temporary phenomenon. There is now again a remarkable interest in spiritual things, though it is perhaps too early to say to whom, on the whole, Japan will turn for leadership.

There are those who hold that Japan will neither follow her old religious guides nor turn to the newly introduced old religion of the West, but that there will have to be a New Religion if her allegiance is to be won. This new religion may borrow some things from the old but not exclusively from any single one of them or even all of them. It will have to be a sort of <term>syncretism</term> made up from the best elements that can be gathered together, no matter where they come from. Just as in other spheres Japan has borrowed the best that could be found and adapted these things to her needs; so she must do in religious matters. And since all religions are made of essentially the same material, there ought to be no insurmountable obstacle in fusing them into one grand whole; if not into an organic union, then at least into one great cooperative enterprise for promoting righteousness and peace.

Insofar as these broad-minded leaders would do away with the bitter jealousies and conflicts between existing religions, one cannot help but have profound respect for their good intentions; but when their efforts are based on the assumption that all religions are essentially one in their great fundamentals and differ only on minor points or expression, one can only pity their lack of understanding. Of course, there is a sense in which all historical religions may be said to be but different forms of Religion, *i.e.*, different aspects of one and the same reality, but this is true only in such a general sense that the statement is practically meaningless. The very fact that it is almost impossible to make a definition of religion which is anything but an empty generalization—which includes everyone only because it includes really nothing very vital of anyone—should be sufficient proof. Even in such advanced religions as Buddhism and Christianity, the radical differences in fundamentals ought to be apparent to anyone who is at all familiar with their central teachings. It is inconceivable that the two could ever be merged into one without one or the other giving up some of its essential characteristics. The view that the religions of the East are one and all like crumbling ancient castles that will soon turn to dust reveals a rather shallow knowledge of the real nature of religion. It seems to regard religion as something external—a garment which can be cast off as the style changes. As a matter of fact, nothing changes as slowly as a nation's religion and religious customs. Japan, *for example*, has changed its army and navy from a medieval type to one thoroughly modern and strictly up-to-date within the space of a few decades. Her educational system, her transportation facilities, and industrial enterprises have likewise been revolutionized within that period. But with her religion, the matter stands quite differently. A leader like Constantine may make Christianity the state religion overnight—and Japanese officials once thought of doing the same—but that would only be a change of name. For the thought-life of a nation and the spirit of a people to be made Christian, even to the extent to which this has been accomplished in some of our Western nations (there is, of course, no such thing as a truly Christian nation anywhere), will take decades and perhaps centuries. is in general an expanded and developed <term>Buddhism</term> which in many respects—even in fundamental things—is often radically different from original <term>Buddhism</term>. We do not mean to say that <term>Northern Buddhism</term> does not contain much that goes back to the teachings of the founder and, perhaps, even some things from his life and teachings which are not preserved in the <term>Pali</term> literature; but there is in it so much that is different and even radically opposed to what seems to have been the main thought and life of <term>Gautama</term>’s religion that we are ready to accept this time-honored division of <term>Hīnayāna</term> and <term>Mahāyāna</term>.

These great differences in <term>Buddhism</term> are, of course, the result of the growth and expansion which this religion underwent in the course of its history as it marched northward and eastward through <term>China</term>, <term>Korea</term>, and <term>Japan</term>. Orthodox Buddhists hold that both these great forms of their religion, in spite of the most glaring contradictions, are the teachings of the master, and they resort to the most elaborate schemes of harmonization to resolve the obvious difficulties. But modern scholars see more and more clearly that it is impossible for even the main points of <term>Mahāyāna</term> and <term>Hīnayāna</term> Buddhism to have all come from the same mind. It seems rather certain, as we have said, that the <term>Pali</term> scriptures of the south contain, on the whole, the purest form of the teaching of the <term>Buddha</term>, though they too show a considerable development. Meanwhile, the scriptures of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>—which are written partly in <term>Sanskrit</term> and in a mixed dialect of <term>Sanskrit</term> and <term>Middle Indian</term>, or the <term>Gāthā</term> dialect, and partly in Chinese, Tibetan, Mongolian, and Japanese—contain not only what is found in the <term>Pali</term> scriptures but a great deal more. It is this extra material which leads the <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhists to claim that their teachings are superior to the <term>Hīnayāna</term> and that they represent the full mind of the master; but to the unbiased scholar, it is rather evidence of *extra* Buddhist elements which entered as <term>Buddhism</term> readjusted itself to meet the attacks of a revived <term>Brahmanism</term>, and as it spread into other countries and tried to absorb the native cults which it encountered along its way.

It is the northern stream—that is, *Mahāyāna Buddhism*—that is of interest for our present purpose, for it is this stream which ultimately reached Japan in the middle of the sixth century. But so that we may understand the significance of this northern stream more clearly, it becomes necessary, as we mentioned above, to take at least a broad overview of the main points of primitive Buddhism and its development. What, then, was the religion of the Buddha? Only by answering this question, at least approximately, can we fully appreciate Northern Buddhism and especially its furthest development in the Buddhism of Japan, which in some of its branches seems Buddhist in name only. This topic is taken up in Chapter I.

# CHAPTER I

## BUDDHIST ORIGINS

The main facts of the life of Gautama, the founder of Buddhism, and the primary points of the religion he proclaimed are gradually coming to light more clearly each year as a result of the diligent efforts of a specific group of scholars. Not everything written on the subject adds to our knowledge; in fact, most of the older popular books on Buddhism are often very misleading, especially regarding the points dealing with the origins of Buddhism. This is largely because most of these books do not distinguish enough between early and late sources. For example, we have a book like Sir Edwin Arnold’s “The Light of Asia,” which has perhaps been read more widely than any other book on Buddhism. It presents a picture of the Buddha and his religion not as they were, but rather as they appeared to a devout Buddhist poet who lived several centuries later. What is written about the Buddha and early Buddhism by the vast majority of Buddhist writers, especially those in China and Japan, is even more misleading, as they view the founder of their religion largely through the eyes of men who wrote five hundred to a thousand years after Gautama’s time. We do not mean that such pictures are entirely incorrect, but rather that a careful scholar should seek to construct the image from the oldest available sources, instead of using all sources without distinction. As we mentioned, it is thanks to the patient efforts of a few careful scholars that some of the actual facts of the matter are gradually being brought to light and cleared of the accumulations of the centuries. This does not mean that students of Buddhism have anywhere near as much reliable data for the life of Gautama

This outline, particularly regarding the religion of the Buddha, becomes even clearer when seen in the light of its historical environment. In fact, our entire understanding of early Buddhism has been revolutionized by our growing knowledge of the circumstances under which it emerged. Let us briefly describe the main features of the era that preceded Gautama’s time, especially the religious life of India.

### A. *Gautama’s Environment*

When Buddhism emerged near the end of the sixth century B.C., India had already passed through several stages of its remarkable religious history. The Aryan conquerors, who invaded India from the northwest in gradual stages during the second or third millennium B.C., had already developed the religion of the Vedic hymns. In fact, the Vedic hymns and the religion they expressed already belonged to the distant past; the noble poetry of the <term>Rig-Veda</term> had been forgotten by the general public and was known only to the priests. Even the priests apparently no longer knew these hymns in their original purity, but rather as fragmented magic spells, or <term>Mantras</term>, through which they exerted authority over evil spirits and, in this way, gained power over the people. That is, the Vedic hymns had been replaced by the <term>Brāhmanas</term>, the prose liturgical texts based upon them. Those who possessed this “divine knowledge” were naturally respected by the common people. This, perhaps more than any other factor, gave them the highest position in India’s social organization and gradually led to the <term>caste system</term>, which has been such a defining element in every aspect of the country’s life ever since.

The <term>Brāhmanas</term>, which are primarily nothing more than detailed instructions for the performance of religious rites, had in turn been expanded by the addition of commentaries in which are frequently found theological and philosophical

This is the brief outline of the primary religious literature produced in India before the sixth century B.C., and a mere glance at it is enough to show that it represents many centuries of religious development. All of this literature is regarded by Indian orthodoxy as equally divinely inspired, and all the orthodox systems of metaphysics claim to base their teachings on these books, especially on the *Upanishads*.

In such a brief review, it is both impossible and unnecessary to describe the full contents of this literature. Not only is it very varied, but the views on the same subject are often quite diverse—which is to be expected when one remembers that these books record, at least in part, the religious life of a mixed race over a period of more than a thousand years. We shall provide a summary of only a few points that have a special bearing on our main theme. These are the concept of God, the theory of the soul (including the doctrines of transmigration and *Karma*), salvation, and the religious and social structure of the time.

1. *The Concept of God.* — The idea of God is exceedingly varied; this is true not only when the literature is viewed as a whole, but also when a single era is considered by itself. Alongside the highest philosophical speculations—which sometimes resulted in semi-monotheism and at other times in pantheism—one finds the lowest forms of animism and the most repulsive polytheism and demonology. <note>1</note> In the later portions of the *Rig-Veda* collection, there are passages that have supported the view that India's oldest literature points to monotheism as the earliest form of the concept of God, but a closer study of the facts hardly supports this. > “The flowers of the garlands he wore are withered, his robes of majesty have grown old and faded, he falls from his high status, and is reborn into a new life.” 

By the century in which Buddhism arose, many of the Vedic gods—even those who at one time or another had held unique places—had succumbed to this fate. Only a few of them remained, and new gods had taken the places of the old ones. What impresses one is that the sharpest thinkers, both in the Vedic age and the centuries which followed, were trying in one way or another to work their way through the animistic and polytheistic maze surrounding them toward the concept that there must be a unitary ground of existence at the origin of all things. In some writers, this thought is expressed by singling out one god from the pantheon and ascribing to him all the characteristics of other popular gods, as we see, *e.g.*, later in the cases of Vishnu and Siva. Other writers conceive of this unitary ground of existence in less personal terms and regard it instead as a self-existent principle which is the source of all phenomenal existence, including the gods. We see the God-idea assume this monistic form especially when we come to the Upanishads. In the Upanishads, this principle is usually called Brahman. Some connect Brahman with the god Brahmā or with Brahmanaspati or Brihaspati—*i.e.*, Brahman manifests itself in a personal god, and so the concept leans toward monotheism; but other thinkers use Brahman in an impersonal sense—*i.e.*, in the sense of a first principle which is the source of all empirical reality. Thus we read, 

> “Brahma, truly, was this world in the beginning. It created the gods and assigned them the rule over these worlds—Agni over this earth, Vāyu over the atmosphere, Sūryā over the heaven, and gods higher than these over the higher worlds.” 

The writer says these worlds and gods are manifest, but Brahman itself has “retired to the half beyond.” That is, the worlds and the gods that rule over them belong to the realm of empirical reality, whereas Brahman belongs to the invisible world of the Noumenon.

Atman, the Self. That is, Brahman is conceived of in terms of the human self; not, however, in the ordinary sense, but rather in the sense of the ideal self, the essential self after the body and the sense-world have been subtracted. The conception is something like Kant's Noumenal Ego as distinguished from his Empirical Ego, though what the nature of such an ego might be remains rather vague. The noumenal ego is not only like the Atman but is identical with it, as the pregnant phrase, “*Tat tvam asi*,” “That you are,” expresses it. The Brahman-Atman, then, represents the furthest development of the God-idea which Indian thought had reached by the end of the sixth century B.C. It was a monistic conception which had monotheistic affinities, but on the whole it is best classified under the convenient though vague term Pantheism.

The spirit of this pantheism is summed up most pithily in Chhandogya Upanishad, III, sec. 14:

> “Brahman indeed is this All. It has its beginning, end, and breath within it; so one should worship it in stillness.
> 
> “Now man indeed is made of will. As is man’s will in this world, so does he become on departing from it. He shall shape his will.
> 
> “Made of mind, embodied with breath, revealed in radiance, true of purpose, ethereal of soul, all-working, all-loving, all-smelling, all-tasting, grasping this All, speaking nothing, heeding nothing, this very Self within my heart is tinier than a grain of rice or a barley-corn or a mustard-seed or a canary-seed or the pulp of a canary-seed. This my Self within my heart is greater than earth, greater than sky, greater than heaven, greater than these worlds.
> 
> “All-working, all-loving, all-smelling, all-tasting, grasping this All, speaking nothing, heeding nothing, this my Self within my heart, this is Brahma; to Him shall I attain on departing from here. He who has this thought has indeed no doubt.”

To sum up, then, in a few words the God-idea current in India when Buddhism arose, we may say that as held by the common people it was either animistic or polytheistic; both terms including a very wide range of beings. In the

minds of the keener thinkers it is quite likely that the concept of God was polytheistic in their practical life; that is, the gods were regarded as having real existence and had to be taken into account. But in their speculative moods, such minds penetrated through this plurality of gods to the conception of a unitary source of all existence, the gods included. This unitary source they conceived of either in terms of their own psychic life, or as an unimaginable First Principle which somehow is the ground of all that the empirical world reveals to us. This latter conception, however, was entirely too abstract to satisfy the religious sense. While the mind demanded a unitary source of all existence, the heart needed more than a mere First Principle. It is in the reconciliation of these two demands of mind and heart that we find the origin of the conception of a supreme personal God, which we find in the great currents of Shaivite and Vaishnavite thought that have divided India into two great camps from pre-Buddhist days down to the present time. The latest and most lofty expression of India’s approach to a true monotheistic concept of God is to be found in the writings of men like Rabindranath Tagore; though, of course, this is no longer purely Indian but borrows much from Western science and Christian thought.

2. *The Soul Theory.* — The soul theory prevalent in India before the sixth century B.C. was equally varied, for the concept of God and the soul theory are most intimately connected. In fact, nothing seems truer than the statement that man makes gods in his own image.

Nothing is more natural to primitive man than the belief in his own soul. He not only believes in the existence of his own soul, but sees a soul in everything else. This is the real heart of animism. Polytheism, too, is really a soul theory. The great objects of nature, or groups of phenomena, behave as they do because they have souls similar to the soul that controls the human body. And many gods are nothing but deified ancestors. But Indian thought had advanced far beyond these simple assumptions by the end of the sixth century B.C. It had attempted a

usually thought of as some refined substance that inhabits

   In the Upanishads, however, we find a much more
advanced conception. To show that the soul is not a material substance,
we are told that it is smaller than a mustard seed or the

all the worlds; in fact, it is of the same essence as Brah-
man and even identified with It or Him.

   In short, we may say that at the end of the sixth
century B.C., India believed in the existence of the soul as a
reality distinct from the body, surviving the dissolution
of the body at death.

   3. *Transmigration.* — One aspect of the soul-theory is
the doctrine of transmigration. This doctrine dates
at least as far back as the eighth century B.C. In the minds of
the uneducated masses, this belief assumed a very crude form.
All objects were endowed with souls. At death, when the
soul seemed to depart from the body, it simply changed its
dwelling from one body to another. It was believed that the nature of the new
dwelling was somewhat determined by the
character and conduct of the soul while it occupied
the body it was leaving. This phase of the doctrine
is the heart of the Karma doctrine, which is closely associated
with the theory of transmigration. We shall speak
of this later, as it is one of the foundation stones of Buddhism. We
only wish to add here that the doctrine of Karma, like that
of transmigration, had been the common belief of the
people of India for several centuries before Buddhism arose.

By the end of the sixth century B.C., it had already been raised into an ethical conception even in the minds of the masses and explained most satisfactorily to them both the inequalities of man’s present life and the rewards and punishments meted out in a future life.

Now just as the soul-theory was held in both crude and philosophical forms, so the doctrine of transmigration and its associated doctrine of karma were also held in higher forms by the better thinkers before the days of Gautama. We read, *e.g.*, in the Upanishads that “Man in truth is made of will. As is man’s will in this world, so does he become on going hence.” That is, where the masses held the doctrines of transmigration and karma in the crude form—that the soul at death simply passes over into another body already prepared for it and of the character which the deeds of the soul justly deserve—the higher form held that the soul is essentially will, and by its own deeds creates its own future environment. In short, man becomes what he desires and strives to be—a doctrine not far removed from some of our modern biological theories regarding the origin of the varied organisms of life.

The destiny of the soul as held by pre-Buddhist thought is already exhibited by the above remarks on the doctrines of transmigration and karma. We only add that India believed in a happy fate for the good and in hells for the evil. Either goal is reached through gradual stages by the law of karma and by means of transmigrating from one body to another. To the masses, heaven was a life of endless bliss conceived of in terms of what seemed pleasant in this life, while hell was a place filled with all the horrors that a fertile imagination could conjure up. To the philosopher, and especially to the philosophers of the Upanishads, the life of bliss was union with the great Source of All Being, the “identity of Brahman-Atman.” This was not simply to be realized after death, but was regarded as a present possibility. The blessed state was realized the moment that the soul became aware of the great fact that it is essentially the same as the Great Atman. Hell, on the other hand, was to be in

To summarize, then, the pre-Buddhist theories regarding the soul and its destiny that were current in India, we may say India believed that the soul had a real existence and that it wandered from body to body, or from state to state, according to the law of Karma, which had reached an ethical level. India believed that the final destiny of the soul was, on one hand, a life of happiness with the gods or in union with Brahman; on the other hand, for the wicked, it was a life of unhappiness in lower realms of existence and in hell, or a life of separation from Brahman.

4. *General Social and Religious Condition.* — But however much Indian thought was occupied with problems concerning the nature of the soul and its destiny, and however much people were taught that at the end of the long road—led through many years of ascetic practices—there lay the highest heaven where one could escape from the Wheel of Life, these beliefs were, after all, rather shadowy. The average Indian preferred to cling to the few pleasures of the present life rather than count on the promised greater happiness of an uncertain future. "It is not good to leave this world, for who knows whether one shall exist in the world beyond or not." And Yajnavalkya, the real founder of Brahmanism, says, "Beyond the grave there is no consciousness." In another place he says, "To be sure, a tree cut down sprouts again from the stump; but from what roots will a dead man grow up again? Do not say, 'from the seed,' for seed is produced only by the living. He who has died shall not be born anew." The religious life of the masses in India before Gautama’s day dealt largely with present material blessings or curses rather than with moral achievements that were to determine future conditions. So prayers and sacrifices to the gods centered then, as they do today, around the things that will feed and clothe the body, and they were not much concerned with the "garments of righteousness" which alone can make men fit companions of God. The average man lived in fear of demons and spiteful

gods, and these he sought to win over so that they might become friendly to him and give him what he needed for a present life of happiness and prosperity. Even the Brahmin priests, the sole possessors of "divine knowledge," were apparently more concerned with keeping the people in terror of their power—so that they themselves might live better by their trade—than with saving men's lives from sin and leading them to a better and higher life. Indeed, these guardians of "divine knowledge" magnified the horrors of hell so that their fees for the work of deliverance might be more profitable.

5. *Signs of a Better Day.* — There was, however, in the sixth century B.C. a growing class of men and women who were exceedingly serious and sincere in their religious life. These were the so-called Wanderers and Hermits. There may have been some impostors among them, but on the whole they seem to have been held in high regard by the people because of their holiness and wisdom. The Wanderers were holy, wise men wandering up and down India talking informally with anyone who cared for religious and philosophical things. They came largely from the ranks of the common people, though it would seem that there were also some Brahmins among them. Their appearance may be said to have heralded and helped cause the change that was about to come over the religious life of India, for these wandering philosophers prepared the way for the greatest of these wandering teachers, namely, the Buddha Gautama. The Hermits, who lived in tangled forests and barren caves, were less numerous than the Wanderers, but still, in their silent haunts of self-denial and meditation, they also had a definite share in bringing in the religion of the "World-Honored One" who was soon to appear.

With these few words regarding the environment in which Buddhism arose, we pass on to a brief sketch of Gautama's life and the essentials of his religious views.

### B. *The Buddha's Life and Teachings*

The Buddha or Siddhārtha — to call him by his personal name — was born at Lumbini near Kapilavastu about 560 B.C.

<header>THE BUDDHA’S LIFE AND TEACHINGS</header>
<page-num>23</page-num>

B.C. and died at Kusināgarā about 480<note>2</note> B.C. His father Suddhodana, "Pure Rice," was not a king as is often said, but probably a noble landed proprietor of the Gautama branch of the S’akya clan. Thus the Buddha is sometimes called Gautama and sometimes S’akyamuni,<note>3</note> Teacher of the S’akyans. The S’akyan clan at that time occupied a district a few thousand square miles in area lying partly on the slopes of the Nepalese foothills and partly on the plains to the south. The capital was Kapilavastu, situated about a hundred miles due north of Benares. The clan was no longer independent but had come under the suzerainty of the adjoining kingdom of Kosala, to the east of which lay the rival kingdom of Magadha, whose ruler Bimbisāra became the Buddha’s first royal patron. The young Siddhārtha lost his mother when he was only a few days old and was brought up by his mother’s sister, whom his father married. His upbringing was probably like that of most young men of his class, being trained more in manly sports and the arts of hunting and war than in the learning of the priests or the wisdom of the Wanderers and the Hermits. In due time he was married and became the father of one son, Rāhula, who became in the course of time a member of the Buddhist order.

Soon after the birth of his son, at the age of twenty-nine, Siddhārtha abandoned his young wife and child and wandered forth "to seek after what was right," as hundreds of others were doing at that time. Many writers, ancient and modern, have given us beautiful pictures of the "Great Renunciation" of the Buddha and his struggle with the tempter who tried to make him give up his quest; but, of course, such pictures should not be taken too literally. Relying upon the oldest sources available, it would seem, however, that the cause that led to this step on Siddhārtha’s part was his growing realization that to be "carnally minded is death," and that the pleasures of the life of the senses are extremely fleeting and can never satisfy the heart; indeed, that life as a whole seems to have more shadows than sunlight.

<page-num>24</page-num>

Legend gives us several instances in which this truth was brought graphically to the attention of the young man. Thus one day, while attending a plowing festival, he saw an earthworm cut in two by the plow. Soon after this, while passing through the city, he met in rapid succession a beggar, an old man, a sick man, and a corpse being carried through the streets. One of the oldest authoritative texts puts the following words in the Buddha's mouth, "An ordinary uneducated man, though he himself is subject to old age and has not escaped its power, when he sees another old man, is hurt, ashamed, and disgusted, overlooking meanwhile his own condition. Thinking that this would be unsuitable for me, the infatuation of youth and youth itself departed from me entirely." That is, youth, health, and the pleasures of life end in old age, sickness, and sorrow; and therefore these transitory things can never give permanent satisfaction. And because they cannot give real satisfaction, it is better to abandon them lest they become too deep-rooted. Let man seek "that which is right," for this alone can give permanent satisfaction.

This, in short, seems to have been the thought in young *Siddhārtha's* mind when he went forth from his home and became a <term>Wanderer</term> in search of <term>salvation</term>. At first he seems to have attached himself to two teachers skilled in the art of cultivating <term>trance states</term>; but finding that this led to nothing permanent, he turned to a life of <term>self-mortification</term> in which he showed such zeal that five disciples attached themselves to him. He followed this path of hardships until it brought him to the very verge of death, without, however, leading him to what he really sought. If a life of luxury and sensual enjoyment leads to pain and death, the other extreme of fasting and <term>self-mortification</term> also seems to lead nowhere but to a miserable death. *Siddhārtha* therefore abandoned the life of the ordinary <term>ascetic</term>, realizing that physical impoverishment is not in itself <term>spiritual enrichment</term>. His five companions in misery abandoned him when he departed from what they regarded as the only true path of holiness. *Siddhārtha*, however, continued his

quest until finally, six or seven years after he first set out, the moment of his <term>Enlightenment</term> came to him. He understood for the first time the cause of the world’s miseries and saw the way to escape from the earth’s sorrows. He had attained <term>Buddhahood</term> and was now prepared to become the teacher of the Way that was to bring salvation to millions in Asia.

What did <term>Siddhārtha</term>—or rather the <term>Buddha</term>, the Enlightened One—see in that hour of enlightenment? To know this is to know the heart of his religion. Furthermore, to know the heart of <term>early Buddhism</term> is to have a standard by which to judge the development of <term>early Buddhism</term> into <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> and its evolution into the Buddhism of Japan, which is the furthest development of <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> and constitutes the real subject of this book.

Answering this question accurately may be difficult, but the general outline seems fairly clear. It is most concisely stated in what are called the <term>Three Conceptions</term> (<term>Trividyā</term>) or the <term>Three Law Seals</term>, the <term>Four Noble Truths</term>, and the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>. These are not three entirely different things; rather, they overlap to some extent. The <term>Three Conceptions</term>, or Law Seals, represent the general philosophical assumptions of <term>Gautama’s</term> religion, whereas the <term>Four Noble Truths</term> and the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term> represent his specific insight into human needs and the way of salvation.

1. *The Three Conceptions.* — The <term>Three Conceptions</term>, or the general philosophical assumptions underlying the <term>Buddha’s</term> religion, may be summarized under the following three headings:
->The Impermanence of All Individual Existence.<-
->The Universality of Suffering Inherent in Individuality.<-
->The Non-reality of an Ego-principle.<-

a. *The Impermanence of All Individual Existence.* — We saw earlier that <term>Brahmin</term> speculation had advanced to the point where it asserted the existence of a unified basis of all beings in the One-All, the <term>Brahman</term>. This conclusion

was a result of speculation based on observation—specifically, the general observation that no individual existence as such is ever permanent, but is always subject to change. If there is permanency in anything, it must be in that which somehow underlies the world of change—that is, in the <term>Brahman</term>. Now, while <term>Gautama</term> had little or nothing to say about the "One-All," or even whether it was unchanging, he did share the view of the philosophers of his day that all individual existence and the entire world of phenomena were subject to change, and that the single word <term>Impermanence</term> best describes the world as we know it.

This is true especially of all living things. An insect lives for only a few days; the average lifespan of an animal is only a few years; the plant world is green today and withered tomorrow. While trees may endure for decades or even centuries, it is still true that all of them undergo changes from day to day. The inanimate world seems more permanent, but it, too, is in constant flux. Rivers change their courses; they overflow in times of flood and dry up during droughts. Rocks crumble to pieces and are worn away by time. Even the eternal hills are made low by the passing of the centuries.

And what is true of nature in general is especially true of human life. A newborn baby soon becomes an active boy, and a few years see him grow into a young man of twenty or thirty. Only a few more years and the prime of life is reached and passed, and then comes the inevitable old age and decay, ending in death. Beggars and princes alike share this fate; indeed, the greater the glory, the faster its end seems to come.

> “The boast of heraldry, the pomp of power,
> And all that beauty, all that wealth ever gave,
> Await alike the inevitable hour.
> The path of glory leads but to the grave.”

Change and decay are not only the fate of man and his immediate environment; this also seems to be the lot of the universe as a whole. Of suns, moons, and stars, it may be said, “Our little systems have their day; they have their day and cease to be.” Worlds are formed and dissolved,

They, too, are bound to the great <term>Wheel of Life</term>, and its eternal revolutions will some day bring their happy circumstances to an end. Nothing, absolutely nothing in the realm of individual existence is exempt. The one word <term>Impermanence</term> must be written across them all.

b. *The Universality of Suffering Inherent in Individuality.*— The second great underlying thought of all the Buddha's teachings—and the one for which the <term>Four Great Truths</term> are really a fuller explanation—is the idea that all individual existence is inherently an existence of suffering. In fact, the very condition of individuality (that is, the effort to remain an individual) means <term>Suffering</term>. There is an elemental force at work which ultimately destroys every individual, as is announced in the doctrine of <term>Impermanence</term>, and therefore any effort on the part of an individual to oppose this elemental force must result in pain. <term>Individuality</term> implies limitation, limitation leads to ignorance, and ignorance leads to sorrow and suffering. This is especially true of humanity. Being an individual, a person's first instinct is self-preservation. Self-preservation leads them to make an effort against the forces that oppose them, and so the fight that can never be won has begun; for even though a person gains what they seek, their desires far outrun their achievements, and even those achievements soon crumble to dust and force them to be separated from all that they have won or sought to win. The Buddha's contemporaries also recognized this second truth to a degree, but they did not hold it in such an absolute form; for the <term>Brahmin</term> philosopher held that as the individual is really identical with the <term>Brahman</term>, the <term>One-All</term>, absolute loss is impossible. And the common people of India believed that though this is a life of suffering and sorrow, and death robs a person of all their worldly possessions, there is nevertheless a future life of happiness as a compensation.

c. *The Non-reality of an Ego-principle.* — The third great underlying thought of <term>Gautama</term>'s religion is the denial of an <term>Ego-principle</term>.

Individuals are real, of course, in a relative sense; but since all things are <term>impermanent</term>, the self (at least the empirical self), too, must be <term>impermanent</term>. The effort of humanity to make provision for the soul in a future life is the most futile of all efforts. It is as if a raindrop sought to retain within itself the rainbow colors caused by the rays of the sun falling on it for a moment or two. The raindrop inevitably falls to the ground and then, united with others, it flows down the stream into the ocean, there to be lost in the eternal depths of <term>Oneness</term>; and what has become of the drop as a drop or the rainbow colors it hoped to treasure up for all eternity? That <term>Gautama</term> did not deny a certain sort of continuity beyond death is seen from the doctrine of <term>Karma</term> which he accepted, but of this we shall speak later.

These three doctrines, then—namely, the doctrine of the <term>impermanence</term> of all individual existence, the doctrine of suffering inherent in individuality, and the non-reality of any abiding <term>ego-principle</term>, or the self—constitute the underlying presuppositions of all of the <term>Buddha</term>'s teachings. And we may say that these are not denied by the Buddhists of any school, though, as we shall see in succeeding chapters, many of the sects of Chinese and Japanese Buddhism proclaim teachings that seem practically the opposites of these.

Now, there is a ring of sincerity and practicality about these words of the Buddha which one misses in the speculative systems of many religious teachers. The Buddha speaks from experience, and while we may not agree with his interpretation of life and his way of salvation, we cannot help but feel that he was completely in earnest in his quest and honest in the solution to life's problem which he offered to the people of India. He knew the two extremes which man is to avoid from his own bitter experience. They are extremes into which not only the people of ancient India had fallen, but they remain with us to this day. Life, indeed, is an art; and, after all, very few can strike the happy balance of using sensory things without abusing them—the happy balance of living in the world without sinking to the level of the world. This discovery by the Buddha is a commonplace truth to us moderns, though actually walking the Middle Path of sane moderation seems almost as difficult today as it did to the ancients.

When we come to the specific content of <term>The Four Noble Truths</term> proclaimed by the Buddha, the Western mind and heart part company with him, though few would hesitate to accept much of what is implied in these Truths. Every man who knows life at all must have experienced that life has much in it of sorrow and suffering, but that is not all that can be said about life. Though not blind to pain and evil, the Western mind has always held to a divine optimism which refuses to give wholehearted allegiance to the statement of the first Noble Truth: that life is essentially sorrow and pain. And the deep-rooted belief in the goodness of a Personal God, known through Christ as the Heavenly Father, will always make the Buddha's solution to life's problems seem quite inadequate and too gloomy. Gautama began his quest as many others had begun before him. Like others, he had found that life as lived by the ordinary man—namely, the life of the senses and physical enjoyment—was fleeting and ended in old age, sickness, and death. If there are pleasures, they are impermanent and seem to be outweighed by sorrow and suffering. Thus, he was led to formulate his first Noble Truth: that human life is suffering and vanity. This, as we have said above, is not exactly a new truth with Gautama, but it must be admitted that perhaps no one had ever held it with such universal application, seeing that he applied it to all individual existence, including the gods of the highest heavens.

Now in the second of the Noble Truths, we find what seems to have been an original<gloss>8</gloss> conception of the Buddha: namely, his explanation of the cause of human suffering. The source of all suffering, he said, is to be found in man's desires, especially in that craving thirst which seeks satisfaction through the gratification of the senses. That is, man, as he is constituted in his ignorance, has a thirst for things which do not really satisfy. This thirst keeps him ever seeking satisfaction without finding it. Some seek happiness in a life of luxury, others seek it in what seem to be nobler ways; and still others, forgoing all earthly pleasures, seek happiness in a life of bliss with the gods in the world to come. But all such seeking can never satisfy nor lead to anything permanent, for the simple reason that it is all a sort of self-seeking—*i.e.*, it is based on the belief that the self is a permanent reality, which, according to the Buddha, is the greatest of all follies, seeing that no individual existence is permanent as such, but is subject to the great law of change.

Is trust in the popular gods of Brahmanism a futile thing? For how can they save humanity when they, too, belong to this world of change and are bound to the Wheel of Life? But there is a way of salvation discovered by the Enlightened One. This way is declared in what makes up the fourth Noble Truth. It is nothing other than the Noble Eightfold Path, which leads a person finally into true salvation—into an enlightenment in which they see things as they are.

And when a person is enlightened and sees things as they really are, what do they see? They see that all things are temporary and that all individual existence is inherently an existence of suffering; they see that in order to escape from this life of suffering, the truly wise must give up all desires for individuality and the things that go toward making up such a life. That is, the Enlightened One sees that what we ordinarily call the self is the greatest of all illusions, and therefore to know this is to become free from the bonds of individual existence. Freedom from the bonds of individuality is what constitutes real salvation.

Now, this denial of the reality of the self seems very strange, at least to the average Western mind; for the thought immediately suggests itself that if the belief in the reality of the self is an illusion, it must be an illusion to something, or someone; and what is that “something, or someone”? And furthermore, if the Enlightened One knows that the belief in the existence of the ego is an illusion, then what, or who, is it that knows this?

Such questions make it clear that the Buddha either did not think the problem through completely, or that, after all, he must have believed in the existence of a “something” that knows. We are rather inclined to believe that both these alternatives are true: that is, the Buddha neither thought his position completely through nor did he absolutely deny that there was a “something” that knew, which we have a perfect right to call the true or higher self.<note>9</note>

The Buddha himself apparently admitted that he did not think his position completely through, for it seems more and more evident that he had no special fondness for metaphysical

problems, and that he tended to sidestep them when he could. What he was primarily interested in was the liberation of suffering humanity from the bonds of sin and passion. While others theorized about the cosmogonical problem, the nature of the soul, and its relation to the <term>Brahman</term>, he was preaching the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term> of practical ethical conduct, which was intended to free humanity from suffering. He was not as concerned with what lay at the end of the road of redemption from suffering; in fact, he felt that speculating on this subject only kept people from achieving liberation. Thus, we read in one of the oldest and most authentic passages on the subject as follows:

> “A person considers unwisely, ‘Have I existed in ages past... shall I exist in ages to come? Do I exist at all? Am I? How am I? This is a being—where did it come from, and where will it go?’ Engaging in considerations such as these is like walking in a jungle of delusions. These are the things one should consider: ‘This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the end of suffering; this is the way that leads to the end of suffering.’ For the person who considers these things, their bonds fall away.”

The Buddha was certain of only one thing at the end of the road of suffering: freedom and perfect peace. Whether this was the freedom and peace of annihilation or a positive existence, he did not state clearly. In fact, his answer to such questions usually consisted of a list of the <term>Great Indeterminates</term>, the most important of which are the following:

(1 and 2). Whether the world in its true substance is eternal or not.

(3 and 4). Whether the world is infinite or not.

(5 and 6). Whether the soul is the same as the body or different from it.

(7 and 8). Whether a person exists in any way after death.

> “The jungle, the desert, the puppet show, the writhing, and the entanglements of such speculations are accompanied by sorrow, resentful arguments, and the fever of excitement. It leads

Thus, while it is generally true that the Buddha seemed to base his teachings on certain philosophical assumptions—the main ones being mentioned above—it seems equally true that he had not fully worked out a clear position on even those points which his main teachings seem to imply. Or, if he did work them out, he did not follow his conclusions very consistently or positively.

3. *<term>Karma</term>* <note>10</note> *and Self.* — Now, while the Buddha was not certain about the continuation of the Enlightened One (the <term>Arhat</term>) beyond this life, and while he apparently denied the reality of the self and placed such problems among the <term>Great Indeterminates</term>, he nevertheless did assert positively that for the unenlightened person there was a “something” which continued beyond death. This “something” was a person’s Karma. In fact, his very plan of salvation was primarily a way by which Karma should be destroyed or exhausted, so that it would not again build up an individual being and cause suffering.

But what is meant by Karma, and how does it differ from the self? This is a question to which no really satisfactory answer can be given, and it illustrates what we said above: namely, that the Buddha did not think his position all the way through, or at least that he did not explain exactly what it was.

The doctrine of Karma, as we said above, is one that was common to India long before the days of the Buddha. It was closely associated with that other great doctrine of Indian thought: the doctrine of the Transmigration of the soul. <term>Gautama</term> apparently denied the latter but not the former. He held to a transmigration from one existence to another, so that a person’s present misfortunes may be the effect of the sins committed in a former existence; however, the identity of the present person with the person of the former existence was not a personal identity, but only a Karma identity. That is, the soul, or the self, does not pass from

one body to another, as was held by most of the thinkers of Gautama’s day, but only Karma passed over. There is no memory or consciousness of a self; there is only Karma that endures. Therefore, if one is to understand the Buddha’s position, one must understand the meaning of the baffling conception expressed by the word Karma.

The word Karma expresses in general the doctrine of the universal reign of the law of Cause and Effect. Of all doctrines, none is more axiomatic than this causal-nexus axiom, and so the Buddha, like every true Indian of his day, accepted it with all its accustomed rigor. Though he refused to go back step by step through the causal-nexus to the First Great Cause, he nevertheless held with others that everything that exists has a cause, and every effect in turn becomes the cause of future effects. That is the meaning of the most famous of all Buddhist stanzas which one finds engraved on thousands of votive gifts to Buddhist shrines in India, and which reads:

> “Of all the phenomena sprung from a cause
> The Buddha has told the cause,
> And he tells, too, how each shall come to its end,
> Such alone is the word of the Sage.”

Now this causal-nexus axiom when applied to the human individual means nothing else than that a person is at any one moment just what their deeds and desires of the past have made them; and in the future, they will become just what their deeds and desires of the past and the present are making them. The words of the poet have for the Buddhist a literal meaning when he says:

> “Our deeds follow us from afar,
> And what we have been makes us what we are.”

Good deeds will produce a good result; and evil deeds, an evil result; or to use the Indian mode of thought, a person’s good Karma will tend to make a good individual, and their evil Karma will tend to make an evil individual. The resultant is the combination of the two. Now at death the

The individual falls apart into the component elements of individuality—namely, the five <term>Aggregates</term><note>11</note>, or <term>Skandhas</term> (physicality, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness)—but the *Karma*, or the *tendency-energy*, of the present life remains. In the future, it will gather other <term>Skandhas</term> which will function as an individual in harmony with the *Karma*, or *tendency-energy*, that creates them. There is, then, no memory or consciousness that passes from one birth to another, but there is this mysterious energy—distinct from the body and the functioning of the empirical ego—that does pass from one individual to another; or rather, it builds up a new individual again when the old individual is dissolved in death.

From this, it seems clear that the Buddha did not believe in the existence of the soul in the sense that the common philosophers of his day did. Furthermore, it seems clear that he did not believe in the existence of the spiritual self in the sense that we moderns do, when we maintain in our doctrine of personal immortality that beyond death there is a continuation of memory and a consciousness of real identity. That mysterious *tendency-energy* known as *Karma* is, then, neither the mere energy resulting from the physical forces that make up the human body, nor is it, secondly, simply the sum total of the functioning of the five <term>Skandhas</term>, since it is the energy that gathers the new <term>Skandhas</term> of the new individual in each successive stage of incarnation. And thirdly, it cannot be said to be like the spiritual self of the modern psychologist; rather, it seems to be like that mysterious energy which we know within us as *Will*—especially like the *blind will*, or the *will-to-be* of Schopenhauer's<note>12</note> system. It is this "blind will-to-be" which is the real cause of all becoming, and as long as it persists, it will continue to create for itself new bodies and individuals after the old ones are dissolved through death. The empirical individual, which is only a composite of the five <term>Skandhas</term> and the seat of all sorrow and pain, ceases to exist when this combination is dissolved at death, but *Karma*, or that *will-energy*, continues and creates the

We cannot define more closely than this what is meant by this baffling conception of Karma and rebirths, and by the Buddha's conception of the empirical ego.

### 4. *The Buddha's Mode of Salvation.* 
Whatever, then, Karma may or may not mean, the aim and purpose of the Buddha's way of salvation is to break the Karma-chain so that it will not continue and form another individual and so prolong the life of suffering. The true <term>Arhat</term> is one whose Karma has been completely exhausted and who is therefore assured of deliverance from the Wheel of Life. 

> "Looking for the maker (Karma) of this tabernacle, I have had to run through a course of many births, as long as I did not find him; and painful is birth again and again. But now, maker of the tabernacle, you have been seen; you shall not make up this tabernacle again. All your rafters are broken, your ridgepole is split apart, your mind approaching <term>Nirvāna</term> has attained the extinction of all desires."

This is one of the best-authenticated passages of early Buddhism and seems to bear out what we have said: namely, that what the Buddha aimed at above everything else was to find deliverance from individual existence.

Another passage which illustrates the way the Buddha expressed himself on this central doctrine reads as follows: 

> "As a flame blown out by the wind goes out and cannot be considered as existing; so a sage delivered from name and body disappears and cannot be considered as existing."

And when his disciple asks him, "But has he only disappeared, or does he not exist, or is he only free from sickness?" the Buddha replies, "For him there is no form, and that by which they say he is exists for him no longer." Whether this may mean that the sage does exist in a higher form though free from the forms of the present life is a question not easily answered. One thing, however, is certain: namely, that the Buddha did mean that the sage was not to be born again into this life, and this was for him the important consideration; that is what constituted the salvation he offered.

Therefore, let anyone who would win this salvation walk in the <term>Middle Way</term>, the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>; for at the end of this path, they shall surely find deliverance. They will become a true <term>Arhat</term> who can face the future in perfect peace, for they know that from now on there is no bondage for them. This blessed assurance gives the only joy worth having; it alone can satisfy human desire. The <term>Arhat</term> feels no need for the gods, for he is infinitely superior to them. They are still bound to the <term>Wheel of Life</term>, even though they may be on the top side for now. The future will certainly bring them to the bottom again, and then they will be no better off than other beings. The <term>Arhat</term>, on the other hand, is neither on the top side nor on the bottom of the <term>Wheel of Life</term>; he is totally free from it.

Now, from all that has been said so far regarding the core of the <term>Buddha</term>’s teachings, it is clear that he placed his emphasis quite differently from the religious teachers of his day or from where it is usually placed. He agreed with the thought of his day that salvation is primarily “an escape from the evils of existence,” and also with much of the contemporary belief that, ultimately, one must save oneself. But he held these two doctrines with a rigor that few others did; because of this, he differed widely from both the thought of his own age and the minds of many in all ages, in that he left practically no room for the <term>God-idea</term> or for a real future life for the individual—two cardinal doctrines of practically all religions.

It is not true that the <term>Buddha</term> was a complete atheist, as is frequently claimed. Of course, if by an atheist one means someone who does not accept the Christian conception of God or the theistic conception in general, then he was an atheist. It is also true that he had very little to say about either the <term>Brahman</term> of the philosophers of his day or the gods of the popular pantheon. But it is not true that he denied either the existence of the former or the relative existence of the latter. The most that can be said is that he regarded speculations about the <term>Absolute</term> as a waste of time, *i.e.*

he seemed to be an agnostic rather than an out-and-out atheist. And the gods of the common people he regarded as not being worthy of either the fear or the reverence given them. As we said, he did not exactly deny their existence, but rather held that they, too, belonged to the world of change and decay; so that no permanent help could come from them. How could these gods really help mankind, since they could not deliver themselves from the "dread cycle of existence" to which they were still bound? Greater than the gods was he who, like himself, had attained enlightenment. And the God of <term>Brahmin</term> speculation was too far removed from the real needs of humanity to be of any true help. In view of the impotence of the popular gods and the unknowability of the <term>Brahman</term>, man must work out his own salvation with patience and persistence. Thus, though theoretically the <term>Buddha</term> cannot be regarded as an atheist, practically he lived as one who was without God and with hope only in himself.

It is only natural that the average Indian did not understand the <term>Buddha</term>'s conception of <term>Karma</term> or his explanation of the cause of suffering. And it also seems that his early disciples did not all follow his general attitude toward the God-idea or the future-life-idea to its logical conclusion. Since he placed these questions among the <term>Great Indeterminates</term>, he could not have been very positive in his teachings on these points, and so it is safe to say that at least the ordinary <term>Buddhist</term> never gave up entirely his trust in the gods nor his hope of a happy future life. Even among the thinkers in the early <term>Buddhist</term> community, it would seem that salvation was regarded as more than a mere "escape from the dread cycle of existence," but to this was also added the thought that it was at the same time a happy future existence of real content. The word <term>Nirvāna</term> may mean the peace of annihilation, but it is not the only expression used by the early <term>Buddhists</term>. To be sure, when the <term>Buddhist</term> speaks from the standpoint of the ethical life and the struggle with the lower passions, salvation is conceived of as the "great emancipation," "the end of craving," "the going out,"

Thus, the state of the <term>Arhat</term> is spoken of as a “state of purity,” “the supreme,” “the transcendent,” “the uncreated,” “the tranquil,” “the unchanging,” “the unshaken,” and “the imperishable.” Such expressions as these are a little too positive in content to represent total annihilation. Therefore, it would seem that while the <term>Buddha</term> himself was not especially interested in what lay at the end of the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>, except that it meant to him deliverance from the bondage of individual existence, his followers put more content into this conception of salvation.

But whether the majority of disciples followed the <term>Buddha</term> in these great questions or not, they could understand his practical ethical teachings, which, after all, was the main purpose of his religion. The <term>Middle Way</term><sup>13</sup>—the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>—was a true way of deliverance from lower passions and coarser sins; and to the extent that India walked in this way, it was a better India.

The weakness of <term>Gautama</term>’s religion, therefore, is not so much in what he taught positively, but rather in the belief that religion is possible without having some positive ideas regarding the great problems of God, the soul, and its eternal destiny. It is not enough to offer mankind a deliverance from a present evil; the heart also craves a present and future good, and fellowship with a power that makes these certain. To be sure, practical ethical teachings and deliverance from lower passions are more profitable than much of the idle speculation about metaphysical problems engaged in by <term>Gautama</term>’s contemporaries, and this is why his religion gained such a rapid hold on India; but, after all, the heart needs more and demands some answer to these great problems. These questions will not be silenced, and while it may be impossible to give perfectly satisfactory answers to them, the teacher of religion who declines to provide an answer, as the <term>Buddha</term> seems to have done as a rule, will find that either his system will soon fade away or that his followers will try to answer these questions for themselves.

This latter fate is what happened to Gautama's religion. Even during the Buddha's own lifetime, it seems, as we mentioned, that the average disciple never entirely gave up their allegiance to the popular gods or their hope for a happier future life. And over the centuries, as we will see in the following chapters, the Buddhist philosophers themselves not only provided answers to these deepest questions of the human heart, but often did so in a way that was quite contrary to the concepts that the Buddha seems to have held, or at least contrary to what some of his explicit teachings seem to imply. All the gods and spirits of the Indian pantheon (and later the gods of the Chinese and Japanese pantheons) returned to Buddhism with a glory they rarely possessed in pre-Buddhist days. And the future life for the individual was depicted in the most positive and vivid colors that the imagination could conceive.

But we are getting ahead of our subject, as this belongs in the following chapters. We must now return to the narrative of Gautama's life after he became the Buddha and describe the success he had in bringing his message of salvation, as outlined above, to the people of India.

### C. *The Success of the Buddha's Ministry*

Tradition says that while Gautama was pursuing the truth, and just as he had achieved enlightenment, he was harassed by attacks from Māra, the Buddhist tempter, but he did not yield to these temptations. To be sure, he gave up the life of self-mortification, as we have mentioned, which appeared to some as a return to the desires of the flesh; however, he only gave up one extreme of life without falling into the other. He strictly followed the Middle Path of moderation. Therefore, the great temptation did not lie in that area, although many Buddhist texts also have much to say about how the Buddha overcame these more obvious temptations. After the hour of enlightenment had dawned upon him, a subtle temptation came to him: that the great truth he had discovered was too profound for this ignorant world, and that he should immediately

The Buddha’s first disciples, it seems, were the five mendicants who had been his companions in the forests of <term>Uruvelā</term>, but who had abandoned him when he left the way of austerities for the <term>Middle Way</term> of moderation. Naturally, they were prejudiced against him after their experience, but his way of salvation was so wonderful that they entered it gladly as soon as he proclaimed it to them. Beginning with these five, his disciples soon became numerous. They came from all classes, for the Buddha’s religion was not a protest against India’s <term>caste system</term>, as some have held. It was rather above caste and welcomed men from every station in life. To be sure, he attacked the <term>Brahmin</term> priests of his day, but largely because he felt that their false conceit about <term>Vedic learning</term> and ritual observances not only did not save man, but became a real hindrance to salvation. They were blind leaders of the blind and needed to be taught as much as those whom they tried to lead. Let them abandon their false learning and enter the one Way which is for all castes because it is above caste. Apparently, a good many Brahmins did leave their own rank and entered the community of the Enlightened One. Some converts came over from rival sects <note>14</note> which were just then coming into life. Some came from the general class of Wanderers and Hermits of whom we spoke above and who belonged to no particular sect or system. The majority of the disciples, however, came from the people in general who were like sheep without a shepherd, lost in the desert of the lower passions and sin.

Just what constituted discipleship may be hard to say; but it seems that rather early in Buddhist history the <term>Triple Confession</term> was established as the door of entrance to the order, namely, the confession: "I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Doctrine, I take refuge in the Order."
