The yellow robe, the shaven head, and the begging bowl seem to have been the outward badges of the monk early on, though the common believer did not go that far in changing his outward life. Beyond subscribing to the previously mentioned triple confession, the common believer probably subscribed to nothing further than the first five of the ten Buddhist commandments, which are a prohibition of: (1) the destruction of life, (2) theft, (3) unchastity, (4) falsehood, and (5) the use of intoxicating drinks. Naturally, the monks had to observe the remaining ten commandments in addition to these, which are a prohibition of: (6) eating at forbidden hours, (7) frequenting worldly amusements or spectacles, (8) using perfumes and ornaments, (9) sleeping on a raised couch, and (10) receiving gifts of money. In the course of time, these simple rules were elaborated and developed into a rather rigorous code of discipline, though it would seem that this was not done at the Buddha's command. In fact, it was over disputes as to what constituted proper discipline that the Buddhist church, even before the death of the Buddha, began to develop the seeds which soon grew into numerous schisms.

Of the Buddha's mode of life and activity during his long ministry of forty-five years, we know very little for certain. It seems that he spent nine months of the year wandering up and down the kingdoms of Magadha and Kosala (modern Bihar and Oudh), proclaiming his way of salvation to anyone who would listen. The remaining three months—that is, the rainy season—he spent with his disciples in one or another of his favorite places, such as Rajagriha in Veluvana or Sravāstī in Jetavana, instructing them in the fuller meaning of his doctrines. The latter place seems to have been a particular favorite spot, as may be seen from the fact that many sutras begin with the formula: "Thus I have heard; once the Master lived at Sravāstī in Jetavana, the Park of Anāthapindika." These gathering places became the centers from which the Buddhist disciples went out in ever-growing numbers. They went out not in groups, nor even in pairs as the disciples of Christ did, but individually so that the teaching might be spread more rapidly. In the course of time, these temporary abodes became permanent places of residence and formed the beginning of that chain of Buddhist monasteries which stretches from Ceylon in the south through central and eastern Asia to the Hokkaidō in northeastern Japan.

Apparently early in the Buddha’s ministry, he gained the sympathy of the ruling classes, and King Bimbisara of Magadha in particular seems to have been his patron. But it was not only because he gained the attention of the ruling classes that the Buddha’s religion spread so rapidly and without much opposition; rather, it seems that a remarkable spirit of tolerance prevailed in the India of that distant day, so that the Buddha and his disciples could go where they pleased and talk with whomever they met. Of course, there was some opposition from the Brahmins and the heretical sects which arose at the same time as Buddhism, but it was the kind of opposition that helps rather than hinders a new teaching.

The most serious obstacle to the new faith came not from the outside, but from within; the real enemies were those of his own spiritual household. Some sources claim that even as early as the ninth year of his ministry there were quarrels and divisions among his disciples. While it is difficult to distinguish between legend and real history in the early Buddhist records, it would seem that the Buddha had among his inner circle of disciples not only his St. John (Ananda) but also his Judas Iscariot (Devadatta). Devadatta was ambitious to become the head of the order after the Master’s death. It would seem, however, that while he did not become the head of the Buddhist order as a whole, he succeeded in gaining a considerable following, and so caused the first serious schism in the Buddhist ranks. As late as the seventh century A.D., there were monks who followed the discipline established by Devadatta, though some sources say that the rebellion was only of short duration.

Another difficulty that confronted the Buddha was the woman problem. What attitude should the new religion take toward the "weaker sex"? Buddhism, as we said, was above caste, but the sex problem seems to have been more troublesome. As a young man of twenty-nine, Siddhārtha, before he became the Buddha, had forsaken his wife and child, for family life was too much a life of earthly fetters for one who wished to walk in the path of holiness. It would seem, however, that afterward the Buddha returned to his home, not to resume his family relationships, but to proclaim his way of salvation to his wife and child and to his father and other relatives. We also read of women from all classes who heard his message gladly. And how could the Buddha deny salvation to women when he professed to proclaim a way of salvation for all sentient beings?

But while the new religion was to be a way of salvation for all, it did not mean that all were equally near the kingdom. And woman, just because she is woman, was regarded by the Buddha as being at least one step further removed than man. When the question arose as to whether she was to be admitted to the Buddhist order on equal terms with men, he hesitated and only with great reluctance did he finally yield the point. The following supposed conversation between him and his beloved disciple Ananda illustrates his attitude.

> “How should we behave toward a woman?” asks Ananda. 
> “Avoid the sight of her,” replies the Buddha.

> “O monks, do not look at a woman. If you meet a woman, do not look at her and be careful not to speak with her. If you do speak with her, say to yourself, ‘I am a monk; I must live in this corrupt world like an uncontaminated lotus blossom.’ Regard an elderly woman as your mother, one a little older than yourself as an elder sister, and a younger woman as your younger sister.” 

Naturally, in going from house to house with his begging bowl, the monk frequently came in contact with women, and so the regulations were rather strict. The monk was to cover his face with his outer garment and, with downcast eyes, was to receive what was offered to him and then take his departure, uttering a blessing but without looking at the generous giver. The scriptures are full of records of temptations overcome, but, alas, also of failures.

While Buddhist nuns have never been as numerous as the monks or played as prominent a part in the history of this religion, it is nevertheless true that woman has played a significant role in spreading the teachings of the Buddha, especially through her deeds of mercy and labors of love. In fact, woman has done a good deal more for Buddhism than Buddhism has done for woman; this especially seems to be the case when compared with what Christianity has done for her. The attitude of the Buddha toward woman was, of course, a very natural attitude for an Indian of that day to take, and it simply shows that he was, after all, very much a product of his own age and environment. The Buddhist apologist may say that it was an accommodation of his teachings to meet the needs of the times, and there is an element of truth in this, but the succeeding centuries in all Buddhist lands have proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that the religion which came to save all sentient beings and which undoubtedly has done much to exalt gentleness and kindness toward all creatures, has done comparatively little for woman as woman.

The Buddha ended his long ministry of about forty-five years, ripe in age and experience. He had been spending the rainy season near Vaisali when he became seriously ill. He recovered somewhat and continued on his way to Kusināgarā. Along the way, he stopped to dine with a disciple who gave him fat pork, which is said to have brought about his end soon after reaching Kusināgarā. Ananda, his favorite disciple, was at his side and wept bitterly when he saw the final hour approaching. The dying Buddha comforted him with these words:

> “Let it suffice, O Ananda; do not grieve, nor mourn. Have I not told you that man must endure separation from all that is dear and pleasant? How is it possible, O Ananda, that what is born, what comes into being, what is compounded and subject to change—that this does not end? It must be so. You, O Ananda, have long served the Perfect One with love and care, with kindness and goodness, without deceit and constantly, in heart, mouth, and hands. You have done well, O Ananda; be diligent, and soon you will be free from evil.”

And again he said,

> “It may be, O Ananda, that you harbor the thought that the doctrine has lost its master, and that there is no longer any master. You should not look at the matter in this way. The Law and the Discipline which I have taught and proclaimed—these are your master after my departure.”

He then made certain arrangements for the future, asked the monks three times whether any of them had any doubts regarding the teachings, and when all remained silent, he said,

> “O Disciples: I speak to you. Everything that comes into being is transient. Work diligently for your salvation.”

With these words on his lips, he passed away.

The funeral ceremonies are said to have continued for seven days; on the eighth day, the remains were cremated, and the ashes were divided among the various rulers and nobles who had become adherents of the new faith. A portion was given to the Sakyan clan, who buried the sacred remains and erected a stupa on the spot. It is likely this stupa that was discovered in 1898 by W. C. Peppé at Piprava in Tarai. This discovery gives the early Buddhist records and traditions an atmosphere of historical reality which, perhaps, they did not have before; and while we are still a long way from knowing the full facts of the Buddha’s life, no one can safely deny any longer the historical existence of the personality of Gautama Buddha.

If, after what we have said about the core of early Buddhism, the reader wonders how it was possible that such a doctrine could win such quick popularity and success, we might remark that the Buddha was himself often better than his logic; and, after all, it was the practical side of his teachings that appealed to the people of India. As a later Buddhist philosopher put it, “The doctrine in its logical fullness was a teaching only for the wise, not for fools,” but in practice, the Buddha preached the importance of conquering evil passions and overcoming the five hindrances: sensuality, ill-will, torpor of mind or body, worry, and wavering. “To have faith and good works, to renounce the pomp and vanities of life, to show kindness to every living thing, to seek salvation, to understand, and so finally to leave no second self behind to suffer again” in this life of suffering—these were the things which appealed to India, and especially to those who were sated with the things of life and were world-weary. ### SUCCESS OF NEW RELIGION

And while Nirvana meant total annihilation to some, we should never forget that life to many in India has never had the fascination and interest that it has for the Westerner, and the highest bliss to many could only be the bliss of non-existence. It is not merely ceasing to exist in this present bodily life—for then suicide would be the remedy—but ceasing to be bound to the Wheel of Life, “the dread cycle of birth, suffering, and death” on and on without end. It may be difficult for the Westerner, with his love and passion for life and self-expression, to understand this point of view; but in India, with its hot climate, its poverty, and its suffering, the pessimistic mood which looks upon life as a great evil rather than an achievable good seems natural. In fact, no matter what system of philosophy or religion dominates the field in India, this pessimistic mood seems to run through all of them. While the Buddha implemented some practical reforms and generally stood for a higher ethical life than the systems of his day, in the final analysis, his system was also consistent with the others. He, too, saw life as incurably evil and held that the only way of escape from this evil was to cut as much as possible the bonds which tie man to life. Even the bonds of love which tie a husband to his wife and a father to his child had to be cut if freedom is to be gained. So, while the Western mind of today may marvel at the rapid success of Gautama’s religion in India, it is not strange when understood in the light of its time and environment.

The Buddha’s religion was undoubtedly the best of its day. It delivered people from the fears and superstitions of a gross polytheism and demonology and taught kindness and the way of moderation to all. But even better than his religion was the founder himself. Strange as it may seem, he who apparently denied the existence of a true personality was one of the greatest personalities the world has seen. The unbiased student will have no hesitation in recognizing his essential sincerity in facing life’s deepest problems. Such sincerity, linked with real ability, was bound to make a great impression upon the life of India. The Buddha

# CHAPTER II

## DEVELOPMENT OF PRIMITIVE BUDDHISM INTO MAHĀYĀNA BUDDHISM

In the preceding chapter, we tried to give very briefly the circumstances under which Buddhism arose in India, as well as a concise statement of what may be regarded as the essence of Gautama’s teachings. We showed how Buddhism was a tremendous reduction of Brahmanism. Much of the metaphysical speculation about the Brahman—the One All—and the relation of the individual to it was brushed aside as vain mental gymnastics; for such problems, the Buddha held, were beyond the powers of the human mind. And many of the beliefs regarding spirits, gods, and demons—innumerable ones which filled the world of the common people—he denounced as mere ignorance and superstition. He went so far in his opposition to the views generally held by the masses that, in some of his sayings, he reached the extreme position of apparently denying the reality of the human self and, therefore, the possibility of a future personal existence. His attitude toward speculations on metaphysical problems, especially the problem regarding the underlying core of all reality, led him to a position which, for all practical purposes, was one of atheism, or at least agnosticism, so that he had little or nothing to say about God.

This is the negative side of the Buddha’s teachings. The positive side clusters around the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Way, or the Noble Eightfold Path. The essence of the teachings, in short, is this: Life is essentially pain and sorrow. Pain and sorrow have their roots in ignorance and our passionate cravings and desires. The taproot, as it were, of all our desires and cravings is the desire for self-

<summary>This chapter introduction outlines how early Buddhism rejected Brahmanical metaphysics and popular superstitions in favor of a focus on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. It characterizes the Buddha's early stance as practically atheistic or agnostic, emphasizing the removal of desire to end suffering.</summary>

<keywords>Gautama Buddha, Brahmanism, Mahāyāna Buddhism, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, metaphysics, atheism, agnosticism, religious evolution</keywords>

expression; indeed, the blossom and fruit on the tree of ignorance is the belief in the reality of the (empirical) self. Now it is possible to escape from this life of sorrow and pain—not by being saved into an eternal heaven by the gods, or by an almighty God, but by a slow process of self-cultivation and discipline until one attains enlightenment. In this state, one sees that all the things of our life are mere shadows and illusions and that our very self (at least the empirical self) has no real existence. This state of enlightenment is attained through obedience to the Middle Way, the Noble Eightfold Path of Right Views, Right Aspirations, Right Speech, Right Conduct, Right Mode of Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Rapture.

We also said that while these teachings about the non-reality of the self and the practical denial of the existence of God were the logical conclusion of Gautama’s main position and the truth as held by the Buddhist philosopher, they were never held in that extreme form by the general population of Buddhist believers. These people never gave up entirely the belief in the existence of God, or the gods, and the belief in the reality of the self and a future personal existence.

Now, in this chapter, we wish to trace very briefly the spread of Buddhism into neighboring countries and its development into what is known as Mahāyāna Buddhism, which, as we shall see as we go on, is often radically different from Gautama’s teachings in its attitude toward even the cardinal elements of religion.

## A. *The Buddhism of Asoka's Day*

When the founder of Buddhism died, about the year 480 B.C., the new religion had already won for itself a real place in India’s life. It was apparently popular with all classes of society, and the Buddha was favored by both high and low, with even kings and noblemen delighting to honor him and help further his cause. Just how far the new religion spread during the lifetime of its founder would be difficult to say. It would seem, however, that the region between the Ganges and the Himalayas, with Patna and Allaha-

However, it should not be supposed that everything went smoothly in the early Buddhist community. Not only were the Brahmins beginning to show active opposition to the new faith, but there were also conflicts within the Buddhist ranks. We have already spoken of Devadatta's rebellion during the lifetime of the Buddha. Immediately after the founder's death, we hear of the monk Subhadra addressing the grieving disciples with these rebellious words:

> "Brothers, stop your wailing and mourning. We are fortunate to be free of that great ascetic. He troubled us with his saying, 'this is proper and that is not proper.' Now we shall do what we please, and whatever does not suit us we shall not do."

These words show that the seeds of discord had long been sown and that they would soon spring up and bear fruit. It is not surprising, therefore, to read that when the first great council<note>1</note> of the Buddha's disciples was held at Rajagriha shortly after the founder's death—at which a part of the early canon was established (probably a part of the *Vinaya* and *Sūtra pitakas*)—there were many monks (five hundred according to one tradition), headed by Purāṇa, who did not accept the findings of the official body and so held a council of their own. And at a second great council, held at Vaisālī about one hundred years after the first council, we find that Buddhism was already beginning to be hopelessly divided, there being some eighteen or twenty different schools.

With these divisions in the ranks of Buddhism, it is not strange that the new religion found it difficult to cope with Brahmanism, which, under the stimulus provided by the heretical teachings of the day, was showing signs of new life. Then, in addition to this, a great calamity from the outside befell the home of Buddhism. Northern and central India were overrun by the armies of Alexander the Great; and amidst war and rumors of war, Buddhism found itself more restricted. Obviously, a religion which made all self-expression wrong and regarded even the killing of an insect as an accumulation of evil Karma, would not be

The glimpse that we get of the Buddhism of Asoka's day—and this is the important thing for our present purpose—would indicate that while Buddhism had undergone some changes since the days of its founder, it had not yet developed into what we now know as <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term>. It was, however, beginning to show tendencies along those lines.

We have already stated above that by the time of the great council of <term>Vaiśālī</term>, eighteen or twenty different schools had developed. These were, of course, minor differences; but in the course of time, the more radical of these schools became the core of the liberal wing of Buddhism which developed into <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term>; the more conservative wing corresponding roughly to what is meant today by the term <term>Hinayāna Buddhism</term>. The tendencies in Asoka's day towards these two great wings may be seen most clearly from the differences in regard to three main points.

In the first place, it seems clear that the old soul-theories rejected by the Buddha and his early followers were getting a stronger hold from year to year. If they did not come back into Buddhism in their exact old forms, the more liberal Buddhists were at least ready to make a compromise with the demands of non-Buddhist thought that the soul is a permanent reality. In the second place, Gautama, who had robbed the gods of their glory by teaching that they, too, were subject to the law of change and decay, was himself being glorified as God, or at least as the revelation of the Divine. Gradually the legends centering around his birth and ministry increased in their miraculous elements (see <term>Jātaka</term> stories) until Gautama the man was disappearing entirely, and we have a superhuman being far removed from the Gautama of history. Then, in the third place, the ideal of salvation which the Buddha had held out as the highest, namely, <term>Arhatship</term>, which meant primarily enlightenment for self, was giving way in the liberal wing to the more altruistic ideal of the <term>Bodhisattva</term> state, *i.e.* enlighten-

It can be seen that these three great changes are closely connected with one another, and that any one of them really implies the other two. For example, the change from <term>Gautama</term> the Great Teacher, or superman, to the divine <term>Buddha</term> implied that the historical personality known as <term>Siddhārtha</term>, or <term>Gautama</term>, had pre-existence. Such goodness and wisdom as he possessed were far "too perfect to have been worked out or developed in a single lifetime." Through ages upon ages, he had exercised himself in the perfection of wisdom and all virtues; therefore, there must have been a real continuity of personality. And especially since the <term>Buddha</term> was said to have been willing to be born again and again for the good of humanity (this is the ideal of the true <term>Bodhisattva</term>), it seems clear that he must have had a real personal identity from incarnation to incarnation—that is, an identity other than the old-fashioned <term>Karma</term> identity.

We do not mean to say that in <term>Asoka</term>'s day any one of these three characteristics of <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term>, as distinguished from <term>Hīnayāna Buddhism</term>, was fully developed, but even at that early date, these tendencies were beginning to manifest themselves. And the third great council of <term>Buddhism</term>, convened by <term>King Asoka</term>, may be regarded as marking the real parting of the ways: one great school remaining more or less true to original <term>Buddhism</term>, and the other diverging gradually until in many respects—even in fundamental things—it often ran quite counter to the way laid down by <term>Gautama</term>.<note>2</note>

## B. *The Rise of Mahāyāna Buddhism*

The period following <term>Asoka</term>'s day down to the first century B.C. is practically a closed book to historians. It would seem, however, that <term>Asoka</term>'s empire, in spite of its apparent greatness, soon fell to pieces. And with its ruin, <term>Buddhism</term> fell on hard times again. To the northwest of India, among the Parthians, the Yuetchi <note>An ancient nomadic people, also known as the Yuezhi.</note>, and the outer branches of the Sakyans, Buddhism apparently found a welcome. What factors worked the profound change—from the religion of the founder and of King Asoka’s day to the Buddhism which won the hearts of central and northeastern Asia during the first six or seven centuries of our era—remains a dark problem. Let us indicate a few of these profound changes.

We have already pointed out that, even in Asoka’s day (that is, in the third century B.C.), there were evidences of great changes coming over Buddhism. Those tendencies became stronger as time went on, and they in turn brought about other changes. Thus, we have not only a tendency to deify Gautama, but in such scriptures as the *Saddharma-Pundarika* and the Paradise *sūtras*, Gautama as a human being seems to have disappeared altogether and is replaced by the Eternal Buddha, or Buddhas. The historical Buddhas are many, each age or cycle having its own, but all these Buddhas are but manifestations of the Eternal Buddha, or Buddhas. Some scriptures speak of five historical Buddhas who preceded Gautama Buddha, others give long lists of names, and still others, without attempting to give their names, say that the Buddhas are millions and trillions; indeed, equal in number to the grains of sand on the banks of the sacred Ganges. “The blessed Buddhas equal in number the sand of the Ganga.”

Emphasis was placed on this by <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhists, for it is not quite true that the <term>Arhat</term> seeks salvation only for himself. His seeking salvation for himself was at least an example to others, and to that extent his efforts were for the good of all. It is true, however, that the older ideal of enlightenment implied that every man must be his own savior, whereas in <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhism the <term>Bodhisattva</term> through his own virtues helped save others. That is, his own merit is somehow transferred to others who put their trust in him. This is especially true of the <term>Bodhisattva</term> <term>Dharmakara</term> who finally became the Buddha <term>Amitābha</term> to whose <term>Western Paradise</term> go all those who in simple faith call upon his great name.

This change of ideal as to what constitutes the highest type of enlightenment and true <term>Buddhahood</term> also implied a radical change as to the way of salvation. <term>Gautama</term> had taught that man is bound by the <term>Karma</term> chain to such a degree that everyone must work out his own salvation through a long process of self-discipline. No one can really help another; not even the gods, for if there are gods they too are subject to the law of <term>Karma</term> and are bound to the <term>Wheel of Life</term> with its endless revolutions. But in certain books of <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhism man is not left to his own strength. He becomes an object of grace, especially the grace of the great Buddha <term>Amitābha</term> who saves by his might all those who believe in him and call upon his name. <term>Amitābha</term> has made the great vow to help all who desire help.

> “In obtaining <term>Buddhahood</term> I shall not enter into perfect enlightenment until all creatures of the Ten Regions (Universe) who wish sincerely to be born into my country or who practice tenfold meditations, shall have been born there.”

> “My mercy towards all you heaven- and earth-born creatures is deeper than the love of parents towards their children.”

A final great change which we must mention here as coming over <term>Buddhism</term> is the love for speculation on <term>metaphysical</term> problems. We said in the preceding chapter that <term>Gautama</term> considered the speculations of the <term>Brahmin</term> priests about the Brahman as an idle waste of time, and that he rather hesitated to express himself on <term>metaphysical</term> questions even when pressed by his disciples, but put such problems in his list of the <term>Great Indeterminates</term>. In spite of the protest of the founder against such things, his religion has become *par excellence* a religion which is couched in a <term>metaphysical</term> mold. Even the earlier <term>Hīnayāna</term> books contain much idle speculation on the problems of metaphysics, and to that extent are also a great change from what seems to have been <term>Gautama’s</term> attitude toward such problems.

Thus while the common ethical teachings as contained in the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>, the <term>Ten Commandments</term> and the elaboration of these in various systems of <term>Monk’s Rules</term>, may not have changed so seriously as the years went by, the great fundamental doctrines of religion—the God-idea, the doctrine of a future life, the conception as to the real nature of human life, and the way of <term>salvation</term>—all these seem to have undergone rather radical changes. Some scholars see in this great change the influence of Western thought, particularly Christian thought. It is, of course, quite possible that when Buddhism spread into the countries northwest of India, it came into contact with and was influenced by the religions of the West; just as it is reasonable to suppose that especially such heresies in Christianity as the <term>Gnostic</term> heresy were in part at least the result of the impact of Buddhism upon Christianity. At any rate, it seems safe to assume that there was a good deal of intercourse between the East and the West after the time of Alexander the Great, if not before. The careful historian will be slow to say what was possible and what was not in this matter of intercourse between the nations in ancient times.

The student of Indian <term>archaeology</term> is finding many traces of Western influence; especially is this true of northwestern India. There are a good many relics of pure Greek art dating probably from the first and second centuries B.C.; and still more numerous are the relics which show a blending of Greek and Indian art. Then, further, the results of recent discoveries in the lands northwest of India would go to show that the great religions of the world seem to have come into contact with one another on their march into China. <term>Asvaghosha</term>’s “Life of Buddha” (*<term>Buddha-Karita</term>*) and especially his “Awakening of Faith” (*<term>Kishinron</term>*) have exerted a tremendous influence on Northern <term>Buddhism</term>, and the latter work is regarded by many as the real foundation of <term>Mahāyāna</term> <term>Buddhism</term>. Now, we have said that nearly all traditions agree that <term>Asvaghosha</term> was originally a <term>Brahmin</term> scholar who was later converted to <term>Buddhism</term>. What is more natural than for this converted <term>Brahmin</term> scholar to bring much of his earlier training into <term>Buddhism</term>? Specifically, it is natural that he should give back to <term>Buddhism</term> those very fundamentals of religion which the human heart demands—namely, the belief in a Supreme Being and a future life for the individual. This is not to say that <term>Asvaghosha</term> introduced these as something new; for it would seem that even in the <term>Buddha</term>’s day, the common person had never given up their faith in some sort of god and their faith in a future life. We have also seen that as early as <term>Asoka</term>’s day, <term>Gautama</term> was being raised to the status of a god. But the contribution <term>Asvaghosha</term> made was that he gave these great beliefs a philosophical formulation and embodied them in the doctrines of the religion; through his writings, he handed them down to succeeding generations as the orthodox teachings of <term>Buddhism</term>.

<term>Asvaghosha</term>’s work was ably supplemented by the work of that second great saint of <term>Mahāyāna</term> <term>Buddhism</term>, <term>Nāgārjuna</term>, who was also a <term>Brahmin</term> converted to <term>Buddhism</term>. He probably lived in the second century A.D. and, as we have said above, laid the foundations for a number of the leading sects of Chinese and Japanese <term>Buddhism</term>. <term>Nāgārjuna</term> was followed by <term>Asanga</term> and <term>Vasubandhu</term>, who lived in the fifth century. Like their great predecessors, these two scholars were steeped in the thought of India and the speculations of <term>Brahmanism</term>. It is only natural that they should bring much from the religion in which they had been trained to their adopted religion. They added to the ever-growing complexity of the <term>Mahāyāna</term> school until it contained in its

# THE RISE OF MAHĀYĀNA

...vast embrace included not only what was in original <term>Buddhism</term>, but also everything that the founder of <term>Buddhism</term> had opposed. <term>Asanga</term> must especially be regarded as the foremost master in matters of religious compromise. Through his influence, <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term>—which was already quite inclusive—increasingly adopted the compromising attitude toward other religions that has been its strength and weakness ever since. On the one hand, it enabled <term>Buddhism</term> to adapt itself to any local conditions it happened to encounter. Not only were the leading <term>Shivaite</term> and <term>Vishnuite</term> gods of India admitted into the <term>Buddhist pantheon</term>, but the gods of all nations found easy entry; it was simple to regard these as various <term>Bodhisattvas</term> or as the different manifestations of the <term>Eternal Buddha</term>, or Buddhas. 

<term>Asanga</term> did not stop with enriching the <term>Buddhist pantheon</term>; he is also credited with incorporating much of the mystical <term>Tantric doctrine</term> from prevailing animism into this newer <term>Buddhism</term>. This doctrine still plays a major role today in the <term>Lamaism</term> of <term>Tibet</term> and the <term>Shingon</term> sect of Japanese <term>Buddhism</term>. This latter move enabled <term>Buddhism</term> to win converts among many semi-civilized tribes who knew nothing of the <term>Four Noble Truths</term> or the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>. The weakness of this compromising attitude lay in the fact that it filled the Buddhist tradition with all sorts of worthless material that is utterly unworthy of the religion proclaimed by <term>Gautama</term>. In its triumphant progress across Asia, <term>Buddhism</term> gathered up everything that crossed its path. Victory through compromise became the ruling principle, and this has remained the primary characteristic of <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> to this day. Buddhist scholars justify this on the grounds that truth must adapt itself to the diverse needs of humanity. However, we shall discuss this guiding principle of <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> more fully in a later chapter.

From what we have said, then, it seems quite clear that <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> originates primarily in Indian thought, though we do not wish to deny that it has been influenced by the West. The point we wish to make...

The queen had suffered hardships at the hands of her own son, and in her distress, she turned to the Buddha for consolation. She asked him why it was that she had to suffer such things because of her son. The Buddha replied in a manner consistent with the Indian doctrine of Karma—*namely*, that the queen was simply suffering for her own sins, committed either in her present life or in some previous existence. Then, in her despair, the queen cried out and said, “Is there no escape from this dreadful chain of Karma?” “Not in India,” replied the Buddha, “but there is a Western Buddha Field where one does not have to atone for all one’s sins.” Whether this is a true story or not, it remains an ancient story, and it shows that the doctrine of the forgiveness of sin was known quite early in Buddhism, though it was recognized as belonging to the Western Buddha Field.

If the Buddha himself spoke these words, it is possible, as Professor Lloyd has suggested, that he knew something about the religion of the Old Testament through the prophets of the Exile. If it is a later story, then it is possible that this doctrine entered Buddhism after the conquest of Alexander the Great. And if we place it as late as the first century <term>A.D.</term> (for which there is good reason), then it may be connected with Christian influences. If it is neither Jewish nor Christian in origin, there still remains the possibility of it coming from the Near West, specifically from Persia, and particularly from the Mithras cult. We realize, of course, that the doctrine of salvation by divine grace is found also in the popular Vishnu and Siva schools of Hinduism; however, whether it existed in these before it entered Buddhism, and if so, whether it was Indian in origin, remains a problem.

### C. *The Spread of Buddhism through China*

Eitel claims that Buddhist missionaries accompanied merchant caravans into China as early as the days of King Asoka—that is, in the middle of the third century *B.C.* Others claim that the first century *B.C.* saw the first Buddhist efforts in that country, but even that seems quite doubtful. It is, however, safe to say that Buddhism did reach China during the first century *A.D.* We are told that in the year 61 *A.D.*, the Emperor Ming-ti had a dream. For several nights in succession, he had a vision of a man standing before him in golden clothing, holding a bow and arrows in his hands and pointing to the West. The emperor was much moved by the vision and so sent eighteen men to the West to seek the "True Man" whom he had seen in his dream. The messengers, we are told, traveled as far as the land of the *Getæ* bordering on India when they met two monks coming through the mountain pass, leading a white horse laden with scriptures and images. The messengers returned to the court with these two monks, where the strangers were well received and given lodging in a monastery which exists to this day: namely, the celebrated Pomash, or White Horse Monastery. The two monks died a few years later, and the only memorial they left behind, it would seem, was the famous scripture of the Forty-Two Sections, which has remained to this day one of the most popular writings of Chinese and Japanese Buddhism.

The legend that St. Thomas reached India is not completely without foundation; furthermore, it is true that the Jews of the Diaspora seem to have had their easternmost settlement in a colony at Kaifong-fu <note>Modern Kaifeng, Henan province.</note> in Honan, China, at this time. (This colony of Jews has survived to our day and is only now disappearing.) Thus, it was quite possible that Emperor Ming-ti could have known something about the "True Man" who had appeared in Palestine. But, of course, the mere possibility of such an acquaintance is a very slender thread on which to hang any claim that Christianity reached China as early as the sixties of the first century. And the further claim that the *sūtra* of the *Forty-Two Sections* has Christian elements is equally weak, as all advanced religions have a great many things in common, so that similarity, as we said before, does not prove dependence.

Whatever these monks were, their influence seems to have been very slight regarding the establishment of either Buddhism or Christianity in China. Between 76–88 A.D., a number of Buddhist books were brought into China from Turkestan, but their influence is also very difficult to trace. Not until 147 A.D. did Buddhism make a real beginning in that land. The Buddhism which won China at first did not come directly from India itself, but largely from the new home of Buddhism among the Scythians and Parthians. (After the fourth century, the connection between India and China seems to have been more direct, with Indians coming to China in great numbers and Chinese pilgrims visiting the birthplace of their new religion.) <term>Asvaghosha</term> and <term>Nāgārjuna</term> had already done their great work in giving Buddhism a new turn. And their work had been advanced by others, so that ideas which they held only in their earliest stages had reached full fruition. The progress of Buddhism in China was not very rapid at first. The first century and a half or more was a period of importation and translation of scriptures. In fact, China seems to have been flooded with books; so that the Emperor Hweiti in 306 <term>A.D.</term>, wishing to free himself of this foreign importation, ordered a great many books to be burned, and for many years the Chinese were forbidden by imperial edict to become Buddhist monks. But after 335 <term>A.D.</term> matters took a turn for the better. The people were allowed to take monastic vows, and many began to give the new religion serious attention. The thing that, perhaps, more than any other won the Chinese to Buddhism was the religion's attitude towards the deep-rooted ancestor worship. Buddhism did not openly antagonize ancestor worship; in fact, it enriched it by a distinct contribution, for it offered the Chinese a way of raising the dead to the exalted position of Buddhas. Ancestors should not only be revered, but they should be worshipped as Buddhas. Then of course Buddhism also satisfied the religious longings better than Confucianism was doing. Especially did the Amitābha faith meet a great need in a land where religion was entirely too much a matter of mere human relationships. Buddhism went, of course, to the other extreme; but even so it filled a great need in the heart of the Chinese people, and from the fourth century on became very popular.

Naturally, when Buddhism began to be really rooted in the hearts of the people, they became interested in the origins of their adopted religion and in the home of its founder. He found Buddhism in a flourishing condition in the countries northwest of India, but when he reached the cradle of Buddhism, he found things in a state of decay. Fah-hian's studies in the field of Buddhism's beginnings soon showed him that the Buddhism which had been introduced into China differed rather widely from the Buddhism of India itself. Under the Ts'in dynasty in 401 A.D., Kumārajīva was brought from Tibet as a prisoner to Sin-an-fu, China. His great work was the translation of numerous books—many of them of purely Indian origin. From these translations and studies, it became increasingly evident that the Buddhism imported into China by the great Anshikao and Lokaraksha in 147 A.D. was not the pure Buddhism of the founder. This discovery gave rise to great discussions and divisions in the ranks of Buddhism and thus weakened the new religion in its conflict with Confucianism and Taoism. But these discussions and divisions, in the long run, led to further developments of the new religion and to the formation of some of the great sects which later were transplanted to Japan, where they are active to this day.

It is from this time on that Chinese Buddhism began to take up many of the elements of Confucianism, Taoism, and the minor local cults. From Confucianism, Buddhism adopted much which made its ethical teachings more practical and suited to the tastes of the Chinese. The growing popularity of Buddhism in China during the fifth century led to a bitter religious controversy with the Confucianists and scholars, so that finally the king of the Wei dynasty in the north was persuaded to issue an edict calling for the destruction of Buddhist books and images. But by 451 <term>A.D.</term>, a king of the same dynasty authorized the establishment of one Buddhist temple in every city of his dominion, and forty to fifty inhabitants of each place were permitted to become monks or priests. This friendliness on the part of the rulers made China a safe place of refuge for the Buddhists of India, who were being persecuted by their Brahmin rivals. Thus, one account has it that at the beginning of the sixth century, the number of Indian refugees in China was more than 6,000. This, in turn, helped raise the prestige of Buddhism, as may be seen from the statistics of that period, which give the number of Buddhist temples as more than 13,000.

The following interview with the Chinese Emperor <term>Liang Wuti</term>, taken from Edkins’ *Chinese Buddhism*, illustrates the temper of the man and the characteristics of his true followers:

When <term>Bodhidharma</term> lived at Nanking, the emperor came to him one day and said, “Since my accession to the throne, I have been constantly building temples, transcribing sacred books, and admitting new monks to take their vows. How much merit should I be considered to have accumulated?” The reply was, “None.” The emperor asked: “And why no merit?” The patriarch replied: “All this is but the insignificant effect of an imperfect cause, not complete in itself. It is the shadow that follows the substance and is without real existence.” The emperor asked: “Then what is true merit?” The patriarch replied: “It consists in purity and enlightenment, depth and completeness, and in being absorbed in thought while surrounded by emptiness and stillness. Merit such as this cannot be sought by worldly means.” The emperor asked: “Which is the most important of the holy doctrines?” The patriarch replied: “Where all is emptiness, nothing can be called ‘holy’ (<term>sheng</term>).” The emperor asked: “Who is it that replies to me in this way?” The patriarch replied: “I do not know.”

Some time after this interview, the emperor became a Buddhist monk, much to the disgust of the Confucianists.

According to the *History of the Wei Dynasty*, says Edkins, the number of Buddhist monks and priests around this time reached 2,000,000 and the number of temples was 30,000. This seems to be an exaggeration, but it shows that Buddhism was exceedingly popular. ...centuries show that <term>Buddhism</term> continued to increase at the expense of its rivals. In 714 AD, for example, we are told that 12,000 monks and nuns were compelled to return to secular life; and the edict against Buddhists issued by Emperor <term>Wu-tsung</term> in 845 AD is said to have led to the destruction of 4,600 monasteries and 40,000 smaller buildings. Again, in the first half of the tenth century, we hear of persecutions which closed 30,000 temples. But none of these or similar oppressions, many of which were purely local, were sufficient to check <term>Buddhism</term> in China; for, after all, it satisfied the spiritual needs of the people better than <term>Confucianism</term> and <term>Taoism</term> could, and so the Buddhists, though frequently oppressed and persecuted, always found their way back to favor and prosperity.

We may say, however, that in these oppressions and persecutions we have an indication of China’s chief objection to the religion of the Buddha. We said above that <term>Buddhism</term> did not openly oppose <term>ancestor worship</term> and that it even enriched it by converting ancestors into Buddhas who are truly worthy of reverence and worship. But, after all, the highest ideal of life for the Buddhist is that of the monk or nun who withdraws from active life and so becomes an economic loss, and by their vows of celibacy, they sever the very heart of <term>ancestor worship</term>. The Chinese are too practical and matter-of-fact a people to accept the monk and the nun as the highest type of manhood and womanhood, and they are especially too deeply devoted to the ancestor cult to accept <term>Buddhism</term> without serious questions; for the sin above all other sins in the eyes of a faithful son of China is the sin of having no children. <term>Ancestor worship</term> demands an unbroken line of descendants, and if there are no children through legal marriage, "either the adoption of a son or polygamy becomes an ethical necessity." And so, however much <term>Buddhism</term> may flatter the Chinese by converting ancestors into Buddhas, or however much it may satisfy other religious

With China as a center, <term>Buddhism</term> spread in several directions—primarily, however, in its <term>Mahāyāna</term> form. During the seventh century, it reached Tibet and developed there into what is now known as <term>Lamaism</term>. <term>Lamaism</term>, during the time of the great Mongolian conqueror <term>Kublai Khan</term>, became the religion of Mongolia and also spread back into China proper, thus adding one more current to the ever-swelling stream of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>. Before this, however—specifically during the latter part of the fourth century—<term>Buddhism</term> had reached Korea. At this time, there was really no unified Korea as we know it today; instead, it was divided into the three small independent kingdoms of <term>Koma</term> (<term>Ko-gur-yu</term>), <term>Kudara</term> (<term>Pakche</term>), and <term>Shiragi</term> (<term>Silla</term>), with some small buffer states between the latter two. In 372 AD, a priest from <term>Sin-an-fu</term>, China, reached <term>Koma</term>. An Indian priest named <term>Masananda</term> came to <term>Kudara</term> from eastern China in 384 AD. And <term>Shiragi</term> received its first Buddhist missionary from <term>Koma</term> in 424 AD. We know very little about the nature of Korean Buddhism in those early days. It seems, however, that the new religion quickly gained influence among the upper classes and enjoyed the protection of the royal families; for it was the king of <term>Kudara</term>, King <term>Seimei</term>, who in the year 552 AD sent <term>Buddhism</term> across the narrow channel that separates Korea from Japan when he sent his Buddhist mission to the emperor of Japan.

With these few scattered remarks, we must leave Chinese <term>Buddhism</term>. The point to remember, however, is that Chinese <term>Buddhism</term> differed quite widely from the religion of <term>Gautama</term> from the very beginning. During its long history in that country and its conflict with <term>Confucianism</term>, <term>Taoism</term>, and minor local cults—and later through the direct influx of Indian thought into China—<term>Buddhism</term> adopted more and more elements that were radically different from primitive <term>Buddhism</term>. In short, in China, <term>Buddhism</term> became a conglomerate system of beliefs and

# CHAPTER III

## DEVELOPMENTS OF BUDDHISM IN JAPAN

### A. *Introduction of Buddhism into Japan*

In the last chapter, we tried to show briefly the development of primitive Buddhism into Mahāyāna Buddhism. We saw that Buddhism, in its spread northward from India and in its triumphant march across China and Korea, underwent some radical changes—not only in minor points, but in the very fundamentals of religion. And so, when Buddhism reached Japan in the middle of the sixth century AD, it was no longer the pure religion of the founder. It was not the Buddhism of the Pali scriptures or the religion which Western scholars usually describe when they speak of Buddhism; rather, it was that expanded and much-modified religion which we know as Mahāyāna Buddhism. A part of the original Indian stream and a great many later streams from Hinduism reached Japan through China; consequently, Japanese Buddhism does go back to India, but the stream had been enlarged by many tributaries from the local cults and religions of other countries. These were so well mingled with one another that it is impossible to say exactly what was Buddhist and what was not.

Now, in this chapter, we shall trace the flow of this great stream of many waters across Japanese life. We shall see as we go on that in Japan, too, it was fed by other streams—principally by that mighty current of the native Shintō. This modified Buddhism so seriously after its union with it at the beginning of the ninth century that the resulting stream was known for many centuries as <term>Ryōbu-Shintō</term>, or Two-sided Shintō.

As we saw at the end of the last chapter, Buddhism reached Korea from China during the second half of the fourth century A.D.; from Korea, it crossed the narrow channel that separates the peninsula from the island empire of Japan. Japan and Korea had been aware of one another for many years. The Japanese claim that as early as 32 B.C., the small province of Mimana (or Kara) sought Japan's protection against the oppression of the kingdom of Shiragi, and for several centuries it remained a type of dependency of the Japanese Emperor. Then, in the year 202 A.D., the great Japanese heroine, Empress Jingō, led her famous expedition to Korea and apparently reduced the kingdom of Shiragi to a Japanese dependency. Empress Jingō's son and successor, Ōjin Tennō—later deified as the God of War—is supposed to have continued this authority over southern Korea, and during his reign, there was likely a vital connection between the two countries. This is a point that some modern imperialistic Japanese thinkers love to emphasize, and it was used by some as an argument to justify Japan's annexation of Korea.

However, Japan’s hold on Korea was never very firm. As we have said, by the time Buddhism reached Korea in the fourth century, the peninsula was occupied by three small independent kingdoms. This was also the political situation about one hundred and fifty years later when, in 552 <note>1</note> A.D., King Seimei of Kudara sent a gold and copper image of Buddha to the Emperor of Japan. This was probably an image of the Buddha *Amitābha* and not of *Gautama*. Along with it, he sent Buddhist books and a letter in which he praised the great merit of Buddhism. In fact, this was only one of many missions sent by this king. It seems that the three Korean kingdoms were always more or less at war with one another, and it is quite likely that the King of Kudara was moved by political considerations rather than religious ones when he recommended his religion to the Japanese court. Gaining the friendship of this island empire would be a real advantage in his conflicts with his rivals; and this seemed all the more

The story of how these Buddhist beginnings were received is an interesting one. The emperor of Japan was apparently greatly pleased with these gifts, for it must be remembered that images and books were exceedingly rare among the simple Japanese of that early day. He said to the messengers, “I have never heard such sublime teachings, yet I myself dare not decide whether to accept this doctrine or not.” The matter was submitted to the council of his vassals, and one Soga no Iname replied, “Western countries all believe this doctrine, and why should not we?” But two other ministers of a more conservative disposition said, in substance, “We have our own gods, and if we now change and worship the gods of other nations, we are in danger of bringing the wrath of our gods upon our heads.” The image was turned over to Soga with the instruction that he was to worship the new god and give the new religion a test; for like the Athenians of old, the Japanese did not dare run the risk of leaving any god without an altar, even though they already had myriads of their own. Soga accordingly converted his own house into a temple, set up the new image, and began the new cult.

But soon after this introduction of the new god, a terrible pestilence afflicted the land, and the conservative party was not slow to see the wrath of their native gods in this event. Soga’s temple was burned to the ground, and the Buddhist image was thrown into a canal of Naniwa (Osaka). The Buddhist god was, however, to have his turn and show what he could do. A great fire suddenly destroyed the great hall of the imperial residence, and, of course, this could have but one meaning. Thus we see how trifling and random occurrences may play a great part in momentous issues. These were not the only or even the main determining factors, however, for in the long run, the success of Buddhism in Japan was due to its real superiority over the native Shintō faith.

Before we proceed with a narrative of the development of Buddhism in Japan from these small beginnings, it may be well to pause a moment and briefly describe what the native Shintō was and what the conditions of Japan were in general at this time; for the successful entrance of a religion into a country depends more or less upon the religious, social, political, and intellectual condition of the people to be won to the new faith.

The population at this time consisted possibly of about two million people—hunters, fishermen, and farmers, divided into many different clans. The center of population was in the Osaka-Kyoto region, and the dominant tribe, whose head was the Mikado, exercised authority over a considerable portion of the main island, though the outlying portions<note>2</note>, especially in the north, were still in the hands of the aboriginal Ainus. The people, though very simple in their manner of life, were intellectually well-gifted and later proved to be endowed with extraordinary aesthetic ability. Their religion was Shintō<note>3</note>—The Way of the Gods. This religion was and is, in some of its phases even today, an animistic and polytheistic nature worship with a strong mixture of ancestor worship<note>4</note>. The forces of nature are personified and humanized, while the heroes and ancestors, especially those of the royal family, are deified<note>5</note>. The soul of Shintō is reverence and implicit obedience to the Mikado; and religion and patriotism are made one. *Yamato Damashii*<note>6</note>, The Spirit of Japan, is largely the product of this religion, and it has played a great part in the conquest, unification, and civilization of the entire country. Japan is regarded by Shintō as the sacred land of the gods; and every

The rising tide of Japanese civilization, quickened as it was by the introduction of new ideas from the continent, made Shintō more and more inadequate, and Japan was on the whole ready for the new and more elaborate faith of Buddhism.

So much for a summary of conditions which prevailed in Japan when Buddhism was first introduced. It was therefore comparatively easy for the new religion to get a firm hold, especially upon the more progressive element. Its success was, however, not due simply to its superiority as a religion, but even more to the fact that it was the vehicle of a higher civilization, namely, the Chinese civilization from whose fountains Japan has ever drunk deeply even up to almost the present day. We have a modern parallel in what is happening in Korea today. The success of Christianity in that land is due in some measure at least to the fact that it is the vehicle of western civilization and not simply because it is a superior religion.

Soon after the incidents connected with the introduction of Buddhism related above, the ruler of Japan, more anxious for the concrete things of Korean and Chinese civilizations than for the new religion, sent a message to the king of Kudara in which he asked the king to send no more Buddhist priests and images, but to supply him with physicians, apothecaries, soothsayers, almanac makers and artisans of one sort and another. The priests, books and images, however, continued to come together with the things specially asked for. This influx of so many new things had very much the same effect that the influx of western things has had in our own day; it caused a temporary upheaval and led to much internal strife and war. But it was not long till Buddhism had won for itself a place in the heart of members of the ruling family and thus secured protection. Empress Suiko (593–628 <term>A.D.</term>) became an ardent Buddhist, giving over the affairs of state to the Crown Prince Mumayado

More important than this was the fact that the Crown Prince himself embraced the new religion and managed the affairs of state in such a way that everything encouraged the spread of Buddhism. In the so-called Constitution of Seventeen Articles he issued, he explicitly ordered his people to pay all due respect to the new religion. He "devoted all his energies to importing scholars, priests, architects, woodcarvers, bronze-founders, clay modelers, masons, gilders, tile-makers, and weavers from Korea; in short, all the skilled artisans whose work was involved in creating and installing a great Buddhist temple such as were already known in the peninsula kingdom." In fact, some scholars believe that the prince was a talented artist himself and that the famous Hōryūji temple near Nara, built under his direction, contains art treasures created by his own hands. It is therefore not at all strange that by the end of Empress Suiko's reign (628 AD), there were already 46 temples in existence, and 816 priests and 569 nuns had been consecrated. Not only did Buddhist missionaries pour in from Korea and China, but Japanese people were beginning to go in greater and greater numbers to the continent to study at the great centers of religion and culture, returning with new learning and enthusiasm for the Buddhist faith.

The influence of this close contact with the more advanced continental civilization on Japanese culture can hardly be overstated. In a relatively short time, this simple island people adopted the fruits of centuries of Chinese culture and made it their own. In fact, the adoption of Western culture in our own time, which has astonished the world, is no more remarkable than what happened in the history of this people during the seventh century. With the founding of the great monastery of Hōryūji early in the seventh century, a marvelous development of the fine arts began, which in a few decades resulted in the production of world masterpieces; for art critics claim that the famous

The great reform, beginning in 645 <term>A.D.</term> and continuing through the rest of the century, known as the Taikwa Reforms, changed the ruler of Japan from what was little better than a tribal chief into a real monarch of an empire.⁸ In short, we might say that the impact of Chinese culture, fostered largely by Buddhists, changed a simple, uneducated people into a people of culture and refinement, at least among the upper classes.

### B. *Rise of the Nara Sects*

It is a rather significant fact that Buddhism was firmly rooted in Japan before any sectarian differences were introduced. For a period of about seventy years, wise missionaries were content with teaching the general tenets of their faith. Perhaps this was due to the fact that the people of Japan were not really intellectually prepared to appreciate the fine points of sectarian speculations and were more interested in the external trappings of religion and the simpler teachings contained in the moral maxims and precepts more or less common to all the sects. Finally, however, sectarian differences made their appearance early in the seventh century.

Curiously enough, the first sect to be introduced was the highly metaphysical Sanron Sect (<term>Mādhyamika</term> school, founded originally by Nāgārjuna). It w<unclear>a</unclear>s brought in from China in the year 625 by Ekwan. Its headquarters was the famous Hōryūji near Nara mentioned above. The Sanron sect belongs to what is called the Provisional⁹ <term>Mahāyāna</term> school. Starting with the <term>Hinayāna</term> position of the non-reality of the ego, it carries the principle of negation to the point at which it denies the reality of all phenomenal ex-

Concurrent with the establishment of the Sanron was that of the Jōjitsu Sect (Satya-siddhi-sastra Sect). This sect never gained a real independent existence but was propagated in conjunction with the Sanron. It belongs to the Hīnayāna school and represents a rather strong subjective idealism in its doctrines.

The third sect to find its way into Japan was the Hossō (Dharma-lakshana Sect, *i.e.*, the Yoga school). It was brought over from China by Dōsho, probably about the middle of the seventh century, though some would place it as early as 625. The Hossō, like the Sanron, belongs to the Provisional Mahāyāna school. This is the sect which, in the person of Gyōgi Bosatsu during the eighth century, initiated that syncretic movement by which the claims of the native Shintō and the new religion were reconciled. We shall speak of this later.

The Kusha Sect (Abhidharma-kosa-sastra Sect) was the fourth to be established in Japan, being introduced in 658 by two Japanese priests who had studied in China, namely, Chitsu and Chitatsu. This sect is usually regarded as the best representative of the Hīnayāna school of Buddhism. The center of its teachings is an elaborate psychological analysis through which it seeks to account for the complexity of the phenomenal world while simultaneously denying the reality of the ego.

About three-quarters of a century passed before the fifth Chinese sect was introduced. This was the Kegon (Avatamsaka-sūtra Sect) brought over in 736. The Kegon was the first sect of the true Mahāyāna school, which later was to be the type<note>10</note> of Buddhism which really won over Japan. Though this sect has now practically disappeared, it has exerted a great influence upon other sects through its chief scripture, the Kegonkyō (Avatamsaka-sūtra), which has always been popular with Buddhist scholars as one of the chief sources of Mahāyāna philosophy.

In fact, it was likely these practical moral teachings, rather than the philosophical speculations of the other sects, that helped Japan embrace the religion of the Buddha so quickly. The Ritsu belongs to the Hīnayāna school. Like the other Hīnayāna sects, it has disappeared, but its teachings have been largely absorbed by the existing Mahāyāna sects and continue to exert an influence in that way.

Today, these six sects are frequently referred to as the Six Sects of Nara to distinguish them from the later Kyoto and Kamakura sects. They are called Nara sects because they reached their highest development in and around Nara during the Nara Epoch (710–794). The remarkable progress Japan made during the seventh century, which was mentioned earlier, continued through the eighth. In fact, we may say that the eighth century marks one of the great peaks of Japanese history. Many significant aspects of old Japan originated during this time. For example, Nara, which became the capital of the realm in 710, was the first real city Japan had until then. It was an impressive city even when compared with the great cities of other lands; some claim its population reached over 500,000. Here, or in the immediate vicinity, many noble Buddhist buildings could be found, filled with art treasures, some of which have survived to our own time to be the wonder of experts. It was during the Nara epoch, specifically in 749, that the enormous Nara Daibutsu—the world's largest bronze statue—was cast. It stands 53 feet high, and its creation required 500 Japanese pounds (about 666 lbs.) of gold, 16,827 pounds of tin, 1,954 pounds of mercury, and 986,180 pounds of copper, along with some lead. The famous Tōdaiji Bell, which is over 13 feet high and weighs 40 tons, <note>11</note> belongs to this century. [Historians] call this age the "Golden Age of Poetry," for during this period the *Manyōshū*, or "Collection of Myriad Leaves," was written, containing more than 4,000 pieces, mostly short poems (*Tanka*) but also some longer ones (*Nagauta*).

All this splendor of culture and civilization was largely the work, either directly or indirectly, of Buddhism and shows the power and influence the new religion had attained by this time. However, it must not be supposed that the common people of the land had been won over completely to the new faith. This outward splendor and magnificence naturally made a very strong appeal to the imagination; but, after all, deep down in the heart of the average man, there was still a strong loyalty to the traditions of the native cults, and he was therefore always ready to blame the gods of the new religion for the misfortunes that befell him or the nation from time to time. This was the case even during the Nara Epoch. A great epidemic of smallpox afflicted the realm. Introduced from Korea into the southern island of Kyūshū, it spread northward until, in 735, it began to devastate even the aristocratic circles in the capital itself. Offerings were made at the various temples by priests and their royal patrons, but all seemed to be of no avail. It was at this time that the Emperor Shōmu contemplated the building of the great Nara Daibutsu. However, before he dared to show his confidence in the Buddhas in such an open manner, he had to find a way to appease the native deities and their devotees. Accordingly, he sent the illustrious Gyōgi Bosatsu, a grandson of a Korean immigrant, to the Ise shrines to inquire of the Sun Goddess what she thought of the emperor's project. Gyōgi remained at the shrine for a week and then returned to Nara with a favorable answer, namely, that the Sun Goddess had declared herself to be identical with the Buddha in whose honor the statue was to be built. A few nights later, the emperor himself is said to have had a dream in which the Sun Goddess said to him, "The Sun is Biroshana." (Biroshana is the Japanese transliteration for Vairochana). This marks the beginning of that syncretistic movement so successfully

carried out during the ninth century by Dengyō Daishi and especially by Kōbō Daishi, which resulted in reconciling the claims of the two religions in the hearts of the people. It should, however, be added that it also resulted in perverting things, and so in the long run really did more harm than good, as every unprincipled compromise must do.

The influence of Buddhism during the Nara period was great, not only in the spheres mentioned above, but it extended perhaps even more into the field of politics and state affairs. This is only natural, for it must be remembered that Buddhism gained its first and chief hold on the upper and ruling classes rather than upon the common people. Frequently this influence was for the good, as might be expected because the men who had studied in China, or under Chinese priests in Japan, were best acquainted with politics and matters of government as conducted on the continent.<note>13</note> This superior knowledge gave these men a natural place as advisers to the court and other officials. But the temptations which this influence gave to the disciples of Buddha were more than could be endured, and it was not long, therefore, until the monks and priests became more interested in the “things that are Caesar’s” than in their true mission. In fact, things reached such a state that during the reign of Empress Shōtoku (765–770) a Buddhist monk, Dōkyō, had managed to make himself the most powerful subject in the land and was even planning to place himself upon the imperial throne. In this, however, he did not succeed; and while the ambitious clergy continued to meddle in such things, the time was fast approaching when not only the guilty were to suffer for their sins, but the whole Buddhist world which had centered around the old capital of Nara—indeed, Nara itself—was soon to wane in importance and yield its place to another.

### *C.  The Kyōto Sects*

In the year 782, Emperor Kwammu succeeded to the throne. He must have been a man of daring and originality, for it

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Emperor Kwammu's efforts to distance the imperial government from the political meddling of the Nara Buddhist sects, leading to the establishment of Kyoto as the new capital and the introduction of new Buddhist traditions from China.</meta>

STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM

It was he who cut the Gordian knot of the political tangle of his day by simply abandoning Nara to the Buddhists and their schemes and setting up his capital first at Nagaoka and then at a place he significantly called Heian (Peace), known today as Kyōto. This took place between 784 and 793, and here at Kyōto the capital of the empire remained for almost 1100 years—specifically until 1868, when the late Emperor Meiji removed his seat of government to Tōkyō. Kyōto soon overshadowed Nara and became indeed one of the world's greatest centers of culture. The decline of Nara apparently had a disastrous effect upon the Buddhist sects entrenched there, for it must be remembered that a Japanese person, true to the fundamental principle of his native Shintō, is first a patriot and then a person of religion. When the two conflict, religion is likely to be the loser. To this day, this seems to be a characteristic of the average Japanese person. Religion is presented by its advocates as something good for the welfare of the state, and by those who oppose it, it is opposed on the grounds that it is harmful to the state. The greatest obstacle which Christianity has met in Japan is the claim on the part of its enemies that it undermines the state. Even a scholar in Japan is very slow to follow where truth would lead him if it should seem to conflict with the sacred traditions of the nation.

Now, this running away from the meddling of the Nara sects did not mean that Emperor Kwammu had turned his back on Buddhism as a religion. He simply wanted the monks to keep their proper place and to leave for Caesar the things that belong to Caesar. But to make sure that he was getting the right type of religious leaders, he sent a promising young man directly to China to bring back a purer religion which would serve in spiritual matters and leave the affairs of state in his own hands. This young man was Saichō, better known as Dengyō Daishi, the founder of the powerful Tendai sect in Japan. He was followed a few months later by the equally famous Kūkai, known best by his posthumous title Kōbō Daishi, the founder of the other powerful sect of this period, the Shingon Sect. These two, Dengyō

## DENGYŌ AND TENDAI SECT

Dengyō Daishi and Kōbō Daishi are the great names in Japanese Buddhism of the ninth century; and the two sects which they founded have occupied a prominent place in Japanese history down to the present day.

1. *Dengyō Daishi and Tendai.* — The Tendai sect may be characterized as the harmonizing, comprehensive sect. That is, Tendai tries to reconcile all the contradictions of the extensive Mahāyāna and Hinayāna scriptures as being the direct teachings of the founder of Buddhism. It was Chi K'ai, the founder of the Tendai (Chinese, T'ien-t'ai) sect in China, who worked out an elaborate harmonizing <note>14</note> scheme by which he tried to show how every Buddhist scripture has its own particular place and is the direct or indirect product of S'akyamuni's mind. Humanity has varied needs and these needs must be met in different ways. Thus, every scripture has its truth, each providing its own unique perspective. This irenic attitude was adopted by Chi K'ai in the face of competing sects, each of which seemed to proclaim a different system. There were, for example, in China at that time the old Abhidharma sects which tried to define all truth with an Aristotelian precision of detail. On the other hand, the Pure Land sects were teaching that all attempts at salvation through knowledge of detailed truth were in vain and that there was only one way, namely, the way of faith in the grace of Amitābha. And still another group of sects were the contemplative traditions which held that neither book learning nor a pious trust in Amitābha saved a person, but that quiet meditation and abstract contemplation were the only true way. Now, in the face of these competing schools, the comprehensive Tendai sect arose and it included *all* ways, rejecting none. Thus, a Tendai disciple may find salvation through philosophical wisdom; or, rejecting the great mass of doctrines contained in the extensive scriptures, he may select merely the comforting doctrine of salvation through faith in Amitābha's great name. Or, again, he may reject all book learning and all simple faith and work out his own salvation through silent meditation and abstract contemplation, as do the contemplative sects.

The broad-minded Tendai philosopher, however, would try to hold to the truth in every way, though as a matter of fact very few ever attained this supposedly lofty ideal. After all, there was developed what we might call an orthodox Tendai system which did reject some things and included others as characteristic Tendai teachings. Thus, while theoretically Tendai accepted all scriptures as of equal value, Tendai teachers looked upon the *Saddharma-Pundarīka-sūtra* with special reverence. This sutra, together with the *Mahāprajna-pāramitā-sūtra*, contains, after all, the loftiest teachings of S'akyamuni; and while the teachings of other scriptures are not false, they must be regarded as incomplete and only provisional. As we have said in the preceding chapter, the *Saddharma-Pundarīka* breathes a Buddhism quite different from the Buddhism of S'akyamuni. S'akyamuni himself is regarded as but one of the manifestations of the Eternal Buddha, or Buddhas. The identification of the historical manifestation with the Eternal Buddha is the great revelation of this scripture. To know this and to trust in this knowledge far outweighs all merit which a person can accumulate by practicing the Buddhist virtues and perfections through countless incarnations. Since, then, Tendai lays special stress on these scriptures, it does have its specific doctrines, but it does not thereby absolutely exclude other doctrines even if they should seem to be contradictory.<note>15</note>

Now this all-inclusive system was brought to Japan by Dengyō Daishi early in the ninth century. But the Japanese Tendai Sect underwent certain changes and differs considerably from the parent sect in China. This is due to the fact that not only Dengyō Daishi, but also other learned Japanese priests, such as Jikaku Daishi who studied in China, drank not only from the fountains of wisdom which flowed from the sacred mountains of T'ien-t'ai, but also from the deep wells of truth guarded by other Chinese sects. Another factor which was operative was that deep-rooted Japanese characteristic which is quick to adopt anything new but always only after some slight modifications and a mingling
