# DENGYŌ AND TENDAI SECT

with something from other sources. Japanese Tendai claims to be eclectic rather than all-inclusive. That is, it does not simply take everything contained in other schools, but it rather chooses what it regards as the best of all schools. But, of course, an eclectic process may be carried so far that it ceases to be eclectic and becomes simply an absorption of things good, bad, and indifferent. And that is what seems to have gradually taken place in Japanese Tendai. It is practically impossible to say what it really stands for. Thus, for example, you will find some Tendai temples littered with innumerable images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They impress one as religious junk shops. Other temples may have only a trinity of Buddhas, and still others seem to honor but one Buddha. In the temples which sprang from the famous Miidera, Amida (Amitābha) seems to be the sole object of worship. Thus the Amida teaching was held in Japan long before the actual Amida sects came into existence. Again, in one and the same temple, one believer may preface his meditations and prayers with the formula, "Namu Amida Butsu," "I adore You, the Buddha of Eternal Life and Light," and another believer may use the equally popular form of "Namu-Myōhō Renge-kyō," "I worship You, the Scripture of the Wonderful Lotus"; the former being today the special prayer of the Amida sects, and the latter the "vain repetition" of the Nichiren Sect.

Now the Tendai harmonist may believe that he can reconcile the varied beliefs and practices of his own sect by saying that they are only different angles of the same truth; to the Western mind, however, it is difficult to see how such a harmony is anything more than an empty formula. And to the practical Japanese mind it also appeared so, and that is the chief reason why the Tendai Sect not only split into several sub-sects but also why many great reformers who could not endure the contradictions left it. Thus, as we shall see later, from the Tendai Sect emerged the founders of the great Amida sects of Japan, the Zen sects, and the Nichiren Sect. In these independent sects these conflicting doctrines found their freest development, and

2. *Kōbō Daishi and Shingon.* — As we stated above, at the time Dengyō Daishi introduced the Tendai Sect, Kōbō Daishi laid the foundations for the beginnings of the Shingon Sect. The latter, like the former, studied at the various centers of learning in China. He remained abroad for several years and seems to have come into contact with various influences—Buddhist and otherwise. When he returned to Japan, he brought with him many scriptures from the Chinese canon, and these he studied assiduously. He soon began to preach his new teachings, the core of which was that man can attain Buddhahood even in this present life since he is essentially one with the Eternal Buddha. His teaching was naturally challenged by the priests of the older Nara sects, but tradition has it that in his disputations with them he usually gained a miraculous victory; because of this, he was held in high esteem by the emperor and the people. He especially gained the gratitude of Japan when once, after a long drought, the heavens responded to his prayers offered at the request of his Imperial patron. Kōbō was not only a man of prayer but also a man exceptionally gifted in other fields. He is credited by some with the invention of one form of the simple Kana script, and his linguistic ability may be seen in the fact that Emperor Saga often summoned him to the palace so that he might hear his beautiful language. As an educator of the common people, he may be said to have been a pioneer, for it was he who founded the Sōgei Shuchiin, which was the first institution in which the general public had access to education; it was the forerunner of those temple schools which were often the chief centers of light during the dark ages in Japan. The cultivation of the silkworm, an industry from which Japan to this day draws its greatest revenue, was apparently greatly promoted by him. As a sculptor, he must have been a marvel, for there are many places in central Japan which boast of relics of his work in stone.

# KŌBŌ AND SHINGON SECT

Although he was popular with the emperor and the people, Kōbō Daishi preferred solitude. After much searching for a quiet spot, he finally found Mt. Kōya, where he built a temple with the emperor’s permission. Later, when his Imperial admirer gave him the Tōji temple in Kyoto, he settled there and made it the center of his sect. However, as old age approached and he saw his end drawing near, he returned to his quiet retreat on Mt. Kōya. There, he died in 835 while fasting and in silent meditation. He is buried there, and the pious followers of this great teacher believe that he sits in his tomb waiting for Maitreya (Miroku), the Buddha of the Future, to come and convert the world. When Maitreya comes, Kōbō will emerge from his tomb and join in the glory of victory.

If Dengyō Daishi’s teachings can be described as a comprehensive system, Kōbō Daishi’s system is characterized by the words Mystery and Magic. In many respects, the Shingon Sect is the furthest removed from the teachings of Sakyamuni. Surprisingly, it also holds the *Saddharma-Pundarika* in the highest regard, and its primary Buddha is the Eternal Buddha Vairochana, of whom Sakyamuni is only one of many manifestations. While the Tendai sect holds to a theory of successive stages in the Buddha’s teachings, Shingon divides the doctrines into exoteric and esoteric teachings, calling its own unique doctrines the "Secret Teachings" (*Himitsukyō*). The great secret is the revelation that man can even now attain Buddhahood because he is essentially one with the Eternal Buddha. Generally, there are two ladders by which this pinnacle of all truth may be reached: one is the intellectual ladder and the other is the moral ladder, each consisting of ten rungs. The intellectual ladder leads upward, step by step, from the lowest being to the highest being—from the finite to the Absolute. The moral ladder is the Buddhist Decalogue <note>The ten Buddhist precepts or commandments</note>, along with its elaborations in the various monastic rules that have been handed down from century to century.

In Shingon, we have “a world of ideas” (*Kongōkai*, literally the Diamond World), which is unchangeable and everlasting,

having existence only in universal thought. Parallel to this "world of ideas," serving as a sort of material counterpart, is the world of phenomena. The center of both worlds is the great Buddha Vairochana. In the "world of ideas," the central sun Vairochana (Dainichi, literally "Great Sun") tends to draw all bodies to himself, and when one has reached the highest enlightenment, one sees that the thought of Vairochana really includes all thoughts, for Vairochana is the All. In the world of the material counterpart, however, the movement is in the opposite direction; that is, the movement is outward, and from Vairochana emanate other Buddhas. From these other Buddhas emanate Bodhisattvas; from the Bodhisattvas, in turn, issue other and lesser beings, and so the emanation process goes on until the whole phenomenal world has evolved. The source of all existence, then, is the Eternal Buddha. All other beings have only relative existence. They are not void, but neither are they permanent in themselves. Vairochana, as the center of "the world of ideas," is conceived through the analogy of a planetary system, where Vairochana is the sun and Akshobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasambhava, and Shakyamuni are four great planets, each of which has lesser beings as satellites. Vairochana, as the center of the world of phenomena, is conceived as the heart of an eight-petaled lotus flower, the eight petals being Amitābha, Avalokitesvara, Dioyagosha, Maitreya, Ratna Shvaya, Samantabhadra, Muktapushpa, and Manjusri.

Thus, as we have said, Vairochana is on the one hand the source of all life and of all beings, and on the other hand, he represents the sum total of all truth. Since man is but a fragment of the sum total of all Being, his knowledge is fragmentary; but the great and saving revelation of Shingon doctrine is the great secret that man, just because he is an emanation from Vairochana, is really one with him. Man's apparent separateness is not real; deeper than this is the fact of his essential oneness with the Great All.

We said that Shingon holds that, parallel to "the world of ideas," there is the world of phenomena, with the former being the underlying cause of the latter. From this, it follows that ideas are the source of things, and thus if one has the correct ideas, one can control things. This is the real meaning of the name Shingon, "True Word." The True Word, which becomes the Magic Word, will become an efficient cause of the desired phenomenon. The person who knows the Magic Word is therefore able to achieve results simply by thinking or speaking the thought expressed by such words. Thus, as we said above, Shingon is characterized by the words Mystery and Magic, and Shingon priests are experts in all the mysteries of magic words and signs made with the fingers and the hands. These occult powers may be used for the benefit of the living or the dead. Specifically, the dead are to be delivered from the sufferings of hell and lower realms of existence by reciting the correct magical formulas or making the required signs with the hands and fingers.

Both in its theory of emanations and in its wealth of magic and mystery, Shingon seems rather far removed from the teachings of original Buddhism and also from other forms of later Buddhism. Some scholars have sought to find historical connections with other religions and philosophies, and it has particularly been pointed out that there is much affinity with Manichaeism. It is doubtful whether it can be shown that Shingon has historical connections with Manichaeism, <note>16</note> nor does it seem necessary to search very far for the source of these peculiarities of the sect. We have already seen in the last chapter that in the fifth century, Asanga had thrown open the floodgates to all the "magic and mystery" connected with the animism of India and the lands west and north of India. This stream was increased in volume later on by a powerful current which had passed through Tibet and then joined the Chinese Buddhist stream again. But whatever its source was, it is clear that this

This prominent aspect of the Shingon Sect is in flat contradiction to the teachings of Sakyamuni, who branded such things as superstition and folly, and the real enemy of the ethics of the Middle Path. <note>17</note>

We said that Kōbō Daishi was a great benefactor of Japan, and his piety and good works must have done much to recommend his religion to his people. The thing, however, which had more to do with making his religion acceptable to the people of Japan than anything else he did was his clever compromise with the native *Shintō*. We have already stated above how, during the preceding century, Gyōgi Bosatsu had begun the movement of religious syncretism by the clever answer he brought back from the Ise shrines—namely, that the Sun Goddess had declared herself to be identical with the Buddha Roshana or Birochana (Vairochana), in whose honor Emperor Shōmu erected the great Nara Daibutsu. How far Gyōgi carried his scheme is hard to say, but as he was one of the greatest artists of his day, it is quite likely that with his marvelous creations in bronze and wood, he made the union of *Shintō* and Buddhist deities very real to the people of his day. But, after all, it was Kōbō Daishi who must be given the honor of being the one who really succeeded—through his *Ryōbu Shintō*—in making the two religions but two sides of the same thing. The Sun Goddess, Amaterasu, was made identical with Vairochana, the great Buddha of Shingon (Vairochana is usually called Dainichi, Great Sun), and the lesser Buddhist deities were identified with the lesser *Shintō* gods, or the latter were declared to be just so many manifestations of the Eternal Buddha. The Shingon theory of emanations lent itself unusually well to this syncretistic movement, for it was easy thus to account for the essential oneness of the Buddhist and *Shintō* pantheons. One and all of the many gods of both religions were but emanations or radiations of the Central Sun which Buddhists knew as Vairochana and *Shintōists* as Amaterasu. Since the Central Sun is one and the same in both systems, the emanations must be essentially alike, no matter what different names they might have.

<header>KŌBŌ AND SHINGON SECT</header>

This movement, of course, resulted in bringing many elements into Japanese Buddhism that were quite foreign to original Buddhism. It furthered the tendencies that manifested themselves as early as the third century B.C.—namely, the tendency to overcome foreign beliefs through compromise and absorption. From the deification of its founder, Buddhism progressed step by step to the admission of countless gods, the greatest of whom were the Buddhas Amitābha and Vairochana, both of whom were symbolized by the sun. And when these had been declared to be identical with the Sun Goddess, Amaterasu, the next steps in this religious syncretism were comparatively easy to take. Even the Shintō War God, Hachiman, was not refused entrance into this new religion—which, in the mind of its founder, was to have been above all else a religion of peace and one that subdues the passions leading to strife and war. It is not strange, then, that Japanese Buddhism has always been and remains to this day—at least as far as the uneducated masses are concerned—a polytheistic and idolatrous religion. And Kōbō Daishi, the saint *par excellence* of early Japanese Buddhism, who succeeded in making his religion popular with the people, may be regarded in a true sense as a perverter of Buddhism.

This clever compromise made not only Kōbō’s sect popular but also the Tendai Sect, for Dengyō Daishi, too, had worked out a scheme by which he harmonized the claims of Shintō and Buddhism. All over the land, temples were built in which both the old Shintō deities and Buddhist saints and Bodhisattvas were worshipped. The two new sects grew by leaps and bounds, so that they soon overshadowed the old Nara sects. Mt. Hiei was gradually being covered with monastery after monastery, and soon branch temples of the famous Enryakuji were being built in other parts of the land. The same was true of Mt. Kōya and the Shingon sect.

Just as in the Nara period, so in the Heian period, Buddhism was closely identified with the ruling classes. Kyōto became the capital of magnificence and splendor that it was, largely

The light of culture and refinement which radiated from Japan’s new capital in ever-widening circles until it reached even the more remote places of the empire was strongly colored by Buddhist influence. What Chamberlain says so well of Japanese Buddhism as a whole is especially true of the Heian epoch when he writes: “All education was for centuries in Buddhist hands, as was the care of the poor and sick; Buddhism introduced art, introduced medicine, molded the folklore of the country, created its dramatic poetry, and deeply influenced politics and every sphere of social and intellectual activity. In a word, Buddhism was the teacher under whose instruction the Japanese nation grew up.” A few instances from the time of Emperor Shirakawa (1072–1086) may indicate how extensive its influence must have been by that time. It is said, for example, that the Buddhist injunction against taking life was so strictly enforced that “eight thousand fishing nets were seized and burned; no gifts of fish were to be offered to the court; hunting and hawking were strictly forbidden, and the hawks set at liberty.” This same emperor spent immense sums of money upon Buddhist temples and equipment. “Besides 5,470 scrolls or hanging pictures painted and presented to various <note>The original uses "fanes," an archaic word for temples or shrines.</note> temples, Shirakawa was responsible for the erection of one huge idol 32 feet in height, 127 half that size, 3,150 life-size, and 2,930 three-foot images. # KŌBŌ AND SHINGON SECT 101

By the end of the tenth century, the great religious centers themselves began to become hotbeds of vice and intrigue rather than seats of learning and virtue. The era itself, of course, was partially responsible for this, as it was beginning to be an age of political disturbances and military conquest resulting from a complex of causes for which no one in particular was responsible. But, ultimately, the Buddhist leaders must be blamed for failing in their duty as spiritual guides. In truth, they sank to the level of their surroundings and, in many cases, became the blind leading the blind. “By the end of the eleventh century,” writes Murdoch,

> “any one of these great temples (that is, Enryakuji, Miidera, and Kōfukuji) could easily place several thousand men in the field at very short notice. Each of them had become a huge Cave of Adullam—a refuge for every sturdy rogue with a soul that felt above earning a living through the common drudgery of honest work. Each of them had, in truth, taken on the appearance of a great fortress garrisoned by a turbulent rabble of armed ruffians. And each of them had degenerated into a hotbed of vice, where the most important precepts of the moral code were openly and recklessly flouted. . . . And yet, despite the foulness of their lives, the prestige of the priests had never been higher, while the resources of the monasteries had never been greater; and year by year, they were adding to their wealth.”

The ex-Emperor Shirakawa expressed the situation well in a witty remark when he noted that although he was the ruler of Japan, there were three things in the Empire beyond his control:

> “the unpredictability of the Kamo River (which often flooded and devastated the capital), the roll of the dice, and the unruliness of the priests.”

Thus we see the irony of history: the very Buddhism that Emperor Kwammu had fostered in his new Capital of Peace to counteract the influence of the old Nara sects ultimately turned out to be a greater nuisance and meddler in state affairs than its older rival ever dared to be. Not infrequently, these residents of Hieizan defied both the pleas and threats of the imperial

### D. *The Sects of the Great Awakening*

But just as the great Protestant Reformation sprang from decadent Catholicism, so the great religious awakening in Japan during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries emerged from this prosperous and degenerate <term>Heian Buddhism</term>.

What might be considered a voice in the wilderness was that of an eccentric wandering priest named <term>Kūya</term>, who according to some was actually an Imperial prince, a son of <term>Emperor Daigo</term>. He went dancing from place to place, incessantly repeating the <term>Nembutsu</term> (the prayer, <term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>), by which he hoped to direct the people's attention to the spiritual side of life that had been so completely buried in the confusion and turmoil of the age. He did not, however, limit his activity to preaching and praying, but expressed his faith in a very concrete way; for he built bridges, improved roads, repaired temples, dug wells in barren lands, tunneled through mountains, and worked unceasingly with his hands—all with the purpose of turning people's minds to the better and higher things of life. It is difficult to say whether <term>Kūya’s</term> preaching did more than arouse a passing curiosity.

A man who indirectly exercised great influence on the later generation of religious reformers was <term>Genshin</term>. While still a young boy, he dreamed that a priest gave him a small mirror and asked him to polish it. He did not understand the significance of the dream until later when, at the age of thirteen, he entered a <term>Tendai</term> monastery on <term>Mt. Hiei</term>. There, under the great priest and scholar <term>Jie</term>, he was led into the deep truths of <term>Tendai</term> doctrines. At the early age of fifteen, he began his lectures on the sacred scriptures and was greatly admired by the emperor, who gave him many beautiful garments as a token of his esteem. Young <term>Genshin</term> was much elated by this recognition and sent these gifts to his mother. But his mother was not so

### 1. *Ryōnin and the First Amida Sect.*

<term>Genshin</term> was followed by <term>Ryōnin</term> (1072–1132), who was also a student at the <term>Tendai</term> monasteries. <term>Ryōnin</term> also studied the doctrines of the <term>Shingon</term> sect, but he felt that in all his studies he was not truly entering the way of true enlightenment. Not only did he himself fail in his search, but he saw that this was the experience of other monks. All of them were so busy with their extensive learning that they did not really take the time to find the heart of truth. He therefore retired to a quiet spot and spent his time reading and repeating the prayer “<term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>,” “I adore you, Buddha of Eternal Life and Light.” It is said that he repeated this prayer sometimes as often as 60,000 times in one day, thus concentrating his mind and heart on <term>Amida</term>. One day, when he was thus absorbed in prayer and deep meditation, <term>Amida</term> appeared to him in a vision and said: 

> “Great is the merit of <term>Nembutsu</term> <note>that is, repeating the prayer, Namu Amida Butsu</note>. If by your own prayers you teach others to pray the <term>Nembutsu</term>, their prayers will become your merit, and in this way there will be mutual benefit. This is entering Paradise through the power of another.”

This thought impressed <term>Ryōnin</term> very much, and so he formed the <term>Yūdzū Nembutsu Sect</term> (Society of Mutual Benefit through <term>Nembutsu</term>). He went to <term>Kyōto</term> with a registration book and enrolled <term>Emperor Toba</term> and many courtiers and officials. Afterward, he wandered from province to province enlisting people in his new sect.

The <term>Yūdzū Nembutsu Sect</term> is the oldest of the four <term>Amida</term> sects in Japan and the first outward expression of that great religious development which took place during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. It is the first distinctively Japanese sect; the <term>Six Nara sects</term> and the <term>Tendai</term> and <term>Shingon</term> sects having been introduced from China. But while it is the oldest of the <term>Amida</term> sects and as a sect the first Japanese product, it must not be regarded as the beginning of the <term>Amida</term> teaching in Japan nor as even a fair repre-

The idea that one can be born into <term>Amida</term>'s Western Paradise by sincerely offering the prayer “<term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>” is a very ancient one in Japan. To begin with, it seems that the image sent by the king of <term>Kudara</term> to the emperor of Japan in the year 552, when Buddhism was officially introduced, was an image of the Buddha <term>Amida</term>; thus, the <term>Amida</term> faith may be said to date from the very beginning of <term>Japanese Buddhism</term>. This may be stretching a point, so we do not emphasize it. Moving down to the end of the <term>Nara period</term> (that is, at the end of the eighth century), we find pictures of <term>Amida</term> and his Western Paradise in most of the main temples of every province. Besides this, it seems to have been the custom at this time to copy the <term>Shosan Jōdokyō</term> (a hymn on birth into Paradise) on the forty-ninth day after a death occurred, and on the first anniversary, it was the custom to erect an image of <term>Amida</term> six feet tall. ## 2. *Hōnen and the Jōdo Sect.*
<term>Ryōnin</term>’s conception of <term>Amida</term>’s way of salvation was, however, very inadequate. He laid too much stress on the idea of the merit of the believer—that is, the merit of repeating the <term>Nembutsu</term>. This was really too much of “a vain repetition of the heathen” to thoroughly satisfy the deeper religious sense of the people of Japan. The great teacher of <term>Amida Buddhism</term> was yet to come. This was <term>Genku</term>, better known as <term>Hōnen Shōnin</term>. When <term>Ryōnin</term> died in 1132, <term>Hōnen</term> was a two-year-old boy. It was an age of civil wars—wars in which not only the <term>Samurai</term> took part, but also the monks of <term>Hieizan</term>, <term>Miidera</term>, <term>Kōfukuji</term>, and the other great monastic centers of the time. One day, the father of <term>Seishimaru</term> (<term>Genku</term>’s name as a boy) was mortally wounded in the conflict, and the young boy, raised in the atmosphere of war, attempted to kill his father’s enemy. The father praised his son for his loyalty and courage, but in his dying words he said:

> “I now die through this misfortune, but you must not take vengeance on my enemy. My death is only the reward of my former life. If you avenge my death, you will in turn be subject to the vengeance of your enemy’s descendants. All living beings fear death. As I suffer from my wounds, other men suffer; and as I cling to life, shall not others cling to life equally? Henceforth pray only for salvation for yourself and your fellow men. Cast away all vengeance and malice and seek to attain enlightenment.”

These words made a profound impression on the boy, and soon after this incident, he entered a monastery of the <term>Tendai Sect</term> on <term>Hieizan</term>. He was a diligent student and delved deeply into the various doctrines of not only the <term>Tendai Sect</term> but

Like Luther more than three centuries later, Genku longed for a deeper assurance of salvation and a more vital religious life than what was offered at the centers of learning on the slopes of Hieizan. One day, as if by chance, he came across Genshin's "*Ōjōyōshū*" (Collected Essays on Entering Paradise). A little later, he became acquainted with the writings of Zendō Daishi, from which he drank deeply; for here he learned that man's salvation does not depend upon his own strength so much as upon the grace of Amida. Even the lowest sinner may find a way of escape from this life of misery and suffering into a life of happiness and peace, if only he has learned to pray in faith to the great Buddha Amida, who has prepared his Western Paradise for those who believe in him. When Genku read these great words of hope, he immediately cast aside the ordinary way of salvation which Japanese Buddhism had usually been proclaiming—namely, the way of salvation through one's own wisdom and virtue <note>20</note>—and he became the prophet of the new way: the way of faith in the mercy of Amida. He became the founder in Japan of the great Jōdo (Pure Land or Paradise) Sect (1175), which has as its chief tenets a semi-theistic conception of God, a doctrine of a personal future life, and salvation for all people who believe in the grace of Amida. This way of salvation, the sect holds, was worked out for humanity by the vicarious sufferings of the (divine) man Hōzō Bosatsu.

With the founding of Hōnen's sect, Amida Buddhism may be said to have been thoroughly established in Japan. The influence of Hōnen's teachings soon became far-reaching. People from all classes of society—from the nobility and the royal family down to the lowest peasants—joined the new sect. Priests of other sects, one after another, began to give their allegiance to this new school and helped spread the way of salvation through faith in Amida. Among Hōnen's followers were many men of great ability, and this naturally gave prestige to the Jōdo Sect. But strong men are often "strong-minded" men, and that frequently becomes a seed of discord. It was not long thereafter—

3. *Shinran and the Shin Sect.* — There was, however, one disciple, Hōnen’s greatest disciple, namely, Shinran Shōnin, who felt that his master had not gone far enough in his explanation of the Amida doctrine, and so felt compelled finally in 1224 to establish an independent sect. This sect is the powerful Jōdo Shinshū, the True Pure Land Sect, usually referred to by the shorter term, Shin Sect.

When Hōnen founded the Jōdo Sect in 1175, Shinran was two years old. He was of noble birth, being a descendant on his father’s side of the great Fujiwara family, and on his mother’s side, of the illustrious Minamoto family. As a boy of four he lost his father, and in his eighth year his mother also died. Acquainted early with the hardships of life, neither his social standing nor the luxury of his condition could satisfy his heart. His mind became more and more set upon deeper things, and at the age of nine he became a pupil of Jichin, the abbot of Shōrenin monastery on Hieizan. He is said to have composed the following beautiful line when he took this step: “The heart that thinks there is a tomorrow is as fleeting as the cherry blossom, for is there not the midnight wind?” He spent many years on Hieizan studying the depths of Tendai philosophy. He also visited Nara and there learned what he could from the scholars of the older sects, among whom there were many men of real ability at this time. So profound was his learning that he was popularly known as “The Genius of Hieizan” and “The Famous Priest of the Future.” He was made abbot of one of the monasteries on the mountain and was well on his way to becoming a high priest of the Tendai Sect and being placed at the head of the Sansenbo—the 3,000 monastic buildings which dotted Hieizan—thus overshadowing with his dignity the whole mountain and the nearby capital of Kyoto. <header>SHINRAN AND SHIN SECT</header>

Buddhism, Shinran, having given up all worldly ambition when he first entered the way of enlightenment, was not going to yield to the temptation of occupying a prominent position as a high priest. Instead, he devoted himself even more diligently to the search for truth and to prayer.

One day, Shinran happened to hear Hōnen preach on the way of salvation through faith in Amida’s great name. After the sermon, he visited Hōnen in his study, and after an earnest inquiry into the full meaning of this teaching, he then and there abandoned the old way of salvation through the Law (<term>Shōdomon</term>) and accepted the doctrine of salvation through faith in Amida (<term>Jōdomon</term>). This happened at the age of twenty-nine. Two years later, influenced by a vision of the Goddess <note>21</note> of Mercy (Kwannon) and urged on by his master Hōnen, he married Princess Tamahi, the daughter of Prince Fujiwara Kanezane, thus setting an example for the Buddhist world of a new type of priesthood. By this step, he broke down the barrier between priest and layman, seeking to demonstrate to the people of Japan that religion should not make a person live an abnormal life or break up the most sacred institution of humanity, namely, the family. Shinran also ate meat and other food forbidden to the priesthood, and in his dress, he followed the style of ordinary citizens of the land. In short, he lived as a man among men, for he felt that religion has to do with the ordinary things of life and should enable the average person to live this life in the best way possible.

It is not surprising that he was fiercely attacked by the priests of other sects, for his innovations were every bit as extraordinary as anything Luther ever thought of. He was accordingly banished in 1219 to the province of Hitachi, but he looked upon this exile as an opportunity rather than a hardship. “If I do not go to my place of banishment,” he said, “how can I convert the people of those remote parts? This, too, is a blessing flowing from the master’s teachings.” After six years, the ban was removed, but he was in no hurry to return to Kyōto and civilization. He took a roundabout way through the outlying provinces,

He preached the new way and built temples as he went. After an absence of twenty-eight years, he finally reached Kyōto, rich in experience and confident in his gospel of salvation through Amida’s Name. He spent the remaining years of his life writing and preaching. People came even from distant places to sit at his feet and learn from this great teacher how to walk in the way of Amida’s grace. He died at the ripe age of eighty-nine, true to the end in his determination to know nothing but Amida and salvation in his Western Paradise. “Empty thoughts flee at the prayer <term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>. Both the mouth that utters these words and the heart that believes them are in Paradise.” “When you see the change that befalls all people, stir your heart to rely upon Amida.” (Shinran.)

At no point in the history of Buddhism would a comparison with the founder of Buddhism and his teachings be as interesting and instructive as right here. If the reader bears in mind what was said in Chapter I about the kernel of S'akyamuni’s teachings, the contrast between that and the teachings of Shinran and his sect will be striking. It is impossible to give the doctrines of the Shin Sect in detail here, and the reader is referred to the author’s translation of “A Catechism of the Shin Sect,” but we must give at least an outline of the main tenets of this remarkable form of Buddhism.

As stated above, Shinran taught salvation through faith in the Name of the Buddha Amida and rejected the old way of salvation through one’s own wisdom and virtue. Just what does this mean? Briefly stated, it means the following:

There may have been a time back in the “golden age” of the human race, said Shinran, when it was possible for man to save himself through his own strength, but in “these latter days” this is quite out of the question; for man is entirely too corrupt and lost in ignorance and sin for this task. There is now only one way of salvation for him, namely, the way of simple faith and trust in the great mercy of Amida. But who or what is Amida?

# SHINRAN AND THE SHIN SECT

Without attempting to provide the history of the Amida faith, we will simply state what is believed about this Buddha Amida. Amida Buddha (Buddha Amitābha), before he became a Buddha and while he was still the Bodhisattva Hōzō (Bodhisattva Dharmakara) many eons ago, made a great vow 23 in which he promised that he would not enter the full bliss of Buddhahood until he had worked out a way of salvation for all people, including even the worst sinners. He remained true to his vow, and after many incarnations of self-sacrificing lives, he finally succeeded in accumulating so much merit that he became the great Amida Buddha, the Buddha of Eternal Life and Light, who offers everyone entrance—or rather, birth—into his Pure Land of Bliss. There is only one thing a person must do in order to win this birth into Paradise, and that is to accept the gift that is offered in a spirit of simple faith and trust. The believer is told to call upon the name of Amida in the prayer <term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>, which probably means, “I adore You,” or “Have mercy on me, You Buddha of Eternal Life and Light.” He who does this shall be saved. Some go even so far as to say that the faith itself, which enables the believer to utter this prayer effectively, is also a gift from Amida. The works of the Law—that is, the good works of a person’s daily life, which most Buddhists regard as an accumulation of merit or good karma—are of no use, according to the followers of Shinran. Faith in Amida’s great Name, and that alone, can save. Good works are not excluded, but they are regarded only as expressions of the believer’s gratitude to Amida for his gift of salvation. That is, good works are not the cause of a person's salvation, but rather the result of having been saved through faith.

The teachings of the Shin Sect regarding the way of salvation differ widely not only from the teachings of the founder of Buddhism and those of the older Japanese sects, but also somewhat from the teachings of other Amida sects. The Yūdzū Nembutsu Sect, which we mentioned above, also preached salvation through Amida’s name; however, in that sect, salvation still had to be earned by a faithful repetition of the <term>Nembutsu</term>. That is, the believer earned merit, or accumulated

While Amida’s grace was held to be sufficient to save, the believer was still warned to be strict in his observance of certain rules of conduct and was made to feel that, after all, good works had a great deal to do with one’s salvation. The follower of Shinran, on the other hand, is taught to rest in perfect peace of heart and to trust solely in Amida. He should not even worry about his moral condition or have any anxiety as to his growth in character. “Whether we are saved because our sins have been blotted out or not, we do not know; it is as Amida has ordained. We have nothing to do with it; we have only to believe.” And Rennyō, one of the great leaders in the Shin Sect, says, “The important thing according to the founder’s (*i.e.*, Shinran’s) teachings is nothing else than this heart of faith. He who does not know this is to be regarded as an outsider; he who knows what faith is has the true marks of a follower of Shinran.”

Now this way of salvation proclaimed by Shinran, and to a certain extent also by other Amidaists, clearly represents a rather radical departure from the fundamentals of S’akyamuni’s religion. In the first place, it would seem that Amidaism, at least in the minds of some of its adherents, not only makes room for a real God-idea, but this idea seems to come very near to a theistic conception. In Chapter V, under the general heading of “The God-idea” and the section on “Theistic Buddhism,” we shall discuss this point more fully, but here we simply wish to point out the fact that in these Amida sects the conception of Amida is very much the same as the conception of God in theistic systems. It is significant that the Buddha S’akyamuni almost disappears in the Shin Sect and is regarded simply as the teacher of the gospel of Amida. He is revered as a great man and the founder of Buddhism, but he is not usually held up as an object of worship. If he is worshipped at all, it is only because he is regarded as an incarnation or partial manifestation of Amida; never

Another fact about these Amida sects, and the Shin Sect in particular, is that salvation means the salvation of the individual into a future life where there seems to be a real continuity and identity of the individual, rather than mere <term>Karma</term> continuity and identity. The Shin Sect teaches that at death the believer truly enters Amida's Western Paradise, and for many, this hope of a future life of happiness seems to have been a real source of joy and peace. There are even cases on record where people have committed suicide to hasten their departure from this world and enter Amida's Paradise. Others have lived in such joyful anticipation of this that this world was turned into a paradise for them; in fact, Shinran emphasized the idea that salvation begins in this life.

A third point of difference is in the conception of sin found in the teachings of the Shin Sect. Humanity is regarded as totally depraved and beyond the possibility of saving itself. Sin is not regarded as mere outward evil or misfortune, as it often is in Buddhist thought, but rather as a condition of the heart that causes outward evil and misfortune. The one thing necessary, then, is to have a change of heart, and this change of heart comes through faith rather than through an effort by the individual to cleanse their heart through their own wisdom or strength. When Amida is received through faith, he controls the heart and thus uproots all sin. “When we firmly believe in this vow <note>that is, Amida’s vow to save all living beings</note> and do not doubt it for a moment, Amida graciously governs our heart. Our evil heart at once becomes united with the good heart of the <term>Nyōrai</term> <note>that is, Amida</note>.” (Shinran.)

...much less emphasis is put upon the evils of our present existence than in Indian Buddhism. This world, S'akyamuni had said, is a world of suffering and sorrow, and therefore its hold on us should be rigorously reduced to the lowest possible terms. The Japanese mind has never fully accepted this doctrine, and the Shin Sect, which is the purest Japanese product of all Japanese sects, has been influenced by it the least. It is more natural for the Japanese mind to look upon life and the things of life as good, for Japan is above all else "the land of the gods," and the Japanese are the offspring of "the sons of heaven." Thus, the religious life cannot be so very distinct from the normal life of a man as a citizen of Japan, and any teacher who can show how religious faith and practical conduct may be harmonized is bound to have a great following. Shinran did have a great following, and his sect is today the strongest of all sects of Japanese Buddhism. In fact, it has a vitality which is rather unique among the old religions of the Orient. Unhampered by any elaborate metaphysical system, it seems to be able to adjust itself to the great changes—political, economic, and social—which have come over modern Japan, and to continue its hold upon the people of this generation while most of the other sects seem to be on the decline. If Buddhism has any future in Japan, it will be the Buddhism of the Amida sects in general and the Shin Sect in particular.

With these few remarks, we must leave for the present this most interesting of all Japanese Buddhist sects and pass on to an account of the other great sects.

4. *Introduction of the Zen Sect.* — Between the founding of the Jōdo and the Shin sects, there was introduced from South China one of the main branches of the Dhyāna school, namely, the Rinzai branch of the Zen Sect. The Dhyāna school of Buddhism reached China from India in the year 520 A.D. when Bodhidharma came to China as a missionary. Bodhidharma (Japanese, Daruma) is regarded as the twenty-eighth patriarch, being in direct "apostolic succession" from S'akyamuni. ...considered the first Chinese patriarch. At this time, China was being flooded with Indian books, and bewildered Buddhists did not know which book or books to turn to for the correct teaching. Bodhidharma came with the message that the true teaching of the master was not contained in any single book, nor even in all the books put together, for truth is too great and deep to be expressed in any written or spoken word. Truth is in the heart itself, and it must be transmitted from heart to heart by a sort of spiritual telegraphy; or even better, the heart must teach itself through silent meditation. The chief characteristic, therefore, of the Zen Sect is silent meditation and abstract contemplation. The true follower seeks to penetrate the inner recesses of reality, into what might be called "the white silence of Truth." It is said of Bodhidharma that he sat for seven years staring at a blank wall and that when he was asked questions regarding religion and himself, he remained silent. And of another Zen philosopher, it is said that when he fell into the hands of bandits who tried to intimidate him by thrusting a sword at his face, he did not so much as blink but sat unmoved. No wonder the ruffians were themselves terrified and fled, leaving this holy man in peace.

Now, this method of approaching truth and salvation as a result of the knowledge thus gained was known in Japan from the early days of Buddhism, having been introduced by the high priest Dōsho, who established the old Hossō Sect in this land. After him, Dōsen, Dengyō, Jikaku, and other prominent religious leaders practiced and preached the Zen way of salvation. By the twelfth century, there were many people, especially those of deep character, who were acquainted with this quiet way of approaching the truth, but the followers of Zen had still never organized themselves into a separate sect; they continued to remain within the existing sects, especially in the all-inclusive Tendai Sect. Finally, however, late in the twelfth century, Eisai appeared. Like other great leaders of his day, he also studied Buddhism at the famous monasteries on Hieizan belonging to the Tendai...

When an opportunity presented itself, he carried out a long-cherished wish and sailed for China, where he studied for a while at the headquarters of the Tendai Sect. However, a few years later, he felt compelled to go to China again, and there at the Tendai center, he was initiated into the true teachings of the Zen Sect. When he started for home, his teacher bestowed upon him—as a special mark of his achievements—the Great Mantle, the symbol of his having mastered the truth as known by the Zen school. The Zen Sect dates its origin in Japan from about the time of Eisai’s second return from China, that is, about 1191. In 1201, the reigning shōgun invited him to establish himself at the Kennin-ji in Kyoto, and later at the Kenkō-ji in Kamakura, which city became the center for the sect. Having its center in this military capital of Japan is one reason why the Zen Sect has always had—and still has to this day—a great many military men among its followers.

Not many years after the founding of the Rinzai branch of the Zen Sect, a sister branch of this contemplative school, namely the Sōtō branch, was established by Dōgen (also known as Shōyō Daishi) with headquarters in Echizen Province. The chief difference between the Sōtō and the Rinzai branches of the Zen Sect is that the former places more weight upon book learning as a secondary aid to silent meditation on the truth.

The Zen Sect claims that it represents the spirit and teaching of the founder of Buddhism most truly. This claim seems supported by the facts of the case. Not only does the historical connection with early Indian Buddhism seem more direct than in the case of other sects, but its emphasis on meditation and self-discipline seems closer to the practices and teachings of Shakyamuni <note>S’akyamuni is an alternate spelling for Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note>. Zen philosophy does not give the Four Great Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path the same importance that S'akyamuni <note>The historical Buddha</note> probably did, but it still insists, as he had done, on the doctrine that people must save themselves through their own strength and must not depend on God, or the gods, for help. In fact, the Zen Sect makes little or no room for the idea of God, or for the idea of the real permanence of the individual in a future life. It has nothing to say about an Eternal Buddha, though it does recognize an ultimate reality that transcends the human mind's power to grasp—a reality which S'akyamuni himself, as we saw, did not deny. While S'akyamuni laid his chief emphasis on the idea of "escaping from the evils of this life," the Zen teachings of Japan emphasize the escape from the limitations of the present and empirical self into the glorious liberty of union with the Greater Self; they do not state, however, what that Greater Self is or what the nature of such salvation might mean.

The practice of Zen, or Zazen, is a kind of mystical self-intoxication by which the believer seeks to rise above the world of the senses, with all its limitations and differences, into the freedom and harmony of the Reality that lies beyond, in which there are no differences and jarring contrasts. Naturally, not everyone who practices Zazen goes through exactly the same experience. For some, it is entering into a feeling of the oneness of all reality, so that the consciousness of the self and all individual existence fades into nothingness and only a "holy vacancy" remains. For others, it may go no further than a heightened sense of the oneness of all reality; consequently, no matter what loss may come to the individual, there can be no permanent loss since the self is regarded as being truly one with the Greater Self, or the Universal Self. But in any case, the believer who has entered this ecstatic state feels no longer bound by the ordinary laws of our everyday experience. "He has ceased to think of good or evil, released himself from a relative idea of wise and common beings, given up any discussion or consideration of ignorance and intelligence, and delivered his mind from

All our ordinary knowledge—*i.e.*, the knowledge of the sensory world in which we make distinctions between things—is regarded as an illusion. Even our moral distinctions have no value and must be treated as the product of the unenlightened mind.²⁵ “The ancients say: ‘When illusion vanishes, quietude will appear; when quietude appears, knowledge will arise; when knowledge arises, truth will make its appearance.’ If you want to put an end to such illusory thoughts, you should abstain from thinking of good or evil; without perceiving objects or performing deeds, you should not think with the mind or do anything with the body. This is the first precaution to be taken. When illusory objects vanish, the illusory mind will consequently vanish. If the illusory mind vanishes, the unchanging entity will appear.²⁶ It always knows things clearly. It is not an object of quietude, nor an object of activity.”

In order to attain this state of mind, which is void of all sensory objects and in which Reality itself will appear, the student of Zazen is given detailed directions as to how and where he is to sit in his silent meditations. > ". . . There are two ways of sitting: the full cross-legged position and the half cross-legged position. The lips and teeth must touch each other. The eyes must be moderately open, neither too wide nor too narrow. Thus, after making the proper arrangements of the body, you should inhale and exhale a few times through the open mouth. Next, settling your body, you should move your body from side to side, decreasing the degree of the motion each time, and finally coming to a firm, upright sitting position. At that point, you should consider "unconsiderableness." How could unconsiderableness be considered? It is "considerationless," which is an important method of <term>*Dhyāna*</term> sitting, by means of which you must immediately destroy evil passions and obtain full enlightenment.

<header># THE ZEN SECT</header>

> “When you wish to rise from your sitting position, you must first place both hands, palms upward, on your knees and move your body from side to side seven or eight times. Each time, increase the range of the movement and breathe out through your open mouth. Then, placing your extended arms on the ground, stand up easily and walk slowly along the left side of the room, always turning to the right.”

As one reads these detailed instructions given to those who practice <term>Zazen</term>, one cannot help but be struck by the contradiction between the methods used to achieve this goal of abstract contemplation and the goal itself. The methods involve a meticulous—almost trivial—attention to the details of the sensory world, while the goal is a state of mind in which the sensory world does not exist. The follower of <term>Zazen</term> may argue that this attention to the body's arrangement is only temporary and that these things vanish along with the illusory mind once the believer has entered the state of perfect quiet and truth. 

That may be so; however, it should then be unnecessary for someone who has reached such a state to return to an ordinary state of consciousness where the details and differences of the sensory world seem so real. That is, the student of <term>Zazen</term> should not be given rules on how to get up from their sitting posture during meditation. Why should they wish to get up and return to the sensory world if they have truly entered a state where Truth has appeared and where they know that the objects of our everyday consciousness are illusions? Obviously, the world of the senses is too real to be dismissed in this way for any length of time. The problems of truth and reality must be approached in a way other than through a mystical state of self-trance that lasts, under the best conditions, for only a few hours at most. No one would question that a “quiet mind” is the most favorable condition for perceiving Reality; however, it cannot be perceived simply by a process of removing and emptying the content of our ordinary conscious states. This can only end in an abstraction and emptiness which may be a pleasant feeling for those who want to escape for a short time from the

It seems a curious phenomenon that a sect which places such an emphasis on the contemplative life and which holds out the "white silence of truth" as the highest goal should have always had many followers from the military class. Even in modern industrial and bustling Japan, it is fashionable for military men to practice "<term>Zazen</term>." Besides the reason already given above—namely, the fact that the Zen Sect made the military capital of Japan its center of activity<sup>27</sup>—there are two other reasons. One is that the Zen Sect has always shown itself very friendly toward Confucian ethics and made them a part of its practical teachings. From the earliest times, Confucianism has been a kind of religious philosophy for the military classes, and it has never been regarded in Japan as antagonistic to Buddhism. The vagueness of the concept of God in Confucianism is exceedingly well-suited to the Zen mind, and the definiteness of Confucian ethics—especially the ethical teachings dealing with the relationship between lord and vassal—formed a good substitute for the ethics of the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term>. At any rate, the former were not regarded as contrary to the latter. The other great reason for the popularity of Zen thought with military men is the fact that it places a strong emphasis on self-discipline and self-control, the primary qualifications of any true soldier. Even the physical discipline of a true student of Zen is Spartan, and the mental discipline is often such that men become indifferent to all dangers and face death without trembling. The capture of Port Arthur in the Russo-Japanese War was, at least in part, the result of Zen discipline. For a further presentation of Zen thought, the reader is referred to Chapter V.

...in Japan or leaders in religious matters, Nichiren is the most colorful and in many respects the most powerful personality. He was born in 1222 in an obscure village of Awa Province. As a boy, he became somewhat familiar with the teachings of the Shingon Sect, but later he went to Mt. Hiei and studied under the great priests of the Tendai Sect. For about ten years, he dedicated himself to these studies and then returned to his native province, ready for his great campaign. Like all great reformers, Nichiren did not start out to found a new sect. He began by denouncing what he regarded as a genuine perversion of the master's teachings. He found such perversions especially in the teachings of the sects that were then gaining great popularity—namely, the Jōdo, the Shin, and the Zen sects. In his Rissho Ankoku Ron, Nichiren's chief writing, he makes a vehement attack on Hōnen, the founder of the Jōdo Sect, and upon all the followers of the Amida doctrine. He laments that the teachings of Dengyō Daishi and the older type of Buddhism were being neglected and that the people had ears only for the writings of Zendō and the Amida scriptures. This testifies to the remarkable success the Amida sects achieved soon after they were founded. He also could not tolerate the Zen sects and opposed them as the invention of the devil. Even his first love, the Shingon Sect, he denounced as "a traitor to the country."

The reason Nichiren so bitterly opposed these other sects was that he felt they were dividing Buddhism, and especially that the Amida sects were taking the glory of S'akyamuni and giving it to another, namely, Amida. On the other hand, he felt that with a divided religion Japan would be a divided nation, and so both religion and state would be destroyed. That is why he cries in one of his impassioned declarations, "Awake, men, awake! Awake, and look around you. No man is born with two fathers or two mothers. Look at the heavens above you: there are no two suns in the sky. Look at the earth at your feet: no two kings can rule a country." But this, he felt, was exactly what was happening in Japan. And since the former political division was the natural result of the latter religious division, there was only one thing to do: uproot the sects that had proved themselves disloyal to the pure teachings of the founder.

He felt that not only were the political and religious worlds divided and falling apart, but because of this, the nation itself was being destroyed. Evidence of this seemed abundant everywhere. In 1257, for example, a terrible earthquake shook everything from its very foundations. This was followed the next year by an equally terrible hurricane; as a result of these two calamities, famine and disease completed the work of destruction. Furthermore, there were signs that whatever was left by these natural disasters would fall prey to a foreign invader—the Mongols, who in 1264 had established themselves in Peking under Kublai Khan and were threatening to subdue the whole of eastern Asia, including the islands of the Sunrise Kingdom <note>Japan</note>. To avoid this impending peril, Japan had to be a united nation both politically and spiritually.

The events that followed in the political world show that Nichiren was not a mere alarmist. The predicted Mongol invasion actually happened, and apparently the only reason it did not succeed beyond the occupation of a few minor islands and a narrow strip of coastline in Kyushu was the timely appearance of a severe typhoon. This storm caused the Mongol ships to share the fate of the great Spanish Armada. The proud Japanese, however, prefer to place greater stress on the bravery of their illustrious ancestors, who, they claim, were the only people of that age able to check the advancing hordes of the Mongols—hordes that at one time or another overran great portions of the two continents of Asia and Europe. If he is worshiped at all, it is only because he might be regarded as one of the historical manifestations of Amida. The Shingon was equally a departure, though in quite a different way, as we have already shown above. Whether his attacks on the Zen sect were justified on the same grounds is a question; for, as we have said above, Zen is nearer to the teachings of the founder in many ways than, perhaps, any other Japanese sect. But on the whole, Nichiren was correct in raising an alarm and trying to bring his people back to the historical Buddha S'akyamuni if Japanese Buddhism was to follow the teaching of the one they professed to follow.

But while Nichiren was eager to restore Buddhism to its original purity, it does not follow at all that he even knew what that original purity might mean. Both the spirit of his religion and the content of his doctrines prove that he actually knew very little on this subject. As a student of the Tendai, he became acquainted—among other books—with the *Saddharma-Pundarīka-sūtra* (in Japanese, *Hokkekyō*), which he made the main foundation of his teachings. As we have already pointed out, this is a relatively late writing and breathes a form of Buddhism quite different from the Buddhism of S'akyamuni. The great Buddha of that scripture is the Eternal Buddha of Original Enlightenment, with whom S'akyamuni is identical, or of whom he is one of many manifestations. But the historical Buddha S'akyamuni had nothing to say of such a Buddha, and he certainly never claimed to be identical with or the manifestation of such a Buddha. Furthermore, Nichiren and his followers lay great emphasis on faith—faith in this sacred scripture, which is regarded with a superstitious reverence. Then Nichiren's bitter attack on other sects was also a great departure from the spirit of older Buddhism, which was nothing if not tolerant of views that differed. This tolerant attitude was especially characteristic of the Tendai Sect, from which Nichiren learned practically all that he knew about Buddhism. This characteristic of Nichiren was not altogether a bad one; for if there is anything that Buddhism needed, it was a firmness that would enable it to hold to some definite things and reject others that were incompatible. But we simply wish to point out that Nichiren, in trying to give Buddhism some backbone, was infusing into it his own vigorous personality, for whom distinctions were real and vital, and he was not restoring a characteristic of the older Buddhism. In his Rissho Ankoku Ron, <note>A famous treatise by Nichiren titled "On Establishing the Correct Teaching for the Peace of the Land."</note> this comes clearly to light; for in this dialogue between the master of a house and a guest, the latter frequently makes the point that the spirit of Buddhism is one that tolerates all views and persecutes none, and the master has great difficulty in proving from the sacred scriptures that heretics should be opposed. The truth of the matter is that Nichiren was anything but a reformer of Buddhism. He thought he was one, but in reality, he was a man who gave Japanese Buddhism a new turn. This new turn was not in the doctrines he taught—for there is nothing new in the teachings of the Nichiren Sect—but in the spirit that he infused into the new sect which he founded. The very fact that it is the only Japanese sect that calls itself by the name of its founder shows that it was founded on Nichiren's spirit and personality rather than upon any new doctrine or upon any old Buddhist teaching restored to life. Nichiren has transmitted his positive spirit to his followers, though it must be admitted that the positiveness which made him a towering figure in Japanese life assumes a fanatical character in most of his followers. This is the enemy of all true progress and has made the sect, as one has put it, "the Ishmael of Buddhism." <note>A reference to the biblical Ishmael, implying the sect is at odds with all other Buddhist groups.</note>

<header>NICHIREN AND NICHIREN SECT</header>

# NICHIREN AND NICHIREN SECT

Nichiren’s bitter attacks on the political and religious leaders of his day naturally led to counterattacks from his many enemies. Priests of other sects accused him of spreading heresy, and his political enemies accused him of inciting rebellion. In 1261, he was arrested and brought before the regent’s court at Kamakura. It is not surprising that he was found guilty and banished to the Izu <note>Spelled "Idzu" in the original text.</note> Peninsula. Three years later, however, he appeared again in the streets of Kamakura, more outspoken than ever. For a while he was safe, because the people believed it was in response to his prayers that the heavens sent rain after a long drought. Like Elijah of old, he mocked the “false prophets” and emerged victorious. But even so, it was impossible for a man of his temperament to stay out of trouble, and he was soon back before the regent’s court. This time the charges were so serious that the court felt compelled to condemn him to death.<note>29</note> He was led to the sands of Kamakura beach, and the executioner’s sword was about to strike the fatal blow when, as if by a miracle, a messenger from the regent appeared on the scene and saved his life. 

Nichiren was instead banished to distant Sado, where he remained until 1272, when he returned once more to resume his preaching and warnings. By this time, he had won so many followers that he was quite safe. He spent the remaining ten years of his life at Minobu and Ikegami; these two places are regarded to this day as the primary centers of the sect. At Ikegami, Nichiren passed away after his strenuous life, and his tomb there remains a sacred shrine to thousands. Every autumn, his many followers gather there from all directions to honor him. But the thoughtful student, hearing the deafening noise of those drunken worshippers—intoxicated not with Nichiren’s enthusiasm and inspiring message but with cheap sake—regrets the thought that one so earnest and, on the whole, so sane should have such unworthy followers. For it is true that while there are some educated people in the Nichiren Sect, the rank and file come from the most ignorant and lowest classes; and

6. *The Ji Sect.* — Another sect that came into existence around this time, and which we mention only in passing, is the last of the four Amida sects: the Ji Sect, founded by Ippen Shōnin. Some hold that it was first founded by Kūya and that Ippen is the second founder; however, if it was founded as early as Kūya’s day, it did not establish a place for itself before Ippen’s time. It is of little consequence today, as it has only about 500 temples in all of Japan, but in its early history, it promised to have great influence and at one time even had an imperial prince as its head. Ippen Shōnin was remarkable for his zeal in spreading his message, traveling from one end of the land to the other to teach people the Easy Way—the Way of Faith in the Mercy of Amida. He seems to have passed this characteristic on to his followers, as the sect has apparently always placed great emphasis on <term>itinerant preaching</term>. One naturally wonders why such efforts have not produced greater results, unless the benefits are being reaped by the more powerful Amida sects, from which the Ji Sect does not really differ enough to justify a separate existence.

All four of these great sects—the Jōdo, Zen, Shin, and Nichiren—came into existence within a period of about three-quarters of a century (specifically between 1175 and 1253). Their beginnings undoubtedly represent the greatest outburst of religious life in Japan’s long history. The student who reads about this movement and the lives of the great men who led the way with an unbiased mind cannot fail to be impressed by the positive contribution Japan has made to at least one of the world’s great religions. Knowing this period of Japanese history will cure anyone of the superficial idea often expressed by Westerners that the Japanese have borrowed everything they possess and are merely imitators. The religion of these four great sects is just as much a genuine development of Indian and

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the development of Japanese Buddhism and the Protestant Reformation, concluding that the Kamakura sects represent the first truly indigenous expression of the religion in Japan.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>
<header>FOUR GREAT SECTS</header>

Chinese Buddhism, just as the Protestantism of Germany, England, and America is a development of medieval and early Christianity; the only difference is that this development took place some three centuries earlier. The old Nara sects and the two Kyoto sects of the ninth century had their influence on Japan because they represented a higher civilization than Japan's at the time, but these four great sects of the Kamakura period gained their hold because they were the first real expression of Buddhism in Japanese terms—that is, with them Buddhism may be said to have been thoroughly planted in Japanese life. It was planted not only in the life of the upper classes, as was largely the case with the older sects, but in the life of the people at large. It is only natural that these sects should become very popular, and while the old Tendai and Shingon sects continued to exercise a great influence, they were relegated to a secondary place, especially in the new Kwanto<gloss>30</gloss> region, the center of the military rulers of Japan. Out of a total of 72,000 temples in existence today, over 53,000 belong to the above-mentioned four great sects, and as we shall see later, they represent the dominant forces of Japanese Buddhism today.

Unfortunately, this reformation of Japanese Buddhism in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries also contained some of the evils of the Protestant Reformation. From the beginning, it held the seeds of schism and division. We saw above that Nichiren was alarmed at the influence the new sects were having and that he sought to rally Buddhists around the single standard of loyalty to Shakyamuni and one earthly ruler; but as a matter of fact, his efforts resulted in further divisions and in bringing about a period of strife and hatred among the various sects. This is not to say that Nichiren was responsible for all these fights and divisions, but rather that he personified the tendency of the age. Any account of these divisions, or even the barest outline of them, would try the patience of even an interested student. It is enough to say that the process went on and on, with old schisms dying out and new ones taking their place, until today, Japan has over fifty Buddhist sects recognized by the government.

Of these, there are thirty-six divisions and subdivisions within the four sects of the Kamakura period.

The differences between the main divisions of Japanese Buddhism, which are usually counted as twelve, are often much greater than the differences between the major branches of Christianity. On the other hand, the differences between the subdivisions of a sect are often very minor. Thus, *e.g.*, the ten subdivisions of the Shin Sect are not due to any doctrinal differences, but sometimes simply to the fact that a certain temple—perhaps hosting a royal or other important person—became so prominent that it could no longer be regarded as a branch temple. It was therefore made independent and became the center of a new subdivision. In other cases, subdivisions were caused by the rise of a great priest who, through his own personality, impressed his followers so powerfully that they formed a brotherhood. They did this without intending to cut themselves loose from the parent body, but they nevertheless became independent over time. In still other cases, the divisions were due merely to geographical conditions; for in a mountainous country like Japan, travel and communication were exceedingly difficult before the arrival of the railroad. This fact had made political divisions very real for centuries before the arrival of Buddhism, and these political divisions in turn made religious differences feel very natural and easy.

Thus, Japanese Buddhism is quite accustomed to the idea of schisms and divisions, just as Buddhism in India and China was from its early days. However, it must be added that the average Buddhist—especially the average Buddhist philosopher—does not see this as something to be regretted, but only as a sign of life. Even a Christian must admit that schisms are often a sign of life, though frequently a misdirected life. The Buddhist philosopher, on the other hand, would hold that because Truth is many-sided and human minds are so finite, it is the glory of a religion to have many divisions, each of which brings out its own unique perspective of the whole truth. Some philosophers carry this half-truth so far

### E. *Political Strife and Religious Decline*

The wonderful religious outburst of the 12th and 13th centuries was followed by a sad decline. For about one hundred years after the founding of the Kamakura shogunate, Japan enjoyed peace and a degree of prosperity. The Hojo regents, who replaced the descendants of the great Yoritomo, were on the whole strong and capable rulers, and under their administration the country was able to recover somewhat from the devastating wars that had preceded this period. But in the beginning of the 14th century, things began to change for the worse again. In 1333, the Hojo regents were overthrown, and this was followed by the long Wars of Succession, when Japan had two rival lines of emperors; for more than fifty years, civil war and private conflicts were the order of the day. Finally, in 1392, the Ashikagas succeeded in bringing the land once more under one central authority, but this did not result in much gain for the average citizen. In fact, the peace under the Ashikaga shoguns was often less bearable than war, for the tax collector was more to be feared than the soldier or the plague and famine that in those days usually followed in the wake of war. It is claimed that in one form or another, the poor peasants had to pay about 70 percent of the produce of their fields as taxes. The money thus extorted from the people was not used to repair the damage of preceding wars but was squandered in extravagant and luxurious living by the shoguns and their followers. The third Ashikaga shogun, Yoshimitsu, for example, spent enormous sums on magnificent palaces and private residences. One writer states that his “Flower Palace” cost about five million dollars, with a single door costing as much as $150,000.

<header>STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM</header>

In this mad craze, he was followed by the upper classes who could—and more often could not—afford it; so that the city of Kyōto had at this time between six and seven thousand such extravagant residences. Even when the land was stricken with a severe plague and famine, as it was, *e.g.*, in the time of the eighth Ashikaga shōgun, Yoshimasa, when in two months about 80,000 people perished, this extravagant style of living was kept up.

It is therefore not strange that in such days the heart for quiet and industrial living was taken out of the common people and that industry and the constructive forces of life lagged. Nor is it strange that finally Japan was so impoverished that when, *e.g.*, in 1500 the Emperor Tsuchimikado II died, it was forty-four days before enough money could be gathered together to pay for the funeral expenses, while his successor, Nara II, had to wait twenty-one years before he had sufficient means to celebrate his coronation appropriately.

That this should be a period of religious decline goes without saying. Of course, in one way religion seemed to gain a firmer hold on the people just because of the adverse circumstances under which they lived. Especially those sects which held out to the common man the hope of a speedy entrance into paradise from this “vale of tears” found a rather congenial atmosphere in which to propagate their doctrines. In fact the pessimistic spirit of Buddhism as a whole, which was born in a world-weary civilization and which regards life as incurably evil and everything as evanescent, fitted in remarkably well with the temper of the age. The very woes of the people became a source of prosperity to the unscrupulous priests, who were usually quite ready to exchange their “spiritual treasures” for deeds to broad acres and stately manors. The pleasure-loving Yoshimitsu and his successors were indeed ever ready to spend goodly sums upon temples and temple decorations. Yoshimitsu was especially generous towards the Zen Sect and gave liberal gifts to the five great temples <note>fanes</note> of Kamakura (Go-zan) and the five great temples in Kyōto and its vicinity.

It further explains how the misery of the era allowed Buddhist sects to flourish by offering an escape from a "vale of tears," even as the priesthood profited from the people's suffering.</summary>

He went so far as to direct that each province should have its own great <term>Zen monastery</term>. The land owned by all the temples and monasteries was exempt from taxation, and many monasteries received funds from the special tax known as <term>Dansen</term>. Furthermore, certain ones directly received the customs duties and transit duties collected at the various barriers that were then being erected all over the land. Thus, *e.g.*, the great <term>Kōfukuji</term> of <term>Nara</term> received the customs of the port of <term>Hyōgo</term>.

With such favors extended to the Buddhist monks and priests, it is only natural that, outwardly at least, religion was flourishing in this age of bloodshed and misery. But a religion which lives on the fears and tears of its adherents is not a healthy product; and as a matter of fact, this period of the great Succession Wars and <term>Ashikaga</term> shōguns was not great in spiritual realities. Very few indeed were walking the <term>Noble Eightfold Path</term> of the founder. Not only had the Buddhist laypeople wandered far from this path, but the priests and monks seem to have gone even further astray. Even the new sects, which had been founded as a protest against the corruption of the old <term>Kyōto</term> sects, had gone the way of all the rest. The great monasteries were great only as formidable camps of <term>fighting monks</term>, for the military monk was the order of the day. Some authorities claim that in the early part of the sixteenth century, the Buddhist priests were, on the whole, the strongest political force in Japan. This is probably not an exaggeration, for it must be remembered that by this time all semblance of a central authority had vanished. The emperors were figureheads and even the shōguns were mere puppets, and the various feudal chiefs were each a law unto themselves. And often greater than the authority of these feudal chiefs was that of the rich monasteries with their extensive lands and their mountain fortresses. But, of course, the priests did not wield this authority as a unit nor in the interest of what might work for the good of the land. When they were not taking part in the general civil wars of the age on one side or the other, the various monasteries fought among them-

Hieizan, Miidera, and Kōfukuji had been in the habit of doing this for centuries, but now they were imitated by the new “centers of light.” The feud between the Jōdo and Nichiren sects was particularly fierce. Even the followers of the great Shinran apparently believed in the power of the mailed fist as much as the rest; for we read that toward the close of this age, a great monastery of this sect was able to successfully resist Nobunaga’s besieging army of sixty thousand.

But it was not only that the religious leaders of this day had exchanged their spiritual weapons for steel swords and spears, and that the foes they were fighting were their own brothers and not the hosts of sin and darkness, that marks the spiritual decline of the times. These “centers of light” were guilty of far more infamous deeds of darkness. We read, for example, of the abbots of monasteries who, after taking the customary vows of poverty and celibacy, spent their days in riotous living with immoral women. And the worst of it was that apparently nobody regarded this as wrong or inconsistent. In the middle of the fifteenth century, when famine and plague stalked through the land and daily between seven and eight hundred peasants fell by the wayside, it was quite common to dispose of the daughters of poor families by selling them to brothels. Meanwhile, the boys were frequently sold to the priests, “who shaved their eyebrows, powdered their faces, dressed them in female clothing, and put them to the most shameful uses. For since the days of Yoshimitsu, who had set an evil example in this as in so many other matters, the practice of pederasty had become very common, especially in the monasteries, although it was by no means confined to them.”

It would, however, not be correct to infer from what we have just said that Buddhism did not exert any influence for good during this period of bloodshed and misery. In fact, there are many cases in which Buddhist priests intervened with the mercy of Buddha to stay the wrath of men.
