It is true that the guilty occasionally escaped well-deserved punishment in this way, but more often the law from which they escaped was not the law of right, but only that of might. At that time, there were individual priests of real power here and there who exercised a great influence for good over the rulers of the day, helping to guide them through these stormy periods toward days of peace. Perhaps the most notable case of such an influence was the relationship between Ashikaga Takauji and the famous Zen priest Soseki. Not only did such men give spiritual consolation to these leaders during their trying times, but perhaps even more often they gave them solid advice regarding the affairs of state. Soseki especially seems to have tried to apply religious truths to the practical problems of life. He sought to show Takauji that mercy, patience, and serving others were not only expressions of the heart of Buddha, but also the quickest and surest road to a peaceful reign. “If one rises above the clouds, the moon can be seen without obstruction,” he once wrote to the founder of the Ashikaga <term>shogunate</term>. Little did he realize how few would be able to do this during the two centuries that followed.

Furthermore, it should be said to the credit of Buddhism that this period marks a wonderful development in pictorial art, *namely*, the rise of the great Zen school of painters, which has dominated the ideals of artists in one way or another until almost the present day. Of course, such an influence may not have been very far-reaching in that age, but the fact that this development of at least one of the fine arts was possible at all shows that, after all, there were individuals here and there who had time and taste for the higher aspects of life.

But after this has been said, it must be admitted that the period of the Ashikaga <term>shoguns</term> was generally one of religious decay. Buddhism, though outwardly strong, was really bankrupt morally and spiritually. Here and there a man—for example, Rennyō (1415–1499) of the <term>Shin Sect</term>—appeared and tried to make Buddhism a real spiritual force in society,

### F. *Religion in the Tokugawa Period*

1. *Reconstruction Days and the Catholic Mission.* — The long period of strife and bloodshed of which we have just spoken was followed finally by the great peace of the <term>Tokugawa shogunate</term>. By the middle of the sixteenth century, the movement had begun which was gradually to bring about a unification of the empire and restore peace and prosperity to a much-afflicted people. There are three great names around which the history of Japan centers during these reconstruction days, namely, Nobunaga, Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu. Of course, there were other great men who helped in the unification of the empire, but these three stand out like great peaks. We shall not stop to give even an outline of their lives, though it would not be out of place even in such a hurried review of the development of Buddhism; for while they were not men of religion, they had a great deal to do with determining the religious development of the empire for several centuries. All three were men who rose from humble backgrounds, and Hideyoshi,<sup>32</sup> the greatest of the trio, was the son of a simple peasant. A Japanese wit has well expressed their respective characteristics as follows: “If you do not sing,” said Nobunaga to a nightingale, “I will wring your neck.” “If you do not sing,” said Hideyoshi, “I will make you.” “If you do not sing,”

The nightingale finally did sing the song of peace and unity for Ieyasu, but each of the three had a major part in making it sing. Their work resulted in the great <term>Tokugawa shōgunate</term>, which ruled the land with such skill and firmness for about two and a half centuries that there was hardly so much as a dogfight on this blood-drenched soil.

It was just at the beginning of this reconstruction period that the <term>Catholic mission</term> under <term>Xavier</term> came to Japan in the year 1549. The mission landed from a Portuguese ship on the southern island of <term>Kyūshū</term>. The missionaries were well received, for in their wake came the merchants and traders with guns and other implements of war so highly valued by a warlike age. We are told that even the Buddhist priests received these Christian missionaries in a friendly spirit, for they regarded their religion as simply one more form of the comprehensive <term>Mahāyāna</term> teaching. And besides, they were not half so concerned with rivals in spiritual matters as they were with worldly power and prestige. It goes without saying that the Catholics were not willing to compromise with the Buddhists, though they did not take an openly hostile attitude until they had first gained favor with certain political factions to whom they looked for patronage and protection.

We thus find the missionary <term>Froez</term>, in the year 1568, seeking an interview with the great <term>Nobunaga</term>. At this conference, apparently, an understanding was reached by which the Catholics were to be utilized for fighting and crushing the Buddhist monasteries, which had incurred Nobunaga's enmity. We do not know the details of the arrangement, but it is a fact that Christianity in Japan at that time advanced by leaps and bounds and that Nobunaga in 1571 destroyed the three thousand monasteries which dotted <term>Mt. Hiei</term>. This wholesale destruction of the historic center and home of Buddhism was but the beginning of similar operations against the other monastic centers in the land. By the zealous Catholics, Nobunaga was regarded as the "true scourge of God." Nobunaga, however, was

He was not a Christian himself; he simply used the Jesuits to serve his purpose. His religion was his own ambition, as he built a great temple and placed a stone image of himself inside, which he expected the people to worship. But as in the case of vain Herod of old, his self-exaltation was quickly followed by his downfall. The hand of the assassin, prompted by his trusted general Akechi Mitsuhide, brought his career to a sudden end.

Nobunaga was succeeded by his friend and lieutenant, Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Hideyoshi was quick to preserve what Nobunaga had begun. He “made the nightingale sing,” not so much by threatening “to wring its neck” as by less drastic measures, though he also resorted to the sword quite often to carry out his program of unifying the nation. Hideyoshi, too, was no friend of the Buddhists and continued Nobunaga's work in reducing their military strength, though he showed some consideration for certain monasteries that he could use to his advantage. He had begun to suspect the Jesuits of political intrigue, and in 1597, he suddenly dropped his mask of friendship and had twenty-six of them crucified on Martyr’s Peak near Nagasaki. This did not mean that all Christians were banned, for he later entrusted the Christian general Konishi with a regiment of Christians to carry out a military expedition against Korea. However, he took the precaution of also sending some Buddhist troops with them, the idea being that the two groups would spy on each other and thus neutralize their influence. Like Nobunaga, Hideyoshi made his own ambition his religion, as seen by the fact that he erected a magnificent temple to the New War God, who was to be none other than himself.

Hideyoshi was succeeded by Ieyasu, the last of the great triad. Nobunaga and Hideyoshi had done the preparatory work for the unification of the empire; Ieyasu completed and consolidated it. He had only one great battle to fight—the famous Battle of Sekigahara—and then he could wait until the “nightingale sang” its song of peace. And sing it did, for Ieyasu became the founder of the illustrious

## RELIGION IN THE TOKUGAWA PERIOD

The Tokugawa shogunate provided peace and order to Japan for more than 250 years. While the emperor at Kyoto was permitted the nominal rule of the empire, it was an open secret that the shogun’s word at Yedo (Tokyo) was supreme. When Commodore Perry opened the closed doors of Japan in 1853, he dealt with the shogun as the real ruler of the land. The relative power of the emperor and shogun may be best understood when it is remembered that the annual allowance for the imperial family and its dependents was only 150,000 *koku* <note>A koku is a traditional Japanese unit of volume, used to measure rice and determine a domain's wealth, roughly equal to 180 liters.</note> of rice. This was not taken directly from the national revenue but was provided by the shogun from his own massive annual income of 4,000,000.

Ieyasu’s attitude toward religion differed from that of his two predecessors because he was himself a practicing Buddhist and took a relatively active interest in religious reform. Whether he was truly a religious man is another question. The truth of the matter seems to be that he was very liberal in his views and looked upon organized religion as a force that might help him in the affairs of state, for Ieyasu was, above all else, a shrewd statesman. That is why he was so close with the priest Tenkai, who became his right-hand man in controlling not only the Christians but also the Buddhists themselves. That is also why he encouraged the revival of Confucianism in Japan, for he saw in the Confucian philosophy of state and its emphasis on the spirit of loyalty a desirable force to help him in his great work of national unification.

2. *The Closing of the Doors and the Suppression of Christianity.* — It may seem strange at first glance that a man so liberal-minded should be the one who closed the doors of Japan to the outside world. The truth of the matter is that this policy, which seems so narrow to us today, was really intended to maintain peace and order. The only mistake was that the doors were kept closed for so long after the danger that Ieyasu sought to avoid had passed. It is safe to say that if his successors had been as open-minded as he was, they would have changed the policy long before they actually did. Ieyasu’s reason for cutting Japan off from the outside

His goal in the world was simply to enable him to consolidate his work of unification. He did not wish for any disturbing element to come in from the outside and upset the peace that had been bought at such a great cost. For too long, Japan had bled from the wounds of discord. Now, Christianity was undoubtedly a foreign element, and in the form in which it had been propagated in Japan from the beginning, it meddled far too much with the things that belong to Caesar <note>A reference to the biblical phrase "Render unto Caesar," implying political or state affairs.</note> to be allowed with impunity. The Buddhists, of course, meddled even more than the Christians did, but Buddhism had been the religion of the people for centuries and could not be opposed too much. It was enough to regulate it through the priests themselves. But Christianity was a new outside element, and if it was not willing to be merged into the national religion of the land, there was only one thing left, namely to exterminate it. An additional reason for this attitude toward Christianity was the fact that the Jesuits were the real agents of the Pope at Rome and that all true disciples were called upon to regard the Pope as not only the spiritual head but also as superior to earthly rulers in temporal matters. It is only natural that Ieyasu should see in the rising Catholic Church in Japan the seeds of future political troubles.

We find, accordingly, that step by step the regulations against Christianity became more and more severe until it was positively forbidden by law after 1611. Whereas under Nobunaga’s regime the Catholics were used as an instrument to fight Buddhist monasteries, Ieyasu turned the tables and used the Buddhist monks to suppress Christianity. In every city and village of the land, certain officials were set over well-defined districts, their sole duty being to spy out those suspected of being Christians. (It is an interesting fact that the second man to become a bishop in the Japan Methodist Church, Bishop Hiraiwa, is the son of such an official, the office having been hereditary in the family for several generations.)

The story of the suppression of Christianity in Japan has been told by others, and we do not need to repeat it here. We

One of the requirements of the time was the registration of every Japanese citizen as a member of one of the Buddhist sects. We might note in passing that this accounts for why, even today, the great majority of the people consider themselves Buddhists, though as individuals they may not care at all for the religion or know even the simplest outline of Buddhist teachings. But not all of these Catholic Christians recanted. Many of them died martyrs' deaths, and despite the government's close surveillance for 250 years, Christianity continued to resurface repeatedly. There are many people still living who saw the edict boards against Christianity along the empire's highways; and the brass crosses <note>These are fumi-e, or "trampling pictures," used to identify Christians by requiring them to step on sacred images.</note>, worn smooth by the feet of those who used them to prove they were not Christians, can still be seen in the nation's museums. However, when the edicts were finally removed, there were several thousand Christians in and around Nagasaki who had kept the faith. In other parts of the country, there are also Christians whose families have passed down precious Christian relics in secret from generation to generation.

3. *Partial Revival of Buddhism.* — We have stated above that the Buddhists were used as an instrument of the government to suppress Christianity. However, this does not mean that Buddhism under the Tokugawa shōguns ever regained its former vitality or even its outward prestige.<sup>33</sup> The truth is that the blow Nobunaga dealt to the famous Tendai monastery on Mt. Hiei proved to be almost fatal. And since Mt. Hiei was essentially the birthplace of all the great leaders who founded the leading sects, this blow was serious for Japanese Buddhism as a whole. It was all the more serious for the religion of Buddha when one remembers that other great centers of the faith were equally disrupted during the stormy times that preceded the "great calm."

# STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM

To return: Buddhism also recovered somewhat from the shock. In almost every one of the leading sects, men of real ability and character appeared. It is therefore customary among Buddhist writers to speak of the "Middle Reformers"—that is, the men who brought new prosperity to the various sects after the devastating wars of the Ashikaga period. Thus, for example, the Tendai Sect, while crushed in and around Kyōto, began to show new activity in the Kwantō with Nikkō and Yedo <note>Yedo, also spelled Edo, was the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate and is the former name of Tōkyō.</note> as centers. In the Shingon Sect, we see the New School party growing in power and influence. The Rinzai and Sōtō branches of the Zen Sect had suffered most severely from the wars because, as we have said, these sects had many military men as adherents; the old law that "he who takes the sword shall perish by the sword" held as true in Japan as elsewhere. 

But when peace was restored, these sects became quite flourishing, especially in outward matters, for it was the fashion of the day among the various feudal lords—who were usually military men—to bestow much property upon Zen temples and monasteries. The Jōdo Sect seemed specially favored from time to time by the Tokugawa shōguns, and it recovered much of its former glory. It possessed strong temples such as the famous Chionin of Kyōto and the Zōjōji of Tōkyō and counted many men of real ability among its priests. What is true of the Jōdo is equally true of the Shin Sect. Its great temples built in the modern period—including some during the past few decades—are numerous. The headquarters of the two Hongwanji branches in Kyōto are especially noteworthy as magnificent specimens of temple architecture. The Nichiren Sect also had its reformers and shared with others a certain degree of prosperity during the peaceful days of the Tokugawa period.

This era of renewal even saw the introduction of a new sect from China: the Ōbaku branch of the Zen Sect, founded in 1659 by a Chinese priest named Ingen and by Chinese refugees who came to Japan after the fall of the Ming dynasty. This sect has never attracted many adherents, but it has exerted a great influence and counts

numbered among its few followers some of the strongest men in Japan. The distinguishing feature of this sect is its use of modern Chinese for its scriptures, whereas other sects still use ancient Chinese—though in very recent years, they have begun to use Japanese translations for the general public.

However, despite all that has been said about the renewal of Buddhism during the Tokugawa period, it cannot be claimed that the religion of Buddha ever again reached the heights it had attained during the great period of religious awakening in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Despite this outward prosperity and activity, which in some cases led to the formation of new subdivisions, the period as a whole cannot be regarded as a great era for Buddhism in terms of actual spiritual influence and strength. The truth of the matter is that the sources of spiritual life during this age were actually outside of Buddhism—specifically, in Confucianism.

4. *Neo-Confucianism*.—Confucian thought has influenced Japan since its earliest days, even before Buddhism was introduced in the sixth century. While this is true, it cannot be said that Confucianism was the dominant current of life in this land before the Tokugawa era. Instead, it was like several minor tributaries feeding the main stream; its influence was felt particularly in the realm of practical ethics. In fact, as previously stated, much of the ethical teaching in Japanese Buddhism is really just a restatement of Confucian ethics. That is to say, the strongest influence that Confucianism exerted on Japan before the Tokugawa period was channeled through Buddhism.

Now, it is a peculiar coincidence that at the very time when Buddhism in Japan burst forth into the four great sects of the Kamakura period—namely, the rise of the Jōdo, Zen, Shin, and Nichiren sects—Confucianism in China was being reshaped by the Neo-Confucian schools of *Shushi* (Chinese: Chu Hi, 1130–1200) and *Ōyōmei* (Chinese: Wang-Yang-Ming, 1472–1528). The foundations for the *Ōyōmei* school were actually laid by *Riku-Shōsan* (1042–1094); so, while *Ōyōmei*, who gave the school its permanent influence, belongs

# STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM

Relating to a slightly later period, we can say that these Neo-Confucian schools emerged around the same time as the great Buddhist awakening in Japan. This specific type of Confucianism was destined to overshadow Buddhism during the Tokugawa period. The <term>Shushi</term> school, in particular, became the dominant force in Japan's official circles, as <term>Ieyasu</term> established it as the authorized system of education. It became so deeply entrenched that anyone who opposed its teachings was considered a traitor to the state.

This reshaping of Confucianism in China into the <term>Shushi</term> and <term>Ōyōmei</term> schools was actually more than just a restatement of an old system; it was, in fact, a syncretism of Confucianism and Buddhism. Even as far back as the days of <term>Mencius</term> and shortly thereafter, Confucianism was being strongly influenced by <term>Taoism</term>. That is to say, Confucian scholars, while holding onto the practical ethics of the <term>Five Relations</term>, began to seek a metaphysical and religious foundation for their morality. Then, with the arrival of <term>Zen</term> philosophy in the sixth century A.D. and the general development of <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> in China, the movement in Confucianism from the external and formal toward the internal and spiritual continued. This was the era when Chinese Buddhism integrated many of the practical teachings of Confucianism, which have ever since formed the practical ethics found in Chinese and Japanese Buddhism.

However, it was not until the time of <term>Riku-Shōsan</term>, <term>Shushi</term>, and <term>Ōyōmei</term> that Confucianism developed a true metaphysical and religious basis for its teachings. These philosophers and their followers were constantly discussing <term>Ri</term> and <term>Ki</term> and the relationship between the two. While the older Confucianism always focused on human relationships, these Neo-Confucianists were more concerned with the problem of the relationship between the human and the divine, the finite and the infinite, and the phenomenal world and the noumenal world. In Confucianism, <term>Ri</term> became what the <term>Tao</term>, or Way, was in Taoism, and what the Eternal and Monistic Substance or the Rational Principle was in Mahāyāna Buddhism. And the <term>Ki</term> in Confucianism fills much the same role

which the transitory and phenomenal world occupies in Buddhism. The chief difference is that the "<term>Ri</term>" in Confucianism is usually more than a mere Rational Principle; it frequently possesses a moral quality. That is, it is the personification of Moral Wisdom rather than the personification of mere Reason. In the writings of some authors, the conception of this Moral Wisdom comes very near to the conception of a personal God, though in others it remains rather pantheistic. And as the Absolute is thought of in terms of Moral Wisdom rather than mere Reason, the relation of man to the Absolute is also thought of more as a moral relation—*i.e.*, man’s chief duty is expressed in terms of righteous conduct rather than in terms of right knowledge, as is usually the case in Buddhism.

While these two Neo-Confucian schools are alike in that both are the expression of a union of Confucian and Buddhist thought, they differ somewhat from each other in other respects. The <term>Shushi</term> school regards itself as a true transmitter of orthodox Confucianism and consequently lays a great deal of stress upon a knowledge of the classics and erudition in general. The <term>Ōyōmei</term> school, on the other hand, while claiming to be a follower of Confucius in spirit, is more free in what it regards as orthodox. It does not lay as much stress upon erudition as upon intuitive knowledge. Much like the <term>Zen</term> Sect in Buddhism, which holds that the true teaching of the master is transmitted from heart to heart and not through books, the <term>Ōyōmei</term> school holds that books are only guideposts to the truth and that the heart must find the truth within itself. Or, as <term>Kumazawa Banzan</term>, one of the chief representatives of the <term>Ōyōmei</term> school in Japan, so well put it when he compared books and the teachings of wise men of the past to the footprints of a rabbit which one wishes to catch. Obviously, the footprints are a help in catching the rabbit, but they are not the rabbit itself. Once one has caught the rabbit, the footprints are no longer necessary. It is not our purpose to give here a detailed account of the introduction of this Neo-Confucianism, nor of its real place in the life of Japan. As already stated before, it was brought in gradually by priests of the Zen Sect who have always been among its chief exponents. The first representatives appear to have been two Chinese Buddhist scholars, Sōgen and Ichizan, the former coming to Japan in the latter part of the thirteenth century. These were followed by other Chinese teachers and by Japanese scholars who studied in China, but the political strife and bloodshed which caused Buddhism to degenerate in Japan also kept Confucianism from gaining much of a hold. It was not, therefore, until the famous trio—Nobunaga, Hideyoshi, and Ieyasu—had restored peace that Neo-Confucianism became fully established in the person of the scholarly Fujiwara Seigwa (1561–1610), who is usually regarded as the first real exponent of the Shushi school in Japan. He was followed by Hayashi Razan (1583–1672), also a descendant of the great Fujiwara family. Both these illustrious scholars had been Buddhist scholars, and the latter became a Buddhist priest after retiring from his position in the Tokugawa government. His opposition to Christianity was pronounced, and the account of his interview with one of the Jesuit missionaries is of special interest to the student of Christianity in Japan. Other great lights regarded as disciples of the Shushi school in Japan are such men as the scholarly Muro Kyuso, the famous educator Kaibara Ekiken, Yamazaki Anzai, and a whole host of strong and earnest men.

Just as the Shushi school had been recognized in China as the orthodox school by the government during the Ming era (1402–1644), so it was made, as we have said above, the authorized system of education by the Tokugawa <term>shōguns</term>. Ieyasu and his successors encouraged this teaching because

because of its great emphasis on loyalty and obedience which a subject owed to the ruling powers. This teaching became so general and was so deeply planted in the Japanese mind that we see its effect even today in the intense loyalty and patriotism so characteristic of the people of Japan. In fact, it was the spirit of this teaching, so zealously fostered by the Tokugawa shoguns, which finally—in the teachings of the Mito branch of the Shushi school—resulted in the overthrow of the shoguns and the restoration of the emperor as the real ruler of Japan.

But while the Shushi school was recognized and encouraged as the official teaching, and while opponents to this system were often suppressed, there were in Japan—as there had been in China before—men whose intellectual life could not be confined to a fixed rut by government edicts or persecutions. These became the followers of Ōyōmei and constituted the Ōyōmei school. The first and in many respects the greatest of these was Nakae Tōjiu, the "Sage of Ōmi." In his philosophy of life, Japanese thought reaches its loftiest form in many respects, and it is not strange that he is still regarded with great reverence. Some say he was really the only true sage Japan has produced. His conception of the nature of "*Ri*" and man’s relation to it and to his fellow man was indeed a close approach to the best Christian thought, and should be a real guide to bring men to Christ. Another man of this school was Nakae’s greatest disciple, Kumazawa Banzan, who was perhaps the most independent thinker of all these Neo-Confucianists and whose views on Buddhism and Christianity are of special interest.

The Ōyōmei school, like the Shushi school, counted many of the leading men of the Tokugawa era among its exponents. In fact, the stream of Confucianism in this school remained purer and fresher than in the official Shushi school, for the latter was too closely restricted by official regulations to allow the freedom so essential for spiritual life. The official school became truly corrupt and helped impose upon Japan that formalism <note>34</note> and dead uniformity so characteristic of much of life during the Tokugawa period.

In addition to these two Neo-Confucian schools, found in both China and Japan, a third school of Confucianism known as the Classical school developed in Japan during the late seventeenth century. The founders of this school were Yamaga Soko and Itō Jinsai; the latter is of the greatest importance, though the former is of particular interest because he is regarded as the father of *Bushidō*, “*The Way of the True Knight.*” This school may be described as a protest against the emphasis that both the *Shushi* and *Ōyōmei* schools were placing upon the life of thought as opposed to the life of action and emotion. That is, Confucianism was becoming much like Buddhism, which conceives of life too much in terms of the intellect and not enough in terms of the feelings and the will. The school deserves to be called the Classical school because it made a conscious effort to return to Confucius and even back to the life-ideal of the wise rulers before him, of whom he was only a transmitter. However, after all, the philosophy of life held by the chief representatives of this school is a great advance over the older Confucianism. This is particularly true of the philosophy of Ogiu Sōrai. Though he claims to go back to the teachings of the sages who preceded Confucius, it is clear that his lofty conception of the divine and man’s relation to it and to his fellow man is more than just an explanation of these ancient texts; rather, it shows that, as the keen scholar he was, he was a true heir of all the ages. Ogiu Sōrai and Nakae Tōjiu represent the best blending of what is loftiest in the teachings of the old philosophies and religions of Japan. Other great names in this Classical school are Itō Togai and Dazai Shundai, the latter being of special importance as a vigorous opponent of Buddhism.

Of less importance in the life of Japan during the Tokugawa period than the three schools of Confucianism mentioned above is a fourth one, known as the Eclectic school. The tendency toward eclecticism is always strong when too many schools of philosophy and religion occupy the field, and there were a number of such movements in Japan at this time. But

This Eclectic school of Confucianism must be distinguished from the others because it claimed to draw its material only from the existing Confucian schools. However, when we remember that the schools of Neo-Confucianism are themselves a syncretism of Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism, this so-called Eclectic Confucian school is actually a broader form of eclecticism.

Now, from this brief summary of Confucianism in Japan during the Tokugawa era, it is clear that Buddhism did indeed have a strong rival. For while, as we have said, this Confucian thought was first introduced by Buddhist priests as a part of Buddhist teachings, the movement gradually became independent of its nurturing source and, in some cases, even opposed it. In fact, some of the most bitter enemies Japanese Buddhism ever had were among these great Confucian scholars who came to Confucianism by way of Buddhism. Gradually, the intellectual leadership and the guidance in matters of moral education passed from the hands of the Buddhists to the hands of men who drew their inspiration from Confucian thought. The role of the Buddhist priests was increasingly limited to matters pertaining to the afterlife and to taking care of the bodies of the dead, rather than directing people's daily lives. The official world in Japan, the military classes, and men of affairs had little to do with Buddhism; thus, it increasingly became the religion of the uneducated masses, who knew nothing of its higher teachings or its past glory. Even the best minds within Buddhism could not cope with this new situation. When challenged by progressive Confucianists to state their religious views in terms applicable to Japanese life, they could not do so satisfactorily. The simple truth of the matter is that the Buddhist philosophy of life—being itself the expression of a world-weary civilization—cannot be made a constructive force in an age of reconstruction.<sup>35</sup>

5. *Neo-Shintō Opposition to Buddhism.* — But Neo-Confucianism was not the only force with which Buddhism had to share the field after the rise of the Tokugawa shogunate. There also developed what might be called a Neo-Shintō.

We saw how, at the beginning of the ninth century, Shintō and Buddhism were merged into one system known as Ryōbu Shintō. What this really meant was that Shintō was virtually swallowed up by Buddhism. This does not mean that Shintō disappeared entirely—for the religion of the masses within Buddhism was often more like the old Shintō than Buddhism—but rather that Buddhist thought dominated the minds of the intellectual sections of society. However, when Buddhism was weakened by the civil wars that preceded the Tokugawa age, the spirit of native Shintō came to life again. It is somewhat difficult to explain this, but one factor in the matter seems to have been a growing national consciousness caused, on the one hand, by the influx of Neo-Confucianism and, on the other hand, by the forced unification of the empire under Ieyasu. That is, the growing knowledge of Chinese matters naturally led men to think of Japanese matters by way of comparison. We know, *for example*, that Hayashi Razan and other Confucian scholars went so far as to develop a theory of a relationship between Japan's first emperor, Jimmu Tennō, and the Chinese Emperor Taikaku of the Shu era, and that these views led Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628–1700) to gather many great scholars into an institution called the “Shōkō Kwan” for the purpose of investigating Japanese history. It was these scholars of the Mito branch of the Shushi school who wrote the *Dai Nihon Shi*, or “Great Japanese History,” which was to play such a significant role in the Restoration of 1868. But this movement in the Mito school was only a part of a wider movement; namely, a movement to understand and restore Japanese traditions.

A better knowledge of Japanese history showed men that Buddhism, which had dominated Japan for so long, was actually a foreign import and that it could be justly blamed for playing a major role in the civil wars which had devastated these beautiful islands for centuries. In fact, it could be argued with a degree of fairness that Buddhism had broken the spirit of native Shintō, the heart of which was loyalty to the ruler and a deep patriotism. Of course,

Even among Buddhists themselves, there was an investigation into the facts of the past that helped weaken its hold on Japan and shook people’s faith in its authority. Attacked from all sides and on historical grounds, some of the more earnest priests took a more critical attitude toward their own religion, and we see what we might call the birth of higher criticism in Japanese Buddhism. Two learned men, Tominaga Nakamoto and Hattori Tenyū, were chosen to make a special study of the Buddhist canon; and particularly the work of the former, though attracting little attention at the time, laid the foundations for future criticism. We shall speak of his work in the chapter on the Buddhist Canon, but we wish to state here simply that he reached the general conclusion that Mahayana Buddhism was not the pure Buddhism of its founder. It is only natural that such views should have a rather serious effect on the minds of those who placed all their emphasis on external authority.

The Tokugawa shogunate itself, which had been instrumental in establishing the Shushi school, was affected by these developments. If Buddhism was seen as a usurper in the spiritual world, then the shogunate itself was certainly an even greater criminal; for had it not robbed the emperors in Kyoto of all real authority? Little did Tokugawa Mitsukuni imagine that when he founded the “Shoko Kwan” at Mito and encouraged scholars to study Japanese history, he was helping to bring about the overthrow of his own successors. We should not say that this was the only factor in the situation; long before it was viewed as a usurper, the Tokugawa shogunate had decayed and lost control over the powerful clans in the south. Nevertheless, the leaders from these southern clans, who took the lead in the movement that ended in the Restoration of 1868, drew much of their inspiration from the Mito scholars. The Restoration was, of course, accelerated by the arrival of Commodore Perry’s ships in 1853, but it was not actually caused by this, as some Westerners like to imagine. This was really a very minor factor in a very complex movement, the core of which lay in the religious and philosophical life of the nation during the two preceding centuries.

### G. *Buddhism in the Meiji Era*

With the end of the Tokugawa shogunate and the restoration of the emperor as the actual ruler of the empire, Buddhism entered a new world. Despite the opposition it faced during the Tokugawa period, and despite losing its intellectual and moral leadership to men raised in a Confucian environment, it still held a position as a state religion. Even the fierce advocates of native Shinto could not succeed in removing Buddhism from its official status as the national religion or in breaking the union of Shinto and Buddhism. However, a few years after the Restoration—specifically in the year 1870—Buddhism was finally disestablished as the state religion and separated from Shinto. Instead, Shinto was divided into two parts: Shinto as a religion, and Shinto as a system of rites and ceremonies to be used on state occasions as the official form for such events. This second division (<term>Shinshoku</term>) takes charge of all national shrines and the tombs of great statesmen and patriots, which are not officially regarded as having any religious significance. In fact, the Constitution of Japan recognizes the principle of religious liberty, and so puts all religions on the same footing before the law. 

However, the fact that the government draws its ceremonies for state occasions from Shinto and has Shinto priests officiate at such times, along with the fact that the great Shinto shrines are designated as national shrines, gives the people the impression that the government regards Shinto as the state religion. The distinction in Shinto mentioned above has no meaning to the average Japanese person, and all the explanations from government officials as to what they mean by it have not changed matters much. The simple fact is that the general public regards the great Shinto shrines as having religious significance and as more than simply nurseries for patriotism.<note>36</note>

As a result of this disestablishment of Buddhism as a state religion, it has found it rather difficult to readjust itself. Throughout its history in Japan, it had depended a great deal upon government patronage, and frequently its interests had been identical with those of the rulers of the nation. Thus, being cast off and thrown upon its own resources naturally led to many hardships. A great many temples have found it impossible to continue and have been abandoned, and still more are in a dilapidated condition. Anyone who visits the numerous beauty spots in Japan so frequently occupied by Buddhist temples is struck by the fact that their glory belongs to a past age rather than to the present. ...many repeated prayers, but rather groups of middle school students out on an autumn or spring excursion with little knowledge or interest in the ideals for which these decaying temples stood in the past. Of course, there are certain parts of the country where these temples still represent the authority of the past; this is especially true in some of the more traditional sections on the west coast of the main island. However, no serious student of Buddhist history would claim that Buddhism plays anything like the role in Japanese life that it played up to or even throughout the Tokugawa period.

In certain circles, however, attempts have been made to reform Buddhism and restore it to its former place in Japanese life. Two or three of the leading sects seem to have rediscovered their purpose and are succeeding fairly well in meeting the economic pressures that have come over Japan in our day. Some of the more progressive leaders say that the disestablishment of Buddhism as the state religion is actually a good thing and will enable it to fulfill its mission as a spiritual force in society. These sects are even trying to expand their field of activity by carrying on mission work in the newer portions of the empire and by trying to revitalize the declining Buddhism of Korea and China. New methods of outreach are being adopted, taken directly from Christianity. Consequently, on all sides we see the emergence of Young Men’s Buddhist Associations, Buddhist Sunday Schools, Women’s Societies, orphanages, homes for ex-convicts, and so on. Even street preaching and special “evangelistic campaigns” are becoming quite common, and the content of some of the sermons and hymns is sometimes taken directly from Christianity, with the name Buddha simply taking the place of Christ. It must be added, however, that recent scandals involving the headquarters of almost every one of the leading sects have gone a long way toward undermining this forward movement, and many earnest Buddhists are wondering what the future of their religion will be in Japan.

However, these reform efforts face significant challenges due to recent administrative scandals within the major Buddhist sects.</summary>

### H. *The Buddhist Sects and Their Numerical Strength*

In the closing chapter, we will discuss more fully the place of Buddhism in the life of present-day Japan and its outlook for the future. At this point, however, it might be useful to give the names of the various sects and subdivisions of Japanese Buddhism as well as their relative strength.

1. *The Twelve Sects.* — Following the traditions of Chinese Buddhism, Japanese Buddhism has long held that twelve is the proper number of sects. This has necessitated a readjustment from time to time as old sects died out and new ones came into existence. The old way of counting them, when given in their chronological order, was as follows:

1. Sanron introduced in 625 <term>A.D.</term>
2. Jōjitsu introduced in 625 <term>A.D.</term>
3. Hossō introduced in 625 or 653 <term>A.D.</term>
4. Kusha introduced in 658 <term>A.D.</term>
5. Kegon introduced in 736 <term>A.D.</term>
6. Ritsu introduced in 754 <term>A.D.</term>
7. Tendai introduced in 805 <term>A.D.</term>
8. Shingon introduced in 805 <term>A.D.</term>
9. Jōdo founded in 1175 <term>A.D.</term>
10. Zen introduced in 1191 <term>A.D.</term>
11. Shin founded in 1224 <term>A.D.</term>
12. Nichiren founded in 1253 <term>A.D.</term>

Four of these sects have died out—namely, the Sanron, Jōjitsu, Kusha, and Ritsu. Their places have been filled by regarding the three main divisions of the Zen Sect as independent sects and counting the small Yūdzū Nembutsu and Ji sects, so that the current list is as follows:

(The "Priests" in the second column are some of them also included in the third column and others in the fourth, so they are actually counted twice in the figures above.)

It is impossible to say exactly how many followers the various sects have. This is due to two reasons. First is the fact that during the <term>Tokugawa period</term>, everyone was required to register at one of the temples; thus, many still call themselves Buddhists even though they have practically no connection with any temple or sect now that this registration is no longer required. The other reason why it is impossible to give the number of followers is the simple fact that nothing special is required to be a Buddhist. Not even the simple confession, "I take refuge in the <term>Buddha</term>, the <term>Law</term>, and the <term>Priesthood</term>," once used as a test of discipleship, is required of the average people who are claimed as Buddhists. The numerical strength of Buddhists in Japan today, therefore, can be measured only by such figures as we have given above; even this is rather misleading for the simple fact that practically all those numerous temples are an inheritance from the past, and it is exceedingly doubtful whether many of them will be maintained or rebuilt as economic pressure continues to increase.

# CHAPTER IV

## THE BUDDHIST CANON AS KNOWN IN JAPAN

The <term>Christian Bible</term> is a collection of books, sixty-six in all; the <term>Buddhist Canon</term> as known in <term>Japan</term> is a good-sized library. It is the boast of Buddhist priests that their sacred Canon contains no less than 6,771 books. This may be an overstatement of the facts, but it is still true that the Canon of <term>Northern Buddhism</term> does contain more than 5,000 books, which according to <term>Nanjo's Catalogue</term> of the <term>Chinese Tripitaka</term> represent 1,662 different works. <term>Edkins</term> in his "Chinese Buddhism" states that the Buddhist scriptures in some of the standard Chinese versions are about 700 times as large as the New Testament, and as Japanese Buddhists include books not found in the Chinese collections, their scriptures are even more voluminous. <note>1. Reference to the comparative size of the Chinese scriptures.</note> The <term>Pali Canon</term> of <term>Southern Buddhism</term>, made known to Western students through the splendid efforts of the <term>Pali Text Society</term>, is only about twice as large as the English Bible. A simple calculation would then show that the Northern Canon is about one hundred times larger than this Pali Canon. When it is remembered that even this relatively small Bible of Southern Buddhists is still very little known by Western students—though the great bulk of the scholarly work done on Buddhism has been performed on the Buddhism of the South—it will not seem strange to say that the massive Northern Canon is practically an unknown library to all but a handful of scholars. It will take the untiring efforts of several generations of students before even the more valuable of these many books can be made accessible to scholars who are not familiar with the puzzling Chinese characters. Strictly speaking, of course, there is really no such thing as a Canon of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>, for the line between books included and those excluded is not drawn very clearly. In fact, some of the books included are merely titles and are no longer in existence, whereas there are books used in <term>Japan</term> by the various sects which are not ordinarily included in the Canon, but which for all practical purposes have replaced the canonical writings.<note>2. Reference to books used in Japan that have supplanted canonical writings; specific footnote text not provided in the original transcript.</note> Throughout the history of Northern Buddhism, the Canon has constantly been changing; old books once included have disappeared, and new ones have taken their place. This becomes very clear from a study of the introduction to <term>Nanjō's Catalogue</term>, referred to above. A few facts about the thirteen existing catalogues of the <term>Chinese Canon</term> (or Canons) may be summarized as follows:

The oldest existing catalogue dates from about 520 AD. It mentions 2,213 works, of which 276 can be identified with those in existence at the present day.

The second oldest catalogue (594 AD) mentions 2,257 distinct works in 5,310 books. This does not mean, however, that these were all in existence at that time, as some were known only as names.

The third catalogue (597 AD) lists 1,076 different works in 3,325 books as admitted to the Canon at that time. Perhaps the reason why two lists published so closely together differ so widely in the number of books given is that the third catalogue includes only the books then positively known to be in existence, while the second catalogue includes all books once recognized as canonical, even though many had been lost.

The fourth catalogue (602 AD) mentions 2,109 works in 5,058 books.

The fifth catalogue (664 AD) lists 2,487 works in 8,476 books, but of the works actually in existence at that time

From the summary above, then, it should be clear, as we have said, that strictly speaking there is no such thing as a true <term>Canon</term> of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>. It would almost seem as if, at times, any book produced by Buddhists was given a place within its wide boundaries. The only reason the <term>Canon</term> has become more or less fixed in the modern period is because Chinese Buddhism has declined and ceased to produce any literature of value. In Japan, where Buddhism remained vital for longer, valuable books were produced later; as stated above, there is a tendency to include these among the sacred scriptures of Buddhism even though they may not be technically regarded as part of the <term>Canon</term>.

The standard edition of the <term>Canon</term> held in Japan today is probably the one published by a group of Japanese scholars in 1885, known as *The Official Canon of Japan* (<term>Dai Nippon Kōtei Daizōkyō</term>). It is a somewhat critical work carried out by men who have had some training in modern methods of criticism, though it should not be assumed that it will satisfy future scholars. It is based upon four older editions published in Korea and China from the eleventh to the sixteenth centuries. These are the following:

(1) The <term>Kōraibon</term>, published in Korea at the beginning of the eleventh century and containing 1,521 different works in 6,467 (or 6,589) books. A copy of this was brought to Japan between 1469–1486 and is in the possession of the <term>Zōjōji</term> of Shiba Park, Tōkyō. Only two volumes are missing from the original collection.

(2) The <term>Minzō</term> (Chinese, <term>Min Tsan</term>) edition of the sixteenth century, consisting of 1,662 works. This edition is very widely circulated in both China and Japan, and a copy of essentially the same work is found in the India Office in London.

(3) The <term>Sōzō</term> edition, which appeared in China in 1239 and contains 1,421 works in 5,714 (or 5,916) books. This was brought to Japan in 1275 and is located at the <term>Zōjōji</term> in Tōkyō.

(4) The <term>Genzō</term> edition, which appeared in China at the

The first copy of this standard edition of the <term>Japanese Canon</term> to be sent abroad was sent to the <term>Bodleian Library</term> at Oxford, where Western students have access to it; but as it is written in difficult <term>Chinese characters</term>, it is not very likely that its contents will become public knowledge very soon. Even in the university libraries of Japan, these sacred books have a forbidding air about them, and none but a few students of Oriental philosophy ever look into them. A few copies are finding their way into the older Buddhist lands of Asia, and there, among the more zealous disciples of the <term>Buddha</term>, they may be read with interest; but for the average modern student in the East, the majority of these books have only an antiquarian interest. A few of the books, as we shall see later, still exercise an influence over certain sections of Japanese society, and these may be said to constitute the real Bible of <term>Japanese Buddhism</term>.

From what we have said thus far, it is already clear that there is an enormous difference between the scriptures of <term>Northern Buddhism</term> and those of <term>Southern Buddhism</term>, which are best preserved in the <term>Pali Canon</term>. At the very least, there is the obvious difference in size. But the difference is more fundamental than simply that of size; it pertains to the content equally well. The <term>Northern Canon</term> contains practically everything found in the <term>Pali Canon</term>, but it also contains a great many treasures and a great deal of rubbish peculiar to itself. The <term>Pali Canon</term> was, of course, a growth and represents several centuries of development. That is, it is not simply the teachings of the <term>Buddha</term> and his immediate disciples handed down from generation to generation, but it is the expression of the religious experience of several centuries, guided more or less by the original impression communicated by <term>Gautama</term>. The <term>Northern Canon</term>, however, is more than the evolution of a few centuries of <term>Indian thought</term>; it is really a library of books written during a period extending over many centuries and by people of varying civilizations on subjects as varied as are the interests and whims of

Their contents vary from the most profound speculations regarding the nature of the <term>Absolute</term> to the most childish nonsense about the trivial things of life. One critic speaks of the <term>Northern Canon</term> as a house in which nothing old and worn out has ever been thrown away, even though many new things have been added from time to time. The reverent Buddhist, however, sees in this bewildering variety a wise provision for the varied needs of humanity. He says the <term>Buddhist Bible</term> is like a well-stocked apothecary shop, and the wise druggist knows which of the countless bottles and cases he should turn to for the specific disease he is called upon to treat.

As a result of this conglomeration of books written over a period of many centuries and by thinkers of different civilizations, it is not surprising to find the most flagrantly contradictory teachings and practices represented. We speak of the differences among Christians, and an <term>Abelard</term> was able to write his <term>*Sic et non*</term> regarding the Catholic Church, but these differences are rather small when compared with what we find in these scriptures of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>. The differences and contradictions extend to the very fundamentals of fundamentals. In fact, there is as much agreement between the varied systems of religion and philosophy which have occupied the hearts and minds of men in the West during the past 2,500 years as there is in the teachings of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>. There is nothing that has ever entered the heart or mind of man which does not find its counterpart somewhere in these Buddhist scriptures.

And yet, in spite of these glaring contradictions in the <term>Buddhist Bible</term> in both essentials and non-essentials, all Buddhists claim to follow the teachings of the founder <term>Gautama</term>, though it should be added that at least one sect in Japan, the <term>Shin Sect</term>, does not lay very much stress upon this point.

To say, as some modern Buddhist apologists do, that <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term> is simply the developed form of what was really contained in seed form in Gautama’s teachings, is to say that a system may develop to a point where it is practically the exact opposite of what it was at the beginning. That there is a historical connection between <term>Southern Buddhism</term> and <term>Northern Buddhism</term> is beyond doubt, as we have shown in Chapter I, and in that sense, the latter is, of course, a development of the former. But the development was so revolutionary in some points that often the new version remained Buddhist in name only. Original Buddhism, as we saw in Chapter I, was itself a development of <term>Brahmanism</term>, whose fundamental ideas about the <term>Absolute</term> and the human soul it rejected, though it accepted other teachings of <term>Brahmanism</term>, such as the doctrine of <term>Karma</term> and <term>Transmigration</term>. Some 500 years later, however, Buddhism had developed (or degenerated, if one speaks from the standpoint of Gautama’s views) to the point where it once again affirmed these very concepts which it had originally either denied or ignored as idle speculations. In short, the old theories about God, the soul, and the afterlife reasserted themselves, and they have always played a vital part in at least some of the sects of <term>Northern Buddhism</term>, as we shall see in the following chapters. Many minor things were added to this change in fundamentals from time to time; so that gradually the sacred Canon gathered up into itself, like a rolling snowball, everything which Buddhism encountered on its way through central and eastern Asia.

Of course, few Buddhists will admit there is such a radical difference between the teachings of the founder and the later doctrines of <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term>. <page-num>165</page-num>
<header>THE BUDDHIST CANON</header>

The plant differs from the seed; otherwise, they rely on a convenient theory long held by <term>Northern Buddhists</term>. This theory suggests that the founder taught all of these varied and apparently contradictory doctrines, but that some of them must be viewed as provisional and adapted teachings, while others are the pure and perfect truths.

The <term>Buddhist Canon</term> as a whole is therefore divided by Northern Buddhists into two major categories. These are the Little Vehicle (*Sanskrit*, *<term>Hīnayāna</term>*, *Japanese*, *<term>Shōjō</term>*) and the Great Vehicle (*Sanskrit*, *<term>Mahāyāna</term>*, *Japanese*, *<term>Daijō</term>*). Many Japanese writers establish three divisions, specifically adding the Provisional *Mahāyāna* (*Japanese*, *<term>Gondaijō</term>*). A few writers even speak of five Vehicles and, in a broader sense, it is sometimes said that there are as many Vehicles of salvation as there are differences between the various living beings to be saved. Normally, however, the division of the Buddhist Canon into <term>Hīnayāna</term> and <term>Mahāyāna</term> is the accepted standard. These terms were created by <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhists and clearly show the controversy that raged during the early centuries of the Christian era regarding the founder's actual teachings. The second half of the two words, *yāna*, means Vehicle—a vehicle of salvation that carries people safely from this life into the next and better life. *Hīnayāna* means Little Vehicle and is actually a term of contempt. The name indicates the nature of the teachings this vehicle of salvation contains: the "Little Teachings," or the undeveloped and provisional doctrines. *Mahāyāna*, on the other hand, means Great Vehicle and is a term of boastful superiority. It contains the "Great Teachings"—the full and perfect doctrines that the master is believed to have taught after his disciples had been prepared for them through their knowledge of the *Hīnayāna*. We will explain later how this theory was developed in more detail by the founder of the *<term>T’ien T’ai</term> Sect* in China, in what is known as the Five Periods of <term>Gautama</term>’s ministry.

divisions called <term>Pitakas</term>, or Baskets (Japanese, <term>Zō</term>). Some say that the divisions were called Pitakas because, when scholars classified the sacred scriptures, the books were put into baskets. A better explanation is to see in this term the idea of how the scriptures were handed down from one generation to another. In the East, it is a common custom to have workmen stationed in a line who pass a series of baskets from man to man, filled with materials to be moved from one place to another. (It is similar to a bucket line in a fire drill.) So, we are to understand by this term Pitaka a long line of teachers who have handed down the teachings of the founder of Buddhism to generation after generation.

The three Pitakas, or <term>Tri-pitaka</term>, are the following:
1. <term>Sūtra-pitaka</term> (Japanese, <term>Kyōzō</term>).
2. <term>Vinaya-pitaka</term> (Japanese, <term>Ritsuzō</term>).
3. <term>Abhidharma-pitaka</term> (Japanese, <term>Ronzō</term>).

The <term>Sūtra-pitaka</term> contains teachings in the form of collected sayings, dialogues between the Buddha and his disciples, and sermons with stories and parables which relate and illustrate the events that happened at that time.

The <term>Vinaya-pitaka</term> contains the precepts and rules given by the master for the instruction of those who have dedicated themselves to following the doctrine. It is a sort of set of rules for the brotherhood of the elect.

The <term>Abhidharma-pitaka</term> is a collection of treatises and commentaries and often contains the most profound philosophical discussions on points arising from the teachings contained in the <term>Sūtra-pitaka</term>. The contents of this third division are not regarded as the Buddha’s own words, but as explanations of his teachings presented from the standpoint of psychology and philosophy.

It is unnecessary to say that this classification is somewhat flexible; for the <term>Vinaya-pitaka</term> sometimes contains sermons and discourses, and the <term>Sūtra-pitaka</term> often includes discourses on points of discipline, while both of these divisions frequently have the characteristics of the third division. In fact, this threefold division, while fairly accurate for the

The <term>Pali Canon</term> classification really breaks down entirely when applied to the <term>Northern Canon</term>, for the simple reason that many of the leading <term>sūtras</term>, though put into the mouth of the <term>Buddha</term>, are no more his actual teachings than the whole <term>Abhidharma-pitaka</term> is. The classification should therefore not be taken too seriously and should be regarded as one of those convenient expedients of the human mind by which a bewildering variety is reduced to a unity by simply affixing a label.

This gives us, then, a double <term>Tri-pitaka</term> for the Buddhist Canon taken as a whole; namely, a <term>Hinayāna</term> <term>Tri-pitaka</term> and a <term>Mahāyāna</term> <term>Tri-pitaka</term>. The relative sizes of the two can be seen by referring to <term>Nanjō's Catalogue</term> of the canonical writings to which we referred above. Nanjō's divisions are a little different from what we have just given, but they are similar enough to shed light on the subject. <term>Nanjō</term>’s classification of the Canon is based largely on older classifications made by Chinese scholars and, therefore, should not be regarded as a truly critical analysis. It is only one method among many. For instance, a handbook on Buddhism published in Tokyo several years ago provides the following broad classification, using individual books in the Canon as the units of division rather than distinct works:

A. <term>Mahāyāna</term> <term>sūtras</term> . . . . . . . . . . . 2883 books
B. <term>Hīnayāna</term> <term>sūtras</term> . . . . . . . . . . . 680 books
C. <term>Mahāyāna</term> <term>abhidharmas</term> . . . . . . . . . 555 books
D. <term>Hīnayāna</term> <term>abhidharmas</term> . . . . . . . . . 695 books
E. <term>Hīnayāna</term> <term>vinayas</term> . . . . . . . . . . . 441 books
Total . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 5254 books

According to the orthodox branch of the <term>Mahāyāna</term> school, the Canon—with these divisions of <term>Mahāyāna</term> and <term>Hīnayāna</term> and the subdivisions of <term>Sūtra</term>, <term>Vinaya</term>, and <term>Abhidharma</term>—was largely established the year after <term>Gautama</term>’s death at a great council of his disciples held at <term>Rajagriha</term>. It is, of course, quite probable that a council was held by the Buddha’s disciples shortly after his death, as Buddhist tradition claims; however, it is completely impossible that the Canon could have been established then and there in anything like its current form. Even in the simpler form preserved in the <term>Pali Canon</term>, it could not have been finished at such an early date. As it exists now, the <term>Pali Canon</term> is actually only the Canon of one of the sects of early Buddhism and clearly shows evidence of being compiled at later dates. Regarding the <term>Northern Canon</term>—or rather, the series of canons—one only needs to look at the thirteen Chinese catalogs mentioned above to see how absurd such a claim is.

It is doubtful whether or not any part of the Canon was committed to writing immediately after <term>Gautama</term>’s death. The <term>Pali Canon</term>, for example, was not fixed on the written page until the first century B.C. Great portions of the <term>Northern Canon</term>, even large sections of the <term>sūtra</term> division, could not possibly have been fixed in their present form before the beginning of the Christian era. But while this is true, we do not mean to say that no books in the Canon were finalized at an early date. Even if they were not written down immediately after <term>Gautama</term>’s death, it seems quite likely that sections of the <term>Vinaya-pitaka</term> were fixed more or less definitely at the <term>Rajagriha Council</term> or soon after. At any rate, the core of these Monks’ Rules, it would seem, must have taken shape almost from the beginning.

If, then, portions of the Canon were fixed before they were committed to writing, may it not be that the <term>Pali Canon</term> was fixed long before it was committed to the written page in the first century before Christ? And is it not therefore the oldest and most authoritative Canon of primitive Buddhism in existence, and so should be made the standard by which Buddhism as a whole is to be measured? We may admit that the <term>Pali Canon</term> was fixed, at least by one sect, before it was committed to writing. We may also admit that it contains the main teachings of <term>Gautama</term>, though it contains more than simply the teachings of the founder. And still further, we must admit that, taken as a whole, the <term>Pali Canon</term> comes much nearer to representing the teachings of original Buddhism than the <term>Northern Canons</term> do when taken as a whole. But this does not mean that it should be taken as the only source for <term>Gautama</term>’s teachings, nor should it be assumed that those portions of the <term>Northern Canon</term> which are essentially the same as portions of the <term>Pali Canon</term>—for example, the four <term>Nikāyas</term> (<term>Agamas</term>)—were taken from the latter. In fact, it seems quite likely that some of the <term>Sanskrit</term> scriptures of the <term>Northern Canon</term> and some of the <term>Pali</term> scriptures go back to an older redaction in <term>Magadhi</term>, the language of <term>Magadha</term> which <term>S’akyamuni</term> probably used. So it is quite possible that the <term>Northern Canon</term> contains books just as

This is made possible by the form in which the teachings of <term>Gautama</term>’s day were usually presented—namely, a style that seems like tiresome repetition to the Western mind, but which made them relatively easy to remember. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the Buddhist Canon, specifically addressing how oral tradition and memorization have preserved the teachings, while noting the historical development of the Mahāyāna scriptures and later attempts to harmonize contradictory texts.</meta>

<page-num>171</page-num>
<header>THE BUDDHIST CANON</header>

The system of education in the East has been, for centuries, a method of memorizing what others have said. It is astonishing how much the human mind can retain when trained in this way from youth. It is said that even today there are men in India who can, *for example*, recite the whole Rig-Veda—1,028 songs, many of them quite long—without a single slip. So it is not at all unlikely that we have in the Pali Canon, and in some of the scriptures of the Northern Canon, something of the real teachings of the founder and sometimes even his actual phrasing. 

But once this has been said, it is nonetheless absurd to hold, as some Buddhists in Japan do, that the entire *Sūtra-pitaka* and *Vinaya-pitaka*, especially those of the *Mahāyāna* school, date back that far. Even King Asoka, in the third century B.C., apparently knew nothing of the threefold division of the sacred scriptures; and, as we have said in Chapter I, the entire system of *Mahāyāna* Buddhism had not yet been born in his day. The most we can say is that there were only tendencies pointing in that direction. 

In short, then, we may grant to the Buddhists of China and Japan that in their voluminous Canon they possess the teachings of the founder as truly as do the Buddhists of the South, and they may even have some of the master's teachings not found in the Pali Canon. However, we cannot admit that the scriptures which they usually regard as the very words of Shakyamuni's deepest teachings—namely, the distinctively *Mahāyāna* scriptures—are such. Many of the most popular books in Japan cannot date back further than the beginning of the Christian era.

The broad division of the Buddhist Canon into a *Hīnayāna Tri-pitaka* and a *Mahāyāna Tri-pitaka* did not resolve all the glaring contradictions found in the Northern Canon. In the last half of the sixth century A.D., the learned Chinese priest Chi K'ai, founder of the great T'ien T'ai Sect, developed an elaborate scheme of harmonization. He divided Gautama's teachings into five great periods, and into these he tried to fit the various scriptures by arranging and rearranging them until he had cleared away, as he thought, all the difficulties and

contradictions. Briefly stated, the scheme was as follows:

1. The first period of the Buddha’s long ministry extended over a space of only two or three weeks immediately following the hour when the Great Enlightenment had dawned upon him. In this first period, he preached the undiluted and perfect truth as he saw it in his Buddhahood. His audience was not the ordinary people of India, but the innumerable Bodhisattvas, gods, and heavenly beings. This period is called in Japanese the Kegon period, and the teachings are recorded in the famous *Kegonkyō* (*Buddhavatamsaka-Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*), which has been used, perhaps, as widely by Buddhist scholars in Japan as any other scripture.

2. When the Buddha realized that his exalted teachings were beyond the capacity of the average human being, he began to dilute his teachings, as it were, and adapted them to the understanding of the common person. It was during this period that he taught the Four Noble Truths about suffering and salvation from suffering and the Noble Eightfold Path. To know these truths and to follow this path led to the Arhat state, which is the goal of Hīnayāna teachings. This second period extended over twelve years, and the teachings are to be found in the ordinary Hīnayāna scriptures.

3. But when the master perceived that his disciples took this adapted teaching of the Hīnayāna scriptures as the full truth, he began to show them that he still had many things to say to them and that what he had taught them thus far was only preparatory to the higher truth. He now began to teach them the way of true enlightenment—the enlightenment not of the Arhat who seeks only their own salvation, but that of the Bodhisattva who is interested also in the salvation of others. This period is called the Hōdō period and lasted eight years. The teachings of this period are recorded in the ordinary Mahāyāna scriptures.

4. Now when the disciples heard these lofty teachings of the third period, they felt that they were too high for the average person and that for them the Hīnayāna doctrines were

<meta>This page continues the chronological classification of the Buddha’s ministry, moving from the transitional teachings to the final revelation of the highest truths in the Mahāyāna tradition.</meta>

<page-num>173</page-num>
<header>THE BUDDHIST CANON</header>

better suited. They felt that only the one destined to be a *Bodhisattva* could comprehend the profound truths of the *Mahāyāna* teaching. The Buddha then showed them that nothing hindered even the average person from becoming a follower of *Mahāyāna* truth and attaining true enlightenment. The disciples were thus led to see that there was no chasm between the *Hīnayāna* and the *Mahāyāna*, but that the former was really a vehicle for the first part of the journey; from it, the passenger could transfer to the latter and continue his journey until he arrived at his true destination. This fourth period is called the *Hannya* period and extended over twenty-two years of the master’s long ministry. The leading scripture containing the teachings of this period is the voluminous *Mahāpragnāpāramitā-sūtra*, which teaches the deep *Mahāyāna* doctrines with simplicity.

5. Finally, when the Buddha reached the advanced age of seventy-two, he began to preach the deepest and highest truths of all: namely, that all sentient beings are able to attain Buddhahood and enjoy the blessings of *Nirvāna*. For this purpose, he had left his heavenly home and endured hardships during many incarnations so that he might lead all living beings into the bliss of *Nirvāna*. These teachings are contained in the famous Lotus Scripture, *Saddharma-Pundarīka-sūtra* (*Myōhō Renge-kyō*, or *Hokkekyō*). In this closing period, the Buddha also preached the teachings of the Paradise Scripture (*Mahāparinirvāna-sūtra* (*Ne-hankyō*)), in which he showed that all beings, animate and inanimate, have the nature of Buddha and so can attain Buddhahood. This period is called the *Nehan* or *Hokke* period and extended over eight years.

According to the Amida sects of Japan, the teachings of the famous Paradise or Amida scriptures also belong to this last period: namely, *The Larger Sukhāvati-vyūha* (*Daimuryōjukyō*), *The Smaller Sukhāvati-vyūha* (*Amidakyō*), and *Amitā-yur-dhyāna-sūtra* (*Kwammuryōjukyō*). These scriptures teach the great doctrine of salvation through faith in the Buddha Amida, who has prepared his Western Paradise for those who trust in him.

<page-num>174</page-num>
<header>STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM</header>

This concludes Chi K’ai’s classification of the founder’s teachings. It was undoubtedly an ingenious piece of work and would do credit to some of our modern harmonizers. For a period of about one thousand years, it calmed the doubts of skeptics and gave authority to the most contradictory teachings found in the sacred scriptures. Just as people used various means of transportation, so in religion there are various ways of salvation. The founder of Buddhism knew all these ways and taught them all, and the pious Buddhist must recognize in this a wise provision for the varied needs of humanity; indeed, a provision for the needs of all beings, for the heart of Buddha seeks to save everyone. But in the eighteenth century, when the Neo-Confucian and Neo-Shintō movements began to make themselves felt in Japan, the Buddhists, too, began to question the explanation of the Five Periods. As we stated in the last chapter, a man named Tominaga began to advance views that were designed to upset this convenient solution offered by Chi K’ai. Tominaga’s contention, in short, was that the scriptures which Chi K’ai assigned to the first, fourth, and fifth periods of Gautama’s ministry were actually the products of later centuries, and that his real teachings were contained in the *Hīnayāna Tri-pitaka*. Although these views attracted relatively little attention at the time, they marked the beginning of that Higher Criticism among Japanese Buddhists which is finding more and more champions as the years go on, and which should one day help solve the great problems presented by the Canon of Northern Buddhism.

The majority of Western scholars who are in a position to have an intelligent opinion on this complicated problem side with the liberal wing; but they would go a step further and say that <term>Mahāyāna</term> is not simply a developed form of Buddhism, but that it also has in it much which is not strictly Buddhist. It has a historical connection with primitive Buddhism, but it also has vital connections with other systems and streams of life, so that in many of its phases it is Buddhist in name only.

But the problems which confront the scholar who attempts to trace the historical development of Buddhism and unravel the many strands—Buddhist and non-Buddhist—which go to make up the Canon of <term>Northern Buddhism</term> are so stupendous that it may take centuries before even an outline of a satisfactory solution will be worked out. No one set of scholars, whether Oriental or Occidental, is sufficient for the task. It is like digging a long tunnel in which the work must be carried on from both ends. It is high time that Western scholars take a wider outlook upon the world, and through a knowledge of Oriental thought help lay the foundations for that sympathy for Asia's millions which alone can make the inevitable meeting of East and West a blessing rather than a curse. STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM

The scripture of the Northern Buddhists is far too voluminous to be used as a whole in any practical way. Even the Christian Bible is too large for most Christians, and many portions of it remain closed books; how then could a Buddhist be expected to make use of his massive Bible with its more than 5,000 books? In general, there are three different attitudes taken by the Japanese sects. At one extreme are sects like the old Sanron and the Tendai, which claim to use all the scriptures, regarding each scripture as having its own peculiar function. At the other extreme is the Rinzai branch of the Zen Sect, which holds that no scripture can truly be a vehicle of truth, for truth cannot be transmitted by the written page but must be communicated from heart to heart, or must be discovered in one's own heart through silent meditation. To them, the sacred scriptures are only the footprints on the sands of time left by the wise men of the past who walked in the way of truth. Between these two positions are the majority of the sects, which for practical purposes select one or more books from the Canon and make these their Authoritative or Basal Scriptures, to be used specifically by the adherents of the sect. Thus we have, *e.g.*, the Amida sects selecting the three Amida books as their Authoritative Scriptures: namely, the *Dai-muryōjukyō*, the *Amidakyō*, and the *Kwammuryōjukyō*. The Shingon and Nichiren sects regard the famous Lotus Scripture as especially sacred, though each of these adds several other books as Basal Scriptures. The old Kegon Sect was founded on the *Kegonkyō*, and the Sanron Sect on three scriptures. And so it is with other sects, each regarding certain scriptures as especially valuable and authoritative for the teachings of the sect, without, however, denying the teachings of other scriptures in the Canon which may seem quite contradictory. As we have said before, the average Buddhist philosopher is exceedingly tolerant of other views and regards even direct opposites as but two sides of the same shield.

Instead of translating all these writings, the clever priests have resorted to much simpler methods of providing their followers with the benefits of their contents. Among other things, they have introduced from China a sixth-century Chinese invention: namely, the huge revolving bookcase in which the sacred scriptures are placed.
