Another method in use in the Tendai Sect is what a visitor to the famous Tennōji in Osaka, *for example*, may see. The priests, eight or ten in number sitting in a row, read the scriptures by simply letting the pages glide through their fingers so that each reader can finish a set of ten books every two or three minutes.

But even the sects which choose only a few scriptures from the voluminous Canon do not always succeed in making these the common possession of their followers. The number of Japanese homes that have Buddhist scriptures is very small, and even fewer are the homes where the scriptures are read. The scriptures are considered too profound in their content to be understood by the masses, who are taught to worship the books blindly rather than to know what these books have to say. This is especially true of such a sect as the Nichiren. It has as its chief scripture one of the loftiest in the entire Canon, and if its contents were really known by the people, it would have a profound influence on their lives; but the average disciple of Nichiren is taught a superstitious reverence for the book and nothing more. The prayer, *Namu Myōhō Rengē-kyō*, "Hail Thou Scripture of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law," is on every disciple's lips, but what that Wonderful Law might be, few indeed have the slightest idea.

This superstitious reverence for the sacred scriptures as such, regardless of knowing their contents, has found expression in many ways. For example, it has always been regarded as a work of great merit to be engaged in copying the scriptures, and at times even emperors and princes have labored faithfully in the capacity of scribes of the sacred law. There are some manuscripts in existence written in human blood, the zealous scribe thus literally pouring out his lifeblood for the transmission of the holy text. # CHAPTER V

## OUTLINE OF MAIN DOCTRINES OF JAPANESE BUDDHISM

In providing an outline of the main doctrines of Japanese Buddhism, one is naturally tempted to follow the general divisions into which the fundamentals of Christianity are usually divided by modern writers on Systematic Theology. This has the great advantage of enabling the reader to make a comparison between the main teachings of the two religions, and for this reason, we shall not depart entirely from such a course of procedure in this chapter. But to be true to the subject at hand, we must depart from this course at least at the beginning and deal first with subjects which are very fundamental but which, in books on Systematic Theology, are usually left to works on philosophy and psychology.

### *A. Summary Statement of Teachings*

Perhaps the most concise expression of the essence of Buddhist teachings is the meaningful phrase, "*Tenmei Kaigo*": "*Turning from error and opening understanding.*" Man is in error and ignorance, and he must turn from this and open his understanding. The entire mode of Buddhist salvation is expressed primarily in terms of right thinking rather than in terms of right moral purpose, and the great obstacle in man's way is error rather than sin. Enlightenment is the great word of Buddhism, and Enlightenment means to know the truth. We do not mean to say that Buddhism does not also have a good deal to say about sin and righteous conduct, but only that these are secondary.

To the meaningful expression given above, two other expressions are sometimes added, and all three taken together

The complete statement is, “<term>Tenmei kaigo</term>, <term>riku tokuraku</term>, <term>shiaku shuzen</term>.” “Turning from error and opening understanding, escaping from suffering and obtaining bliss, ceasing from evil and doing good.” All living beings have clouded their reasoning regarding things, and so through error, they commit evil deeds and consequently are doomed to suffer. Through the teachings of Buddhism, man is to learn the truth. This will show him what is right, and by obedience to the right, he escapes from suffering and enters bliss. Or to put it in Western thought, man is to think the truth, do the good, and feel the beautiful. This, in short, is the general summary of Buddhist teachings, and when given in this general form, there would seem to be little difference between Buddhism and Christian thought. But when we come to inquire into what is meant by the true, the good, and the beautiful, we shall find great differences between Buddhist and Christian thought, and also between the different schools and sects of Buddhism.

### B. *Theory of Knowledge*

The first step in the explanation of Buddhist doctrines must necessarily involve a few remarks on the problem of knowledge. This problem is, of course, important in any system of thought, but in Buddhist philosophy it is particularly so, and it is quite impossible to make any progress in our understanding of it unless we always keep in mind what Buddhists mean by knowledge and truth.

As the expression, “Turning from error and opening understanding” implies, all human knowledge may be divided into two great categories: namely, Error and Truth. Such a division is, however, too clear-cut, for there is much of our knowledge which can be called neither pure truth nor absolute error; and so Buddhists usually divide knowledge into three categories: namely, Illusion, Relative Truth, and Absolute Truth. Or, in the case that we divide knowledge into Error and Truth, Truth itself is divided into two categories: namely, Relative or Accommodated Truth and Perfect or Absolute

It then introduces the Buddhist theory of knowledge, which categorizes human understanding into illusion, relative truth, and absolute truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Buddhist philosophy, moving from the general summary of doctrines to the specific Theory of Knowledge, focusing on the three levels of truth and their relation to Western philosophical concepts like Kant’s "thing in itself."</meta>

<page-num>185</page-num>
<header>BUDDHIST THEORY OF KNOWLEDGE</header>

Truth: All human knowledge, then, is either Illusion, Relatively True, or Absolute Truth. An ancient and popular illustration of this threefold division is that of a piece of rope seen in the twilight. Seeing its general shape, one may take it for a snake (Illusion). One may see that it is a rope and not think any further about its constituent elements (Relative Truth). Or one may know that it is a rope made of grass—*that is*, understand its real make-up (Absolute Truth). 

The knowledge of the average man is largely illusion and error. He holds a naive realistic view and thinks that everything is, in reality, exactly what it appears to be. Relative or Accommodated Truth is a step towards perfect knowledge or Absolute Truth. This kind of knowledge penetrates somewhat into the reality of things, but it does not see things in their real essence. Practically all of our so-called knowledge of the phenomenal world and the things we deal with in our practical lives belongs to this class of knowledge. In our practical lives, *for example*, we make distinctions between things. We say this is good and that is bad, this is beautiful and that is ugly, this is large and that is small, this is light and that is heavy, and so on. All these distinctions have a practical value, and such knowledge is to be regarded as knowledge when contrasted with error; but, after all, this is only relative knowledge. These distinctions which we make in the world of phenomena may seem important and real, but in the final analysis, they are not what they seem. They are mere appearances of a reality in which these distinctions have no real meaning. 

The wise man must go beyond this sort of knowledge of reality; he must attain perfect knowledge of the Absolute Truth and see things as they really are. He must get behind the appearances to the things themselves. He must know not merely the phenomena but the noumena—or rather the Noumenon, Kant’s "*Das Ding an Sich*."

The Western student of philosophy is, of course, quite familiar with Kant's epoch-making work on this problem of human knowledge. He knows what a great contribution Kant made when he showed that in all our thinking the

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Buddhist epistemology, specifically comparing the Buddhist concept of Absolute Truth and the noumenal world with Immanuel Kant's theories on the "thing in itself" and the nature of the self.</meta>

<page-num>186</page-num>

The thinking subject contributes something to the object perceived, so that what we know seems to be a sort of "construct" composed of the object known and the knowing subject. That is, knowledge is not a mere impression of the object on the thinking subject, or mere writing on an empty tablet; rather, the thinking subject is active rather than passive in the process. This much of Kant's theory of knowledge must be accepted as valid. But when Kant proceeded to show how our knowledge is not a knowledge of things as they really are in themselves, but only as they appear (with the implication that appearance does not give us reality), we cannot follow Kant. And especially when Kant tries to draw a line between what he calls the Empirical Ego and the Transcendental or Ontological Ego, and says that we know the former but not the latter, we must reject his epistemology at this point altogether. The self knows nothing better than the self of self-consciousness, and if this is not the real self, or the noumenal ego, then there is no noumenal ego, nor does Kant even have the right to express the judgment that the empirical ego is not the noumenal ego.

Now Buddhism makes this same distinction between the phenomenal and the noumenal world and says that all our ordinary knowledge is only of the phenomenal world and so is only relatively true. The knowledge of the noumenal world is possible only to the one who has reached perfect enlightenment—*that is*, to one who has attained Buddhahood. He who has attained this stage is able to see that the distinctions which the ordinary man makes between things have no real existence in being, but are instead due to the unenlightened mind. It is not that existence is absolutely void, but that the phenomenal world appears to us as it does because we are what we are, rather than because it is so in itself. The enlightened one knows that the complexity and multiplicity of the phenomenal world is really a simplicity and Oneness of Being. On the high plane of Absolute Truth, one enters the "Dharma of non-duality" where all distinctions and antitheses are absorbed in a higher synthesis, where one can see the "identity of differences" and the

"indifference of opposites." (And we might also add, one enters the realm of Fichte's Absolute in which, as Hegel put it, one is in "the night in which all cows are black.") Even the distinction between error and truth disappears, "because," says a modern exponent, "those who have entered a meditation in which there is no sense-impression or thought are free from ignorance as well as from enlightenment. This holds true for all the other dualistic categories." When one has entered this stage, one has entered the Nirvana of true Buddhahood—the heaven in which even the distinction between existence and non-existence has no meaning.

According to the orthodox Buddhist theory of knowledge, then, all ordinary human knowledge deals only with the phenomenal world and not with reality itself. This knowledge of the phenomenal world is "<term>Hōben</term>," or Accommodated Truth—that is, it is the truth adapted to meet the needs of unenlightened minds. There is an Absolute Truth and a perfect knowledge, but it exists only for the fully enlightened—that is, for those who have attained Buddhahood.

If it is asked on what grounds Buddhism asserts that there is an Absolute Truth for the enlightened mind, the answer is that this must be taken on the authority of those who have attained Buddhahood. Clearly, to make the statement that our knowledge is only relative and concerns the phenomenal world implies a knowledge of the real or noumenal world; therefore, this judgment—that our knowledge is relative but that an Absolute Truth exists—cannot be made by ordinary people as a matter of knowledge, but must be accepted on faith. That is, the ordinary Buddhist accepts on faith this theory of truth: that what the unenlightened mind regards as true is true only relatively, and that the Buddha knows reality as it is in itself. The Buddhist theory of truth is, then, in the final analysis, a "<term>credo ut intelligam</term>" <note>Latin for "I believe so that I may understand."</note>.

Of course, even Christian epistemology would not claim that human knowledge is a perfect knowledge of the truth, and would say that only God can know the truth perfectly.

That is, Christian epistemology may also speak of human knowledge as relative, but not in the Buddhist sense. It is relative in the sense that it is fragmentary and incomplete, but not that it is entirely erroneous when compared with perfect truth. In the words of Paul:

> “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away.”

That is, our partial knowledge is a real stepping stone to the full truth, and it is true knowledge as far as it goes. A Buddhist illustration will clarify the difference between the two views of truth; namely, the illustration of the shield. A shield seen from one side appears convex in shape, and from the opposite side, concave. To say that the shield is convex in shape is a true statement. But the Buddhist would say that it is only relatively true, because one can say from the opposite point of view that it is concave in shape. “Therefore,” proceeds Buddhist epistemology, “the shield is both convex and concave; and because these are opposites, it is neither one nor the other, and so its real nature cannot be known.” Christian epistemology would say that the shield, as we see it, is convex. This may be only a partial view of the object. If it is also concave when seen from the other side, then the two appearances must be harmonized to do justice to all the facts known about the shield. They cannot be harmonized in the way Buddhist epistemology tries to harmonize them—specifically, by saying that we really know nothing about the object we call a shield. But if our knowledge of an object contains contradictions, we must proceed on the basis of the knowledge we have until we clear these away. At any rate, we must trust our knowledge of things as true knowledge, even though we admit that it is not perfect and that only the absolute mind can know the full truth.

The Buddhist theory of knowledge is, however, not adequately understood until one grasps the Buddhist explanation of the origin of ignorance, or the theory of <term>Nescience</term>. All human knowledge is really a <term>Nescience</term>. If the phenomenal world does not represent the noumenal world, how is it

Either it appears without a cause, or if it has a cause, the cause is present in the phenomena in some way; and to that extent at least, one would think the <term>noumenal</term> world can be known through the phenomenal world. That the phenomenal world does appear to us no one can deny without ending in absolute skepticism. The question is, why does it appear, and to what does it appear?

The orthodox Buddhist reply to this question is the so-called theory of <term>Nescience</term>. The phenomenal world as known to man has no existence as such; and if by existence we mean the things that appear to us, Buddhism holds that existence is <term>void</term>. It is, however, not void in the sense that nothing at all exists, but only in the sense that nothing really exists in the way in which it appears to us to exist. That is, Buddhism asserts the reality of a noumenal world, and the true <term>Mahāyāna</term> school even affirms the presence of the noumenal in the phenomenal, but denies that the phenomenal world is in reality such as it appears to us. It appears so to us only because of our <term>ignorance</term>. “Everything that is subject to the law of birth and death exists only (*that is*, in the way it appears to exist) because of ignorance and <term>Karma</term>.”

But how does <term>ignorance</term> arise, and by what process do we come to look upon things as we do? The first answer to this question is that our present state of ignorance arose, according to the law of cause and effect, from past states of error and illusions, and our present state, by the same law, will give rise to future states of ignorance. Our past states of ignorance were produced by the law of <term>Karma</term> from states of ignorance still further back, and so this chain of ignorance stretches backwards into an indefinite past, just as it will stretch forwards into an indefinite future unless it is broken by the “gospel of <term>enlightenment</term>.”

It is possible to distinguish twelve links in this Chain of Ignorance, the so-called <term>Twelve Links of Cause and Circumstance</term> (<term>Jūni inen</term>).¹ These links give us one form of the Buddhist conception of the nature of man. If the reader

The following are the twelve links (<term>Nidana</term>):

1. Ignorance—the error of desires and cravings in a previous life.
2. Latent Impressions—the good and evil deeds of a previous life.
3. Thought Substance—the beginning of the psychological aspect of <term>uterine life</term>.
4. Name and Form—the physical beginnings of <term>uterine life</term>.
5. The <term>Six Roots</term>—the development of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and will during <term>uterine life</term>.
6. Contact—the <term>Six Roots</term> mentioned in number five come into contact after birth with the <term>Six Dusts</term> (that is, the physical environment).
7. Sensation—the feeling of pain and pleasure arising from the sense organs.
8. Desire—the cravings of the flesh.
9. Clinging to Existence—the passion and pride of life which drives a person toward actions that produce a new <term>Karma</term> of good or evil.
10. Becoming—the completion of <term>Karma</term> in the present life.
11. Birth—the new life which shall be born in the future as a result of the deeds done in the present life.
12. Decrepitude and Death—the pain, trouble, sorrow, old age, and death in the future.

Numbers 1 and 2 refer to the desires and actions of the previous life. Numbers 3 through 10 refer to the present life, beginning with the start of <term>uterine life</term> and ending with death. Numbers 11 and 12 refer to the birth, pain, sorrow, and death in the next <term>incarnation</term>. In the future as in the past, the twelve links mentioned above are discernible. Each of the twelve links becomes, in turn, the effect of a preceding cause and the cause of a succeeding effect.

Some writers end their explanation of the origin of ignorance with this description of the various links in the <term>Karma</term>-chain, even though Ignorance constitutes the first link in the chain and thus leaves the explanation exactly where it began. But if it is asked, "How do we explain the origin of the first link?" the reply is that it arose from preceding links *ad infinitum*. And if the question is pushed even further, the reply is that the very question about the origin of ignorance is itself ignorance. How can one demand that a rational answer be given for the origin of the irrational? Or, better yet, why explain the origin of that which does not truly exist? For on the high plane of true enlightenment, one can see that ignorance has no real existence.

Some Buddhists, however, recognize the fact that such answers are either wordplay or circular reasoning; therefore, they meet the question about the origin of ignorance with the bold assertion that the irrational is an original element of existence. That is, some hold that it is co-eternal with the rational (a sort of dualism), or that it is inherent in the Absolute and arises spontaneously. Ignorance, which is really synonymous with consciousness—for without consciousness there would be no ignorance—is caused by "the waves of mentation which are ever stirring up the ocean of eternal tranquillity." No one can say what causes these "waves of mentation," beyond the fact that it is a part of the eternal nature of things as they appear to ignorant man.

Ignorance, then, is the real source of the phenomenal world as it appears to us, since it is the first link in the <term>Karma</term>-chain by which the Absolute individualizes itself and becomes conscious in man. Man’s finite mind, in turn, gives rise to the phenomenal world as known to the common man. "Things are fundamentally and in themselves non-existent; only through the law of cause and circumstance

### C. Buddhist World Views

The Buddhist world view is naturally built upon the Buddhist theory of knowledge; or rather, world views, for there are three more or less distinct ones. These are the Hīnayāna, the Provisional Mahāyāna, and the True Mahāyāna. From the standpoint of the Mahāyāna school, the other two are only relatively true and so correspond to the second division of human knowledge mentioned above, *that is*, Relative Truth. The world view of the ignorant masses corresponds to the first division, namely, Illusion; whereas the True Mahāyāna world view corresponds to Absolute Truth.

Both the Hīnayāna and the Provisional Mahāyāna, as we said, are regarded by Mahāyāna Buddhists as relatively true. They are said to be two extremes, and the truth lies in the middle—the Middle Path of Mahāyāna. We shall state briefly what these two extremes are and then explain what the true Middle Path is.

1. *Hīnayāna World View.* — The Hīnayāna view is more or less a realistic world view. It does not, of course, accept the naive realism of the unenlightened masses who hold that the world is just what it appears to be and that there is no mystery about it. It approaches the problem with a critical spirit, and through an analytical method, it seeks to penetrate into the inner nature of existence. To begin with, it divides reality into two great spheres: namely, the phenomenal and the noumenal, or Nirvāna, spheres. The

...the phenomenal sphere, which it divides into two subdivisions: namely, the physical and the psychic. It treats the phenomenal sphere as having a real objective existence, but as being in a constant flux and therefore lacking any element of permanence. It has little to say of the Nirvana sphere, except that it is empty of everything found in the phenomenal sphere. Therefore, the Nirvana sphere cannot be known through the phenomenal sphere, for there is no real connection between them. The objective of Hinayana philosophy is to free man from the aimless wandering of the phenomenal world and lead him into the Nirvana sphere by showing him the real nature of his life and the entire realm of phenomena.

Thus, Hinayana philosophy proceeds further to analyze the things that make up the world of phenomena. The analysis begins with man himself, for he is the best example of the two aspects of existence: namely, mind and matter. Man is shown to be composed of the five so-called Skandhas<note>2</note>—Form, Feeling, Notion, Predisposition, and Discrimination. Of these five Skandhas, the first is physical and the remaining four are psychic. The physical aspect of man is then divided into the Five Indriyas (Japanese: *Gokon*), *that is*, the five organs of sense, and into the five Alambanas (Japanese: *Goriki*), the five senses as distinguished from the organs themselves. The psychic elements are divided into two groups: the first three constitute one group, and the fourth stands by itself. The fourth—Discrimination—is said to be the "Mental King," and the other three—Feeling, Notion, and Predisposition—are spoken of as the servants of the Mental King. Sometimes the analysis is carried even further, and the result is that by this division of the psychic and physical aspects of human life, Hinayana Buddhism tries to account for the phenomena of our mental life. It reaches the startling conclusion that the "self" of self-consciousness is but an illusion and is simply the product of this aggregate of Skandhas.

Hinayana seeks to understand the external world through the same analytical process. Thus, it holds that matter in general is made up of minute particles, which correspond

...very much like the atoms of modern science. These minute particles are composed of the four Great Kinds (Japanese: *Shi-daishu*, or *Shidai*); namely, Earth (Solids), Water (Liquids), Fire (Heat), and Wind (Movability). These four great elements, or natures, remain ever the same, and by combining in different degrees, they constitute the various kinds of atoms; and these, in turn, compose the things which make up the phenomenal world.

While Hīnayāna asserts the reality of both the psychic and the physical aspects of existence, it shows a monistic tendency in that it regards the four Great Kinds, which make up the physical world, as qualities rather than elements, and holds that if the process of division were carried far enough (some say seven raised to the seventh power in the case of an atom), matter would change into spirit. The real dualism in Hīnayāna philosophy is the dualism of the phenomenal and Nirvāna spheres. It asserts the reality of both, though it has little or nothing to say of the latter.

2. *Provisional Mahāyāna World View.* — The Provisional Mahāyāna world view also begins by speaking of the two great spheres of existence: the phenomenal and the noumenal. But where Hīnayāna philosophy divides the phenomenal sphere into two subdivisions and speaks of both as real, Provisional Mahāyāna denies the reality of the outside world and holds it to be the product of impure thought. The outside world exists only in the mind and has no objective existence. “In Buddhism, the mind is made the source from which all laws (phenomena) come.” “Mind takes the form of hell, devils, animals, and heavenly beings; in fact, all that has shape and form is the product of the mind.” Starting with the analysis of the nature of man advanced by the Hīnayāna school, Provisional Mahāyāna speculation goes a step further; it not only declares the self of self-consciousness to have no real existence, but also tries to show how this illusion arises in the mind and how the mind produces the illusions of the outside world and everything that appears in consciousness.

### BUDDHIST WORLD VIEWS

A great deal of Buddhist literature seems to express this worldview, and Western writers usually take this to be the true Buddhist position. Everything is regarded as a mere illusion and devoid of reality. As we stated above, even the self is said to be non-existent and an illusion. One might well ask how this can be; for if the self is also an illusion, it must be an illusion perceived by something, and at least that "Something" must exist. According to the Provisional Māhāyan school, a "Something" does exist: specifically, the noumenal world; however, nothing can truly be affirmed about it. The only thing that can be done is to destroy the errors and illusions of the phenomenal world. That is, progress toward the truth is achieved only by destroying error. Thus, *for example*, the old Sanron Sect, which is the best representative of this school in Japan, held that all progress in truth is made by denying all affirmations.

> "Add a negation and you clear away all illusion; in this way, you destroy and deny every error and misconception. If, *for example*, you hold to the principle of birth, clear it away with the idea of death; and if you hold to death as a principle, destroy it with the principle of birth. If you hold to a 'non-death, non-birth' principle, destroy it with the 'non-non-birth, non-non-death' principle, and so on and so forth. Since we have relative and finite minds, we must clear away everything; for, after all, not one thing in our minds is real."

Thus, negation follows negation *ad infinitum*.

3. *Mahāyāna World View.* — However, this worldview which denies the reality of the external world is regarded by the True Mahāyāna school as an extreme position. This view is correct to the extent that it seeks to destroy all illusions, but it is wrong to make the phenomenal world an absolute void. Mahāyāna holds that the phenomenal world is real because it is identical to the noumenal world. That is, the noumenal world is within the phenomenal world, and the phenomenal world rests upon the noumenal. But this does not mean that reality is as it appears to the unenlightened mind. The Mahāyāna school also says that the phenomenal world, as it appears to the average person, is a shadow world and has

In reality there are no such differences, even though it may seem that there are.'"

> "Shin Shinnyō is that which is the essence of all things and principles; it is the ideal changeless and imperishable. The distinctions and differences in things are but the product of our illusory ideas, and these differences do not exist apart from the mind. Therefore the laws of all things are originally and in their real essence identical, changeless, without real differences and imperishable when all explanations, naming, and thought are subtracted from them. And because they are all one Mind they are called <term>Shinnyō</term>."

This third view of what constitutes the essence of reality — and as we have said, this is the orthodox view of the <term>Mahāyāna</term> school to which most Japanese sects belong — holds, then, in short, that while for practical purposes in

In our state of ignorance, we may say that there are real differences (*Sabetsu*) in things; in reality, Existence is a oneness or a sameness (*Byōdō*) about which no further assertion can be made. Even the statement that the universe is "Being" would be too specific and must be balanced by the concept of "Non-Being," if one wishes to keep to the Middle Path. "We cannot say," writes a modern Buddhist, "that things either exist or that they do not exist. If we ask whether things are fixed in their Being or fixed in their Non-Being, we can give no positive answer to either question. We can only say that things exist, or that they do not exist, or that they are midway between Being and Non-Being." If this seems strange to the reader, let them remember that our own Hegel has tried to show that the essence of Being is Being plus Non-Being—whatever that may mean.

But the Mahāyāna Buddhist, too, recognizes that, after all, we live in a world where differences seem very real and where we must treat them as real despite their supposed metaphysical identity. And so, if we wish to make progress in our understanding, we must leave this problem of the ultimate reality and this high plane of the "Dharma of non-duality" and descend to the world as it is—or, at any rate, as it appears to be. We shall, however, not leave the aforementioned theories of knowledge and theories of the essence of reality too far behind, for they appear in almost every problem that is discussed. In fact, we must remember that all exposition and explanation belong to the realm of Relative or Accommodated Truth and not to the realm of Absolute Truth. And so when we explain certain definite views regarding the cosmos, God, humanity, salvation, etc., we must always be ready to add at the end that these are views expressed in terms of Accommodated Truth. This is extremely frustrating to the average Western mind; for just when one thinks that they have finally reached solid ground regarding what Buddhism really teaches on this or that point, one must be prepared to have the foundation knocked from under this stately mansion of knowledge by the awareness that these ideas are expressed only through the concepts of Accom-

Accommodated Truth and therefore are not really true. We should add here that it is this theory of truth that makes Buddhist teachings so inconsistent when taken as a whole, and so tolerant of views that may be the direct opposite. For if, in the final analysis, all differences are really a sameness, then it would be foolish to insist too much on any one view. All contradictions are but opposite sides of the same thing, whose real nature transcends the power of the finite mind to comprehend. Therefore, as we have said, Buddhism is very tolerant; at least this is true of Buddhist philosophers.

## D. The Pluralistic World of Experience

If the universe is Sameness from the standpoint of Absolute Truth, then from the standpoint of Accommodated Truth it is a universe of Differences. The world of experience is a pluralistic world, even though the final word of speculative thought may be a monism of one sort or another. Now, Buddhism divides this pluralistic world in many ways, and all schools generally agree on these divisions. That is, the distinctions between Hīnayāna, Provisional Mahāyāna, and True Mahāyāna do not have much meaning here. The differences are rather sectarian and pertain more to the religious application of the teachings than otherwise.

1. *The Two Spheres.* — First of all, Buddhism divides all existence into the two great spheres mentioned above: namely, the phenomenal sphere and the noumenal sphere. This has already been discussed, and we mention it here simply because even this distinction belongs to the realm of Accommodated Truth and not to the realm of Absolute Truth.

2. *The Three Worlds.* — The second great division that Buddhism makes is what is called in Japanese *Sanse*, or the Three Worlds—that is, the Past, the Present, and the Future. In Western thought, we are, of course, familiar with this division of time; but in Buddhist thought, it is not so much a division of time as it is a division of the Causal Nexus that runs through all things. The Past world caused the Present

world and the Present world becomes in turn the cause of the Future world. There is really nothing in the Present which was not in the Past, and there will be nothing in the Future which is not in the Present, so that the Past cause may be seen in the Present effect and the Future inferred from the Present cause. The universe is really a closed system and it repeats its perpetual rounds in strict conformity to the law of cause and effect.

3. *The Timeless, Boundless Cosmos.*—According to Buddhist cosmology the cosmos had no real beginning and has no end in time. It has always existed and it always will exist. It passes, however, through various stages as time goes on. Four stages are recognized; namely, (1) Completion, (2) Inhabitation, (3) Destruction and (4) Voidness. In the state of Completion the world is being formed from the great Void and prepared for living beings. In the state of Inhabitation it is filled with all manner of living beings. In the third state, the state of Destruction, the cosmos is disintegrating and preparing to enter the fourth state, the state of Voidness. This last state is, however, not an absolute void nor does this state continue forever, for after an immeasurable length of time the cosmos will again form from out of this void and enter once more upon the first of the above mentioned states, and so a new cycle begins. One such cycle follows upon another in endless succession. Each stage in a cycle is millions of years in length, so that a single cycle is immeasurably long. And when it is said that such cycles follow each other in endless succession it becomes clear that this is simply an attempt to express in finite terms the infinity of Time. The cause of the destruction of the cosmos in the third state is said to be a destructive fire which breaks out and consumes everything with an intense heat. The cause which reforms the cosmos in the first state is a cool wind which arises spontaneously and blows across the hot waste. Lest the reader take this too literally, let them be reminded that this Wind is really the "Wind of Ignorance" which stirs up the "waves of mentation" on the "Ocean of Eternal Tranquillity." The universe is not only timeless but also boundless in space. The cosmos spoken of above is the cosmos known to humanity. But this is only one among countless worlds. Thus, Buddhist speculation says that "a thousand such worlds make a 'group of Lesser Thousand Worlds,' a thousand such groups make one group of 'Middle Thousand Worlds,' and a thousand groups of 'Middle Thousand Worlds' constitute a group of 'Larger Thousand Worlds.' Let the reader, however, be reminded again not to take this too literally, for space and time are regarded as merely the laws of thought, and everything which appears in space and time is but the product of unenlightened minds.

4. *The Three Realms.* — We said that the second stage of each world is the state of Inhabitation, *i.e.*, the state when a world is inhabited by living beings. Buddhism divides these living beings roughly into three great classes or realms; namely, the so-called Sankai, Three Realms³ (Sanskrit: Trailokya). These are the Realm of Desire (Yokukai, Sanskrit: Kāmadhātu), the Realm of Color or Pure Form (Shikikai, Sanskrit: Rūpadhātu), and the Realm of No-Color or Formlessness (Mushikikai, Sanskrit: Arūpadhatu). The first is called the Realm of Desire because all beings in this realm, or state, are subject to the bondage of sexual desires, eating, drinking, sleeping, and all that goes with physical existence. The Realm of Color, or Pure Form, is a kind of ethereal world. The beings in this realm are free from the ordinary lusts of the flesh, but their state is still a sort of bodily existence; namely, a bodily existence of a refined and etherealized sub-

In fact, the highest beings in this realm are not only free from bodily existence, but their state is even more refined than spirit and reaches almost the vanishing point; for they are said to have entered the heaven of No-Thought and No-Non-Thought. What this means is that such beings have reached the borderland of the phenomenal world where it recedes, as it were, into the noumenal world and so eludes our grasp; for as we have repeatedly said, our knowledge is only a knowledge of the phenomenal world and not of the noumenal world. Our knowledge can therefore reach up to the very threshold of the noumenal world, but it cannot go beyond.

5. *The Six Ways.*— Another division of phenomenal existence which covers the same range of beings as the Three Realms but in greater detail is what is known as the Six Ways (Rokudō, Sanskrit: Gāti). The Six Ways are really six great classes of beings. Within these great divisions, there are many subdivisions and grades. In fact, one is very much reminded of the Monadology of Leibniz, which arranged all beings in an ascending or descending scale so that no two were exactly alike—all being of the same essence but in different degrees. It is exceedingly important to understand this Buddhist "scale of beings," for it is only another way of stating the two great doctrines of Indian thought which have been the common property of Hinduism and Buddhism; namely, the doctrine of Karma and its corollary, the doctrine of Transmigration. Without a knowledge of this "scale of beings," it is also impossible to understand the absence in Buddhism of a clear line between God and man on the one hand, and between man and other creatures on the other hand. Therefore, the ease with which men are exalted into gods, and gods are made to appear as men or lower beings, will be understood only after one gets clearly fixed in one's mind at least the main outline of the doctrine of the Six Ways. These Six Ways, or Realms of Beings, are located in relation to <term>Mt. Sumēru</term> (Japanese: Shumisen), which is regarded as the center of every world. Hell is located many leagues below this central mountain. It has eight great subdivisions located one below the other, and each of these has four gates with four antechambers at each gate, thus actually making a total of 136 hells. These are all hot hells, but there are also eight great divisions of a cold hell.<note>4</note> The picture which Buddhism provides of the fate of the beings in these various hells surpasses the imagination of Western readers, even if they are well-versed in *Dante’s Inferno*.

The Realm of Hungry Spirits has two great divisions; one is located under Mt. Sumēru but above Hell, and the other is above the surface of the earth in the air near the base of the mountain. The characteristics of beings in this realm are greed and passion, which exist in varying degrees.

The Realm of Beasts also has two main divisions; one is in the “great sea” and the other is on land around the base of Mt. Sumēru. Folly and passion are the characteristics of beings in this realm, and their variety is as vast as the number of living beings in the waters and on land, excluding humans.

The Realm of Fighting and Bloodshed again has two main divisions, one being in the sea and the other on land. Pride, conflict, and cruelty are the characteristics of beings in this realm. Some Japanese Buddhists omit this fourth realm, for it is not entirely clear what is actually meant by it. The beings in it seem to be a type of hybrid between animals and humans.

The reader is not expected to master all the details in the above outlines of the Six Ways, but simply to get a general idea of the conception which Buddhism has of living beings. All these beings, from the lowest hell to the highest heaven, are bound together by the one inexorable law of <term>Karma</term>. Beings pass from one state to another, either up or down, according to the law of merit and demerit. If merit outweighs demerit, a being will be born into a higher state, and if demerit is the greater, the birth will be in a lower state. No state is a permanent condition. Even the beings that have obtained birth into the highest heaven are still in the clutches of the law of <term>Karma</term> and Transmigration. Their life may be a happy one and it may last for thousands of years, but at the end of that time, unless they accumulate further merit, they are doomed to sink again in the "scale of beings." And even though they have obtained birth into a world where life lasts eighty thousand years (that is, in the higher heavens mentioned above), when this happiness ends they are doomed to fall into the way of the <term>Three Evils</term>." The beings in the <term>Six Ways</term>, then, are all still bound to the <term>Wheel of Life</term> and compelled to wander about in the "dread cycle of existence."

6. *The Four Holies.* — Now Buddhism offers salvation from this "dread cycle of existence" by opening a way of escape to all beings. This way is the way of the <term>Four Holies</term> (<term>Shisei</term>). These are the four great stages of enlightenment, beginning with those who hear the law of Buddha and ending with those who have fully attained <term>Perfect Enlightenment</term>, or <term>Buddhahood</term>. These four stages are the following: (1) <term>Hearers</term> (Japanese: <term>Shōmon</term>, Sanskrit: <term>Srāvaka</term>), (2) <term>Enlightened One</term> (Japanese: <term>Enkaku</term>, Sanskrit: <term>Pratyēka Buddha</term>), (3) <term>Bodhisattva</term> (Japanese: <term>Bosatsu</term>, Sanskrit: <term>Bodhisattva</term>), (4) <term>Buddha</term> (Japanese: <term>Butsu</term>, Sanskrit: <term>Buddha</term>). There are several degrees in each of these four stages of holiness, as can be seen at a glance from the following outline:

**Four Holies (<term>Shisei</term>)**

1. **<term>Shōmon</term> (<term>Srāvaka</term>)**
    a. **<term>Sudako</term> (<term>Srotāpanna</term>)**, a beginner on the path to Enlightenment.
    b. **<term>Sudagon</term> (<term>Skridagamin</term>)**, one who returns but once to the <term>Three Worlds</term>.
    c. **<term>Anagon</term> (<term>Anagamin</term>)**, one who does not return to the <term>Three Worlds</term>.
    d. **<term>Arakan</term>**, or **<term>Rakan</term> (<term>Arhat</term>)**, a true saint, free from evil and one who has attained the first stage of <term>Buddhahood</term>.

2. **<term>Enkaku</term> (<term>Pratyēka Buddha</term>)**
    One who has broken the twelve links in the <term>Karma Chain</term>.
    This state is also called **<term>Dokugaku</term>**, or self-enlightenment. This enlightenment is still shallow, and this kind of Buddha, like the <term>Arhat</term>, seeks salvation only for himself.

3. **<term>Bosatsu</term> (<term>Bodhisattva</term>)**
    The <term>Bodhisattva</term> makes four great vows and practices the six virtues (<term>Pāramitās</term>):
    
    *The Four Vows:*
    a. To save all beings.
    b. To destroy all passions.
    c. To know and teach others all laws.
    d. To lead others to understand all Buddha's ways.
    
    *The Six Virtues (<term>Pāramitās</term>):*
    a. Almsgiving and teaching the ignorant.
    b. Keeping the Commandments.
    c. Patience and long-suffering.
    d. Diligence (in fulfilling the vows).
    e. Meditation.
    f. Wisdom (for oneself and others).

4. **<term>Butsu</term> (<term>Buddha</term>)**
    a. **<term>Ōjin Butsu</term> (<term>Nirmanakāya</term>)**, Buddha in human form, like the historical Buddha <term>S'akyamuni</term>.
    b. **<term>Hoshin Butsu</term> (<term>Sambhogakāya</term>)**, Buddha as an ideal person or the personification of virtue and wisdom, such as the Buddha <term>Amitābha</term>.
    c. **<term>Hōshin Butsu</term> (<term>Dharmakāya</term>)**, Buddha as the Absolute or the reality (noumenon) that underlies all phenomenal existence.

### E. *The God-idea of Japanese Buddhism*

What is actually the concept of the Divine held by Japanese Buddhists? The answer is very complex.

In our first chapter, we briefly discussed what seems to have been <term>Shakyamuni's</term> teaching on this point. We saw that he regarded speculations about the <term>Brahman</term> as an idle waste of time. On the other hand, he stripped the numerous gods of the common people of their glory, either by ignoring them completely or by assigning them a much lower place than someone who, like himself, had attained enlightenment; for the gods too, according to <term>Shakyamuni</term>, were still subject to the laws of birth and death and the dreaded cycle of existence, which is incurably evil. In our second chapter, we saw how the idea of a Supreme Being reasserted itself in Buddhism as it spread through northwest India and then into China, and that <term>Shakyamuni</term> himself—

The self was exalted into a being like God, or at least was regarded as a special manifestation of the Supreme Being. We saw how <term>Buddhism</term>, in its forward progress, gathered into itself practically everything with which it came in contact, so that by the time it reached <term>Japan</term>, it had assumed a complexity that is quite difficult to analyze. As was the case with other fundamental doctrines, its <term>God-idea</term> was no longer one <term>God-idea</term> but many, ranging all the way from a low animistic nature cult through ancestor worship and various stages of <term>polytheism</term> to a philosophical <term>monism</term>. In some branches, this was atheistic; in others, semi-theistic; and in still others, pantheistic. And what <term>Buddhism</term> was in China before it reached <term>Japan</term>, it has been and is today in <term>Japan</term>, except that here it has added to itself the legends and myths of the primitive <term>Shintō</term>. This tradition saw a special god in every phenomenon and regarded the <term>Imperial family</term> in particular as the descendants of the gods and as worthy to become gods after death. Thus, it is clear that if one tries to set forth the conception which Japanese Buddhists have of the Divine, no clear-cut presentation should be expected. It is no wonder that there is such a divergence of opinion among writers on <term>Buddhism</term> as to exactly what the Buddhist conception of God is.

But while it is difficult to make a clear-cut presentation of the subject, we shall try to analyze, at least to some degree, this maze of contradictory ideas. To begin with, we must again refer the reader to the hierarchy of beings which we have provided above. There are ten great realms of living beings in the Buddhist universe, and man finds himself near the middle of this scale. That is, he is superior to some and inferior to others. Those above man, though differing from one another in excellence, may be regarded as gods. And since all beings are bound together by a universal <term>causal nexus</term>, so that the higher may return to the lower and the lower may rise to the higher stages of existence, the boundary between the human and the divine—or any other stage—naturally disappears. Thus, men can become gods and gods can become men. And it must be further remembered—

[It must be remem]bered that all these graded realms of beings are superior or inferior only as seen from the standpoint of unenlightened humanity, but that from the standpoint of true enlightenment these differences have no meaning; for all are mere manifestations of what is essentially one and the same reality. This one reality is the Absolute of Buddhist philosophy. Western writers usually speak of the Buddhist conception of the Absolute as being a pantheistic conception and say that Buddhism as a religion is pantheism. Perhaps pantheism is the best word we can use in English to designate the Buddhist idea of God, but only because it is a very vague term open to an almost indefinite number of shades of meaning. In fact, Buddhist philosophers do not use the term. The Ultimate in Buddhist thought is not an "All-God," but a Oneness which transcends the categories of all existence as known to humanity. The Absolute is really the Great Unknowable, and an agnostic attitude is the proper one for all true Buddhist philosophers.

But while the agnostic attitude is regarded as the most profound and should logically lead to silence on this great problem, few Buddhists are consistent on this point and, like Herbert Spencer, have a good deal to say about the Great Unknowable. What they have to say differs rather widely, for with some the conception of the Divine is practically atheism (that is, the idea of God ends in zero), with others the conception is not far removed from theism, and with still others, who represent the majority, the conception fluctuates between atheism and theism, so that it may be designated by the vague term pantheism. The conception held by the general run of believers is incurably polytheistic, for polytheism is not, as some suppose, inconsistent with pantheism, but its necessary complement. That is, polytheism and pantheism are but two sides of one and the same shield; the former being the pluralistic view of everyday experience, and the latter the monistic view of the speculative thinker.

If then we speak of the idea of God as held by Japanese Buddhists, it depends largely upon what Buddhists we are

While for the sake of convenience we will discuss the God-idea of the thinking classes under the three categories of Atheism, Theism, and Pantheism, we do not wish to give the impression that these are clear divisions, or that they are held as such in actual practice. There are two reasons why these divisions cannot be clear-cut. The first reason is that in the religious life of the average follower, all three are accompanied by an undergrowth of polytheistic nature worship with a strong mixture of ancestor worship; this constantly grows up and chokes any clear distinctions that the philosophers might seek to make. The second reason is that Atheism, Pantheism, and Theism, by their very nature, cannot be clearly distinguished from one another. For example, if in Theism one places great emphasis on what Western thought calls the Immanence of God, one is not far removed from Pantheism; likewise, the lower end of Pantheism, which denies consciousness to the "One-All," is not far from Atheism. It is best, then, to think of the Buddhist idea of God as a tree whose trunk is pantheistic, with atheistic branches on its shady side and semi-theistic branches on its sunny side. Or, to use the Hegelian way of thinking, Atheism might be regarded as the "thesis" of original Buddhism and the Buddhism of those Japanese and Chinese sects that have stayed closest to the teachings of the founder. Theism is the "antithesis" proposed by the worshipers of Amida, and Pantheism is the "synthesis" of the two, representing Buddhism as a whole. Not only the sects that openly claim a pantheistic view, but even the atheistic and semi-theistic sects, would not object to being classified as pantheists. 1. *Atheistic Buddhism.* — It may seem a contradiction in terms to speak of an atheistic idea of God, but the student of Buddhism should not be too sensitive about using contradictory terms if they wish to advance in their understanding of its mysteries. Even an atheistic Buddhist will call his philosophy of life a religion, though according to our Western way of thinking, a religion without a god would hardly be regarded as a religion. It can at least be a religion of humanity, as we Westerners have been taught by Comte and his followers; and in reality, atheistic Buddhism is far more than this, for while the idea of God does seem to end almost in zero, the Buddhist of this type gives at least a passive worship to the mystery of the unknowable Absolute.

Atheistic Buddhism finds its best representative among Japanese Buddhists in the three branches of the Zen Sect; namely, the Rinzai, Sōtō, and Obaku sects. It is the boast of the Zen Sect that it is nearest to the teachings of the founder of Buddhism. It often calls itself the Buddha Heart Sect. The student of primitive Buddhism must admit that Zen, both in theory and in practice, is far nearer the religion of the founder than are the other Chinese and Japanese sects. As we said in our first chapter, Gautama may not have been an outright atheist, but he certainly had very little to say about God. If he did not deny the existence of the gods of the common people, he robbed them of the glory they once had. And so these true modern followers of Gautama may not deny the existence of beings higher than ordinary man—beings which the ignorant may fear and worship as gods—but such beings would not be regarded as gods or as God, worthy to be worshipped. And just as Gautama held that through self-discipline man can attain enlightenment and Buddhahood, which is higher than all the gods, so the Zen philosopher of today holds that man can, in his own strength through self-discipline, attain the highest condition of existence. If the reader will again consult the chart of the Ten Worlds given above,

He will see that above humanity is the realm of heavenly beings, with grade upon grade. The Zen philosopher may not deny the existence of these beings, but they are not gods to him. Above the realm of these heavenly beings are the <term>Four Holies</term>, each of which represents higher and higher stages of <term>enlightenment</term>. All of them are far above the realms of heavenly beings, which still belong to the realm of individual existence with all its limitations. Furthermore, all these levels of beings with their differences are, in the last analysis, only the product of impure thought and so have no real existence outside the mind of the thinker. He who has entered the highest <term>meditation</term> of Zen thought, "the white silence of truth," will see that these differences do not exist and that all individuality is swallowed up in the ocean of the Eternal.

But what about the <term>Four Holies</term> and especially the highest of these, the <term>Buddhahood</term> state? If the Zen philosopher ignores or denies the existence of God or the gods, is not <term>Buddhahood</term> itself, which man may attain, the God of Zen teaching? If the Zen philosopher believes in a god at all, we might say it is Buddha. But then the question arises as to what is meant by Buddha. Is Buddha regarded as a personal being, and does he exist now as a personal being?

The historic <term>Buddha Gautama</term> existed as an individual human being (or what appears so from the standpoint of <term>Accommodated Truth</term>). But when that historic being attained enlightenment and entered into <term>Nirvāna</term>, he became free from the bonds of individual existence. He passed out from the <term>Three Worlds</term> and so ceased to exist in the sense that one can declare anything of his state of being. Or it may be said that he entered a state which transcends all the categories of beings known to man. Therefore, if anything is asserted about him, it must be in the form of negating any particularization, and the wisest attitude is one of silence. Buddha is certainly not a personal being, not a personal God; nor can one assert anything about him. The Zen Sect thus consistently lays great stress on <term>meditation</term> which should lead to silence, not only of words,

Even to say that Zen teaches <term>Atheism</term> regarding the <term>God-idea</term> is not quite accurate, for that would be asserting something definite, since every negation is really an affirmation.

It might be asked, then, whether the Zen philosopher teaches that all existence is God, and that the <term>God-idea</term> is an idea which includes everything. To this, the answer is that the words “all existence” represent something definite to the person who uses them—namely, a summary of all individual beings. But all so-called individual beings have merely a phenomenal existence; therefore, it cannot be said that the ultimate goal of <term>Zen philosophy</term> is the <term>One-All</term>, for the All itself does not exist in the sense in which the mind attributes existence to anything. Thus, the height of <term>Zen philosophy</term> not only denies the existence of God and gods, but it refuses to assert the opposite, or to make a synthesis of the two and assert <term>Pantheism</term>. The consistent Zen philosopher passes through <term>Atheism</term> and <term>Pantheism</term> into absolute <term>Agnosticism</term>, which consistently ends in silence. If this silence is broken at all, it is merely to assert the existence of the <term>Great Unknowable</term>, toward which the philosopher may take an attitude of reverence and even worship with a passive spirit; however, this can hardly be compared with the conscious fellowship which the <term>Christian</term> has in his experience of God.

Sometimes it is claimed that the Zen believer experiences that mystical communion with the Divine which <term>Christian</term> mystics claim to have, and this may be so; but when this is a real communion of the soul with God, it transcends what Zen theology holds to be true. The true communion in Zen teaching is the communion of self with self, for there is no Divine with which to commune except within the heart of the one who communes. That is, the real God of Zen is the human heart—the heart freed from the distractions of specific thoughts. This God may be called the <term>Higher Self</term>, and this may be identified with the <term>Universal Self</term>.

## 2. *Theistic Buddhism.*

Theistic Buddhism finds its best representation among Japanese Buddhists in the four Amida sects; namely, the great Jōdo and Shin sects and the two small Yūdzū Nembutsu and Ji sects. Let us, however, state from the start that strictly speaking we cannot call these sects theistic, for they allow for other gods or Buddhas besides Amida, and in the final analysis, as we shall see, they really deny the personality of God as the Absolute. Like all Mahāyāna sects, they hold that the Absolute is neither personal nor impersonal but transcends human knowledge.

But while the Amidaists make room for other Buddhas and gods, on the whole, the Buddha Amida occupies such a unique place, and his name is on the lips of his followers so much, that we speak of the Amida sects as theistic, or at least semi-theistic sects. They hold that to worship Amida is sufficient, for he embraces all others; he is, as it were, the <term>pleroma</term> of the Godhead. Some moderns, influenced by Christian thought, speak of Amida as the Creator and the Father, and ascribe to him practically all the attributes which a Christian would ascribe to God. And even in some of the older canonical scriptures we find, *e.g.*, such sentences as this: “Buddha (Amida) said, ‘My mercy toward all you heaven- and earth-born creatures is deeper than the love of parents toward their children.’” And in the famous Lotus scripture we read, “Now the Three Worlds are mine and all living beings in them are indeed my children.”

While these sects treat Amida Buddha with attributes similar to the Christian God, they ultimately maintain the Mahāyāna view that the Absolute transcends human definitions.</summary>

It is the same with the love of the *Nyōrai*; though it is equal toward all beings, it hovers in a special manner over those who are in sin." These may not be exactly characteristic thoughts of Amida Buddhism, but there is enough of this element in it to make one feel that it is indeed an approach to the Christian conception of God. This will come more clearly to light in what we have to say under the heading of Salvation, and has also been touched upon in Chapter III, in the section on the Shin Sect.

In our second chapter, we spoke of the beginnings of the *Amitābha* (*Amida*) faith. We saw how early in the Christian era this Buddha was known to *Asvaghosha* and *Nāgārjuna*, though they saw him only "as through a glass darkly." By the beginning of the fifth century, *Kumārajīva* seemed to have had a clearer conception of him as the supreme Personal God. But the name that is prominent among the Amida sects is that of *Zendō* <gloss>5</gloss>, who lived at *Sin-an-fu*, China, in the first half of the seventh century. In 635 AD, the Nestorian mission under *Olopun* arrived in the same city. This mission must have been quite successful, as can be inferred from the celebrated memorial stone, the *Nestorian Monument*, erected in 781 AD. Is it a stretch of the imagination to suppose that *Zendō* might have been influenced by the Christian conception of God taught by these Nestorian missionaries? This is not to say that the Amida doctrine is a purely Christian product, for as we showed in Chapter II, it may have originated in purely Indian or Persian thought; but it does seem possible, if not probable, that Nestorian Christianity in China strengthened this theistic tendency in Buddhism—the practice of singling out one of the many Buddhas and making him the one and only Buddha. This theory seems all the more plausible when one remembers that *Zendō*’s teachings were regarded as heretical by other Buddhists.

But the Amida doctrine breaks down as a theistic conception also because no Buddhist philosopher is willing to think of the Ultimate in terms of personality. Amida is spoken of as a personal being, but the term "Personal" is what Buddhist philosophers of all schools would consider an accommodation of language when used for the Ultimate. Even in the West, it is a common objection to the doctrine of a Personal God to say that personality implies limitation, and that therefore God as the Absolute cannot be personal. The Buddhist philosopher raises the same objection and says that if Amida is spoken of as personal, it is only as an accommodation to suit the doctrine to the intelligence of the average person who cannot think in philosophical concepts. The Christian theist admits, of course, that God as the Absolute necessarily transcends human comprehension, but he holds that the term Personality represents the highest conception that can be held of God, so that we must think of God either as personal or as sub-personal. Super-personal concepts are beyond us. The Buddhist philosopher, regarding the idea of Personality as inadequate to express the nature of God, rejects it and, without realizing it, lapses into the sub-personal. Instead of reaching an idea more adequate than the conception of a perfect Personality, he either arrives at one less so, or the concept ends in the zero of Agnosticism or in the confusion of Pantheism.

But to understand more clearly in exactly what sense these semi-theistic sects regard Amida as a personal Buddha, we must take up at this point what is known as the doctrine of the Three Bodies of Buddha (<term>Sanshin</term>, Sanskrit: <term>Trikāya</term>). This doctrine is not unique to the Amida Buddhists, but it throws special light upon the God-idea as held by these

Now, Buddha may be thought of in three different ways, and these three ways are the so-called Three Bodies of Buddha. These are: (**a**) The Law Body of Buddha (Sanskrit <term>Dharmakāya</term>, Japanese <term>Hosshin Butsu</term>), (**b**) The Compensation Body of Buddha (Sanskrit <term>Sambhogakāya</term>, Japanese <term>Hōshin Butsu</term>), and (**c**) The Accommodated Body of Buddha (Sanskrit <term>Nirmānakāya</term>, Japanese <term>Ōjin Butsu</term>).

The first of these three, or the Law Body of Buddha, means Buddha conceived as the embodiment of Law. It is Buddha regarded as the essence or underlying substance of the universe, or Buddha as the Noumenon behind the phenomenal world. Or, if the doctrine is stated in the language of modern thought, it is almost synonymous with the Laws of Nature conceived as metaphysical entities, constituting a monistic whole of which nature is a visible and pluralistic expression.

> “Buddha makes Law his body.”
> “The realm of Law is the <term>Nyōrai</term>, and this is the true body of Buddha.”
> “The Law Body is the Law without birth and without death. It exists neither in the past nor in the future, for it transcends time.”

The Law Body of Buddha, then, means Buddha conceived as the Absolute and the underlying substance or essence of all reality; as such, Buddha is not a personal being.

The second way in which Buddha may be thought of is what is called the Compensation Body of Buddha. The meaning of this conception is rather difficult to state clearly, but in it lies the key to understanding theistic Buddhism and the explanation of what is meant by the so-called personal Buddha, or God, <term>Amida</term>. We have already said above that according to Buddhist philosophy, the Absolute as such is not personal, but personality is something which is evolved in the process of phenomenal existence and, like all phenomena, personality cannot be a permanent

According to the Buddhist <term>cosmogony</term>, this universe has always existed very much as it exists today; at least the essence of the universe has always existed. From the above, it must be clear, then, that when we speak of theistic <term>Buddhism</term> and call <term>Amida</term> a personal God, we are using language in a very loose sense. While the average <term>Amidaist</term> prays to <term>Amida</term> and speaks of him in personal terms, the <term>Amida</term> philosopher looks upon him as merely the personification of a principle, or the idea of mercy and wisdom. In Christian language we say, “God is love.” If by this we meant that God is simply the personification of love and not that love is the expression of a real personal being, we would have a parallel case with the Buddhist idea of <term>Amida</term> as the embodiment of Mercy.

Of the <term>Three Bodies of Buddha</term> mentioned above, the <term>Law Body</term> is the ultimate one; and insofar as the <term>Amidaists</term> recognize this, they agree with all the <term>Mahāyāna</term> sects that, while for practical purposes they may make room for the idea of a personal god or of personal gods, the ultimate as such cannot be said to be personal. It is the <term>Great Unknowable</term> concerning which no affirmation can be made.

3. *Pantheistic Buddhism.* — Pantheistic <term>Buddhism</term> finds its best representation in such sects as the <term>Tendai</term> and <term>Shingon</term>. It asserts the reality of the Divine and so is perhaps a little more positive in its idea of God than are the sects which we have designated as atheistic. In the second place, pantheistic sects see the divine in everything, and so differ somewhat from the so-called theistic sects which tend to see the divine primarily in the <term>Buddha Amida</term>. The pantheistic idea of God is the true philosophical basis for the polytheism of the common believer who is to be found in every sect. Even if in the pantheistic sects there are some gods who seem to occupy a peculiar preeminence—and the <term>Buddha Vairochana</term>, *for example*, is spoken of as the Supreme <term>Buddha</term>—the lesser gods and <term>Buddhas</term> will be considered as so many manifestations of these supreme beings, and these supreme beings will not be regarded as having an independent personal

It was this pantheistic basis of <term>Buddhism</term> which enabled <term>Kōbō Daishi</term> and the men of his day to bring the countless gods of the old <term>Shintō</term> into the already overstocked <term>Buddhist</term> pantheon, forming what is known as <term>Two-Sided Shintō</term>. Under theistic <term>Buddhism</term>, we spoke of the <term>Three Bodies of Buddha</term> and said that the first of these, the <term>Law Body of Buddha</term>, is regarded by all <term>Mahāyāna</term> sects as the deepest reality and the underlying essence of all things. Both the so-called atheistic and theistic branches hold this view. Pantheistic <term>Buddhism</term> also recognizes this threefold distinction and makes the <term>Law Body</term> the deepest reality. It is simply more insistent in its religious application of the idea by making all individual beings—especially the gods of the common people—the real manifestation of this ultimate divine reality. Or, to put it the other way around, the ultimate reality has no existence except as it exists in individual beings. All things are not merely the manifestation of the Divine, but they *are* the Divine. While there may be forms and manifestations of the Divine unknown to man, the phenomenal world with its many gods and many <term>Buddhas</term> is the Divine. The <term>Accommodated Bodies of Buddha</term> are the <term>Law Body</term>, and the <term>Law Body</term> is in the <term>Accommodated Body</term>. The phenomena are the <term>Noumenon</term>, and the <term>Noumenon</term> is in the phenomena.

If, then, personal beings appear in the phenomenal world, the essence of reality is personal to that extent; however, the Infinite is personal only as it is personal in the finite. In other words, God is personal only insofar as he is personal in human beings and in the gods of popular polytheism. But inasmuch—

Inasmuch as the personality of each human being and these popular gods is regarded as only a temporary state brought about by certain conditions which are constantly changing, God is not permanently personal in any one being. The Divine is permanently personal in finite beings only in so far as it has always manifested itself in them and probably always will. The Great Ocean of Reality is ever breaking into waves. No wave, however, is permanent, but soon sinks back again into the waveless depths. In the same way, the Divine ever wells up into personal beings, but none endure as such, and soon sink back into the depth of Being which is neither personal nor impersonal.

The God-idea, then, of pantheistic <term>Buddhism</term> is that God is personal in finite personal beings and impersonal in finite impersonal beings; the latter are as truly the essence of the Divine as the former. To the question as to whether God is personal, the reply would be both "Yes" and "No." That is why we said at the beginning of the section on the God-idea that <term>Pantheism</term> is the synthesis of the thesis <term>Atheism</term> and the antithesis <term>Theism</term>, including both and being neither. Speaking in the figure of a shield, <term>Pantheism</term> is the main body of the shield. <term>Atheism</term> is the smooth and barren concave surface, while the convex surface represents the theistic phase. The convex surface faces the foe of practical life and it may have on it one central decoration (<term>Semi-theism</term>), or it may be decorated with many symbols (<term>Polytheism</term>). Whether they be many or only one they are, after all, only surface decorations. The surface decorations may be the picture of those who have attained <term>Buddhahood</term> and so are an encouragement to the one who bears it, but they can be hardly more than that; for again let us remember that <term>Buddhism</term> really knows of no personal God except such as man can himself become, *i.e.* the Divine is only such as is within man.

While philosophic <term>Buddhism</term> is monistic with a strong bent towards agnosticism, popular <term>Buddhism</term> is pluralistic and realistic. The average <term>Buddhist</term> believer is incurably polytheistic, and the philosophical dis-

These are among the more popular deities worshipped by the masses, and to them might be added a long list of other <term>Bodhisattvas</term> and <term>Buddhas</term>, angels, and saints that receive more or less worship as superhuman beings. In fact, the creation of gods is not entirely a lost art even in modern Japan, as can be seen from the fact that the late <term>Emperor Meiji Tennō</term> and <term>Admiral Tōgo</term> are being rapidly enshrined in the hearts of the common people as superhuman beings. This may seem strange to the Western mind, but it is a very natural process from the Buddhist or <term>Shintō</term> standpoint, which refuses to make a clear-cut distinction between the human and the divine.

As we have said above, these realistic gods of popular polytheism play a far more important part in the life of the average Buddhist follower than do the abstract monistic concepts of <term>Mahāyāna</term> philosophy. In fact, even to the Buddhist philosopher, this realistic polytheism is not entirely disagreeable and provides more substance to his monistic abstractions than is usually realized. For the gods of polytheism may be regarded as temporary beings like humans, who are personal now but have no ultimate existence as personal beings; they may be regarded as subject to and manifestations of the one Supreme Being (<term>Semi-theism</term>), or they may be regarded as mere parts of the pantheistic whole into which they, like man, are ultimately absorbed. But as we have said, the most compatible philosophic background for polytheism is pantheism. Or to put it the other way around, polytheism is the popular aspect of the philosopher's pantheism. Thus, polytheism is not a separate category alongside atheism, theism, and pantheism, but it is the popular complement of these, especially of the latter.

As we have already said, Buddhism was polytheistic before it reached Japan, but it became even more so after it absorbed the innumerable gods (*<term>Yaoyorozu no kamigami</term>*, or Eight hundred myriads of gods) of the native <term>Shintō</term>. If the result of the union between Buddhism and <term>Shintō</term> is strongly Buddhistic on the philosophical side, on its popular

On its religious side, it often seems more <term>Shintoistic</term>. The truth is that <term>Buddhism</term> in Japan could only win its place by giving the popular <term>Shinto</term> gods a conspicuous place in its pantheon; and while the Buddhist philosopher has reduced these gods to mere manifestations of the older Buddhist deities, they have more or less kept their former place for the average Japanese believer. This alone can explain the fact that even today, after thirteen centuries of Buddhist history in this land, small shrines to <term>Shinto</term> deities exist by the tens of thousands, and the greater <term>Shinto</term> deities such as <term>Amaterasu</term>, <term>Hachiman</term>, and <term>Inari</term> occupy a prominent place in Japanese religious life. Despite the separation of <term>Shinto</term> from <term>Buddhism</term> made in the <term>Meiji era</term>, the people in general do not give their allegiance exclusively to one or the other, but regard themselves as being Shintoists and Buddhists at one and the same time.

And now let us refer for a moment to the Chart of the Ten Buddhist Worlds and see how this gradation of beings, which is essentially Indian in origin, was well adapted to absorb the <term>Shinto cosmology</term>. This scale of beings fixes humanity near the center and provides for four grades below and five grades above. The grade immediately above humanity is the Realm of Heavenly Beings, or the Realm of the Gods. Now, <term>Shinto</term> had no scale like this, but it, too, believed in beings lower than man and beings higher than man. The beings higher than man were the gods; in fact, the very word for "God" in Japanese probably meant originally simply that which is "above" or "superior." It is a rather striking fact that the realms below humanity in the Buddhist scale were not enriched from the <term>Shinto cosmology</term>. There was comparatively little of the horrible <term>demonology</term> of India, China, and Korea in primitive <term>Shinto</term>. There were many spirits and ghosts, and some of these were more or less malicious, but on the whole, <term>Shinto</term> had little of the horrors of hell and demonology which we find in other Asiatic religions. It was rich in deities—nature deities, personifications of abstractions, apotheoses of great ancestors and heroes, etc.—and these "eight hundred myriads of gods" were added to the

The God-idea, then, in Japanese Buddhism is, as we said at the beginning of this section, an exceedingly complex one. It varies all the way from a low animistic conception up through ancestor worship and a diverse polytheism until it reaches, in the minds of the philosophers and better-educated classes, a monistic form. This form leans toward atheism on one side and semi-theism on the other, but its real core is best expressed as a vague pantheism. And all three philosophical conceptions are, in the final analysis, undermined by an agnosticism which makes every assertion about the nature of the divine futile, and seeks to remind us that all human knowledge is merely seeing things from the standpoint of <term>Accommodated Truth</term>, and not as things really are.

But we cannot close these remarks on the God-idea in Japanese Buddhism without adding a few supplementary words. Among educated Japanese, there is quite a large number of those who would classify themselves as Buddhists, but who know little or nothing of the specific teachings of Buddhist philosophy; yet their general intelligence prevents them from believing in the polytheistic ideas of the uneducated masses. It seems safe to say that many of these have at least a vague belief in a Personal God who is the Great Intelligence that controls our universe, and who is the Moral Power that in some way will reward the righteous and punish the wicked, both in this life and in the life to come. And there are still more whose conception is less theistic but rather <term>neo-pantheistic</term>. They draw their inspiration from modern science, which in its most reverent moods dimly recognizes an eternal mysterious life or energy permeating all things. This <term>neo-pantheism</term> differs from the old Oriental pantheism because it places a greater value upon the physical universe.
