It is from the ranks of such men that Christianity makes its converts, for they are the ones who have breathed most deeply the modern Western atmosphere which, though it contains much that is evil, also contains much that is Christian.

## F. *Man and His Condition*

1. *The Nature of Man.* — In Christian thought, there is a clear distinction between God and man on the one hand, and between man and the lower beings on the other. It is true that the distinction between man and the rest of nature has been somewhat blurred in modern thought by certain schools of philosophy, and no thinkers in the West would deny that man is linked closely with nature, at least on one side. But after this has been granted, Western thought still maintains that man is a unique being in nature and that there is a wide gap between him and other animals; at least, man has within him capacities which, when developed, make him a decidedly higher order of being. In Buddhism, these lines of demarcation between God and man on the one hand, and between man and lower beings on the other side, are not so clear. As we have repeatedly said, man is placed somewhere near the center in the scale of beings who inhabit the Buddhist universe. The Ten Realms of beings into which the universe is divided merge into one another so that the lower constantly becomes the higher, and the higher degenerates into the lower. Man’s good karma leads him to birth in a heavenly realm, or if his

But what is the origin of man according to Buddhism? In Genesis, we read that God created man in his own image. However much modern thought in the Christian world has changed the formulation of this idea, the Christian of today believes as firmly as the Old Testament writers that God existed before man and in some way created man, either directly or through a slow evolutionary process. And he also believes that man is created in God’s image; *that is,* man, like God, is a rational, personal being. Buddhism does not assume a Personal God existing before the universe, nor does Buddhist thought hold that God has created man. It rather holds that when man thinks of the Divine in terms of a personal being, he is creating God in his own image. The universe has always existed, and man, or beings like him, have always existed. And such beings probably always will exist as long as the monistic whole breaks up into the pluralism of individual beings. Ever since the wind of primordial Ignorance has broken up the ocean of Sameness into the waves of individual beings, man has existed, and human beings will continue to come and go as long as the waves of mental activity disturb the eternal Calm. Man is, then, not the creation of an all-wise and loving God, but, like all individual existence, is an accident of primordial Ignorance which, once it begins to function, works on and on by the law of Karma unceasingly, or until it is exhausted.

The inner constitution of man and the way in which the law of Karma works is explained by the doctrine of the Twelve Links in the Karma-chain. This has already been given above in the section on the Theory of Knowledge. This is exceedingly difficult for the Western mind to understand, largely, however, because Western psychology realizes too clearly that the self is a unity which cannot be understood by such an analytic process and by what is essentially a mechanistic conception.

This is true in the sense that Buddhism refuses to claim that the ego is a permanent reality, but not in the sense that Buddhism denies the reality of the psychic within human nature. In fact, Buddhism regards the psychic as the deepest reality in human nature. What the West understands as the "self," Buddhism would call the Provisional Self, regarding it as a byproduct of the body's physical organism.

This does not mean, however, that the physical organism, or matter, is considered the deepest reality; matter itself is the product of a deeper reality. This deeper reality should be understood more in terms of man’s psychic nature than in terms of his physical form. This psychic reality is similar to the "Will" found in Schopenhauer's philosophy. It is that blind "will-to-be" which gives rise to individual beings, especially to beings such as man, who is self-conscious and therefore mistakenly thinks that the conscious self is a permanent reality.

It is not a permanent reality, but only a fleeting phase in the chain of life. This chain has as its only permanent element, or core, this psychic power or blind "will-to-be." It is, then, neither the conscious self nor the physical organism that creates this self as a permanent reality; rather, it is that mysterious "will-to-be" that gives rise to both the physical organism and the conscious self. 

Strangely, this energy continues to "will-to-be" as long as it remains ignorant of the nature of true being—and especially ignorant of the nature of the conscious self. This is why man is born again and again into this world. Only when the blind energy which makes up the real core of his being has been enlightened will it be free from manifesting itself as an individual human being. Thus, according to Buddhism, the real source of man, as well as the source of all individual existence, is that ignorance which somehow enters reality and causes the eternal Oneness to form itself into individual beings. The first link in the chain of Karma is the link of Ignorance.

Even this concept is not held consistently, for the average Buddhist in Japan also makes room for the *Shintō* explanation; specifically, that the people of Japan are actually the descendants of the Imperial Family, and that their ancestry traces back to the gods of heaven and earth. This is, at least, the orthodox Japanese doctrine that no Buddhist dared to challenge in the past. Today's educated classes within the Buddhist community—who are ignorant of the Buddhist explanation and find the *Shintō* explanation too childish—naturally accept, at least vaguely, the Western naturalistic explanation of human origins: namely, that Nature, spelled with a capital letter, has somehow produced man and made him as he is. For practical purposes, they would say, we must treat the self as real; however, exactly what the self is or what becomes of it need not concern the practical person. This type of Buddhist would argue that religion should focus more on developing strong people who are capable of doing the world's work than spending its time speculating about the nature of the self or its final destiny.

2. *Man's Condition.* — Since man finds himself near the center of the scale of living beings, his condition is better than that of beings lower on the scale, but worse than those above him. His is an existence of joy and sorrow, pleasure and pain. Overall, however, the dark side of life outweighs the bright side, because all pleasures are fleeting and end in sorrow; all youth and strength end in old age, weakness, and death. In our first chapter, we spoke of the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism, and we saw that the first of these is the truth that life is essentially sorrow and suffering. We repeat this truth here because Japanese Buddhism—though much less pessimistic than Indian Buddhism—still accepts this assessment of life as substantially correct.

Christianity, too, has a great deal to say about the vanity of life as lived by the average person. Paul’s philosophy of suffering in the eighth chapter of Romans could not have been written by a Buddhist.

### 3. *The Cause of Life’s Evils.*

— What is the cause of the sorrow and suffering in human life according to Buddhism?

We have seen above that the very origin of man is due to the primordial Ignorance, or that blind desire for individual existence which somehow is inherent in the universe. Naturally this blind desire constitutes the core of man’s being, and so is the seat of his sorrows and sufferings. The second of the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism given in Chapter I is the truth about the origin of suffering, and it is formulated as follows:

> “Now this is the Noble Truth as to the origin of suffering. Truly; it is the craving thirst that causes the renewal of existences, that is accompanied by sensual delights, and seeks satisfaction, now here and now there — that is to say, the craving for the gratification of the senses, or the craving for a future life, or the craving for prosperity.”

In short, then, it is the desire for the pleasures of life, the desire for self-assertion, which causes the sufferings of life. And why is it that man desires the things which,

It leads to the formation of the individual, until in the eighth link of the <term>Karma-chain</term>, we reach <term>Desire</term>, that is, the lust of the flesh. This <term>Desire</term> leads to a clinging to existence and a passion for things that cannot provide permanent satisfaction. This, in turn, leads to rebirth into this world of evil, and so the <term>Wheel of Life</term> continues its endless revolutions.

In <term>Buddhism</term>, therefore, it is not so much that "the wages of sin is death" as it is that the wages of ignorance is suffering. Man's condition is not so much a state of sin as it is one of ignorance. It is true that <term>Buddhism</term> uses the word <term>Sin</term>, but hardly with the significance it has in <term>Christian</term> thought, because without the <term>Christian</term> concept of <term>God</term>, the <term>Christian</term> idea of sin is incomprehensible. In fact, it is more accurate to say that <term>Buddhism</term> speaks of <term>Evil</term> rather than <term>Sin</term>. And <term>Evil</term> is an effect rather than a cause; specifically, it is the effect produced by ignorance or error. In the practical ethics of <term>Buddhism</term>, the concept of sin seems to find a place, but hardly in the context we are discussing now. It is better to say that <term>Buddhism</term> makes no distinction between sin and evil. That is, if <term>Job</term> suffers more than his neighbors, it is because he is the greater sinner, and those "eighteen upon whom the tower in <term>Siloam</term> fell" were worse sinners than their neighbors and deserved the punishment.

This is a natural answer for <term>Buddhism</term> to provide, and it follows directly from its fundamental doctrine of <term>Karma</term>. The evils of human life belong to the human condition, and only a being who deserves to be there is born into that state—or rather, one who has caused themselves to be born into that state through the relentless workings of the law of <term>Karma</term>. That is, the character of one's environment corresponds to the nature of one's being, and the reverse is also true; so an evil being exists in an evil environment, and a good being in a good environment. This harmony between being and environment is known as the <term>Two Fruits</term> of *Shōhō* and *Ihō*. The evils of life are the fruits of past deeds, which

<header>STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM</header>

Past deeds may be called sins, or acts of ignorance; and the sins, or acts of ignorance, of the present life may be regarded as the cause of present and future evils.

<term>Sin</term>, then, in <term>Buddhism</term> is not to be regarded as a moral affront to <term>God</term>, but rather as a foolish act which necessarily brings the one who commits it a present or future evil. No true <term>Buddhist</term> could have written the fifty-first <term>Psalm</term>, and especially not the words, “Against thee, thee only have I sinned.” <term>Sin</term> is essentially folly, for what sane man would do that which is sure to bring evil upon himself? The real trouble with man is that he is ignorant, rather than that he is in moral rebellion against <term>God’s</term> will; he needs a renewal of mind rather than a change of heart. This is why the <term>Buddhist</term> gospel of <term>salvation</term> is presented as an <term>Enlightenment</term> of the mind rather than a <term>Regeneration</term> of the heart; and the whole teaching of <term>Buddhism</term> is cast in the form of right thinking rather than right moral purpose. Man is to be saved from evil rather than from sin, and <term>Sin</term> as the cause of evil is <term>ignorance</term> rather than wrong moral purpose. Men are not sinners so much as fools, and <term>Buddhism</term> seeks to make of them sages rather than saints. But this brings us to a new subject; namely, the subject of <term>Salvation</term> in <term>Japanese Buddhism</term>.

### G. *Salvation*

The subject of <term>Salvation</term> naturally falls into two general divisions; namely, the Essence and Goal of Salvation, and the Way or Means of Salvation. Of course, it is impossible to keep these two aspects entirely separate in one’s presentation of the matter, for the essence and goal of salvation are in part the way and means. Thus, for example, it may be said that in <term>Buddhism</term> the essence and goal of salvation is <term>Enlightenment</term>, and that the way and means to achieve this is through <term>Enlightenment</term>. It is also difficult to say which of these two aspects should be taken up first, but it seems best to state first what <term>Japanese Buddhism</term> means by <term>Salvation</term>, and then show what it regards as the Way to attain this.

<page-num>241</page-num>
<header>SALVATION</header>

The goal of the salvation offered by <term>Buddhism</term> is expressed most generally by that mystifying word <term>Nirvāna</term> (Japanese: <term>Nehan</term>). Salvation is to enter <term>Nirvāna</term>.

But what is meant by entering <term>Nirvāna</term>?

The meaning of this word, even in <term>primitive Buddhism</term>, has led to much discussion among scholars. It used to be maintained that <term>Nirvāna</term> means a cessation of being, extinction, or total annihilation. Salvation therefore meant an “escape” from life—a life which is incurably evil. In recent years, however, there has been a reaction against this interpretation, and <term>Nirvāna</term> is taken to mean not only an “escape” from evil, but also an “entrance” into a life of bliss. But whether that life of bliss is to continue beyond physical death is not always so clear. That question in <term>primitive Buddhism</term>, as we pointed out in Chapter I, was placed among the Great Indeterminates. At any rate, it seems true that if the founder of <term>Buddhism</term> believed in the continuation of the <term>Arhat</term> beyond death, he hesitated to say anything very definite as to the nature of such a life. But as we pointed out in Chapter II, when <term>primitive Buddhism</term> began to develop into <term>Mahāyāna Buddhism</term>, the doctrine of a future life of bliss began to assert itself in one way or another. In <term>Chinese Buddhism</term>, the chief function of the Buddhist priests seems to have centered on funerals and matters relating to the world to come. And in <term>Japan</term>, too, both in popular and philosophical <term>Buddhism</term>, salvation means not merely an “escape” from the dread cycle of existence, but often the “entrance” into a present and future life of positive content. Thus we have as one of the great summaries of Buddhist doctrine the profound phrase, “*Riku Tokuraku*,” meaning “Escaping from Suffering and Obtaining Bliss.” That is, salvation is both an “escape” and an “entrance.”

It is true that some philosophers say that “obtaining bliss” simply means the “escape from suffering” and not the obtaining of a positive good, but the majority of Japanese <term>Buddhists</term> would hold that “obtaining bliss” does mean the entrance into an existence of real content. There are various ways of interpreting the meaning of this “con—

We must again refer to the Buddhist chart of the <term>Ten Worlds</term>. The <term>Human World</term> is placed fifth from the bottom. Above the <term>Human World</term> is the <term>Realm of Heavenly Beings</term>, and above this are the <term>Four Holies</term>, the highest of which is <term>Buddhahood</term>, or the <term>Buddha World</term>. Now salvation consists in passing out of the <term>Human World</term> into the worlds above the human. Thus, salvation is naturally a matter of degrees and is only perfect when one has entered into the highest of the <term>Ten Worlds</term>; namely, into the <term>Buddha World</term>. This passage from the lower worlds into the higher worlds is naturally both an "escape" from evil and an "entrance" into bliss. Thus, when man passes into the world above him, he escapes from the sufferings and limitations characteristic of the human sphere and becomes a sharer of the bliss characteristic of his new environment. But as the <term>Realm of Heavenly Beings</term> still belongs to the <term>Six Ways</term> or the <term>Three Worlds</term> in which the law of <term>Karma</term> is operative, beings in this heavenly world are in danger of falling back into the human and lower worlds. Therefore, entrance into the world of heavenly beings is not true salvation, however desirable it may be when compared with human life. Buddhism offers a full salvation, and so it must save man out of this realm of heavenly beings. Other religions, the Buddhist would say, may accomplish this limited salvation, but only Buddhism brings man the complete salvation; it offers salvation into the <term>Four Holies</term>, yes, into the Holiest of Holies, the Buddha state.

The lowest of the <term>Four Holies</term> is the <term>Hearer State</term> (<term>Srāvaka</term>, Japanese: <term>Shōmon</term>), and this has four grades. To enter the lowest of these four grades is to enter the Fellowship of the Saints. He who has entered the second grade is subject to return only once more to the <term>Six Ways</term> or the <term>Three Worlds</term> where the law of <term>Karma</term> reigns. The second of the <term>Four Holies</term> is the <term>Pratyēka Buddha State</term> (Japanese: <term>Enkaku</term>). One who has entered this state has broken the twelve links of the <term>Karma-chain</term>, and has thus escaped from the dreaded <term>Wheel of Life</term> and entered the beginnings of true enlightenment. Of course, such enlightenment, when compared with that of the perfect Buddha, is still very shallow. To such a person, <term>Nirvāna</term> is void of all passions and sufferings and is filled with the bliss of knowledge.

But a fuller salvation than that of the <term>Pratyēka Buddha</term> is that of the <term>Bodhisattva</term> (Japanese: <term>Bosatsu</term>). One who has attained this lofty degree of salvation has not only escaped the evils of life and entered bliss himself, but finds that the bliss of salvation consists in helping others to escape from the <term>Wheel of Life</term> and enter a life of positive bliss. A <term>Bodhisattva</term> returns to the human world again and again—not because he is bound to the <term>Wheel of Life</term> and thus dragged down, but because he is bound by the law of love and sympathy for suffering humanity. That is, to a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, <term>Nirvāna</term> is not an extinction or total annihilation; rather, it is the great work of annihilating the passions and sufferings in the lives of others. This he does by practicing the <term>Six Virtues</term> ⁶ of almsgiving and teaching, keeping the commandments, patience and long-suffering, diligence, meditation, and wisdom, in fulfillment of his <term>Four Great Vows</term> ⁷ to save all beings, to destroy all passions, to know and teach others all laws, and to lead others to understand the ways of Buddha, however lofty they may be. With these characteristics, it is not strange that popular polytheistic Buddhism derives its leading deities from the ranks of the <term>Bodhisattvas</term>.

When the <term>Bodhisattva</term> has finished his noble work of providing a way of salvation for others, then—and only then—does he enter the bliss of true <term>Buddhahood</term>. But while it is clear that <term>Nirvāna</term> is an escape from, or an annihilation of, the lower and an entrance into the higher, it is not yet clear from what has been said what the condition is of one who has entered into the highest state. What is the condition of one who has obtained the complete salvation which Buddhism offers?

The answer to this question is that it is Buddhahood. But then, what is really meant by Buddhahood? This, as the reader will observe, brings the subject back to what we have already discussed in the section on the God-idea. Without repeating in full what we said there, let us state briefly the substance in its bearing upon the matter in hand.

We saw that the God-idea in Buddhist philosophy falls under three general heads; namely, Atheism, Theism or Semi-theism, and Pantheism. The perfect salvation which Japanese Buddhism offers to all beings may likewise be divided into three kinds; for in Buddhism, as in all religions, the God-idea conditions the idea of salvation, and vice versa. It is a real case of “we shall be like him; for we shall see him even as he is.”

To the Buddhist whose God-idea ends practically in zero, <term>Nirvāna</term> also approaches the vanishing point.<note>8</note> But just as no Buddhist in Japan would say that existence is absolutely void, but rather that the essence of existence is a "Something" which transcends the categories of all beings known to man, so <term>Nirvāna</term>, or the perfect Buddha State, is not a condition of absolute void but a state which transcends the categories of human life. It is a total annihilation of everything which makes up this present phenomenal world, but it is not therefore an absolute void. To describe such a

Of course, he would not say that it is an absolute void, but that it is a state which transcends all categories of human thought. Indeed, even to say that it is “a state which transcends all categories of human thought” is really saying too much. As a result of this agnostic spirit, which always flows as an undercurrent of Buddhist thought, there is much less joy in a real salvation from life’s sin and sorrows, and much less hope for a victorious life and an eternal fellowship with God than one would expect among <term>Amida</term> Buddhists. The two letters quoted above, with their note of joy and confidence, are the exception rather than the rule.

And now, what must we say regarding the meaning of salvation and <term>Nirvana</term> to the pantheistic Buddhist? He, too, would say that salvation, or <term>Nirvana</term>, is a progressive “escape” from evil and an “entrance” into a continually higher good. He differs from the semi-theistic Buddhist in that while the former ordinarily thinks of <term>Nirvana</term> as a fellowship of the <term>Buddhas</term>, the latter conceives of <term>Nirvana</term> instead as a merging of the individual with the All-inclusive <term>Buddha</term>.

Salvation consists in knowing that <term>Buddha</term> is in all and all are in <term>Buddha</term>. But just what that state is in which the saved are merged with the Divine is not very clear. In fact, the pantheistic philosopher will give essentially the same answer which has already been given above to represent the atheistic and semi-theistic philosophers. As the true essence of the Divine-All transcends all human knowledge, it is impossible to state in human language the condition of those who have attained perfect salvation. It is, of course, a freedom from the suffering inherent in all individual existence. It is a rest and peace which is void of all that characterizes our present life, but it is not therefore an absolute void. One can only speak of it in negative terms—that is, a negation of all that might be affirmed of life as we know it.

Thus we see that while several answers may be given to the question of what is meant by <term>Nirvāna</term> or salvation in Japanese Buddhism, they merge in the last analysis into the same answer. They all agree that it is an “escape from evil and an obtaining of bliss,” but what that highest bliss may be is impossible to say. This answer, as we have stated in other connections, grows logically from the Buddhist theory of knowledge, which claims that all human knowledge is relative and belongs to the shadow world.

> “All things are unstable, for this is the law of life and death. When life and death are completely done away with, extinction is happiness.”

> “The great and wide expanse of space is called empty space. The peace of <term>Nirvāna</term> is like this empty space, being an immense void. In this place lives no ruler, nor is it the abode of the ego.”

> “Life, death, and <term>Nirvāna</term> are nothing but dreams that have passed; for there is no beginning and no end, there is no coming and no going.”

But while the meaning of <term>Nirvāna</term> and salvation in philosophical Buddhism vanishes into thin mist, it is quite the opposite in popular Buddhism. Here it is often crudely realistic. The common man knows comparatively little

To some—though it must be confessed that their number is not very large—the meaning may not be so very different from what it is to the average Christian. These "more noble" ones seek earnestly to conquer their lower passions and to walk in the path of righteousness and truth to the extent of their ability. And they would think of salvation beyond the present life in terms of our present higher life and a fellowship with <term>Buddha</term> and the saints. The passages quoted from the letters of two Buddhist women throw light on the faith of this nobler type. There are others who would have less to say about the help of <term>Buddha</term> and their hope for a better future, but to whom salvation means something real in the form of a higher ethical life lived in obedience to the commandments and maxims of Buddhism. That is, there are devout people in all the sects to whom <term>Buddha</term>’s salvation is something real and rather noble.

There is, however, a darker side to the picture. Just as the concept of God held by the general run of believers is incurably polytheistic and often revoltingly crude, so the conception of salvation is on an exceedingly low plane. It is real enough. Indeed, just because philosophical Buddhism has lost itself in the clouds of abstract speculation and has not been faithful in proclaiming the higher life in comprehensible terms, the common man has been left to himself; thus, he thinks of salvation largely in terms of life on the lowest plane. He has made gods a little higher (and sometimes a little lower) than himself, and the salvation which such gods offer is naturally in harmony with their nature. Thus, the common man turns to one or the other of the gods in the crowded pantheon and expects from each the help for which the deity has special qualifications to bestow. But in all the help which the various deities render to mankind, there is a surprising absence of the higher aspects of life. Salvation as a conquest over sin and a growth in righteousness is a conception not generally shared by the great mass of those who call themselves Buddhists. In fact, it is not difficult to show that <term>popular Buddhism</term> is often responsible for keeping the people bound with the fetters of sin and ignorance. If anyone doubts this statement, let him visit some of the most popular centers of Buddhism and look around with open eyes. Whatever may be said about the lofty teachings of Buddhism as to salvation and <term>Nirvāna</term>, it must be admitted by the unbiased observer that Buddhism, in the lives of the great majority of its adherents, is often a real hindrance to the higher life. If the religion of the Buddha ever was a power for salvation to Japan's millions, it cannot be said to fill such a function today, at least not on a very large scale.

## 2. *The Way of Salvation.*

If the essence and goal of salvation in Buddhism is an "escape from evil and an entrance into a life of bliss," and if the cause of evil and the hindrance to entrance into the life of bliss is Ignorance, then it follows that the Way of Salvation must be a way which leads away from Ignorance into Knowledge. Thus we have the great summary of the Buddhist mode of salvation, <term>Tenmei Kaigo</term>, "Turning from Error and Opening Understanding." Man is saved by knowing the truth, the Truth of Buddhism.

But what is that saving truth which man must know and which Buddhism offers him? This is a question which has a very complex answer.

There is at least one school which holds that this saving truth consists in "breaking error," *i.e.* truth has no positive content, and the spirit of truth is the spirit which denies all things, for this world is a shadow world and therefore must be destroyed by a process of negations. Light, this school would say, is not a positive reality, but simply the absence of darkness.

But just as we saw in the preceding section that the essence of salvation in Japanese Buddhism ordinarily has a rather positive content, so the way of salvation is usually not simply a "breaking of error" but also a real "opening of the understanding." The way, however, in which this

The way in which the breaking of error and the opening of understanding are to be achieved varies somewhat among the different sects.

It is customary to divide these various methods into two great divisions. These divisions correspond roughly to the two great divisions known in Christian thought as the Way of the Law and the Way of Grace; or the Way of Good Works and the Way of Faith. There are several ways in which the chief aspects of these two great divisions are expressed. Thus the Way of the Law is called the <term>Holy Way Division</term> (Japanese: <term>Shōdōmon</term>), or <term>Self-reliance</term> (Japanese: <term>Jiriki</term>, literally meaning "self-strength"). In less technical language, it is called the <term>Way of Hardships</term> (Japanese: <term>Nangyōdō</term>). On the other hand, the doctrine of the Way of Grace is called the <term>Pure Land Division</term> (Japanese: <term>Jōdomon</term>), from the fact that it teaches a salvation in Paradise which is not prepared or earned by the believer, but by <term>Amida</term>. In contrast with the way of Self-reliance, it is called <term>Reliance upon Another</term> (Japanese: <term>Tariki</term>, literally meaning "another’s strength"), and in contrast with the Way of Hardships, it is called the <term>Easy Way</term> (<term>Igyōdō</term>).

a. *The Way of the Law.* — The first of these two great ways of salvation—namely, the Way of the Law of Self-reliance—is, as we saw in Chapter I, the way proclaimed by primitive Buddhism. It recognized apparently no salvation except that which a person can work out for themselves through perfect obedience to the law and through a strict walking in the Holy Way of self-discipline. This one must do in one’s own strength and without trust in the assistance of another. The majority of Japanese sects are usually classified as teachers of this rigid way, and at least one sect—namely, the great <term>Zen Sect</term>—really carries this doctrine into practice. As we saw in the section on the God-idea, the <term>Zen Sect</term> is practically atheistic, and, of course, the logical corollary of atheism is that man cannot look to God for help, but that he must save himself. Every man is the sole architect of his own future, and whatsoever he sows, that shall he also reap. Not even a heavenly being can intervene and save man from the inexorable workings of the

Therefore, examine yourselves constantly so that you do not lose wisdom; for this, according to my teaching, is the way of deliverance. If anyone loses wisdom, he is no longer on the path, nor a white-robed man, but only a nameless one. True wisdom is a strong ship which carries us across the sea of old age, sickness, and death. And again, wisdom is the great light which illuminates the outer darkness; it is an effective medicine for all patients, and a sharp ax to cut down the trees of passion.”

But while one branch of Buddhism teaches a rather rigid doctrine of salvation through one’s own strength, there is usually some room left for the doctrine that help may come from another. Even the architect of his own future can receive suggestions from another as to how to build that future. Gautama himself, although he rejected the assistance of the gods of the people and did not trust in the unknowable God of the philosophers, felt that the way of salvation which he had achieved would at least show the way to others, and so be a real help. In fact, he gave his life to the task of showing others his way of salvation and preached it as the way in which all the Buddhas before him had walked. And so among Japanese Buddhists who hold the doctrine of salvation through self-reliance, there is at least the recognition of the possibility of one person helping another to the extent of showing him the right way. Even when the doctrine of “Help Thyself” is held in the most extreme form, it is usually accompanied by the doctrine that in the last analysis everything has, as the core of its real being, the <term>Buddha nature</term>, and so the most depraved may have a hope of ultimate deliverance from the bondages of existence even though there is no immediate prospect of entrance into a positive salvation.

b. *The Way of Grace.* — The second great Way of Salvation taught by Japanese Buddhism is the Way of Grace, or salvation through the Strength of Another. The best representatives of this way are the <term>Amida</term> sects, especially the <term>Shin Sect</term>. We saw in the section on the God-idea that the <term>Amida</term> sects are at least semi-theistic, and it is natural that with such a God-idea these sects should recognize more clearly the principle of Divine Grace in human life than is done by the atheistic and pantheistic sects. In fact, these <term>Amida</term> sects not only recognize this principle, but they seem to carry it to an extreme in their popular presentation of the matter. They do not deny that salvation through one’s own strength is possible — it is possible for the few strong men, and especially was it possible for strong men back in the golden age of humanity

Not only do the <term>Amida</term> sects preach this doctrine of salvation through the Strength of Another, but we might say that all popular <term>Buddhism</term>, in one way or another, holds that man receives aid and salvation from the gods, <term>Buddhas</term>, and <term>Bodhisattvas</term>. Each one of these many deities has his own peculiar function as a helper of man, for what is the use of deities if they cannot help man in the hour of need? The way of the Law and Self-discipline is largely confined to the better-educated classes. The masses, whether <term>Amidaists</term> or not, as a rule expect their gods to take care of them. The gods, of course, must be propitiated through various rites and ceremonies, and to that extent man must earn their help and protection.

We said above that the salvation prepared by <term>Amida</term> needs only to be accepted by man to receive the full benefit; but how is man to accept it? By faith and faith alone, say the true <term>Amidaists</term>. It is sometimes customary among believers in <term>Amida</term> to divide <term>Buddhism</term> as a whole into two great divisions, and to say that one teaches that man is saved through philosophical wisdom, and the other that man is saved solely through faith. Such a clear-cut division is a little arbitrary; for in a true sense <term>Buddhism</term> as a whole is a faith, and the very foundation of its theories of knowledge, as we saw above, is a "<term>credo ut intelligam</term>" <note>Latin: "I believe so that I may understand."</note>. Then also the formula which the <term>Buddhists</term> of all sects use is a formula of faith; namely, "I take refuge in <term>Buddha</term>, the Law, and the Priesthood." > "Faith is the gift of Another because it is not a faith which is fixed through the believer's own efforts, but entirely through the influence of the great, merciful heart of <term>Amida</term>. This faith is wrought through the enlightened vow of <term>Amida</term>, and to fill the believer's heart with faith is <term>Amida's</term> desire."

This principle of grace is carried so far in its popular presentation that the listener is told that repeating the prayer, *<term>Namu Amida Butsu</term>*, just once or a few times is enough to ensure his birth into the <term>Western Paradise</term>. Some <term>Amidaists</term> are still too conscious of the old <term>Karma</term> doctrine to admit that a deathbed repentance can lead to immediate birth into Paradise. They hold that a deathbed repentance in <term>Amida</term> will ultimately lead to birth into Paradise. Such a man's lotus—to use Buddhist terminology—will one day, perhaps tens of thousands of years later, open up, and he will thus be born into <term>Amida's</term> Paradise. As a rule, however, the <term>Amida</term> believer is taught that he will enter Paradise immediately after death and that even now he is in Paradise, for he lives in the assurance of that great hope.

Good works, the careful <term>Amidaist</term> says, are necessary as signs of the believer's salvation, and they should be done out of gratitude for the gift of <term>Amida's</term> grace. Good works are not causes of salvation but rather effects of salvation.

But there is another side to this beautiful doctrine of salvation through faith in <term>Amida's</term> saving grace. In practice, this doctrine is often an <term>antinomianism</term> <note>the belief that faith alone is necessary for salvation, regardless of moral law</note> of the worst type. In fact, the <term>Amidaists</term> sometimes boast that their doctrine of grace is more lofty than the Christian doctrine because Christians seem to pay a great deal of attention to moral conduct, after all, while <term>Amida</term> saves everyone no matter how vile they are. As one Christian critic, who is well acquainted with the practical workings of <term>Buddhism</term>, puts it: where the Christian doctrine teaches that man is saved *from* sin—that is, from its guilt, pollution, and power—the doctrine of these followers of <term>Amida</term> is that man is saved *in* sin. This doctrine of grace has been carried to such an extreme that the indifference of the <term>Amidaists</term> to self-culture in the past gave rise to the jibe, "<term>Zenshū</term> zeni nashi, <term>Monto</term> mono wo shirazu," which means, "The Zen followers have no money, the <term>Monto</term> (<term>Shin</term>) followers have no knowledge."

But this doctrine of salvation through the grace of <term>Amida</term> is not only much abused in its popular presentation—often leading to a mere superstitious repetition of the prayer <term>Namu Amida Butsu</term> without working a change of heart or enlightening the mind—it also breaks down philosophically in the last analysis. We have already seen in the section on the God-idea that <term>Amida</term> is, after all, only such a "god as man can and has become." The so-called <term>vicarious savior</term> in <term>Amida</term> Buddhism is not God come in the flesh, but man who has become a god through his own strength. <term>Hōzō Bosatsu</term> was first an ordinary man and then became the Buddha <term>Amida</term>. Perhaps this would not be such a serious defect to many minds, for it would mean that a man has demonstrated the possibility of becoming god, and such a one could truly help other men escape from the evils of this world into the bliss of another world. But there is another weakness in this Buddhist savior-idea. The man <term>Hōzō Bosatsu</term> has not a shred of historicity about him, but is a mere fiction of a fertile imagination. And further, according to the <term>Amidaists</term> themselves, <term>Amida</term> has no real personal existence but is only the personification of the ideas of mercy and wisdom. Thus the savior in <term>Amidaism</term> is reduced to a mere savior-idea, and this idea has no real <term>ontological</term> reference. If my creditor thinks the check I hand him is worth five dollars, then it is worth five dollars to him and to me; but unless I have a deposit in the bank on which I draw the check, and unless the bank backs the checks it issues with a value equal to five dollars, then the man is a fool to accept my check. Similarly, if there is no real God or Savior behind the "Savior-idea" and the "God-idea" in <term>Amida Buddhism</term> (as the <term>Amidaists</term> themselves admit there is not), then it would not be strange if the savior-idea ceased to function effectively as the believer is educated in the teachings of their own religion. And that is exactly what happens in nine out of ten cases. For the uneducated Buddhist, the savior-idea functions—indeed, it functions quite realistically—but for the enlightened Buddhist, it also becomes merely one of those ideas used to attract the common masses, but which must not be taken too seriously. To them, salvation through faith in <term>Amida</term>’s grace is only a metaphorical use of language and does not represent anything truly real.

Thus, despite the strong resemblance between Christianity and <term>Amida Buddhism</term> regarding this doctrine of salvation, there is this radical difference: the Christian Savior-idea has its ontological reference in the historical personality of Jesus Christ, while the Buddhist idea admittedly has no such reference. "The inexhaustible fountain of religious strength," writes <term>Cumont</term> in his small volume on <term>Mithras</term>, "which flowed from the doctrine of the Passion and Crucifixion of the Son of God, never flowed for the disciples of Mithras." The same may be said with equal truth about the savior in <term>Amida Buddhism</term>; no real "fountain of religious strength" has ever flowed or can ever flow from him, because he admittedly never existed.

### 3. *The Extent and Speed of Salvation.*

There are some aspects of the <term>Way of Salvation</term> that were not clearly brought out in the previous discussion but are quite important from the Buddhist perspective. These aspects relate to the extent and what we might call the "speed" of the salvation process.

Regarding the extent of salvation, Buddhists are usually universalists. In fact, not only will all of humanity be saved eventually,<note>9</note> but every living and moving thing shall share in this universal salvation. If it is possible for an evil person, through the law of <term>Karma</term>, to be born into a state lower than human, it is also possible through the operation of that same law for beings in lower states to be born into higher and higher states until they finally achieve <term>Buddhahood</term>. Thus, we read in the <term>Paradise Sutra</term>, "In every living being dwells the essence of Buddha," and therefore, "everything that has a heart can surely attain <term>Buddhahood</term>."

As might be expected, this doctrine of universal salvation rests on slightly different foundations in various sects. Pantheistic Buddhists find the basis for their belief in the idea that since every individual existence is part of the <term>Great-All</term>, there can be no permanent separation or loss. Better yet, they believe the idea of separation and loss is merely an error and does not exist in reality. On the other hand, the <term>Amidaist</term> finds hope for universal salvation in the thought of <term>Amida</term>’s boundless mercy. This mercy is so great that it cannot fail to save all that lives and moves: "The Buddha heart is great mercy. With this absolute mercy, which is not bound by circumstances, it saves all living beings."

The older Buddhists, conscious of the workings of the inescapable law of <term>Karma</term>, usually held that the process by which a being passes through the various grades of existence until it reaches the highest state of <term>Buddhahood</term> is a very long and gradual one. Thus, <term>Gautama</term> is said to have lived through many incarnations before he finally attained enlightenment. But as <term>Buddhism</term> developed—and especially after it reached the northern peoples—Buddhists became impatient with this slow process and in one way or another developed a path by which salvation can be attained quickly. Thus, we have in Japanese and Chinese <term>Buddhism</term> the two ways known as the <term>Gradual Way</term> and the <term>Abrupt Way</term>. These two ways are actually subdivisions of each of the two great paths mentioned above; namely, the <term>Way of Self-reliance</term> and the <term>Way of Reliance on the Strength of Another</term>. That is, the goal in either of these two ways may be reached either gradually or abruptly.

To reach the goal gradually in the <term>Way of Self-reliance</term> is called <term>Lengthwise-going-out</term> (Japanese: <term>Shu-shutsu</term>). In this view, the way of deliverance from the <term>Three Worlds</term> is the long route of self-discipline extending through many incarnations until, after grade upon grade of existence has been passed, the final goal is reached at last. The old <term>Sanron</term> and <term>Hossō</term> sects taught this gradual way.

To reach the goal abruptly in the <term>Way of Self-reliance</term> is called <term>Lengthwise-passing-over</term> (Japanese: <term>Shu-chō</term>). This means that the long way leading from the lower to the higher stages of existence is crossed rapidly. It is not necessary to go through many rebirths and so ascend the scale of beings gradually; instead, the believer—possessing, as it were, the right password or the key of wisdom which unlocks all doors—can pass through gate after gate in rapid succession and reach the highest goal quickly. The nature of this password or key differs among the various sects. To some, it is a magic word or sign. To others, it is a knowledge of the mystery of all being—a correct philosophical insight. To others still, it is right conduct, or a combination of both correct knowledge and conduct.

That is, the one who attains salvation by this path goes through the long scale of beings which separates him from the final goal by gradual stages. His final salvation is certain because Another (<term>Amida</term>) has prepared for him his <term>Western Paradise</term>; but he must pass through many rebirths before he can be born into Paradise. This differs from the gradual way in the <term>Path of Self-reliance</term> in that the goal and the power to reach the goal depend not upon the believer, but upon Another. Some <term>Amidaists</term> walk by this way.

To reach the goal abruptly in the <term>Way of Reliance on the Strength of Another</term> is called <term>Crosswise-passing-over</term> (Japanese: <term>Wō-chō</term>). That is, the believer passes freely over all the stages of existence which separate him from his goal because he is carried by another’s power. It is not necessary to stop along the way, for <term>Amida</term> has cleared away all difficulties. This abrupt way differs from the abrupt way in the <term>Path of Self-reliance</term> in that the believer has nothing to do but to trust and believe. He need not have the key of knowledge nor the password of mystery to allow him to pass on. Sufficient for him is the hand of faith and simple trust in <term>Amida</term>; indeed, <term>Amida</term> carries him like a ship across the ocean of life into his haven of rest and peace. Among the <term>Amida</term> sects, the <term>Shin</term> regards itself as being the true representative of this way of salvation. All other ways are regarded as provisional ways. They are not wrong ways, for just as all roads lead to Rome, so all ways of salvation lead finally to <term>Amida’s Paradise</term>, but it is better to go by the short and easy way provided for sinful humanity.

### H. *Things to Come*

In the Buddhist doctrine of <term>universal salvation</term>, we have part of the answer as to what Buddhism teaches about the Things to Come. Not only is all of humanity ultimately to be saved, but everything that lives is to be delivered from the bonds of individual existence into the bliss of the All-One. But when shall this fulfillment be reached, and what will the intermediate process be?

To begin with, for ages to come, life will go on very much as it is. The great majority of beings shall be born again and again into the <term>Six Ways</term>; that is, they shall be born as human beings or into the realm of heavenly beings (not the final Buddhist heaven) if their good <term>Karma</term> outweighs their evil <term>Karma</term>. However, if the evil outweighs the good, then their birth will be in the lower realms; namely, <term>Fighting and Bloodshed</term>, the <term>Realm of Beasts</term>, <term>Hungry Spirits</term>, or <term>Hell</term>. It is hard to escape from this dreaded cycle of the <term>Six Ways</term> and, if measured by a human lifespan, this condition of things seems almost permanent. "A blind turtle and a floating tree are more likely to meet and see each other than ignorant and foolish humanity is to obtain a human body." And if the chances for humans are so meager, then what must the chances be for beings lower on the scale of existence! Obviously, the situation looks rather gloomy despite the hope of universal salvation.

But the Buddhist speculative thinker is not daunted by time. In fact, he loves to dwell upon the endlessness of time and express this in finite terms. Thus, while the present state of affairs may seem to be an endless state, it will one day be followed by another situation. First, there is to come a golden age for humanity when the Buddha of the Future, the Buddha <term>Maitreya</term> (Japanese: <term>Miroku</term>), shall appear. When he appears, then life will be long and

# CHAPTER VI

## BUDDHIST ETHICS

### A. *General Aspects*

To discuss the ethics of Buddhism in a separate chapter may at first sight seem rather arbitrary, for the ethics of a religion would seem most naturally to belong to the very core of the religious life flowing from the fundamental doctrines. If we were dealing simply with primitive Buddhism, or with only certain phases of <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhism, such a separation as we are making would be impossible; but as we are discussing primarily Japanese Buddhism, the treatment is not only justifiable but essential, for in a peculiar way religion and ethics seem strangely divorced in this land.

The history of religion in all lands shows tendencies to divorce the ethical elements from the purely religious. There are various forms which this separation has taken, but three general types seem rather universal. Thus we have, in the first place, systems which may be regarded as ethical systems but which have no real religious basis. <term>Confucianism</term> and primitive Buddhism are the best examples of this type. In the second place, there are systems which may be said to be truly religious systems but which have no vital ethics, that is, they are ethics-less religions. Many of the animistic and polytheistic systems show this characteristic. Not, of course, that these are altogether without the ethical element, but that this is very insignificant. And in the third place, there are systems in which the religious elements and the distinctively ethical elements exist side by side without there being always a vital connection between the two, or even with a fundamental antagonism between the two; so

<summary>This page introduces the study of Buddhist ethics, noting that in Japanese Buddhism, ethics and religion are often treated as separate entities. The author categorizes systems into those that are ethical without religion, religious without ethics, or systems where the two exist side by side with little connection.</summary>
<keywords>Buddhism, ethics, Mahāyāna, Japanese Buddhism, religion, Confucianism, animism, polytheism, ethical systems</keywords>

--- Page 295 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the three types of separation between religious doctrines and ethical principles, specifically focusing on how Buddhism exemplifies these divisions.</meta>

that ethical principles not only fail to flow from religious doctrines but are more or less in direct opposition to them. This type finds its best representative in Buddhism taken as a whole.

Even in the history of Christianity, we find evidence of these strange tendencies to separate fundamental religious doctrines from ethical principles, or at least to neglect one aspect or the other. Thus, we have had periods when great emphasis was placed on certain fundamental doctrines without a corresponding emphasis on practical Christian ethics. And again, there have been periods—and the present is such a one—when the emphasis was laid exclusively upon Christian ethics, and the underlying theology was regarded as suited only for a few impractical theologians. In the third place, we see the spectacle of professing Christians being perfectly “orthodox” and scrupulously careful regarding ritual and ceremony, but viewing the Sermon on the Mount as a beautiful but impractical ideal.

But while the West is more or less familiar with the various tendencies to separate religion and ethics, it is in the Orient that we most commonly find the divorce of the two; and of all the religions of the world, no system shows the three types of separation mentioned above more markedly than Buddhism does in its various phases.

Primitive Buddhism, as we have said, shows the first type of separation: namely, the type which divorces religion from ethics by practically eliminating what would seem, at least to a Western mind, to be indispensable elements of religion. This is so much the case that some scholars have hesitated to call Gautama’s system a religion at all, though no one would refuse to recognize later Buddhism as such. Of course, it is possible to use the term "religion" in such a broad sense that any attitude toward life may be called religious. Thus, a thinker like Comte, after discarding religion as a phenomenon belonging to the primitive mind, advocates for his own anti-religious system as the "Religion of Humanity." Or again, in our own day, we have materialists and atheists speaking of the Religion of

In this broad sense, Gautama’s system was certainly a religion, and had even a better right to the title than these, for it had at least one of the cardinal elements of religion in that it had a doctrine of redemption. But if religion is essentially “a quest for the enrichment of life by establishing vital relationships with superhuman powers or persons (power or person),” then Gautama’s system, with its indifference, if not opposition, to the idea of God, can hardly be called a real religion. Of course, as soon as Gautama himself was lifted into the place of a superhuman being, as happened rather early in Buddhist history, the essential elements of religion were present. But the system which he himself proclaimed may be said to be a practical ethical system which, above everything else, sought to make man independent of the gods and dependent solely upon himself. The Buddha did not seek to show men the vital relationships which may be established between them and the divine, but he wanted them to see the vital relationship which their present state sustains to their past deeds and which their present deeds will sustain to their future state.

But while primitive Buddhism was primarily a practical system of ethics growing out of a certain view of life—namely, the view of life summed up in the Four Noble Truths—we have even here a divorce between this philosophy of life and some of the practical ethical teachings. The ethical teachings which have as their object the cutting of all the bonds which bind man to this life flow naturally from the view of life expressed in the Four Great Truths, but when ethical ideals center around the thought of self-discipline and self-culture, it is difficult to reconcile them with the doctrine of the non-reality of the self so important in primitive Buddhism. In short, then, many of the ethical principles even in primitive Buddhism were based upon what India had found to be practical for a moral life, but which in reality failed to grow out of the fundamental doctrines of Gautama’s view of life and which were even in flat contradiction to it.

Since Japanese Buddhism contains such a complex of philosophical doctrines, and its ethical teachings are based only in part upon this complex and in part taken from other sources, it becomes practically impossible to give a systematic presentation of the subject at hand. How is it possible to say that "moral and intellectual perfection of personality" is the highest aim of a system when personality itself is said to have no real existence? It is possible only by admitting, as Professor Anezaki does admit, a flat contradiction between Buddhist ethics and one of its fundamental doctrines. The reader will, therefore, forgive us if in what follows, things do not always hang together, or if they appear contradictory.

To the extent to which Buddhist ethics is grounded in Buddhist doctrines, we might say that it has its basis and aim in the philosophy of the good. What is meant by "the Good" we have already discussed in the previous chapter under the heading of the essence of salvation, and in what was said there about the essence of true enlightenment. All moral principles have as their criterion the essence of enlightenment; and since enlightenment is a matter of degree, it follows that ethical principles are also matters of degree. There is no categorical right and wrong, but right and wrong are purely relative. The good varies with the true, and the true changes with the point of view, so that what is true and good for one being is not necessarily so for another. In the long scale of beings<note>1</note> into which Buddhism divides the world of phenomena, each being has its own laws and may appropriate the true and the good in its own way. Thus the standard of ethics is necessarily varied and relative. There is one standard only in the sense that all beings have the capacity for attaining Buddhahood, and will attain this if they obey the varying ethical principles as they advance from stage to stage.

In the beginning of the preceding chapter we gave, as the complete summary of all Buddhist teachings, the significant sentence, "Tenmei kaigo, Riku tokuraku, Shiaku shuzen," the last phrase of which presents the ethical side of the system; namely, "Ceasing from evil and doing good." “Avoid sin (evil), do good, and purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all the Buddhas.” All Buddhists would agree with this general way of stating the core of all Buddhist ethics, and even a Christian would have no objection to expressing their ethical ideal in such terms. But when it comes to defining more specifically what is meant by the “sin” which is not to be committed, and the “good” which is to be done, then, of course, the differences begin to appear.

Roughly speaking, Buddhist ethics may be divided into two great types: namely, the older *Hīnayāna* type and the later *Mahāyāna* type. The two have much in common regarding the ethical principles which pertain to a person as a citizen of this world; however, insofar as they pertain to a person as a candidate for salvation out of this world, the older type may be said to be less altruistic <note>2</note> than the later *Mahāyāna* ideal. It will be remembered that the *Hīnayāna* ideal of salvation was the *Arhat*, and the *Arhat* was above all else interested in his own salvation. He walked in the path of righteousness for his own sake—not so much for the positive good which he sought to achieve, as for the sake of escaping from a positive evil. He perfected his personality in order to destroy the conditions of individuality and personality.

The hindrance to this goal of the ethical ideal of *Hīnayāna* Buddhism lies not so much in a person’s will as in their mind. In order to overcome the obstacles in the path of righteousness, the mind must be enlightened with the truth. This necessary truth is, above all else, the truth about the nature of existence—that is, the nature of human life and the causes which have brought about humanity's present condition. Thus, the beginning of all ethical conduct is correct knowledge. This knowledge is formulated first of all in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path, and then in the various moral maxims suited for practical life. To be sure, the mere knowledge of the truth does not bring deliverance; one must walk by the knowledge they have received, for it is only in the union of theoretical knowledge and the practical application of it to life that deliverance is found.

But what is it that gives humanity the motive power to walk in the way of truth as it is presented to the mind?

It is the truth itself which gives this motive power, for truth expels ignorance, and ignorance is the core of all sin. Hence, to know the truth is to be free from sin and to do good.

It is a question of whether this is good psychology, and whether Buddhism does not give too much prominence to the intellectual aspect of the human personality and not enough to the aspect we call the Will. Of course, a knowledge of the truth is necessary as a step toward freedom from sin, but it does not always follow that to know the truth is to obey it. After all, there is that mysterious aspect of our personality called the Will which enables a person to choose whether they will obey the truth as they see it, or not. It is true, as Buddhism says, that humanity is in ignorance and that ignorance is a source of sin, but sin is more than mere ignorance. It is not merely an intellectual mistake, but rather a rebellion of the will. In short, a person is not simply a mind, but a personality. Personality has at its core the Will aspect as truly as the intellectual; consequently, abstract truth does not make a sufficiently strong appeal to enable a person to forsake sin and do good, but the appeal must be made by a perfect personality. And here is exactly where the ethics of primitive Buddhism must inevitably break down. It can never consistently present the ethical appeal in the truth of a perfect personality, for it denies that personality is a permanent reality. It can therefore never have the drive of Christian ethics, which is grounded in the perfect personality of God expressed in human terms in the historic perfect personality of Jesus Christ. It can never say to a person, “Be perfect, therefore, even as your Father in heaven is perfect.” The best it can say is, “Be perfect as S’akyamuni <note>Also spelled Shakyamuni; a name for the historical Buddha.</note> was perfect in order that you may escape from the evils of life.” The appeal which this older ethic makes is therefore more of an appeal to a person's sense of fear. It is, “be good lest you suffer the consequences.” This was a powerful appeal to a world-weary civilization, but it can never be as powerful as the appeal to a person's higher

Now, the newer ethics of <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhism have a more positive goal than the older, and they are also more altruistic in their tone. That is, they lead not only away from a positive evil but also toward a positive good, and this good is for both the self and others. Its ideal is the <term>Bodhisattva</term>, who is one who achieves perfection for himself but refuses to enjoy the fruit of his labors fully until he has helped others achieve the same benefit. In fact, the <term>Bodhisattva</term> is one who might say of himself, “For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth.” This type of ethics, therefore, makes a stronger appeal than the older type in that it directs itself to the higher self in humanity and centers more on what good one may achieve rather than on what evil one is to escape. The <term>Mahāyāna</term> ethics have, however, some of the weaknesses of the <term>Hīnayāna</term> in that they, too, make the intellectual aspect of human nature central and do not give due recognition to the Will. In this system, sin is also primarily a matter of mere ignorance and not the perversion of the entire personality. Furthermore, while these ethics make an appeal to the higher self, the philosophy on which they rest, after all, denies that personality is really permanent. The <term>Bodhisattva</term> may be personal as long as he chooses to be a <term>Bodhisattva</term>, but when he enters into full <term>Buddhahood</term>, he disappears as a person. And so it follows that though the highest aim of <term>Mahāyāna</term> ethics may be “the moral and intellectual perfection of the personality,” this end, when achieved, is really not permanent but is only a step into that which is neither personal nor impersonal. One might wonder why one should strive to achieve a perfect personality if the real goal is as much the impersonal as the personal.

It is not that the priest is actually so much more holy or learned than the layman, but that he is theoretically so. The lay Buddhist is expected to continue his life much as he did before he became a Buddhist; almost nothing is required of him. But the monk and priest are expected to leave behind not only the evil ways of this world, but also much of what is normal and good in human life. The very expression in Japanese for entering the monk’s life indicates his break with normal life. He is said to “forsake home” and to “ascend the mountain.” (Most monasteries are in the mountains, far removed from the human world.) Only the monk is expected to read and know the sacred scriptures, and an advance in knowledge is expected to bring an advance in holiness. Only the Shin Sect has sought to spread a “household religion,” but even here the sect has not remained true to the high ideal of its founder. The writer is, of course, aware that in Christianity, and in almost every religion, these wide gaps between the religion of the layman and that of the professional religionist have existed. However, in Protestant Christianity at least, there is an attempt to make the knowledge of the Lord cover the earth as the waters cover the sea, and to establish only one standard of conduct for both layman and clergy—the standard of perfect manhood revealed in Jesus Christ.

The contrast between ignorance and enlightenment which <term>Buddhism</term> makes in its fundamental doctrines is carried out in its ethical teachings by the contrast between the vices and virtues; for ignorance may be said to be the cardinal vice and wisdom the cardinal virtue. <term>Buddhists</term> are exceedingly fond, not only of classifying all ethical teachings under these two main heads, but of making list upon list of the various major and minor vices and virtues. This is often done in a rather mechanical way; in particular, the methods of instilling these ethical teachings frequently degenerate into a mere mechanical process which kills the real spirit of the teaching.

1. *The Vices of Life.* — The cardinal vice is the vice of <term>egoism</term> grounded in ignorance; or to put it the other way around, it is ignorance expressing itself in <term>egoism</term>. <term>Egoism</term>, whose taproot is ignorance, is the trunk from which grow all other vices, so that whatever specific vice may be under consideration, it can always be traced back to a form of <term>egoism</term>, and this always grows out of ignorance. For in <term>Buddhism</term>, all individual life is essentially nothing but the desire of <term>Ignorance</term>, or the expression of an unconscious desire — a blind "will-to-be."

This <term>egoism</term> manifests itself in three primary vices usually spoken of as the <term>Three Poisons</term>: namely, <term>Lust</term>, <term>Anger</term>, and <term>Folly</term>. 2. *The Virtues of Life.* — Let us next consider very briefly the virtues of life which <term>Buddhism</term> seeks to instill. If <term>egoism</term> rooted in ignorance is the primary vice, then the suppression of this egoism through knowledge is the primary virtue. That is, all virtue is rooted in right thinking. Thus, Buddhists regard mental discipline, rather than a discipline of the will, as a matter of first importance, and among the primary virtues, methods of mental discipline occupy a prominent place.

But if the suppression of <term>egoism</term> is the primary virtue, a question arises as to whether this means the suppression of a lower egoism by the self-assertion of a higher and nobler egoism, or does it mean the suppression of all egoism and self-assertion? Or to put it in another form: Is enlightenment positive knowledge or simply a “breaking of error”? Some Buddhists hold—and it would seem that to be consistent with Buddhist psychology a Buddhist must hold—that it means the latter, and that virtue is not a positive goodness but simply the absence of a positive evil. This is why most of the teachings of <term>Buddhism</term> are cast in a negative mold. The <term>Ten Commandments of Buddhism</term> are ten prohibitions, ten “Don’ts.” Keeping these ten negative commandments constitutes the <term>Ten Virtues</term> which the average Buddhist is supposed to cultivate, just as breaking them is to commit the <term>Ten Vices</term> mentioned above. The <term>Ten Virtues</term>, then, are the following: Not to Kill, Not to Steal, Not to Commit Adultery, Not to Lie, Not to Exaggerate, Not to Slander, Not to be Double-tongued, Not to Covet, Not to be Angry, and Not to be Heretical. Thus, as we have said—at least according to the form in which these virtues are stated—they seem to be negative virtues, or merely the suppression of vices.

But while Buddhist ethics focuses more on the suppression of vices than on the teaching of positive virtues, there is,

<page-num>281</page-num>
# BUDDHIST ETHICS

After all, there is a good deal in Buddhist ethics built upon the conception that virtue is the expression of the higher and nobler ego. That is, not only are the vices of a lowly egoism to be suppressed, but a higher self expresses itself in this suppression and goes beyond this by exerting itself in positive virtues. For example, a person is not only to suppress his feelings of anger and hatred toward his fellow man, but his heart should go out to him in sympathy and love. Even in the older Buddhism, which made the denial of the reality of the self a cardinal doctrine, one finds ethical principles based upon the conception that "the intellectual and moral perfection of the personality" is the highest aim of ethics. Thus, the Noble Eightfold Path itself is a path of rather positive virtues and more than a mere suppression of vices.

In enumerating the main positive virtues, one must begin with the virtues of walking in the Noble Eightfold Path: *i.e.*, the virtues of Right Opinion, Right Decision, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Contemplation. <note>3</note>

When the virtues are thought of in terms of psychological faculties, Buddhists speak of them as *Organs*, and of these they usually distinguish five; namely, Faith, Exertion, Mindfulness, Contemplation, and Wisdom. Three of these are regarded as cardinal virtues and are included in every list. These three are Faith, Exertion, and Wisdom; the greatest of these is Faith according to some, and Wisdom according to others. Other virtues emphasized in Buddhist ethics are the following: a sense of shame, conscientiousness, a clear conscience, thoughtfulness, sympathy, gentleness, kindness, mercy, pity, and benevolence. The latter is divided into the Four Benevolences directed respectively toward parents, people in general, the ruler, and the Three Treasures (*i.e.*, Buddha, the Law, and the Priesthood).

Of these major virtues, Buddhism has been especially successful in inculcating widely the virtues of gentleness, pity, and sympathy. It is not strange that this is so, for especially the virtues of pity and sympathy for others grow

directly from the Buddhist view regarding the nature of human life. Life is suffering, and sympathy (suffering with others) becomes a natural attitude of the mind and heart. The German words "*Leid*" and "*Mitleid*" express the relationship in a nutshell: *Das Leben ist Leid und darum ist die höchste Tugend Mitleid* <gloss>Life is suffering and therefore the highest virtue is compassion.</gloss> To be sure, the Buddhist conception of Pity and Sympathy lacks something of the positive element found in the Christian conception of Love, for it lacks the underlying conviction of the eternal value of human life. Human life seems very cheap in Buddhist lands, and the life of the masses especially seems like nothing more than foam on a turbulent sea. Yet Buddhism has done much to promote a feeling of solidarity within the human race. Humanity is a great brotherhood of suffering; indeed, even the speechless animals are our fellow-sufferers and are bound to us by the strong links of the Karma-chain. Who knows but that the ox drawing the driver’s heavy load is a great ancestor of the driver, appearing in the form of an ox in obedience to the law of Karma? Should the driver not, then, be kind to his beast?

So far we have spoken of what might be regarded as rather ordinary virtues. There are higher virtues which are practiced by those who are truly serious about attaining Buddhahood. These are the so-called Perfections. The full list consists of ten<note>4</note> virtues: Charity, Morality, Resignation, Wisdom, Exertion or Diligence, Forbearance, Truthfulness, Persistence, Love, and Equanimity. Ordinarily, Japanese Buddhism reduces these to six: Charity (almsgiving and teaching), Morality (keeping the various commandments), Patience and Forbearance, Exertion or Diligence (in keeping the vows of a Bodhisattva), Meditation, and Wisdom (for oneself and others).

These virtues were originally regarded as the special virtues of the few rare souls who sought to be Bodhisattvas and finally Buddhas; however, in Mahāyāna Buddhism, the theoretical purpose of every believer is to become a Bodhisattva and a Buddha. Consequently, these virtues are theoretically virtues which every believer should practice. But as

As a matter of fact, in practice, Mahāyāna Buddhism makes as true a distinction between the ordinary believer and the candidate for Buddhahood as the older Buddhism ever did, and these Six Perfections are therefore not a very vital part of the ethics of the average Buddhist. In fact, a great many Mahāyāna Buddhists hold that these difficult steps toward perfection are not necessary, as they have been taken by the various Bodhisattvas whose accumulated merits the believer may claim for his own benefit through the simple act of faith. So it comes back to this: for the common man at least, the only necessary virtue is the virtue of faith in the holiness and all-sufficient merit of the saints and Buddhas who have gone before. That is why the great formula of faith for every Buddhist is the confession, “I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Law, I take refuge in the Priesthood.” Even the sects which make the doctrine of “Save thyself” their primary teaching combine this severe injunction with the comfort that somehow the goodness of the good and the wisdom of the wise who have gone before will help those who put their trust in them.

The above may be enough to give the reader a general idea of Buddhist ethics, but it is too much like a skeleton without flesh and blood. We therefore give below extracts from the sacred scriptures which set forth the ethical ideals succinctly. The reader should not think, however, that the Buddhist scriptures always maintain this rather lofty level. The extracts are choice bits, “golden words” as the Japanese compiler calls them, or “Buddhist Gold Nuggets” as we have called them in the *Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan*, Vol. XL, from which they are taken.

<margin>Rules of Friendship</margin>
There are three rules which a friend should follow toward a friend, namely: He should correct him when he is at fault, rejoice with deep joy in whatever good is in him, and stand by him in times of trouble. (Ingwakyō)

A friend should not be abandoned simply on the strength of someone else’s bad report. If you hear your friend spoken of poorly, be all the more careful to find out the truth of the matter. (Komponbinakyō)

<margin>The Family</margin>
Let fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, husbands and wives, all the members of the family, and all relatives love and respect each other; and never let them harbor a feeling of bitterness or hatred. Those who have great possessions should not be greedy toward those who have little. Words and conduct should harmonize, and all inconsistency in dealing with one another should be avoided. (Muryōjukyō)

If everyone is faithful, there will be peace in the home, and good fortune will smile upon the family naturally and without any need to have it granted by the gods. (Ananfumbe-tsukyō)

<margin>Duties of Husbands and Wives</margin>
A husband should support and please his wife by observing the following five points: He should respect her with a sincere heart, never harbor any ill will toward her, love her with a pure affection, give her whatever food and clothing she may need, and from time to time present her with gifts to adorn herself. (Zenshoshikyō)

A good wife does not spare her own life, and under no circumstances does she do anything contrary to her husband’s will. (Zōichiagonkyō)

Only a virtuous, wise, and clever wife is fit to raise children; and children who have such a mother cannot fail to become men and women of great character. (Zōichiagonkyō)

# CHAPTER VII

## THE PLACE OF BUDDHISM IN JAPANESE LIFE — PAST, PRESENT AND FUTURE

### A. *The Influence in the Past*

**AN** interesting but exceedingly difficult problem is determining what place Buddhism has had in the life of the Japanese people. The answer to this question is particularly difficult because Buddhism is not and has not been the sole religion of Japan; rather, during the greater part of its long history in this land, it has been closely bound up with Shintō and Confucianism. So even today, though it is officially separated from Shintō, a great many Japanese are Shintōists, Confucianists, and Buddhists all at the same time. Some writers speak of Shintō as the root, Confucianism as the branches and leaves, and Buddhism as the flowers and fruit of the tree of Japanese civilization. This conception is not altogether wrong, for it is true that historically Shintō comes first, and that in organizing legal and educational institutions Confucianism has played a prominent part, and finally that the chief contribution of Buddhism lies in the realm of art, philosophy, and religion. But since art, philosophy, and religion are not only the flower and fruit of a civilization but also in turn become the root and branches of the succeeding stages, Buddhism from the ninth century onward has been a real part of the roots, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit of the Japanese tree of life. That is, its influence has been so profound that there is no aspect of Japanese life which has not been greatly modified by it. This influence cannot be measured by simply enumerating the major points, though this is all that we can do here, but so far—
