reaching has it been that one can also see it in countless minor ways that apparently have little to do with religion as such.

Among the major contributions that Buddhism made to Japanese life, we must place first and foremost the fact that it has been a vehicle for the higher civilization of the continent. This was true not only during its beginnings in this land, when it was so obviously the means of bringing in the wealth of Korean and Chinese culture, but until the Tokugawa period, the Buddhist monks and priests continued to be the chief means by which Japan kept in touch with the rest of the world. The point cannot be overstated; for just as truly as Christian missionaries from Europe and America have been the apostles of a superior civilization to the backward nations of the world, so Buddhists have often been the messengers of progress and light to Japan. In a real sense, Buddhism has been the "Light of Asia," and perhaps no part of Asia has received as much through it as Japan has. In saying this, we do not wish to imply that Japan would have remained in darkness if it had not been for the religion of the Buddha. It is naturally impossible to say just what would have taken its place. Perhaps Shintō, though a very primitive religion, would have developed into a higher and, on the whole, more satisfactory religion. Nor do we wish to imply that Buddhism is not today an actual hindrance to the coming of the "Greater Light," the "Light of the World." But since the history of Japan was what it was, it is correct to say that Buddhism has been a determining factor, and that the sources of Japanese culture have been, either directly or indirectly, mainly Buddhist.

Since Buddhism was both a vehicle for a higher civilization and the expression of such a civilization itself, its influence on the intellectual life of the nation was naturally incalculable. Shintō was the religion of an immature people, while Buddhism was a philosophy of life as worked out by a profoundly meditative and speculative India. Thus, the first really deep-seated influence that Buddhism exerted upon Japan

# BUDDHISM'S CONTRIBUTION

was that it led the people to think more profoundly about the problems of human life. This intellectual stimulus extended in all directions. First of all, it affected the native religion, and <term>Shintō</term> was elevated from a jumble of contradictory legends and myths into what was at least the appearance of a reasoned philosophy of life. The various legends were systematized and organized into a more or less connected whole. The Japanese began to develop a connected account of the past and wrote the first history of their race. It is true that the <term>Kojiki</term> and <term>Nihongi</term> are not actual histories, but they are attempts to weld together the traditions of the past into a historical narrative. 

Furthermore, this intellectual stimulus soon showed its effect upon the language. With the arrival of Buddhism, the Japanese language was elevated into a true medium of education and culture. A very large percentage of the current vocabulary came either directly from Buddhism or was added from Chinese to give adequate expression to the new ideas that arrived with the new religion. The spread of literacy, and thus education in general, was largely due to the influence of the Buddhists. Buddhism taught Japan the elements of logic, psychology, and natural sciences as they were then known in India and China, as well as the subtleties of philosophy and metaphysical speculation. 

The first sects introduced placed special emphasis on dialectics and psychological analysis, which certainly contributed significantly to sharpening the intellectual powers of the people. And what was true in the early days remained true for centuries: namely, that whatever the Japanese knew of philosophy and science, they owed largely to Buddhism. This intellectual development explains why, when Western culture came to Japan in the modern period, the Japanese were able to assimilate it in such a surprisingly short time, and why today there are Japanese scholars in every field of learning who can hold their own with the scholars of any nation. In short, Japan has been a cultured nation for centuries, and she owes to Buddhism a great debt for the major part of this culture.

STUDIES IN JAPANESE BUDDHISM

Now, this spread of general culture and this development of the intellectual powers of the people naturally had a profound effect on every phase of life. Thus, *e.g.*, in the political world, it helped create a new Japan. When Buddhism reached these shores, as we saw in Chapter III, Japan was not yet a real nation. It was instead a land inhabited by various tribes, with the tribe in the Kyoto-Osaka region gradually gaining dominance. Buddhism expanded the horizons of the people with its constant emphasis on universals, so that the tribal concept naturally had to give way to the national ideal. It is true, as we said above, that the organization of the political institutions came from Confucianism, but it came largely through the Buddhist missionaries and educators. And again, it is true that Shinto has been the political weapon through which patriotism was cultivated and the various tribes subdued and unified, but, after all, it was a Shinto profoundly modified by Buddhism. It was the Buddhist philosopher who laid the real foundations of the Japanese state by inspiring the early historians to build up the myths and legends of prehistoric times into a more or less connected whole. Even to this day, the Japanese state has as one of its main pillars the legendary history of the *Kojiki* and *Nihongi* which, in an indirect way at least, owe their very existence to the impact of Buddhist culture upon early Japan. Then further, the part which Buddhist monks and priests played in the actual political development of the nation through the centuries is immeasurable. It is true that this was far from being a noble part in all cases. In fact, there were times when the rulers of the nation were little more than mere puppets of ambitious priests who shielded themselves behind their sacred robes or the hallowed walls of a powerful monastery. What we wish to point out, however, is that whether for good or evil, the part which Buddhism has played in the political life of Japan has been not only an indirect influence but often a very direct and decisive one.

But not to claim for Buddhism too much either of good or evil in a field usually claimed for Shinto and Confucianism,

# BUDDHISM'S CONTRIBUTION

Let us turn to the sphere in which the influence of this religion is self-evident; we mean the field of art, philosophy, and religion.

In the field of art, it is more correct to say that Buddhism created certain branches of Japanese art than simply that it influenced them. Thus, Japanese architecture, sculpture, and painting are what they are because Buddhism has made them so. Music and poetry have also been influenced, though perhaps to a lesser degree.

If, in the field of architecture, we were to remove the Buddhist temples, monasteries, and flights of stone steps leading up to them from these pine-clad hills and valleys, very little grandeur or beauty would remain. The average Japanese house seems to be a development of the primeval hut, and as a work of architecture, it cannot claim a very high place. What makes it attractive is not any architectural feature, but rather the cleanliness, neatness, and simplicity of the interior; or perhaps it is its picturesque environment. The Shintō shrine, too, cannot be said to rank very high, though the shrine entrance, the Torii, may be regarded as a real work of art. But it is really only when we come to Buddhist buildings that Japanese architecture can make any claims. We are not saying that these measure up to the architectural monuments of the West, but only that whatever there is in Japan that merits any attention in this regard belongs to Buddhism.

In the field of sculpture, Japan is relatively much richer, and this is almost purely the product of Buddhism. What existed of this art before the introduction of Buddhism may be classified with the crude clay figures produced by most primitive peoples. It is surprising in how short a time truly world-class masterpieces in bronze, clay, and wood were produced. As we saw in Chapter III, within a hundred years after Buddhism had reached these shores, the Buddhist sculptors were performing wonders. The world’s largest bronze statue belongs to Japanese Buddhism of the eighth century. It is true that this does not rank very high as a work of art, but there are many smaller relics of that period which do

The tens of thousands of images and statues found in temples and temple grounds, along the highways and backroads, in cities, towns, and villages, and in valleys, on hills, mountainsides, and mountain peaks—all these are the handiwork of Buddhist artists. Not only is the Buddhist pilgrim surrounded by the symbols of invisible things on his journey through life, but when he is dead and buried, Buddhist art in stone and bronze marks his resting place and "implores the passing tribute of a sigh."

If Buddhist ideals have guided the chisel and the knife, they have also inspired the pencil and the brush. Here the influence, though perhaps less evident to the casual student, is equally striking. In a land of such natural beauty as Japan, one would naturally expect the painter to be inspired largely by his wonderful environment; instead, practically all the older schools of painting were inspired by Indian and Chinese masterpieces introduced through Buddhism. Thus, one student of the subject says that "it can safely be asserted that not one in twenty of the works of these painters—who to the present day are considered to represent the true genius of Japanese art—was inspired by nature as seen in their own beautiful country." In fact, the very neglect of perspective in landscape paintings and the "impossible mountains" seen in them are well-known characteristics. It may be that the very exquisite beauty of the scenery in Japan has made the artist despair of ever reproducing it on canvas, and so instead he seeks only to suggest it, leaving everything but a few bold strokes marking the outline to be supplied by the imagination. The oldest Japanese painting, believed to date from the seventh century, is a mural decoration in Hōryūji, a Buddhist temple near Nara. Thus, while Buddhism has created and nurtured the art of painting in Japan, it may also be said to have hindered its highest development because it has imposed a slavish adherence to classic Buddhist models. Only occasionally have artists been able to break away from this tyranny and paint as they really saw with their own eyes.

The influence of Buddhism on music—the most subtle of the arts—would be difficult for anyone who is not a true student of Oriental music to estimate. For a Westerner, the subject is practically impossible, for there is nothing among Oriental things which seems more weird. It takes years for someone whose ears are attuned to the harmonies of our Western masters to be willing to admit that Japan has anything worthy of the name. It often seems more like the twang of loosely strung chords, terribly out of tune. One of the best authorities on the subject of the scale in Japanese music says that it consists "of five notes of the harmonic minor scale, with the fourth and the seventh omitted, because—as there are five recognized colors, five planets, five elements, five viscera, and so on—there must also be five notes in music." Since it is written in the minor key, its dominant note is one of melancholy and despair, rather than joy and victory. Because of this, Japanese music—whether influenced by Buddhism or not—is, after all, a real expression of that pessimistic philosophy of life of which Buddhism is the best formulation. As one's understanding of this philosophy of life grows, one's ears also become more sympathetic to its music; especially do one's ears respond to the one distinctively Buddhist instrument of Japan—namely, the rich, mellow tones of the temple bell. Japanese poetry, to continue the Hegelian order of the arts, also shows the influence of Buddhism. It may be difficult to prove that the form of poetry has been much influenced, but its content reflects every aspect of Buddhist thoughts and ideals. This is particularly true of the short stanzas called <term>Tanka</term>, consisting of no more than five lines and thirty-one syllables, and even more so of the <term>Hokku</term>, consisting of only seventeen syllables. These short poems are really more like epigrams and so are suitable vehicles for sentiments too deep for thought, or ideals too lofty for many words. The favorite subject matter of these short poems is “the flowers, the birds, the snow, the moon, the falling leaves in autumn, the mist on the mountains . . . and the shortness of human life,” but the point of view from which these are treated is usually Buddhist. Thus, the favorite cherry blossom is the symbol of the brave knight who does not cling selfishly to this life; the moon is the symbol of the change to which all things are subject; the falling leaves in autumn point the way of all life; and the shortness of human life is, of course, a recurring theme in Buddhism. The short stanza is especially well-suited to express a sigh over life’s fleeting nature. Even the subject of love is dealt with in Japanese poetry from the standpoint of the Buddhist doctrine of <term>Karma</term>. But if the influence of Buddhism on Japanese life has been strong in the field of art, it has been perhaps even greater in the realm of philosophy and religion. It is true, of course, that it had to divide the field with <term>Shintō</term> and <term>Confucianism</term>, but largely on terms laid down by itself. In fact, it is very doubtful whether <term>Shintō</term> would have survived at all if it had been opposed by Buddhism and not incorporated into it; for <term>Shintō</term> was entirely too primitive to have satisfied the growing intelligence of the Japanese for much longer. Buddhism's victory might have been delayed, but it would have been inevitable. And <term>Confucianism</term>, too, gained its hold in Japan largely because Buddhists propagated it. It was fostered by them because it supplemented the Buddhist teachings, especially in the field of practical ethics. Thus, as we have said, both <term>Shintō</term> and <term>Confucianism</term> had their place in Japanese life largely on terms laid down by Buddhism. This, of course, in turn affected Buddhism and made it quite different in Japan from what it was in other lands. But still the genius of the religion of the Japanese people, especially in its higher intellectual and philosophical aspects, has been for centuries and still is today, more Buddhist than anything else.

What, then, are the chief contributions to the distinctively religious life of Japan which Buddhism has made?

First of all, Buddhism elevated and enlarged the conception of the Divine. <term>Shintō</term> was a rather childish animism and crude polytheism, and the Japanese had not yet advanced to the idea of the universal or the monistic whole. The elements of monism or monotheism found in present-day <term>Shintō</term> were not there when Buddhism first reached these shores; for, as we have said above, not until Buddhism had

But it is the very breath of the philosophy of <term>Mahāyāna</term> Buddhism to reduce the plurality of being to an all-embracing Divine Whole, and to regard the myriads of gods and individual beings as in some way the expression of the All-One. It is true, of course, that in popular Buddhism the gods of polytheistic <term>Shintō</term> and other cults have always played a prominent part; and, on the other hand, it is true that the conception of the Divine All in philosophic Buddhism frequently faded away into a thin mist or the “Unknowable” of agnosticism; but even so, it must be admitted that Buddhism did give the Japanese a loftier conception of the ultimate source of all reality than <term>Shintō</term> had. In fact, as we have seen, <term>Amida</term> Buddhism in particular entertained a conception of the Divine which did not differ very far from the Christian conception of God.

Secondly, Buddhism greatly enlarged the conception of man’s destiny. The early <term>Shintō</term> ideal went very little beyond the conception of man as a creature of sensory experience. The gods were implored or propitiated in order that they might bestow upon the worshiper what he wanted for a prosperous and happy existence. And the happiness of existence lay not so much in the realm of an enriched personality, as in the realm of those things which satisfy the desires of the senses. What lay beyond the realm of sense, or the point in time when the sense organs are dissolved in death, did not concern the early Shintōist so much. Buddhism, however, taught Japan that man’s present life is but a moment of his existence and that the real life is more than the life of the body. In spite of the doctrine of the non-reality of the self, Buddhism has impressed, through its doctrine of <term>Karma</term>, the thought of the far-reaching effects of the psychic forces in human life. It taught the Japanese to think of all things *sub specie aeternitatis* and to regard especially the individual human life in its relationship to the past and the future. Thus it both minimized and mag-

magnified the place of man in the universe. It minimized man by showing him as only a fragment of the Whole. But it also magnified human life by showing that, however small this fragment might be, its destiny is wrapped up with the destiny of the Great All. To be sure, Buddhism did not always have a very clear idea of what this destiny might be, and it often seemed to be the destiny of Vacuity; however, occasionally at least, it offered man a hope for a future life that was truly inspiring. And even in areas where the hope of a larger future was not emphasized, or where it was left among the great uncertainties, the emphasis that such Buddhist thinkers placed on self-culture carried with it the implied thought of a higher destiny; for what would self-culture mean if no real, positive goal lay at the end of the road? That is, the schools in Japanese Buddhism that apparently denied the future life still held out some sort of desired future for the individual, and thus ennobled the conception of man’s destiny.

A third great contribution that Buddhism made to the religious life of Japan is the conception, or conceptions, regarding the way man can reach his higher destiny. Whatever the perversions of these conceptions have been—and they have been gross and many in popular Buddhism—higher Buddhism has always insisted that it must be achieved through obedience to the truth. Man must know the truth, and the truth shall set him free from the bonds of his small self into the liberty of the greater Something. The doctrine of <term>Karma</term>, which runs throughout Buddhist thought, at its best means that this universe is governed by law. To know this law is to know the truth, and to obey the truth is to become superior to the law, or rather to direct the operations of the inexorable law in a way that brings man into a better and fuller life. Even the schools that teach the doctrine of salvation through faith in <term>Amida</term> do not deny the necessity of obedience to the law of <term>Karma</term>; they only hold that the obedience was performed once and for all by <term>Amida</term>. Thus, as we have said, whatever perversions there

...have been in popular Buddhism, and whatever superstitious practices of magic the ignorant masses may indulge in, the higher side of Buddhism has always stood for the conception of a universe of rational laws which man must obey if he would advance into a larger and nobler life.

This thought of obedience to the truth naturally leads us to the moral and ethical side of the religious life. We saw in the preceding chapter what the moral ideals of Buddhism are. There may be nothing distinctive in these ethical teachings when compared with the ethics of other advanced religions. But when seen in the light of Shintō ethics—if it is possible to speak of such a thing—it will be realized what a great contribution Buddhism has made. And when it is further remembered that Buddhist priests were largely the medium through which Confucian ethics were made known in this land, we will have to say that practically all the moral training which the people of Japan have had up to the modern period they owe, either directly or indirectly, to Buddhism.

Buddhism influenced not only the intellectual side of religion and its practical application in ethical conduct, but it also exerted a great influence on the less important aspect of religious trappings. One reason why Buddhism appealed to the ancient Japanese was the fact that it had much more elaborate and impressive outward settings than their native religion had. It brought with it images, statues, pictures, bells, incense, and all that goes to make an impressive ritual; and, in the course of time, it developed a complex ecclesiastical machinery in Japan. Buddhism is so rich in these outward things that even a Roman Catholic might feel perfectly at home in these surroundings. A few years ago, a writer in one of the leading Christian papers made a comparison between Buddhism and Catholicism, and he showed over thirty points in which the two were in agreement regarding these externals of religion. It is not strange that when Xavier and his fellow workers came to Japan, they were regarded at first by the Buddhist priests as but one more sect of their own religion.

Such, then, are some of the main influences that Buddhism has exerted upon the lives of the people of Japan. In some fields, these have been so decisive that, among the major Asian states, Japan is the most Buddhist; certainly, in no other land does Buddhism have so much to its credit. It has been the dominant religion in this land for about a thousand years, and during that time Buddhism has developed aspects that make it a more nearly adequate religion for an advanced people than the forms it has taken in other Asian countries. That is to say, Buddhism has not only exerted a great influence on Japan, but the Japanese genius has also, in turn, left its mark upon Buddhism.

But having said this much about the influence that the religion of Buddha has exerted upon Japanese life in the past, we must now come to the question of what place it holds in present-day Japan, and then to the still more difficult question of what its place will probably be in the future. No one is more ready to admit than educated Buddhists themselves that a new day has dawned for the old religions of this people, and that, though the past may have belonged to Buddhism, the present—and especially the future—is uncertain.

### B. *The Place of Buddhism in Present-day Japan*

The Japanese saying that “what goes before becomes master” gives us a partial clue to this question. The fact that Buddhism has dominated the life of Japan in the past means that the present, too, belongs largely to it, in spite of outward appearances to the contrary. As has been pointed out in the introductory remarks, a nation cannot suddenly cast off its old religions like a worn-out garment; and even this rising generation of Japanese, which laughs at the superstitions and beliefs of its fathers and glibly denies that it is Buddhist, nonetheless breathes the Buddhist atmosphere much more than it realizes. By this, we do not mean to say that Buddhism has not lost much ground in the modern period and that there are not forces at work now which seem destined ultimately to undermine the old founda-

Perhaps the simplest way to answer this question regarding what place Buddhism holds in modern Japan is to ask the reader to keep in mind what we said in the preceding section about its place in the past, and then show simply to what extent Buddhism has lost this position.

We have already provided a partial statement of the situation in the latter part of Chapter III, and what we provide here should be regarded as supplementary. The most important fact to remember is that the entire movement which prepared the way for the Restoration in 1868—and all that this implied and brought with it—was from the beginning not a movement of the Buddhists, but rather of the Neo-Confucianists and Neo-Shintoists. To be sure, both Neo-Confucianism and Neo-Shinto owed much to Buddhism, but when these reached a stage of self-awareness, they drew their main strength from the spirit of opposition to the latter. It is not surprising, therefore, that when this movement was crowned with success, Buddhism was disestablished as a state religion. The Buddhist priests, who for centuries had basked in the sunshine of government favor, were cast out into the cold and forced to look after themselves. Not only was Buddhism removed as a state religion, but there was even an attempt made to suppress it altogether. Many temples were stripped of their precious statues and decorations; the priests were evicted and forbidden to spread their teachings. These drastic and aggressive measures were, of course, doomed to fail, for Japan was too thoroughly devoted to its past. After a few years of mild persecution, the priests were allowed to keep their religious organizations and share their views, but they were compelled to stand on their own feet and to work under certain limitations.

This seemingly hard fate was, however, not an entirely bad thing, for it served to wake at least the leaders from their lethargy

This was further accelerated by the impact of Western civilization, which from that time on poured into Japan. Initially, this influx was met with a spirit of opposition by the old-time leaders. They stood against not only Christianity but also Western science and philosophy. This was especially true in the early 1880s, when the Japanese official world seemed to embrace everything from abroad without question. But as the Buddhist leaders became better acquainted with Western thought—and especially when they noticed that in the West itself there was a sharp conflict between the newer philosophies based upon <term>Darwinian evolution</term> and Christianity—they soon sought to form an alliance with Western science and use it as their primary weapon against the religion of the West. As time went on, this union between progressive Buddhists and certain schools of Western philosophy became closer and closer, and the teachings of Buddhism were restated in such a way as to make it appear that parts of <term>Kantian philosophy</term>, <term>Hegelian dialectics</term>, <term>Spencerian agnosticism</term>, and so on, were merely Western forms of the fundamental elements of Buddhism. In short, the progressive Buddhist used from Western philosophy and science whatever suited his purpose to fight the religion of the West.

Toward the end of the 1880s and early in the 1890s, a reaction against everything Western occurred, and conservative Buddhists sought to profit from this. They were the most vocal among those who pointed out the self-sufficiency of everything Japanese. Had Buddhist thought not preceded the highest development of Western science and philosophy by centuries? Why, then, should Japan learn from the West? This movement to exalt everything Japanese was so strong that some Buddhists were quite ready to forget their differences with the <term>Shintōists</term> and <term>Confucianists</term>, at whose hands they had suffered so recently, and unite with them in one "Great Way" of Japanese culture.

The motto of a leading Buddhist, "Defense of the country and love for the truth," crystallizes this spirit in a single sentence. For a while, the conservatives had their way, but Japan had, after all, put too much new wine into old wineskins. They had to burst; or rather, some of them have burst and others will do so as the new wine continues to ferment. This is true not only in the general fields of education and politics but also in the field of religion. The students who studied abroad in the 1880s and 1890s are now the leaders of intellectual life in Japan. They are steeped in the scientific spirit and devoted to the <term>historico-critical method</term>. The Neo-Confucianists and Neo-Shintoists had begun to use this method, and this led to the Restoration and an attack upon Buddhism as a foreign religion. But now this deadly weapon, in a more perfected form, is being used by the more advanced Buddhists themselves, and the results are beginning to show.

Just what the results will be in the long run is hard to tell, but the first effect of a wide application of this method is bound to give a tremendous shock to the ordinary claims of Japanese Buddhists. It is bound to show that the whole fabric of Japanese Buddhism cannot possibly stand as a consistent whole, and certainly not as being entirely either the direct or indirect teaching of the founder of Buddhism. It is nine-tenths historical development, and in many of its essential points, this development runs counter to the teachings of <term>S'akyamuni</term>. To be sure, these views are not very widespread yet, and the great masses of the uneducated do not question the authority of the priests; however, every year's work of Japan's great educational system is bound to help undermine the present foundation of Buddhism in Japan.

While the advanced Buddhist scholars are occupied with the perplexing problems raised by modern thought and methods, the common Buddhist is left to go his own way. On the one hand, he is being taught the new learning of the West in the public schools, and on the other hand, the great hordes of ignorant priests seek to continue binding him to all the superstitions and worn-out forms of the past.

## PRESENT-DAY BUDDHISM

Very little has been done by Buddhists to effectively bridge the chasm between the old and the new. The result is disastrous. Elderly women in the countryside and some of the older men are still earnest followers of traditional ways. However, the younger generation, though Buddhist in name, is completely ignorant of and indifferent to the religion of their ancestors. Their interest in their neighborhood temples usually does not extend beyond the occasional festival or street fair held on the temple grounds. And, of course, since everyone must die and the priests hold a monopoly on funerals, even today’s indifferent youth must occasionally have their attention directed toward things that transcend worldly interests. This indifference toward Buddhism, so characteristic of the rising generation, does not mean that the religion no longer exerts a strong unconscious influence on young Japan; it only means that young Japanese people do not consciously and zealously identify themselves with the religion of the Buddha. Instead, the current generation—especially the uneducated class—is turning to the ancient religion of Japan, Shintō, in the form of new sects such as Tenrikyō, which counts its followers by the hundreds of thousands. It is true, of course, that Tenrikyō and other popular Shintō sects contain as much Buddhism as Shintō, but they regard themselves as pure Shintō and tend to emphasize their differences from Buddhism. In any case, these are forces that Buddhism must increasingly reckon with if it is to continue its influence over the hearts of the people.

This is beginning to be recognized by more progressive priests. They are being driven to action not only by their enthusiastic Shintō rivals but also by the growing influence of Christianity, from which they borrow various methods of outreach. As a result, Buddhists are finally making a real effort to make their sacred scriptures accessible to the average reader. The leading sects are distributing what might be called "Sectarian Bibles"—namely, volumes bound in a convenient format that contain the primary scriptures of the sect along with standard commentaries on them. One cannot help but be impressed with the contrast between the present-day situation and the early days of Buddhism in Japan when the Buddhist priests and monks were the apostles of China’s superior civilization, or the days of the great religious awakening in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries when Japan had religious leaders of real power and influence. Today the leadership is in other hands. The apostles of the new civilization of the West are, as a rule, those on whom Buddhism has the lightest hold, and the leaders in the spiritual realm are decidedly those who have drunk most deeply from the fountains of Christianity. Almost every movement of any consequence in Japan today which is working toward individual and social righteousness has Christian men and women as its leaders. The best that can be said for the Buddhists is that they occasionally attempt to imitate these movements, but an imitation is seldom equal to the real thing. The truth of the matter is that the great days of Buddhism in Japan—the days when its power and influence counted for progress—lie in the distant past. The present, and even more the future, belong to others. But this brings us to the third aspect of our subject, namely, the question as to what place Buddhism will probably occupy in the future of Japanese life.

### *C. The Place of Buddhism in the Future*

Just what place Buddhism will occupy in the future is even more difficult to determine than what place it holds today. We shall try to answer the question more from the standpoint of its adequacy as a religion of the future than by speculating as to what place it will really hold. Only the future can answer the latter question, for it does not follow at all that although Buddhism is inadequate as a religion, it may not dominate the life of Japan for decades and even centuries. We can only point out why it is not an adequate religion for the highest development of Japanese life.

<page-num>315</page-num>
<header>BUDDHISM AND THE FUTURE</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

One of the striking differences between Japanese Buddhists and Japanese Christians is their attitude toward the future. It would be difficult to find a sincere Christian in Japan who does not hope and believe that Japan will one day be a Christian land. However small the mustard seed may be, it will one day grow into a large plant and provide shelter. The leaven will ultimately leaven the entire batch. In short, the Christians of Japan have absolute confidence in the future of their religion, and it is this faith that overcomes the world.

Among Japanese Buddhists, it would be difficult to find such confidence in their own future. There are many Buddhist parents today who, though clinging to their old faith, have little hope that their children will do the same. They vaguely feel that "the old order changes, giving way to" something they do not know. This lack of confidence has been increased in recent years by the discovery that those very sects which have shown the most marked signs of revival have been nearly bankrupted by the dishonesty of their leaders. And the anxious believer rightly concludes that "if they do these things when the tree is green, what will be done when it is dry?"

It is, of course, true that some Buddhists have confidence in the future of their religion, but it is not a widespread trait. In fact, even the optimists hope for little more than that the future will be like the past, in which Buddhism shared the field with others and maintained its dominance through clever compromises. There is a growing number among the liberals who would unite Buddhism with other religions to create one new and all-inclusive system. That is, they are not looking for a reformed Buddhism—a Neo-Buddhism—but for a new religion in which the Buddhist elements would perhaps be the most prominent.

But if Japanese Buddhists themselves have little confidence in the future of their own religion, there are good reasons for it. A statement of these reasons is essentially an answer to the question: what are the great defects in Japanese Buddhism that make it inadequate as the religion of the future?

Before answering this most interesting of all questions from our own Christian standpoint, we will give what is at least a partial answer made recently by one of Japan’s most enlightened thinkers: Professor Inouye Tetsujiro of the Tōkyō Imperial University. Writing on the subject of Religious Reform in Japan, and especially on the need for reform in Buddhism, this learned author points out what he considers the great defects in this religion.

The first outstanding defect is the character of the priests. “Buddhist priests—despite a few notable and brilliant exceptions that only serve to make the general darkness more visible—are behind the rest of the world in education, character, morals, and influence; and though Christian rivalry has stirred some of them to emulate Christian educational and charitable enterprises in recent years, these works of charity have been far from vigorous.” That this adverse judgment is not an overstatement of the situation is clear to any careful student. In fact, many Japanese writers express themselves with even less restraint when dealing with this subject. One naturally wonders what future a religion can have when its leaders lag behind those whom they seek to lead.

The second reform needed, according to Professor Inouye, is the abolition of idols and the substitution of the Japanese language for the unintelligible Sanskrit and Chinese in the Buddhist ritual and scriptures. Idols may have had their place in the past, says this critic, but the modern Japanese should be beyond these crude representations of the Divine. Equally important is “the abolition of the practice of reading and chanting the <term>sūtras</term> in a language which, practically, neither the priests nor the congregation understand.” It is true that modern Japan should be beyond these crutches of religion, but popular Buddhism is still so bound up with idolatry that the abolition of idols would mean to many the giving up of their gods. Not that the idols should not be abolished, but rather that it must be accompanied by constructive work. The substitution of Japanese for the unintelligible Chinese is finally being tried, but Jap-

The third great defect pointed out by Professor Inouye is even more serious, and if the reform he suggested were carried out, it would not leave enough Buddhist elements in the reformed religion to enable even a Bodhisattva to recognize it as Buddhism. The proposal is so naive that we must provide the full text on this point: "The pessimism of India, which is the essence of Japanese Buddhism, is not suited to our needs. Pessimism is the creed of a decaying nationality in the hour of adversity, when this world looks dark and life has no hope to offer us. Then, in despair, we turn from this miserable world and seek comfort in the hope of something better after death. In ancient India, pessimism was perhaps natural, but pessimism can never raise a nation to a higher life; and what Japan, with its new hopes and aspirations, requires is a religion of hope, full of noble ideals and aspirations. In the final analysis, it is a philosophy of defeat and therefore cannot satisfy the "hopes and aspirations" of an awakened nation. But when the suggestion is made that "Buddhism must shed its pessimism or lose its hold on the people," one wonders how a professor of philosophy in a great university could conceive of anything so naive. For Buddhism to "shed its pessimism" is not like a snake shedding its skin, but rather like shedding its backbone. It is like the night shedding its darkness; for just as the night ceases to be night when the darkness is gone, so Buddhism without its pessimistic spirit would no longer be Buddhism. To be sure, the night sheds some of its darkness when the moon shines with its light borrowed from the sovereign of eternal day; and so Buddhism, in the future, may illuminate its pessimism by borrowing elements of "hope and aspirations" from sources other than its own. But for it to truly "shed its pessimism" and for it to become "a religion of hope, full of noble ideals and aspirations" seems impossible without be—

It is true, of course, that Japanese Buddhism has tried to shed the pessimistic philosophy of India, and in the development of <term>Amidaism</term> with its semi-theistic idea of God, it has to some extent grasped elements of hope and aspiration; but, after all, this reaching out for the living God has always been hindered by the agnostic philosopher who reduces Amida and his salvation to mere ideals which have no real <term>ontological reference</term>. And furthermore, just to the degree that Buddhism has succeeded in shedding its pessimism, it has moved away from the religion of the founder. If it is ever to shed its pessimism entirely and become truly a religion of hope and aspiration suited for an awakened people, it will have to cease being Buddhism in its essential elements, whatever name may be attached to it. Of course, the Buddhist might say that such a change would be a “developed Buddhism.” That might be so, but would it not be more correct to say that it would be a new religion rather than a “developed Buddhism”? The basic elements of a religion may undergo some outward changes while the religion remains essentially the same, but for a religion to abandon its basic elements and build itself upon others is really to become a new religion, even if the old name is continued.

The fifth defect in Japanese Buddhism pointed out by Professor Inouye refers to Buddhist ethics. He points out that the ethical ideals of Buddhism are those held in India over two thousand years ago, "and the men who live by them make themselves unfit to become the ethical teachers of a modern, commercial, and industrial generation of men. Japan wants a system of religious morals, but it must be one suited to her present needs. Buddhists may yet be the moral teachers of this nation, if they will bring their ethical system into harmony with present-day needs." But, as has already been pointed out in Chapter VI, the philosophical basis of Buddhist ethics is inadequate for a real, vital moral life. On the one hand, the spirit of agnosticism, which is the dominant current in all Buddhist thought, forever cuts the nerve of any vigorous morality because it makes good and evil, right and wrong, but mere "practical differences" which, however, have no basis in reality. A mere "practical difference" which is not a real difference is, in the last analysis, flawed and anything but practical in the long run. It may be practical for me to lie, and tell the truth at another time, but unless my truthfulness is based on something more firm than on what seems merely practical, it will fail to be even that, for surely no one could be expected to put much confidence in my words if convenience, or the merely practical, were the measure of my honesty. And further, Buddhist psychology runs absolutely counter to the higher ethical ideals, as we also pointed out in Chapter VI. Buddhist psychology has ever asserted that the self has no real existence, and it has contented itself with a "provisional self," and yet Buddhist ethics claims as its highest goal the "intellectual and moral development of the personality." Surely for one to strive to achieve a goal which one knows to be an illusion is the greatest sort of folly. Surely, if Buddhism is what the above-mentioned critic says it is, and if it has these great defects, there is not only a need for reform, but a need for a revolution in its very fundamentals; and when this is accomplished, it would practically mean a new religion, no matter what its name might be. Can this change be made, and does modern Buddhism have sufficient vitality to attempt the undertaking? It is one thing to recognize defects, but quite another to overcome them. Can this be done by a religion which has never given the human personality its proper place and whose spirit of pessimism forever cuts the nerve of aspiration and achievement?

But these defects in Japanese Buddhism pointed out above are not the only ones which, in our judgment, prevent it from being an adequate religion. When we say this, we are not contradicting what we said at the beginning of this chapter, where we spoke of the many things Buddhism contributed to Japanese civilization. At this point, we are measuring Buddhism by Christian standards and not by Shintō or Confucian ones.

The most fundamental defect in Buddhism as we see it—a defect which has almost endless ramifications and accounts largely for its spirit of pessimism and the other defects mentioned above—is the Buddhist conception of truth. It is this essentially agnostic attitude which, in the first place, accounts for the conglomerate nature of Buddhism as a philosophy or a practical religion, in which the nobler elements are so often buried by the accumulated rubbish of passing centuries. It accounts for the fact that in Buddhism can be found every shade of thought common to man, and why the most contradictory doctrines and practices can exist side by side without anyone thinking it strange. Contradictions become but two sides of the same thing, and from this viewpoint, a system with the greatest contradictions is *ipso facto* the most comprehensive statement of the full truth. Thus, it is the boast of Buddhism that its philosophy is much more profound than that of Christianity because, where the latter teaches certain definite views as true, Buddhism teaches both these views and their opposites and every shade between. And so, if it be asked what Buddhism teaches on this or that point, it can be said that it teaches almost anything you please. Or, to put it in the true Buddhist way, Buddhism teaches "This" from one point of view and the "Opposite" from the opposite point of view. (And since both are equally true or good, there is good reason for following neither very seriously.)

But can Buddhism do this? Can it lay hold on a faith in God the Heavenly Father? No, it cannot and at the same time remain true to its generic elements, for it was founded on the thought of man’s inability to know the “Unknowable Absolute,” and through all the centuries, in spite of the various counter-currents in the Buddhist stream of life, this has been the dominant current; this has been the generic element of Buddhism, North and South, Mahāyāna and Hinayāna.

If Japanese Buddhism cannot lay hold on the Living God without undergoing a radical change in its fundamentals, it does not follow that Japanese Buddhists cannot fling away their pessimism and lay hold on Him and so find satisfaction for their hopes and aspirations. That this is possible is best shown by what is taking place today in Japan. But this is another story; it is the story of Christianity in this land. Of this story only the first chapter is history; the remainder is written in the hearts of the rising generation and will be written in the lives of the generations to come,

> “For the old order changes, yielding place to the new,
> And God fulfills himself in many ways.”

# NOTES

## CHAPTER I

1. It seems that even before the emergence of Buddhism and the religious complex we call Hinduism, the general characteristics of religious life in India were essentially the same as they have been throughout the centuries. On one hand, we have the philosophers' profound speculative thoughts regarding the deeper realities of life, and on the other hand, we see the crude and simplistic beliefs held by the common people. There is always a wide gap between the two. India has seemingly never succeeded in framing the results of its philosophical efforts in a way that the common person can apply to daily life. Buddhism was an attempt to set aside the empty and impractical theories of traditional philosophers and to focus people's attention on a practical path of conduct intended to lead them from a lower to a higher and better life. However, it also failed in the end; for one of the most prominent characteristics of Buddhism throughout the centuries has been this same vast chasm between the ideals and thoughts of a few leaders and the lives of their uneducated followers.
2. According to Buddhists themselves, the dates of the Buddha range from the eleventh to the sixth and fifth centuries before the Christian era. Northern Buddhists, wanting their master to precede Confucius and Lao-tse, claim his birth occurred in the late eleventh century B.C.; the year 1026 B.C. is a date accepted by many in Japan. The date generally accepted in Burma, Siam, and Ceylon is 623 B.C. for his birth and 543 B.C. for his death. Western scholars and modern scholars in the Orient generally agree in placing his birth around the middle of the sixth century B.C. and his death somewhere around the year 480 B.C. This conclusion is reached from the fact that King Asoka’s inscriptions on certain stone pillars mention cer-

3. The names by which the Buddha is known are numerous. Not only are there many forms of the word "Buddha," as S. Hardy has pointed out, but he is given many different names by his followers in the various Buddhist lands of Asia. Of course, the name Buddha is not actually a proper name, but a generic title. According to Buddhists, there have been many Buddhas; therefore, one should prefix the proper name Gautama or use the definite article "the" when speaking of the Buddha who lived in India around the sixth or fifth century B.C. Perhaps the most common term by which the Buddha is known is S'akyamuni, *that is, the Teacher of the S'akyans.* In fact, in Japan, one seldom hears him spoken of as "the Buddha" (Jap. Butsu), but usually as Shaka, Shakasama, Shaka Butsu, or Shaka Nyōrai. A term frequently used in Buddhist literature is the word Nyōrai (Sk. Tathāgata). In early Buddhist literature, "Tathāgata" frequently refers to Gautama Buddha, though it is not applied exclusively to him. There are many Tathāgatas. In later Buddhist literature, "Nyōrai" often refers to one of the great Buddhas of Northern Buddhism. Amida, in particular, is often designated by this term. Japanese Buddhists are accustomed to speaking of the Ten Names of Buddha, the first being the name Nyōrai, which probably means "the Perfect One" or "the One Who Comes in the Likeness of the Truth." It is the highest term applied to a Buddha. The other nine names similarly describe some attribute characteristic of a Buddha. Thus, he is spoken of as the one filled with all virtue and wisdom, the supreme Lord, the Teacher of heaven and earth, the world-honored One, and so on. Beyond these expressions, there are others that are less technical but also more or less descriptive of the true characteristics of a Buddha.

9. There are several reasons why the careful student must hesitate to agree with most writers on early <term>Buddhism</term> who claim that the <term>Buddha</term> denied the existence of the self. Of course, everyone must admit that he did not accept the soul theories current in India at that time; however, as most of these viewed the soul as a refined substance which passed from one body to another, it does not follow that the <term>Buddha</term>, in rejecting such theories, rejected every theory of the soul. The very fact that he placed the question of whether the <term>Arhat</term> continues beyond death among the great <term>Indeterminates</term> should make us hesitate to say that he positively denied his continued existence. In fact, if this question belongs to the great <term>Indeterminates</term>, then there is as much reason for saying that the <term>Buddha</term> believed in the continuity of the soul as that he did not.

Even if it is admitted that his primary interest was in freeing man from the bondage of existence and that the <term>Arhat</term>’s chief joy consisted in the awareness that at death the <term>empirical ego</term> would come to an end because its <term>Karma</term> had been exhausted, it still remains possible that the <term>Buddha</term> could have believed in the continuity of a higher ego—one that is not to be conceived of in terms of the <term>empirical ego</term>, but is nonetheless a true self. <term>Kant</term> has made us familiar with the concept of a distinction be-

Between the “empirical ego” and the “transcendental self,” though we must admit that at first sight it is difficult to understand just what the “transcendental self,” as distinguished from the “empirical self,” might be. For if the self known in self-consciousness is not the real self, then it is difficult to see how one can even assert the existence of another self that is the real self. Of course, it is true that the self is greater and more than what appears in self-consciousness from moment to moment. That is, every person feels that the flow of consciousness is never the full expression of his entire self. Thus, when a bank clerk is adding up columns of figures day after day and this work represents the stream of his consciousness for six or eight hours every day, it is not true that the whole self is expressing itself in this operation. And that is true, more or less, with the life of every person. In fact, everyone has experiences in which a depth of his being is revealed to himself of which he had never dreamed. And great crises in people’s lives often bring out qualities that are startling, not only to their friends but also to themselves. All of this simply goes to show that there is room for the distinction between the ego of the ordinary stream of consciousness and the full ego, or the real ego, of which even we ourselves get only glimpses, as it were, from time to time.

Now, is it not possible that the <term>Buddha</term> had in mind some such distinction, and that when he said that the ego was an illusion and fell apart at death, he meant this empirical ego whose life is made up of the world of sense—the world of physical pleasures and pains which, for the average person, makes up almost the whole of life—but that he did not deny the existence and continuity beyond death of a higher and deeper self? The successive dwellings which <term>Karma</term> creates constitute the seat of the successive empirical egos, and these were the fetters of the higher ego from which it could only be freed after the higher ego was perfectly enlightened and saw that the life of the senses and the pleasures of the empirical ego were not the core of its real life. That is, it is <term>Ignorance</term> which somehow attaches itself to the higher ego, giving rise to the twelve links of the <term>Karma</term> chain (the twelve links of the <term>Karma</term> chain, or the twelve segments of the <term>Wheel of Life</term>, are: <term>Ignorance</term>, <term>Latent Impressions</term>, <term>Thought-substance</term>, <term>Name and Form</term>, the <term>Six Roots</term>, <term>Contact</term>, <term>Sensation</term>, <term>Desire</term>, <term>Clinging to Existence</term>, <term>Becoming</term>, <term>Birth</term>, and <term>Decrepitude and Death</term>. For a fuller statement of this with some slight changes see note 8 of Chapter I

It is true that if the Buddha believed in the existence of this higher ego, one would expect him to have placed greater emphasis on the state of this ego after death, and one would think that he would have made salvation less negative—*that is*, not a mere “escape from evil,” but rather a future positive good. In answer to this objection, however, it may be said that the early Buddhists did use fairly positive terms to express the concept of salvation. If the Buddha himself did not use these terms, it may have been because he sought to avoid defining the concept of *Nirvāna* using details taken from the experience of the empirical self. *Nirvāna* was void of these things, but it may nevertheless have had a content which transcends human experience and so could not be expressed in the language of this experience. Even union with the Brahman was inadequate to express the idea, for the Brahman was regarded as the singular foundation of all empirical existence; thus, union with the Brahman savored too much of the things of this world to be acceptable to the Buddha as an ideal of salvation. No, salvation was to be a deliverance from the bondage of the empirical self, and therefore, when spoken of in terms of this self, *Nirvāna* must be regarded as absolutely void. But the Arhat may nevertheless continue in the realm of the “transcendental self,” and his *Nirvāna* is therefore a state which is beyond human language to express.

Now, in saying all this, we do not wish to state definitively that the Buddha held such a view, but the facts known so far regarding the core of his teachings should make one hesitate to say that he denied the reality of the self in the sense described above. The “illusion of the self” may have referred to the illusion that the sensory life of the body and the craving thirst for earth’s fleeting pleasures possess real significance for the deeper self. At any rate, since the Buddha placed the continued existence of the Arhat in a future state among the great Indeterminates, there would seem to be as much ground for holding that he believed in such a continuation as that he did not. Even among Christians of our own day, there are those who have no firm convictions about the nature of the spiritual self and its destiny. He was positive in asserting that life, as lived by ignorant humanity, is not worth living, and that a knowledge of its nature and the cause of its sufferings constitutes true wisdom; and further, that the truly wise will seek to end such a life by walking in the Middle Way, the Noble Eightfold Path. Everything beyond these practical and immediate interests he regarded as belonging to the realm of the unknown, about which speculation is futile.

### CHAPTER II

1. It is customary to speak of four Great Councils of Buddhism. These are: (1) The Council of Rājagriha, called soon after the death of the Buddha. (2) The Council of Vaiśālī, called about one hundred years after the first council. (3) The Council of Pātaliputra, called by the great Buddhist King Asoka in the eighteenth year of his reign (about the year 245 <term>B.C.</term>). (4) The Council of Jalandhara, called by the Indo-Scythian King Kanishka. The first and second councils are recognized by all Buddhists. The third council is regarded by Southern Buddhists as being on the same level with the first two, while the fourth is not admitted to have had any real authority. On the other hand, Northern Buddhists look upon the fourth council as being next in importance to the first council of Rājagriha; for it may be said that King Kanishka plays in Northern Buddhism much the same role that Asoka plays in Southern Buddhism, both being regarded as great defenders of the faith.

## CHAPTER III

1. While this was the first public and successful introduction of Buddhism into Japan, it seems that it was not the first attempt by Buddhists to gain a foothold in the island empire. We are told that about 25 years earlier, a Chinese priest had come to the southern shores with an image which he set up in a grass hut; but the record continues by saying that the people among whom he worked did not understand its meaning, and none were led to follow the new faith.
2. The southern portion of Japan had long before been cleared of its indigenous inhabitants and occupied by the Japanese, but it can hardly be said to have come completely under the control of the Yamato chieftains of central Japan. Even for a considerable length of time after this, southern Japan continued to be a rival of central Japan rather than subject to it.
3. The word Shintō is a Chinese word and means "the Way of the Gods." Obviously, this name was given to the native religion after Japan had come into vital contact with China. Before that time, there probably was no such thing as a Shintō Religion, but rather only a number of primitive local cults which were gradually being welded together into a sort of connected whole as the nation was being unified politically. That is, the native religion developed *pari passu* with the state, moving from disconnected elements into at least a semblance of unity.

Additionally, Emperor Tenchi, who as Prince Naka-no-Ōye was one of the leaders in these reforms, is still regarded today as one of Japan's three greatest emperors.

10. In fact, there are as many types of sects within the so-called Mahayana division as there are in Buddhism as a whole; this is especially true if one considers the popular religious teachings of these sects. The Mahayana sects agree with one another only in a very general way—specifically, in the philosophical foundation of their teachings. However, the religious application of these general teachings varies widely among these sects.

It is, however, no longer the individual mind that does this, but it is rather the Universal Mind within the individual that becomes conscious of itself. "The Entity that never changes will appear." 28. When Nichiren appeared, Yoritomo’s work had been completed. The Kamakura shōgunate was firmly established, and the emperor at Kyōto had been stripped of all but symbolic authority. The Kamakura shōgunate had succeeded in unifying at least the nation's military strength and in providing the land with an administrative system that was effective and, overall, a benefit.

29. This is one of the few instances in the long history of Japanese Buddhism where a religious leader was sentenced to death; it should be noted that even in this case, the sentence was not so much for his religious views as for his supposedly dangerous political opinions. Religious persecutions in the severe forms seen in medieval Europe were practically unknown in Japan. The most severe form was usually banishment to some remote part of the empire which, as we saw in the case of Shinran, for example, was not always entirely a bad thing. On the other hand, it must be admitted that the causes leading to persecution were usually much less noble than in Europe and were frequently of a very sordid nature.

34. A point which Western students of Japanese culture usually overlook is that the formalism and the strict observance of all the niceties of an elaborate etiquette—which often seems to put a straitjacket upon the normal and free development of human personality—is really no more inherently natural to the Japanese than to any other people. It is largely the product of a deliberate effort on the part of the leaders in the Tokugawa period. What strikes the student of Japanese history is that the men and women prior to that period seem more like the free Westerner in their spirit than like the older Japanese of the present generation. We say the “older Japanese” of the present generation deliberately, for anyone acquainted with the younger generation must know that the love for freedom and unhindered self-expression is as strong among the young men and women of Japan as it is even among Americans.

The constructive influence which Buddhism exerted in those days did not spring from the forces inherent in Buddhism itself, but rather from the fact that Buddhism was the vehicle for the superior continental civilization whose chief elements were other than Buddhist.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the tension between religious freedom and state-mandated patriotism in Japan, specifically focusing on the distinction between National Shrines and ordinary Shintō shrines. It then begins the notes for Chapter IV.</meta>

Regarding National Shrines and the ordinary Shintō shrines, the people in general do not make such a distinction; therefore, making an obeisance at the National Shrines is regarded by them as having a real religious significance. It is more than merely showing respect for national heroes; it is real religious worship. Not only do Japanese Christians object to being compelled to worship at such shrines, but the Buddhists, too, feel that it interferes with their religious liberty. Of course, both Christians and Buddhists are as loyal to Japan as the Shintōists are, and they do not hesitate to show all due respect to national heroes; however, they feel that the distinction which the Government is trying to make is truly absurd. It is absurd for the simple reason that many of Japan's national heroes have been deified over the course of centuries, and from a Shintō standpoint, religion and patriotism have been one and the same. If the Government truly wants to be consistent and make its position rational, it will have to go one step further and state that these national heroes who were deified in the past are actually only great men and not gods, and that they should receive only the reverence due to great men. Japanese Christians are second to none in true loyalty to their country and its great heroes, but they will always insist that there must be a distinction between the respect and reverence given to great men and the reverence and worship given to God, and to God alone. The truth of the matter is that this attempt by the Government to separate National Shrines from ordinary Shintō shrines is simply one of those naïve efforts being made by modern statesmen to bridge the chasm between the old and the new. It is an effort that seeks to preserve the old spirit of loyalty and patriotism while simultaneously shifting it from its old basis of traditional emperor- and hero-worship to a new basis of loyalty to human rulers and institutions; in making this shift, they are trying to occupy a halfway position. However, a halfway position cannot satisfy either the followers of the old or the advocates of the new, so a certain amount of friction over this point may be expected for some time to come.

4. The Chinese canon has as its core the older Sanskrit canon, *that is*, translations from the Sanskrit pure and simple. But it also has a great many books written originally in Chinese. And the canon in Japan, in the wider sense, has in the same way many books written originally in Japanese.

However, it is hardly correct to designate them as sects of Hīnayāna Buddhism, for the term Hīnayāna was probably not coined until several centuries later.

### CHAPTER V

1. The Twelve Links of the Karma-chain are known in Japanese by various terms, such as: Jūni Inen, Jūni Inshō, Jūni Yushi, Jūni Engi, and Jūni Enmon. These terms differ slightly in the atmosphere surrounding them, but all are attempts to express the meaning of the chain of existence. Sometimes the order of these links is inverted, so that the first link, Ignorance, is given as the last link, and the last link as the first. The order depends upon whether one reasons from effect back to cause or starts with the cause and proceeds to the effect. Following the order we have provided, the Sanskrit and Japanese terms are as follows:
    (1) Ignorance (Sanskrit: Avidya, Japanese: Mumyō).
    (2) Latent Impressions (Sanskrit: Samskāra, Japanese: Gyō).
    (3) Thought-substance (Sanskrit: Vidjnana, Japanese: Shiki).
    (4) Name and Form (Sanskrit: Namarūpa, Japanese: Myōshiki).
    (5) The Six Roots (Sanskrit: Chadāyatana, Japanese: Rokusho).
    (6) Contact (Sanskrit: Sparsa, Japanese: Shoku).
    (7) Sensation (Sanskrit: Vedana, Japanese: Ju).
    (8) Desire (Sanskrit: Trichnā, Japanese: Ai).
    (9) Clinging to Existence (Sanskrit: Upādāna, Japanese: Shu).
    (10) Becoming (Sanskrit: Bhava, Japanese: Yu).
    (11) Birth (Sanskrit: Djāti, Japanese: Shō).
    (12) Decrepitude and Death (Sanskrit: Djarāmavana, Japanese: Rōshi).
2. Compare note 11, Chapter I.
3. This division of every universe into three realms, or classes of beings—like so many other things in Buddhism—was borrowed from Brahmanism. It is an imitation of the Brahmanic Four

<summary>This page details the sectarian splits within early Buddhism following the Council of Vaisali and provides a comprehensive list of the Twelve Links of the Karma-chain in Sanskrit and Japanese. It also notes the historical connection between Buddhist cosmology and Brahmanism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the endnotes for Chapter V, concluding the discussion on the Three Worlds and detailing the various Buddhist hells, the lineage of the Shin Sect, the Six and Ten Virtues (Paramitas), and the vows of the Bodhisattvas.</meta>

<page-num>347</page-num>
<header>NOTES</header>

Worlds (Bhuvanatraya); except that Buddhists substitute the ethical or spiritual categories of Desire, Pure Form, and Formlessness for the physical categories of Earth, Heaven, and Atmosphere used by the Brahmans.

4. In addition to these eight Hot Hells and eight Cold Hells, one finds mention of eight Dark Hells, ten Larger Cold Hells with a hundred million smaller hells attached to each, and 84,000 Smaller Cold Hells. In no area has the Indian imagination been more extravagant than in this. Japan has adopted some of this nonsense, as may be seen especially from such writings as Genshin’s description of the Buddhist hells; but, after all, the Japanese mind has never lost itself very seriously in such morbid speculations.

5. Zendō is regarded as the fifth of the seven great Church Fathers of the Shin Sect who preceded Shinran. These seven are the two Indians, Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu; the three Chinese, Donran, Dōshaku, and Zendō; and the two Japanese, Genshin and Genku.

6. The Six Virtues (Sanskrit: Paramita) are known in Japanese as the Roku Baramitsu (*Baramitsu* is simply a transliteration of *Paramita*) or Rokudo (Six Crossings). These Six Virtues are the following: Charity (Sanskrit: Dāna, Japanese: Fuse); Morality, that is, Keeping the Commandments (Sanskrit: Sila, Japanese: Jikai); Patience and Forbearance (Sanskrit: Kchānti, Japanese: Ninniku); Exertion or Diligence (Sanskrit: Virya, Japanese: Shōjun); Meditation (Sanskrit: Dhyāna, Japanese: Zenjō); and Wisdom (Sanskrit: Pradjna, Japanese: Chie).

Sometimes four other virtues are added to these six, creating the so-called Ten Virtues or Ten Crossings (Japanese: Judo). These four added virtues are: Use of Proper Means (Sanskrit: Upāya, Japanese: Hōben); Knowledge or Science (Sanskrit: Djnāna, Japanese: Chi or Jakuna); Pious Vows (Sanskrit: Pranidhana, Japanese: Gwan); and Force of Purpose (Sanskrit: Bala, Japanese: Goriki; literally meaning "Five Powers"). Compare Chapter VI, Section B, Subsection 2.

7. The Four Great Vows (Japanese: Shiguseigwan) must be made and fulfilled by all Bodhisattvas. Some Bodhisattvas, however, bind themselves by even more self-sacrificing vows than these. Thus we have the famous Forty-eight Vows of Amida, made by him before he entered the state of Buddha, and especially the famous Eighteenth Vow of these forty-eight, in which this unselfish Bodhisattva declared that he would not enter the bliss of Buddhahood until he had worked out a way of salvation for all beings.

<meta>This page concludes the endnotes for Chapter V, focusing on the internal Buddhist critiques of the Paradise doctrine and the extreme difficulty of achieving human rebirth, before providing cross-references for the start of Chapter VI.</meta>

<page-num>348</page-num>
<header>NOTES</header>

8. Although the Paradise doctrine is very popular among the masses in Japan, there are some Buddhists who regard this desire to be born into Paradise as the worst kind of evil Karma, which actually lands whoever possesses it in Hell.

> “The heart that desires Paradise is already in Hell. In the case of Shaka (Shakyamuni) or a deity, there is no Paradise.”

9. There are some Buddhist scriptures which may not categorically deny the possibility of salvation to all people, but which nevertheless seem to hold out very little hope to the masses who are lost in sin and misery. Thus we read,

> “A blind turtle and a floating tree are more likely to meet and see each other than ignorant and foolish humanity is to obtain a human body.”

That is, the ignorant masses in their next incarnation stand very little chance of being born as human beings, but will instead be born in one of the lower four realms. Their salvation from the bondage of this evil world then seems almost hopeless. It is only when one measures time by Kalpas that one can speak of such beings ultimately attaining salvation.

# SELECTED BIBLIOGRAPHY OF WORKS IN JAPANESE

### Dictionaries.
1. Bonkan Taiyaku Bukkyō Jiten . . . . . . Dr. U. Hagiwara
   Sanskrit-Chinese Buddhist Dictionary.

   Great Dictionary of Buddhism.

   Great Dictionary of Philosophy.

   Dictionary of the Zen Sect.

### Texts and Commentaries.
1. Dai Nippon Bukkyō Zenshō.
   Collected Literature of Japanese Buddhism. (This great series, when completed, will contain about 200 large volumes. It will comprise the Chinese Tripitaka, original Japanese works, and standard commentaries.)
2. Kokuyaku Daizōkyō.
   The Canon Translated into Japanese. (This is a work of twelve large volumes containing translations into Japanese from the leading Buddhist scriptures.)
3. Bukkyō Seiten . . . . . . . . . Drs. Murakami and Maeda
   Buddhist Bible. (Selections from the leading scriptures arranged topically.)
4. Jōdoshu Seiten.
   Bible of the Jodo Sect. (Containing the "Basal Scriptures" of the sect and standard commentaries.)
5. Nichirenshu Seiten.
   Bible of the Nichiren Sect.
6. Shingonshū Seiten.
   Bible of the Shingon Sect.
7. Shinshū Seiten.
   Bible of the Shin Sect.
8. Zenshū Seiten.
   Bible of the Zen Sect.
   (The material in numbers 3–8 is contained, of course, in number 1, but here it is in a more convenient form for a study of the particular tenets of the respective sects.)

# Japan Today and Tomorrow

## By HAMILTON W. MABIE
->Author of "American Ideals, Character and Life"<-

->*Decorated cloth, 12mo, illustrated, boxed, $2.00*<-

The purpose of this volume is to convey a clear and definite impression of the spirit of the Japanese people—what they are interested in and what we may expect from them in the future. Following this goal, it offers chapters on the manners and habits of the Japanese, their family life, their love of art and nature, and their attitude toward religion. Their historical development is sketched very briefly, and their education and political development are covered somewhat more fully. Perhaps no American is better suited to write a book like this than Dr. Mabie. As a lecturer to Japan for the Carnegie Peace Endowment not long ago, he had an excellent opportunity for a close study of the country and its people.

> “A thoroughly readable book. Its literary style is excellent, while the features of Japanese life which have been selected for emphasis and comment have been chosen with rare good judgment. It is an important contribution to the thorough understanding of the true spirit of Japan.” — *Brooklyn Daily Eagle*.

# Japanese Expansion and American Policies

## By J. F. ABBOTT
->Of Washington University<-

->*New edition. Cloth, 12mo, $1.50*<-

In this book, Professor Abbott summarizes dispassionately and impartially the history of diplomatic and social relations between Japan and the United States. In particular, he provides the facts that will enable an American to form their own opinion regarding the possibility of future conflicts between these two countries. The work is neither pro-Japan nor anti-Japan, but seeks, rather, to present the case fairly. The author emphasizes the importance of an intelligent understanding of the subject, believing that despite the current lull due to intense interest in European affairs, this is still a problem that will periodically and persistently come to the forefront until it is satisfactorily solved. Professor Abbott has carefully studied Far Eastern matters for the past fifteen years, has traveled at various times throughout the Orient, and, prior to the Russian War, was an instructor at the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy.
